My doctor referred me to an endocrinologist. A woman about my daughters' age. Clean office. Framed degrees on every wall.

She sat me down and told me the way things were going to have to change.

No more of the banana bread I bake every Sunday morning for Robert. No more of the pasta I have been making for my family for 38 years. No more of the apple crisp my daughter Emily brings to every holiday dinner. No more of the cranberry scones I make for the teachers' lounge when I substitute. No more rolls. No more rice. No more of anything I had grown up cooking and eating.

I want to tell you what that felt like, because unless you are a Type 2 diabetic woman sitting in that chair for the first time, you can't know.

It felt like being told the last third of my life was going to be spent eating things I didn't want to eat and watching everyone else at my own table enjoy the food I made for them.

She prescribed Metformin, 500 mg twice a day. Told me to walk 30 minutes a day. Told me to come back in 3 months for a repeat A1C.

I walked out of her office and I did every single thing she told me to do.

For three years I was the most compliant patient she had ever had.

I took the Metformin every morning at 7 AM with breakfast and every evening at 6 PM with dinner. I set two alarms on my phone. I never missed a dose. Not once. Not in three years.

I cut my evening glass of wine entirely. I cut the half and half in my morning coffee. I switched to black coffee. I hated it. I drank it anyway. Every morning. For three years.

I ate egg whites and a single slice of dry toast for breakfast. Grilled chicken and steamed vegetables for lunch. Baked salmon and a side salad for dinner. No dressing. No butter. No bread on the side.

I walked 40 minutes every morning at 6 AM. In the dark. In the rain. In the snow. Through three Massachusetts winters. On the mornings it was 14 degrees and the sidewalks were iced over I still laced up my shoes and went out.

I sat through three Thanksgivings at my daughter Emily's house eating plain turkey breast and green beans while my family ate stuffing and mashed potatoes and Emily's apple crisp with vanilla ice cream. I sat through three Christmases at my sister's house eating a naked salad while everyone else ate her lasagna. I sat through three of my granddaughter's birthdays watching her blow out candles while I drank a glass of water. She went from five to seven years old during the time I wasn't allowed to eat cake at her party.

I made banana bread for Robert every Sunday morning for three years and didn't eat a single slice.

I made cranberry scones for the teachers' lounge and watched other women eat them while I ate almonds out of a plastic bag I brought from home.

I cooked Thanksgiving dinner. Christmas dinner. Easter dinner. Sunday dinner. I set the table. I served the food. I sat down with my family and I ate something different from what I had made for them. Every time. For three years.

I want you to understand what three years of that does to a woman.

It doesn't just take your food. It takes your place at your own table. It turns you into a guest in your own kitchen. You are the woman who cooks for everyone and eats nothing. You are the woman who watches. You are the woman who says "no thank you" when your own granddaughter offers you a bite of the cake you baked for her.

After three years of that, something inside you goes quiet. You stop being angry about it. You stop being sad about it. You just accept it. And that acceptance is the worst part. Because it means you have given up on ever getting your life back.

At the same time I was watching things in my own body get worse year after year.

The tingling in my feet at night. It started in the first year. Just a low buzzing that showed up when I got into bed. By the second year it was a burning. Some nights I would push the blankets off my feet because they felt like they were wrapped in something hot. By the third year I couldn't wear socks to bed anymore. Some mornings the bottoms of my feet were numb until I had been walking for ten minutes.

The blurry vision that came and went. In the first year it was occasional. I would sit down with a book in the evening and the words would go soft around the edges. I bought a pair of reading glasses at CVS. They didn't help. By the third year it was happening every day. I stopped reading at night because I couldn't trust my eyes to hold the page.

Getting up at night to use the bathroom. Once a night the first year. Twice the second. Three times by the third. Robert slept through it. I didn't. I hadn't slept more than four hours in a row in over a year.

The exhaustion after every single meal. In the first year it was an afternoon heaviness. By the third year it was a collapse. I would eat lunch and by 1 PM I would be sitting in my reading chair unable to keep my eyes open. My daughter started joking that I was turning into her grandmother. I didn't think it was funny. I was 63 years old and I was falling asleep in the middle of the day like I was 90.

The breathlessness walking up the stairs to my bedroom. Fourteen steps. I used to take them two at a time. By year three I was stopping halfway, holding the railing, waiting for my chest to stop pounding. I counted those stairs every night because I had started dreading them.

The weight I couldn't lose. I had gained 22 pounds since my diagnosis despite eating like a bird for three years. My endocrinologist told me to "be more disciplined." I wanted to scream.

And one more thing. The one I didn't tell my endocrinologist. The one no woman my age talks about at appointments.

The intimacy with Robert had been disappearing for three years. Not just desire. Everything. The sensitivity. The response. The warmth. The things that had worked between us for over three decades. It started fading before my diagnosis and it got worse every year after. I told myself it was menopause. I told myself it was age. I told myself it was stress. But it wasn't any of those things.

By the third year Robert and I slept in the same bed like two strangers. He never complained. He never pushed. He just quietly stopped reaching for me. And I quietly stopped wishing he would.

That was the loneliest part of all of this. And I never said a word about it to anyone.

Over three years my endocrinologist adjusted my protocol nine times.

She increased my Metformin from 500 mg twice a day to 1000 mg twice a day after my first follow up. My A1C had moved from 7.6 to 7.5. She said it wasn't enough.

Six months later she added Glipizide. My A1C went to 7.3. She said it was progress but not enough.

A year in she switched me to extended release Metformin because the regular was destroying my stomach. The diarrhea had gotten so bad I had to excuse myself from a third grade reading group twice in one morning. I started bringing a change of clothes to the school in a bag I kept in my car. I never told anyone why.

At the 18 month mark she added Jardiance. My A1C dropped to 7.0. She said we were getting somewhere. I was taking three medications, walking every morning, eating food I hated, and my number had moved six tenths of a point in a year and a half.

At two years she started talking about Ozempic. I told her I didn't want an injection. She said we might not have a choice.

At two and a half years she started talking about insulin.

At every single appointment she asked me the same questions. Are you taking your medication. Are you walking. Are you following the diet. Yes. Yes. Yes. Every time. For three years.

My A1C bounced between 6.9 and 7.6 for the last 18 months. Up one visit. Down the next. Never below 6.9. Never stable. I was taking three pills a day, walking every morning, eating nothing I wanted, and the number wouldn't break.

Then came the appointment that changed everything.

She pulled up my chart. She read it. She read it again. Then she looked at me.

"Caroline. Your A1C is 7.6. We are back where we started."

I didn't say anything. I just sat there.

"Caroline, I have to be direct with you. We have tried Metformin. We have tried Glipizide. We have tried Jardiance. Your numbers are not responding the way they need to. I want to start you on Ozempic this week. And if we don't see significant movement in 3 months, we are going to add basal insulin. We have to be aggressive here. We are running out of options."

I sat in the chair and I felt something I hadn't felt in a doctor's office in my life.

I wasn't scared.

I was angry.

I told her I had been doing everything she asked for three years. Three Thanksgivings. Three Christmases. Three birthdays. I had walked in the dark in 14 degree weather. I had given up wine. I had given up bread. I had given up cooking for myself at my own table. I had taken every pill. I had swallowed every side effect. I had done every single thing she told me to do for three years.

She looked at me the way you look at a student who doesn't understand the lesson.

"Caroline, women your age who fight the protocol don't live long enough to regret it. I need you on board here. Otherwise you are looking at a heart attack in five years. Maybe a stroke. Maybe less."

That was the sentence.

I sat there for about ten seconds. I remember the second hand on the clock behind her because I was staring at it.

Then I stood up.

"Doc. You can go f*ck yourself."

She blinked.

I said it again, calmer this time, because I wanted her to hear it.

"I have taken your pills every morning and every evening for three years. Three different medications. I have lived with the nausea. I have lived with the stomach cramps. The bloating. The diarrhea that sent me to the bathroom in the middle of a third grade reading group. I have given up every food I love for three years. And my number is back where it started. Now you are telling me to add a needle on top of three pills that didn't work and call it aggressive care. I am not the problem here. You are. The pills are."

She tried to say something. I don't remember what.

I picked up my coat and I walked out.

Robert was in the waiting room. He stood up when he saw my face.

I told him what happened in the car on the way home. He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "Caroline, please go back. Take the prescription. We'll figure out the rest later."

I told him no. I told him whatever the answer to this was, it wasn't in that woman's office. It hadn't been in that office for three years.

That night I sat at my kitchen table with my laptop open.

I started reading. Actually reading. Not diet blogs. Not Facebook posts from women sharing smoothie recipes.

Medical journals. Diabetes studies. Research on compounds that support glucose metabolism in ways that medications don't even attempt.

I did that Tuesday night. And Wednesday night. And Thursday night.

Thursday around 1 AM I found a research paper that referenced a meta analysis of thirty four clinical trials. More than fifteen hundred people with elevated blood sugar. Testing a standardized extract against the markers that actually matter. Fasting glucose. Insulin levels. Insulin resistance.

The extract moved them. All of them. Consistently.

But it wasn't the numbers that stopped me. It was what the lead researcher wrote in the discussion section. He said something that made me put my coffee down and read the paragraph three times.

He said the conventional approach to Type 2 diabetes focuses almost entirely on managing blood sugar after it has already spiked. Metformin reduces sugar output from the liver. GLP 1 drugs slow stomach emptying. Glipizide squeezes the pancreas to produce more insulin. But none of them address the system that controls how fast the food you eat turns into sugar in the first place. He said that system is the upstream problem. And as long as it stays broken, everything downstream will keep flooding.

I read that paragraph three times.

And for the first time in three years, I understood why nothing my endocrinologist had done had worked.

Let me tell you what I learned, because it was the first time in three years that anything about this disease made sense to me.

Your body has a system that controls how fast the food you eat turns into sugar. Food comes in, the system breaks it down, sugar enters your blood. When it's working at the right pace, sugar trickles in slowly. Your insulin sees it coming, handles it calmly, and your numbers stay steady. You eat a meal. Energy goes up gently. Then it comes down gently. No spike. No crash. No 2 PM fog. That's how it worked when you were younger. That's why you could eat almost anything and your body just handled it.

But that system is fragile.

Stress wears it down. Processed food wears it down. Environmental toxins your grandparents never had to deal with wear it down. Soil that's been farmed flat for decades produces food with a fraction of the nutrients it used to carry. That wears it down too. Add aging on top of all of it, and the pathway that controls how fast food becomes sugar slowly stops being able to do its job.

A little bit at a time. Year after year. Quietly. Without you noticing.

Until one day it can't control the speed anymore.

Now food hits and turns into sugar almost instantly. The carbs in your meal aren't trickling into your blood. They're flooding in. And that flood is the problem.

When sugar hits your blood faster than your insulin can keep up with, it pools. Your blood sugar spikes. Not because you ate too much, but because everything got converted at once. Your pancreas panics and dumps a wave of insulin to catch up. That wave is too much, so an hour later your blood sugar crashes. And that's when the brain fog hits, the exhaustion sets in, and the cravings start screaming. Your body wants more sugar to climb out of the crash. So you eat. And the whole cycle starts again.

That was why I was getting winded on the stairs. My muscles were being flooded with sugar they couldn't use efficiently because it was all arriving at once instead of gradually.

That was why I was falling asleep after lunch. My body was spiking and crashing every time I ate.

That was why I couldn't lose the 22 pounds no matter what I ate. The constant insulin surges from the floods were telling my body to store everything as fat.

That trapped, pooling sugar had been grinding through my blood vessels every hour of every day for three years. Through the tiny vessels feeding the nerves in my feet. That was the tingling that had gotten worse every year. Through the vessels in the back of my eyes. That was the blurry vision. Through the filters in my kidneys. That was the nighttime bathroom trips. Through the vessels that feed the nerve endings and blood flow that make intimacy possible. That was what had been disappearing between Robert and me.

That same grinding sugar was going to reach my heart. And that was where the heart attack or the stroke my endocrinologist was warning me about was going to come from.

But the sugar flooding my blood wasn't the disease. The sugar flooding my blood was the RESULT of the disease. The disease was the broken pathway. The system that had lost the ability to control how fast food became sugar.

Metformin doesn't address the pathway. It tells the liver to produce less new sugar. Reduces the supply. Never touches the speed of the breakdown.

Glipizide doesn't address the pathway. It squeezes the pancreas to produce more insulin. More insulin chasing a flood that shouldn't be happening in the first place.

Jardiance doesn't address the pathway. It forces the kidneys to flush sugar out through the urine. That was why I was in the bathroom three times a night.

GLP 1 drugs don't address the pathway. They slow how fast your stomach empties so less new food enters the system at once. Never address the pathway itself.

Insulin injections don't address the pathway. They flood the body with even more insulin. But when the pathway is broken, more insulin doesn't slow the flood down.

I had been taking three medications for three years. Not one of them had touched the pathway. Not one of them had addressed the actual system that was letting food turn into sugar too fast. Every single one of them had been aimed at the number on the chart. And the number had barely moved because the disease underneath was still there, untouched, getting worse.

Three years. Three medications. Nine protocol adjustments. And not one of them had done the one thing that needed to be done.

Address the pathway.

The researcher's paper led me to the compound that did.

There's a fruit that's been used in Central Asia for over 5,000 years. The pomegranate.

The healers who used it back then didn't have a name for blood sugar. They didn't know what insulin was. They didn't have a way to measure what was happening inside the body.

But they knew what they saw.

People who ate pomegranate daily had steadier energy. Calmer digestion. They didn't crash after meals. They didn't fall into the slow decline everyone else seemed to. They lived longer. They aged better. The healers called it the fruit of life.

Modern science has finally caught up to what they were seeing.

Pomegranate contains a compound called punicalagins. One of the most powerful compounds your body uses to control how fast food becomes sugar. Your body can't make punicalagins on its own. It has to get them from food. And pomegranate is one of the only places on earth where they show up in meaningful amounts.

When your body had what it needed, the system worked the way it was supposed to. As the years wore that system down through aging, stress, modern life, and a food supply that doesn't deliver what it used to, the punicalagins disappeared along with it.

When the punicalagins are back in your system, the pathway has what it needs to slow the breakdown back to its natural pace. Sugar enters your blood gently, gradually, at a speed your body can actually handle. No flood. No spike. No crash. No 2 PM fog. No cravings dragging you back to the kitchen.

Same meals. Same food. Your body just handles them the way it used to.

This is what makes pomegranate fundamentally different from anything else.

Drugs force your body. They block enzymes, override signals, push your liver into compliance. That's where the side effects come from. The diarrhea, the fatigue, the brain fog, the feeling that the treatment is worse than the condition.

Pomegranate doesn't force anything. It restores. It gives your body the raw material it's been missing. The same raw material your ancestors had access to a thousand years ago. Your body isn't being overridden. It's being supported.

I spent the next two days reading everything I could find. I was looking for a product that matched what the clinical research had actually used. Not a cheap powder capsule from Amazon. Not a grocery store juice bottle with a health claim slapped on it.

The pomegranate at the grocery store was grown in industrial soil that's been stripped of nutrients by decades of chemical farming. Sprayed with pesticides. Picked early so it could survive shipping. The punicalagin content was a fraction of what it was meant to be.

The pomegranate juices people reach for were mostly sugar. Whatever punicalagins were in the fruit were largely destroyed during pasteurization and bottling. Sweetened water with a pomegranate label. And the sugar was doing the opposite of what I actually needed.

The pomegranate powders were heat processed at high temperatures to dry them out. Heat destroys punicalagins. By the time the powder hit the shelf, the active compounds were mostly gone.

I needed organic pomegranate. Standardized extract with verified punicalagin concentration. Low temperature processed so the compounds stayed intact. Third party tested so I could trust what was inside.

I found one that met every requirement.

It was called Alevia's Pomegranate.

I ordered it that afternoon.

It arrived on a Friday. I took two capsules the next morning with my breakfast.

Week 1. I slept six straight hours for the first time in over a year. I hadn't realized how broken my sleep had become until I got a full night of it back. I woke up at 6 AM and I wasn't tired. I can't tell you what that felt like after three years of exhaustion. It felt like someone had turned the lights back on.

Week 2. The tingling in my feet at night went quiet. Not gone. But quiet. Like the volume had been turned down after three years of getting louder. I pulled the blankets over my feet for the first time in months. They felt like my feet again.

Week 3. The energy crashes after meals disappeared. I ate lunch on a Tuesday and I stayed awake through the entire afternoon. I read 40 pages of my book in my reading chair. I hadn't done that in over two years. And I got up once at night instead of three times.

Week 4. I walked up all 14 stairs without stopping. I didn't realize I had done it until I was at the top. Then I stood there and I put my hand on the wall and I cried. Because I had forgotten what it felt like to just walk up the stairs in my own house without my chest pounding. I had been stopping halfway for two years. And now I was at the top. Just like that.

Week 5. The thing I hadn't told my endocrinologist about started coming back. The sensitivity. The response. The warmth. The closeness with Robert that I had been quietly grieving for three years. I am not going to say more than that. But Robert knew. And I knew. And neither of us said anything about it. We didn't need to. He reached for me for the first time in a very long time. And I was there.

Week 6. I bought a home glucose meter at CVS. I tested my fasting glucose one morning. 116. I hadn't seen a number that low since before my diagnosis. My fasting had been running 168 to 182 for the past year.

Week 7. 102. Then 97. Then 93 three mornings in a row.

I stood in my bathroom staring at that meter reading 93 and I couldn't believe it. Three years of pills had never gotten me below 142 fasting. Two capsules every morning for seven weeks and I was at 93.

The walk to the mailbox stopped being a walk. I started walking to the end of the block. Then two blocks. Then around the neighborhood. Then a full mile through the park, the same route I used to walk with Robert before any of this started. My legs didn't ache. My chest didn't pound. I wasn't winded.

I felt like myself again. For the first time in three years, I felt like Caroline.

By week 8 I started doing something I want to tell you about carefully.

I started eating things I hadn't touched in three years.

I didn't go overboard. I know better than that. But one Saturday morning I went to the diner on Main Street and I sat at a booth by myself and I ordered a stack of pancakes. Three of them. Real maple syrup. Butter. Bacon on the side. Coffee with half and half for the first time in three years.

I ate every bite. I sat there for 45 minutes. Then I pricked my finger.

I sat in that booth and I stared at the number. I hadn't eaten pancakes in three years. Three years of dry toast and egg whites. Three years of watching other people eat breakfast while I ate nothing. And my blood sugar after a full stack of pancakes with syrup was 118.

The Saturday after that I baked my banana bread for the first time in three years. I ate a thick slice, warm, with butter, standing at my own kitchen counter. Robert walked in and stopped in the doorway. He looked at the loaf on the counter. He looked at the slice in my hand. He looked at my face. He didn't say a word. He just smiled. Glucose an hour later. 124.

None of those numbers should have been possible in a diabetic body. Not after three years of damage. Not with the complications I had been living with.

The punicalagins had done their work. The pathway that controls how fast food becomes sugar was working again. The sugar from my Saturday breakfast wasn't flooding my blood all at once anymore. It was entering slowly, the way it's supposed to. My body was finally doing what it was supposed to do. What three years of medication had never allowed it to do.

Which brings me to last week.

I baked Emily's apple crisp recipe for Sunday dinner at my house. I served it warm with vanilla ice cream. I ate a full portion in front of my entire family. My granddaughter sat next to me and asked me to share mine because hers was already gone.

I gave her a bite off my plate.

It was the first time in three years I had eaten dessert at a family dinner. My granddaughter doesn't remember a time when grandma ate what everyone else ate. She was four when I got diagnosed. She is seven now. Three of her birthdays passed while I sat at the table drinking water. She never asked why. Children don't ask. They just watch.

Robert caught my eye from across the table. He didn't say anything. He smiled the smile he used to smile at me at Sunday dinners before all of this started. I hadn't seen that smile in three years.

Forty minutes later I stepped into the kitchen to check my meter.

I stood at my kitchen sink and I cried. Not because of the number. Because I had gotten a piece of my life back that I thought I had lost forever. I had spent three years believing I would never eat at my own table again. Three years believing the woman I used to be was gone. Three years accepting that the rest of my life would be almonds in a plastic bag and naked salads and watching.

And it was over. In twelve weeks, it was over.

Two days later I went back to my endocrinologist's office. Same waiting room. Same receptionist who remembered my name and looked nervous when I signed in. Same doctor.

She came into the exam room with my chart already pulled up on her tablet. She didn't say hello.

She said: "Caroline. Your A1C is 5.6. Your last reading twelve weeks ago was 7.6. That is not something I have ever seen without a major medication change. What are you doing?"

I told her.

I told her about the research. About the meta analysis. About the punicalagins. About the pathway. About the speed of the breakdown. About the three years of pills that had never touched the actual system that was letting food flood my blood.

She interrupted me halfway through. "Caroline, this is anecdotal. This is not evidence based medicine. You are describing a supplement. Supplements are not regulated. There is no way a pomegranate extract moved your A1C 2 points in 12 weeks when three years of medication couldn't."

I told her it did.

She stared at the chart.

Then she said, and this is the sentence I won't forget: "That number can't be right. I want to redraw the labs today."

She redrew them.

I sat in the exam room for 40 minutes while the lab ran the panel again. She came back with the printout in her hand.

5.4.

Even lower than the first draw.

She sat down on the stool in the exam room and she didn't say anything for what felt like a very long time.

Then she said, very quietly: "Caroline. I owe you an apology. I don't understand what you are doing. But whatever it is, keep doing it."

I didn't say anything. I let her sit with it.

I wanted to say three years. I wanted to say I gave you three years of my life. I wanted to say I gave up my banana bread and my wine and my Sunday cooking and my reading at night and my sleep and my stairs and my intimacy with my husband for three years because you told me to trust the process. And the process did nothing.

I didn't say any of that. I just let her sit with it.

Then she said: "Can you write down what you are taking? I want to look at this."

I wrote it down for her. She folded the paper and put it in the pocket of her white coat.

She stopped all three of my medications that day. Metformin. Glipizide. Jardiance. All of them. She didn't mention Ozempic. She didn't mention insulin.

On my way out the receptionist smiled at me. I smiled back at her for the first time in three years.

I am 63 years old. I have Type 2 diabetes and my A1C is 5.4. I have eaten pancakes with real maple syrup and banana bread with butter and apple crisp with ice cream in the last four weeks. My blood sugar has stayed in the normal range through every one of those meals.

I am writing this for one reason.

Because if you are sitting where I was sitting three years ago, or one year ago, or last week, angry, scared, cornered by a doctor who is telling you to add another pill or a needle on top of the pills that haven't worked, and you are watching your grandchildren blow out candles from across the room and telling yourself this is just how it has to be for the rest of your life, I am here to tell you it doesn't have to be.

The pathway that controls how fast your food becomes sugar has broken down. Every pill your doctor has given you is aimed at the number on the chart. Not one of them is aimed at the pathway.

There is something that is.

Alevia's Pomegranate. Organic pomegranate superfruit extract. Standardized to preserve the full punicalagin matrix. Low temperature processed so the active compounds stay intact. Third party tested for purity and potency. Made in the USA. Small batch. No fillers.

Two capsules every morning with breakfast. That is the whole protocol.

90 day money back guarantee. If your numbers don't move, you send it back and they refund you every dollar. No questions asked.

I keep 3 paper fans in the top drawer of my desk at Parkview Magnet High School and I have used every last one of them in the past 2 years to hide something my body will not stop doing to me in front of teenagers.

They're the kind of fans they hand out at Baptist funerals in the summer. Cardboard. A wooden stick stapled to the back. A picture of Jesus on one side and the name of the funeral home on the other. Mount Pleasant Baptist. Superior Funeral Chapel. My cousin's home going in 2021. My auntie's home going in 2023. I have been to too many funerals in the past 5 years and I have kept every single fan.

They live in my drawer under the pack of Post-its and the little bag of jolly ranchers I keep for the students.

I use one about 4 times a day.

Not to be cute. Not because I like the picture of Jesus. Because if I don't get air on my face and neck the moment I feel the wave come up my chest, I will sweat through whatever I'm wearing in 90 seconds and every parent standing at the counter in the front office will see it happen.

The move is quick. I open the drawer, pull out the fan, hold it low near my collarbone, flick my wrist 5 or 6 times, breathe through my mouth, put it back. Nobody who isn't looking for it sees it.

I have gotten so good at the church fan trick that I could probably teach a class on it.

I never wanted to be an expert at this.

My name is Alma. I'm 54 years old. I have been the executive secretary at Parkview Magnet High School in Little Rock, Arkansas for 19 years. Before that I was 5 years at Little Rock Central. Before that I was 8 years at a law office on Main Street doing intake.

I run the front office. I know where every teacher is at every hour of every day. I know which kids in the freshman class have older siblings who came through here. I know which parents are going through divorces and which ones are not to be seated together at open house. I know the alarm codes for 4 different rooms and the combination of the safe in the finance closet and the direct cell number of every school board member in Pulaski County.

I am the woman who knows.

That was the identity I built. That was who I was.

I was not supposed to be the woman who has to duck into a supply closet at 10:47 AM to press a damp paper towel to the back of her neck.

My husband Reggie is 57. He retired from the post office 2 years ago after 32 years on the same route in Southwest Little Rock. Now he fixes small engines out of our garage on Arch Street for cash and drives our daughter Camille's kids to karate on Wednesdays. Camille is 32. She teaches 5th grade in North Little Rock. Her twins are 8.

I have been going to First Missionary Baptist since I was 6 years old.

I have sung in that choir. I have taught Sunday school in the basement. I have served lemonade at 4 vacation Bible schools. I know every deacon's wife by name and every deacon's wife knows what I take in my coffee.

I have never in my life been the kind of woman who hides.

The flashes started when I was 51. They started small. A little wave. A little warmth. Nothing worth mentioning. My doctor said it was normal for a woman my age and told me to dress in layers and gave me a pamphlet.

By the time I was 52 they were bigger. I was waking up at 2:30 in the morning with the sheets soaked through and I was changing my nightgown in the dark so I wouldn't wake Reggie. I bought a little battery fan for my nightstand. I bought sheets with the moisture wicking. I bought a cooling pillow that cost 68 dollars off Amazon and didn't work.

By the time I was 53 they were bigger during the day than at night.

I was sitting at my desk at Parkview one morning in September, back to school night was in 4 hours, I had a stack of enrollment forms to file. It was 9:15 AM. The building was cool. My blouse was navy silk. And out of nowhere the wave came up my chest and hit my throat and my whole face went hot like someone had opened an oven in front of me.

I sat there gripping the arms of my chair.

By the time it passed I had sweat clean through my blouse under both arms and down the middle of my back. I could feel my bra clinging to my skin. I could feel my hair damp at the nape of my neck.

Miss Cheryl, the assistant principal, was walking by on her way to the copier. She said "Alma, honey, you okay."

I said I was fine. I smiled.

I went into the supply closet after she passed and I closed the door and I pressed my forehead against the cool metal of the shelving unit and I stood there for 4 minutes until I could breathe again.

That was the day I started buying blazers a size too big.

You would not believe the things I bought in the year after that.

A little pack of blotting papers for makeup that I used on my chest. A silk scarf that I told myself was for style. A stick of clear antiperspirant I put on my chest and shoulders and the back of my neck every morning. A folding cardboard fan I ordered from Etsy because the church fan was starting to look worn out. Then a second one from a different Etsy shop that folded like a Chinese fan and lived in my purse.

I ordered a spray bottle of "cooling mist" for 34 dollars that turned out to be water.

I made an appointment with my doctor. She was young. She was kind. She had a poster on the wall of a smiling older woman doing yoga. She told me my hormones were in the range for a woman my age. She told me I could try hormone therapy if the symptoms became disruptive.

I asked her what disruptive meant.

She said if I couldn't function.

I was functioning. I was doing the church fan trick 20 times a day and I was functioning.

I thanked her and I left.

I want to tell you about one specific day because I think about it a lot.

Camille's oldest, Marcus, had his 3rd grade Christmas program in December of last year. Camille had asked me weeks in advance to come. I sat in the second row of the school gym with Reggie on my left and Camille and her husband on my right and Marcus's twin sister Micah on my lap.

The program started. The lights dimmed. The kids came out singing.

And I felt it start.

Not a small one. A big one. The kind that starts in the middle of your chest and moves up your throat and then it's in your face and you know you have about 20 seconds before your neck starts to shine.

I didn't have my fan. I had left my purse in the car.

Micah was sitting on my lap. I could not get up without making a scene. I could not open my little program and fan myself with it because everyone would see. I sat there and I felt the wave hit my face and I felt my collar go damp and I felt Micah's little arms slide down my forearm because my skin was too slick for her to hold on.

She said "Grandma, you're wet."

She said it out loud.

The woman in front of me turned around.

I stared straight ahead at the stage with tears in my eyes and I sang "away in a manger" with the second graders and I did not move for the rest of the program.

Reggie didn't know what to do. Camille didn't know what to do. Micah went back to her mother's lap 5 minutes later without saying anything else because 3 year old girls are actually much more careful with grown women than we give them credit for.

I went home that night and I sat on the edge of the tub in our bathroom and I cried for a long time.

I told Reggie the next morning I wanted to skip Easter.

He said "you don't skip Easter."

I said "I don't want to sit in the church in a good dress and have this happen in front of every person we know."

He said "Alma, you have been going to Easter service since you were 6."

I did go to Easter service. I wore a linen dress in a light color that would show sweat less. I sat in the back pew instead of my usual place near the deacons' bench.

I did not raise my hands during praise.

I want to tell you about June.

My cousin Everett passed on a Sunday in early June. Everett was 63. He'd had a stroke in his sleep in his apartment in Pine Bluff and his daughter had found him the next morning. It was sudden. It was the kind of loss that comes without warning and knocks a whole family sideways for a while.

The funeral was at Mount Pleasant Baptist here in Little Rock the following Saturday because that was Everett's mother's church and she wanted him buried near her.

June in Arkansas.

The forecast was 91 degrees. The church did not have great air conditioning. The service was at 11 AM.

I wore a navy dress with 3 quarter length sleeves and a pair of low heels and I brought 2 fans in my purse. I sat with Reggie in the fifth pew from the back on the aisle. I could see the whole church.

The service started.

By the time we were 20 minutes in I had used 1 fan and I was on the second and my navy dress was showing wet where my back was against the pew. The woman two rows in front of me had a battery operated hand fan going the whole time. The man behind me was mopping his face with a handkerchief every 90 seconds.

Everyone in Mount Pleasant Baptist that morning was sweating.

Except one woman.

She was sitting in the pew directly in front of me. I hadn't noticed her when I sat down. Older woman. Maybe 63 or 64. Salt and pepper hair pulled back into a low neat bun with a pearl clip. Straight back. Small pearl earrings. A wide brim black hat that she'd taken off and set beside her on the pew.

She was wearing a wool suit.

A full 3 piece wool suit in navy blue. Skirt to just below the knee. Fitted jacket. Silk blouse buttoned to the throat with a little pearl pin. Stockings. Closed toe pumps.

I stared at the back of her neck for the whole 50 minute service.

She did not sweat.

Not a drop. Not a shine. Not the little glisten at the hairline that even the coolest people had going by that point. The little curl of hair at the back of her neck where the bun didn't cover was completely dry.

I could not stop looking.

The service ended. The pallbearers came forward. We stood and we sang. My dress was ruined. Her wool suit sat on her shoulders like it had been pressed that morning.

We filed out into the fellowship hall for the repast.

I told Reggie to fix me a plate. I walked across the room with my purse in my hand and I found her standing near the sweet tea station holding a small plate with 2 deviled eggs and a piece of pound cake.

I said "excuse me ma'am, I don't mean to bother you."

She smiled at me. Kind eyes. Deep laugh lines. A small gap between her front teeth.

She said "you're not bothering me, baby. Sit down."

We sat at one of the round tables in the corner near the coat rack. I did not know how to ask what I was about to ask. I fumbled with the strap of my purse. I looked down at my dress.

She said "you want to know how I'm not sweating."

I looked up at her.

She laughed. She said "sugar, I have been getting that look at every funeral I've been to for the past 8 months. You are the first one to actually come over and ask me."

Her name was Odessa Fields. She was 63. She lived in Pine Bluff. She had known my cousin Everett since they were both in high school at Merrill 45 years ago and that's why she had made the drive up that morning. Her husband Nathaniel had passed 6 years earlier. She had raised 3 children and was a retired guidance counselor from a middle school in Pine Bluff.

She had been having the flashes since she was 51.

She had had them worse than I did. She said hers used to come in twos. Back to back. The kind where you'd finish one and start another before your dress was dry from the first one.

She said she had tried everything.

She had tried the herbs from the natural food store on Main Street. She had tried a soy powder her sister sent her. She had tried the hormone patch her doctor prescribed and had come off it after 4 months because it gave her migraines. She had tried the little battery fans and the cooling mist and the wicking clothes.

She had gone to Everett's cousin's 60th birthday party 9 months earlier and had gotten so hot in the middle of the toast that she had walked out of the restaurant and sat on the curb in her Sunday dress.

Her sister-in-law, a woman she'd known for 40 years who lived in Monroe, Louisiana, had told her about something months earlier and she'd brushed it off because it sounded like every other thing she'd tried. She said pomegranate.

I laughed a small laugh. She waited for me to be done and then she said "I know what it sounds like. Let me tell you what it actually is, because it's not what you're thinking."

She took a sip of her sweet tea and she set the cup down.

She said your body has a whole set of blood vessels whose job is to control your temperature.

She said when you get warm, those vessels are supposed to open up in a certain way to release the heat. When you get cool, they're supposed to tighten in a certain way to keep the heat in. The whole system runs on a signal your body makes called nitric oxide. Nitric oxide tells the vessels when to relax and when to constrict. It's the switch.

She said when the switch is working right, your body handles temperature the way it always has. When it's not working right, the vessels can't respond the way they're supposed to. They flush all at once. They can't get their signal to calm down. And that's what you feel when a flash comes. That's not just your hormones being crazy. That's your vessels not getting the signal to settle.

I sat forward.

She said the reason the switch stops working right is oxidative stress.

She said the same word gets used for what happens to metal when it rusts. Rust. Your body does the same thing on the inside. It rusts. And the little signal molecule that tells your vessels when to open and close, that nitric oxide, gets attacked by the rust the moment your body makes it. The signal doesn't reach the vessels. The vessels don't get the message. And they flush without warning.

She said menopause makes it worse because your hormones change and put more stress on the whole system, but the flashes themselves are your vessels not being able to talk to the switch anymore.

She said the punicalagins support the nitric oxide signal by quieting the oxidative stress that had been destroying it. When the rust eases, the signal survives. Her own father threw molten gold at her.
Then he locked her in a  drum and threw away the key.
He trained her to withstand any situation.
Until she became the best assassin in the world.
He had taken her in as a child with nothing. Built her into the most dangerous instrument he had and aimed her at everything that needed to be destroyed. She killed for him.
She learned piano so she could sit beside his targets at concerts. She learned to cook so she could infiltrate their kitchens. She mastered hacking, marksmanship, combat, five languages, and field surgery.
She gave him everything. One mission more, he promised. Then she would finally be free.
So she completed it. Twelve guards, one drug lord. She killed them all. Bleeding in the silent plaza, she heard clapping. 
Amos Joyce, her godfather, stepped over the bodies in a perfect suit. "twenty-eight years," he said. "You worked so hard." 
"Yes, sir. Now it is time for me to leave," she said with a genuine smile on her face. He sighed. 
"Yeah, time to leave this world… my child!"
Before she could react to what he said, a gunshot rang out. 
The heat tore through her chest before her brain caught up. She looked down.
A dark stain bloomed from her heart and spread fast, unstoppable, absolute. Her legs gave out. She hit the flagstones on her knees and watched him draw the handkerchief from his pocket and wipe a trace of blood from his cheek with it. "Goodbye, Evelyn."
So, that was what twenty-eight years was worth. She wanted a life of her own, but her reward for loyalty was death. Or so she thought….
Nine hundred miles away, at the exact moment she closed her eyes for the last time, a twenty one-year-old actress named Evelyn Hawthorne was being held underwater from behind.
She was an excellent swimmer. Everyone agreed on that…..
She had gone into the water at a private villa party willingly and confidently, the way good swimmers go into water.
Someone had kept both hands on her efficiently, calmly, until the fighting stopped. The scratch marks along their arm told the real story. The alibi told a different one. The defibrillator fired.
The line stayed flat. They increased the power, fired again, a twitch, then another, then a rhythm, uncertain at first, steadying into something that would hold. The room breathed out. But the soul that opened its eyes in that hospital bed was not the one the doctors had been fighting to save. It was hers.
The first thing she did when she opened her eyes was take a hostage. She had no memory of where she was. The ceiling was wrong. The body was wrong, soft-armed and pale. A stranger's hands at the ends of her arms. Her instincts had no interest in that distinction.
She yanked the IV needle free, grabbed the nearest person by the hair, and pressed the sharp end against his carotid artery. "Don't move if you want to live," she rasped. The man she had pinned, Ethan Hawthorne, though she didn't know his name yet, went completely still, reflexively, correctly. The older man across the room raised both hands without being asked.
She scanned the room. Hospital, no guards, no weapons beyond the needle she was holding. Two men, no military bearing, no threat posture, but good instincts, both of them. And they were looking at her with an expression she was unaccustomed to receiving. It took her a moment to identify it. It was grief.
A door opened. Nurses, a doctor, the ordinary machinery of a medical response. A firm-handed older nurse marched over and guided her back onto the mattress before she'd fully processed a counter move. She let her. She needed time to assess. The doctor found nothing wrong with her head. Possible disorientation from oxygen deprivation, he said. Short-term memory disruption. The family should be patient and gentle. So she sat and let them be patient. She catalogued what she had. A name — Evelyn Hawthorne — and a face that stared back at her from the window glass like a stranger's reflection. Pale, wide-eyed, fragile in a way she had never been in any life she remembered. The older man was Richard Hawthorne, the father. The young man whose hair she'd pulled was Ethan, the brother. There was a mother who had fainted in the hallway and been put to bed in the next room. There was significant money, the quiet, embedded kind, that showed itself in the quality of everything around it.
She told them she had amnesia. It wasn't entirely a lie. She knew nothing about the life she had just inherited, and she was not ready to explain the one she had left behind. She used the phone carefully. One search, two words. Amos Joyce. Top result, California governor's race. The man credited with organizing the takedown of a major drug cartel had jumped five points in the polls overnight. His numbers were still climbing. There was a photo of him shaking hands with federal agents in front of a seized shipment. He was smiling. He was celebrating. Somewhere in the world she had just left behind, Amos Joyce was celebrating a mission that she had died completing — a mission he'd sent her on, knowing exactly what he was going to do when she finished it.
She set the phone down. She had no weapons, no money of her own, no connections in this life. The body she was occupying had soft hands, weak arms, and a public reputation that could be summarized by the comment she found in the first ten minutes of scrolling her social media. "I'm tired of hating on Evelyn Hawthorne every day. From now on, I'll just carve the insults on her tombstone." She had forty-thousand followers across all platforms combined, and the positive ones had been purchased by her family's PR budget. Amos Joyce was the governor-elect of California. He had resources she couldn't imagine from where she was sitting. But she had time, and she had every skill he had spent twenty-eight years forcing her to build.
She picked the phone back up and kept reading. The woman who had drowned Evelyn Hawthorne was named Cassidy Reed. She was an actress, a real one. Actual credits, actual fans, the kind of industry position that felt solid until you understood whose protection was underneath it. 
Her protector was a woman named Scarlett Vance, her superior, the daughter of a family so embedded in military and political infrastructure that her name appeared in no press coverage at all, which was itself a kind of power. Cassidy had held Evelyn Hawthorne underwater from behind, face hidden, hands steady, until the fighting stopped. She'd had reasons. Evelyn had witnessed something at the villa she shouldn't have. When the paramedics arrived and shocked Evelyn back to life, Cassidy had already confirmed with the right people that no one had seen anything. The kayak and wet suit were gone. The alibi held. But Evelyn Hawthorne had survived.
Scarlett’s response when Cassidy reported this was careful and unhurried. "Test her. If she has genuine amnesia, she's no threat. If not, let me know before she becomes one." Cassidy passed the message along and lit a cigarette. 
A watch was placed on her before she left the hospital. She didn't know that yet. What she knew was that she had nearly drowned, that the police report called it accidental, and that the woman at whose villa it happened had walked out of the hospital the moment the flatline became a pulse without looking back. She filed that away, and she kept reading.
She had one month before filming began, and she used every hour of it that she could take without attracting attention. She ran before the household woke up — four miles, then five, then six as the weeks progressed — and this body began to remember what bodies were capable of when asked seriously. 
The family's chef received a new meal plan: two eggs, half a pound of beef, a large glass of whole milk, and a high-protein salad at every main meal. Her mother and sister stared at the portions across the breakfast table as if she had developed a second personality, which, in the most literal sense available, she had. The family thought the original Evelyn was preparing for a television show. They were not wrong. They simply didn't understand what she was preparing for.
In the quiet hours, she worked on other things. Ethan's company had suffered a sophisticated cyber attack while she was still in the hospital. Someone on the inside had leaked defense protocols to an external actor and the damage was significant. 
She fixed it overnight from the computer system she'd had installed in her room. Patched the vulnerabilities, embedded a new defensive core that could write its own countermeasures in real time, and while she was already inside the architecture, cleaned up a constellation of legacy bugs that the tech department had been collectively afraid to touch for years because they couldn't predict the cascade failure risk. Ethan received a call from his tech director at five in the morning saying that the company's security system had apparently upgraded itself overnight and the app was running ten times faster. 
Meanwhile, she studied the other contestants. Kyle was the one to take seriously. Solo expeditions in the Amazon, months alone in the Gobi Desert, survival records that read like field operations reports rather than adventure travel. Maya Sutton was a decorated competitive athlete. Cody Nash moved through terrain the way people move through rooms. 
Any of the three of them, in a real survival situation, would be a resource. The mystery guest was Julian Donovan. He returned from studying abroad five days before filming launched, walking through the airport in sunglasses and a mask, an entourage of eight behind him. Security footage she found online showed him stopping in front of the promo poster for the show. 
He looked at each photo in turn. He stopped at hers for a moment that was longer than the others, though not long enough to draw conclusions from, and then moved on without a word. His manager was quoted in a fan account shortly after: "If you must do this show, stay as far from Evelyn Hawthorne as you can. She's a walking disaster." Julian's reported response was a slow smile. "She'll learn to stay out of my way." She read that, set the phone down, and thought about it. Interesting.

September sixteenth. The show launched at eight-o-clock in the evening, but the cameras started rolling that morning. 
The production crew collected every phone before they boarded the bus. She didn't argue. She had already studied everything she needed.
On the bus, the host made the introductions. Each of them waved at the camera. The comment section under her personal live channel — three-lakh viewers, most of them there to see her fail — sent a wave of vomiting emojis when she smiled.
She assessed the other contestants without appearing to. Kyle gave nothing away at all, a blank antisocial stillness that she found instantly reassuring because it was the posture of a man who didn't need anyone else and knew it. 
Maya and Kyle were barely containing excitement. Boone, in a blindingly orange jacket, was trying very hard not to be seen looking at her. Then the partition rose between the driver's cabin and the passenger section. 
The host and camera crew pulled on gas masks. A thick white mist hissed from the back of the bus. Everyone around her was unconscious within ninety seconds. She had taken a full breath the moment she saw the host reach for his mask. She had held it. She had let her body go completely limp and played dead while the production medics checked her pupils with a pen light and found nothing but a convincingly insensible actress. They tied her wrists, blindfolded her, and loaded her into a separate vehicle. She slowed her breathing, kept her face slack, and let the genuine thrill of anticipation rise through her chest. This show was already more interesting than she'd expected.
They untied her after they placed her. She heard the vehicle leave. She waited until the engine noise was fully absorbed by the trees. Then she opened her eyes and took inventory. One backpack, a pop-up tent, a lighter, disinfectant wipes, a water bladder, two protein bars — the barest possible start. She noted what she didn't have and began moving. 
Two million people were watching her personal live feed through cameras hidden in the trees and brush around her. She was aware of the cameras. She factored them in the way she factored in any variable she couldn't remove — as a constraint to work around, not a problem to solve. The operators were good at staying hidden. She'd seen enough surveillance equipment deployed in the field to recognize the signs of professional concealment. She gave them the acknowledgement of not acknowledging them and got to work.
The first thing she needed was water. She found a stream within the hour, small, clear, threading between smooth stones, fed from the mountain above. She checked the current, traced it downstream, found a bend with flat ground, and began setting up camp. She built the fire with controlled airflow and minimum smoke.
The viewers watching, she learned much later, couldn't quite reconcile what they were seeing. The actress who had been publicly mocked for years, the internet's favorite punching bag, the girl they'd shown up to watch fail — was moving through the wilderness like she'd been there her entire life. They kept watching.
She was already thinking about food. Her stomach had been growling for two hours when she found the solution. 
The rabbit burrow announced itself to anyone who knew how to listen. The grass along the approach path was worn thin and angled in a consistent direction. The tunnel entrance was oriented correctly — uphill, sheltered from the prevailing wind. The size and depth of the tracks told her she was working with an adult animal, healthy and well-fed. She pulled the drawstring from her jacket hood — three feet of strong cord — and tied it into a slip knot that required a very specific understanding of load distribution and release dynamics to get right. 
The kind of knowledge you accumulated after someone stood over you in the rain and made you restart from the beginning every time the tension was wrong.
She set the snare on the rabbit's uphill path home, propped it with a Y-shaped branch cut from the thicket, ran a trigger line back to a tree she climbed to wait in.
The viewers on her live feed had been drifting away for twenty minutes. She didn't move. Twenty minutes, thirty. The forest breathed around her. Then she heard footsteps and voices. Julian Donovan and Boone were walking directly through her setup, arguing about cryptids. The rabbit bolted from the noise they made straight down its path and directly into the snare. She yanked the rope from twelve feet up. The slip knot cinched clean around its hind legs. The animal dropped to the ground.
Aiden screamed. He launched himself off the earth with the full body commitment of a man who had decided something large and prehistoric had just attacked him, and he grabbed Julian around the shoulders with the grip of a drowning person finding something to hold. Julian's face went through five distinct expressions before settling on one that could most charitably be described as trapped. Trapped, and also developing a headache.
She slid down from the tree with the rabbit. "It's a rabbit," Julian said to no one in particular. Then, louder: "You can jump that high? You should have been an athlete." Aiden said he had tried but hadn't passed the exam. He said it with genuine earnestness.
She looked at the two of them and made the calculation. Three was harder to manage than one, but both of them had zero survivable options alone in this terrain, and she had already decided somewhere in the last few seconds that she was responsible for them whether she'd agreed to it or not. She kept the rabbit. She kept them, too.

They ate better that night than either of them had expected. The rabbit was gutted, rubbed down with Hawthorne Foods seasoning she'd brought in her pack — a brand partnership she had inherited from the original Evelyn, along with the contract, the deposit, and the complete online reputation — and roasted over a fire she built with controlled airflow and minimum smoke. Julian ate more than half of it without speaking for the first ten minutes. Aiden ate whatever Julian left and kept making small involuntary sounds of gratitude.
After dinner, Aiden fell asleep immediately. Julian held on longer, fighting exhaustion the way overtired people do when their nervous system can't distinguish between tired and threatened. His breathing was uneven, his eyelids working overtime. There had been a spider incident earlier in the day. He wouldn't tell her the details, but the effect on his nervous system was obvious. She gave him twenty minutes to sleep on his own. He didn't. She told him she could help. He covered the back of his neck with both hands immediately. "I'm afraid of pain," he said. "Have you been watching too many action movies?" she said. He considered this. “Probably.” She told him to lie down.
He lay with his head facing out of the shelter, eyes turned up. She squatted at the entrance and held her right hand above his face — index finger first, then middle, ring, pinky — a slow, continuous wave that she kept perfectly even. The kind of technique she'd used on injured teammates in the field who couldn't quiet their own thoughts enough to lose consciousness. You needed to be steady. You needed to clear your own head entirely while you did it, so there was nothing in the motion but the motion itself. Julian's eyes stayed open for ninety three seconds. Then they didn't. He was in deep, even sleep within two minutes.
The comment section, she was told later, went briefly and completely silent. And then the messages began flooding back in. “
What kind of actress knows how to do this?”
“ What is she?”
“ I need to know everything about this woman immediately.”
She adjusted the backpack she'd set beside him so Aiden's feet couldn't reach his head during the night. She added sticks to the fire and listened to the forest.
Three hours later, the drone arrived. She had been waiting for the drone. She had worked out within the first hours of the show that the production crew would send missions this way — midnight drops, dramatic timing, no warning, just the hum of rotors through dark trees. Supplies, task cards, a contained moment that the viewers would find thrilling. She had prepared for it the moment Aiden and Julian fell asleep. She rolled her jacket tight around a fist-sized stone she'd set aside that afternoon and waited by the fire.
When the drone hovered directly above the campsite and its camera found her face, she looked up at it and smiled. The production director, watching from the mobile command center, said afterward that the smile was immediately recognizable as the same one he'd seen before she robbed the squirrel. He lunged for the walkie-talkie. Too late.
She swung the jacket in a long, powerful arc overhead and released it. The weighted end hit the drone's rotors with the flat crack of a stone on water. The machine lurched sideways, tipping hard. She was already moving — three bounding steps, a foot planted against a tree trunk, launched upward, caught a branch at fifteen feet, bolted higher, and snatched the falling drone out of the air with both hands before it could strike the ground. The camera steadied. A completely calm face filled the operator's monitor. "Thanks for the drone," she said. "Don't mind if I do."
Aiden's voice woke Julian. Julian said later that he'd slept more soundly than he had in years. He lay on his back for a few seconds, registered the canvas above him, registered that he was in the wilderness, and then looked at the pile of components on the ground with the expression of a man encountering something that required a moment before responding. "You took it apart," he said. "The propellers can be sharpened into knives," she said without looking up from what she was working on. "The motor rods become tent supports, fishing spears, or grill skewers. The camera lens will concentrate sunlight for fire starting when the lighter runs out. The landing struts are grill material. The signal wire can be braided into a stronger rope. The battery housing is waterproof storage." He stared at her. "You knew they were going to send it," he said. She didn't answer.
He sat down across the fire from her. He was quiet for a long time. And during that quiet, she noticed the thing she had started noticing the night before. The cool, performative distance he carried as reflexively as other people carried keys was giving way to something more honest underneath. Something that looked like a man discovering that a problem he'd thought he understood was considerably more complex than he'd assumed. When he asked how she knew any of this, she told him, "Books.".
She went hunting because she was hungry and because she needed to think. She came back to camp with five quail tied to her belt, the snake hanging from one hand by its tail, a bag of eggs cushioned in her pack, and foraging pouches full enough to make a real meal.
Julian looked at everything she was carrying and did not speak for a moment. Then she handed him the snake reflexively, the way she would have passed equipment to a teammate. And he took it before he'd registered what it was. He looked at it, he looked at her, and then Julian Donovan — a man who had been composed on camera for the better part of a decade — screamed and flung it away from himself with full body revulsion, frantically wiping his hands on his pants, his voice loud enough to startle birds out of the canopy above. Aiden refused to come down from his rock for eight minutes.
"Does your agent have your voice insured?" she asked Julian when he'd managed to stop making sounds. "With a scream like that, you'll blow your vocal cords." "Why didn't you warn me?" he said. "I assumed it was obvious what I was holding," she said. "It's a headless snake," he said. She considered this. "Yes."
She built the grill from the drone — six landing struts, eight propeller blades repurposed as skewers, the whole structure over a fire pit she dug to manage airflow. The quail went on first. Quail eggs into the stainless steel bowl from the supply package, Mushrooms on separate skewers brushed with barbecue sauce. The snake for her, over the hottest part of the flame.
Amos Joyce had spent twenty-eight years building her to walk into rooms exactly like this one.
He had trained her to assess them, control them, and walk back out of them carrying whatever he needed her to carry. He had built this weapon. He had aimed it at everything he needed destroyed. And then, when it became inconvenient to keep the weapon alive, he had tried to bury it.
The man in the doorway was still looking at her. She was still smiling.
And the thing she was thinking — the thought that was sitting just underneath the expression she was wearing like a second skin — was this:
Amos Joyce shot her in a narco compound plaza and called it a clean ending.
He has no idea she is standing in one right now.
He has no idea she survived.
The decision she made in the next thirty seconds would determine whether he ever got the chance to find out.
Does she walk out of that cabin alive and reach Amos Joyce? Whose blood is on the man at the door? Does Scarlett Vance already know where she is?
