I found a wallet in my mailbox last October.

Not mine. Not my wife's. A man's wallet, brown leather, soft as a baseball glove, stuffed between two grocery store flyers and a Penn Power bill.

I'd been retired from the post office for 14 months at that point. I'd carried mail in Erie, Pennsylvania for 31 years, and I'd seen every kind of strange thing a person can put in a mailbox. Live frogs. A wedding ring. Once, a sandwich wrapped in foil with a note that said "for the mailman, God bless." But I'd never found a wallet in my own.

I opened it standing there in my driveway. Driver's license. Robert E. Lassiter. 1962 Buick belonging to him registered at an address on the other side of Presque Isle. $47 in cash. A photo of two little boys in matching church suits, maybe 6 and 8, smiling like they'd just been told a joke.

And a Post-it note stuck to the inside of the bill fold.

In handwriting that looked like a kid wrote it, in pencil: "Grandpa, I will bring this back. I promise. I just need to borrow it for the school thing."

I stood in my driveway holding this wallet for a long time. My hand was shaking, and I told myself it was the cold, because it was the kind of October day in Erie where you can already feel the lake about to turn on you. But it wasn't the cold.

My hand had been shaking for almost 2 years.

My name is Donald. I'm 62 years old. I live on a quiet street in the Glenwood section of Erie, in a brick split-level my wife Caroline and I bought in 1987 for $68,400. We raised our daughter Megan in that house. Megan is 34 now, married to a man named Travis, and they live in Pittsburgh, and they have one little girl named Hazel who turned 4 in August.

Hazel is the entire reason I'm writing any of this down.

I worked the same mail route for 22 of my 31 years. They tried to move me twice and I fought them both times because I knew every porch on that route, every dog, every storm door that stuck in the winter. I knew which old ladies wanted you to wave through the window and which ones didn't. I knew which houses had a kid in the Army and a flag in the window and how to leave the magazines on top so they'd stay dry.

I was good at my job.

What nobody tells you about carrying mail in Erie for 31 years is what it does to your hands.

Sleet in November. Ice on metal mailbox doors in January. That wet, heavy, lake-effect snow that soaks through gloves in 10 minutes. The way you pinch a bundle of mail between your thumb and your first two fingers, hundreds of times a day, for three decades. The way you grip a steering wheel for the parts of the route where you drive. The way you carry your bag on one shoulder, then the other, then the first one again.

My hands started bothering me around 2009. I was 47. I figured it was overuse. I bought better gloves. I started icing my hands after my shift. I took Aleve like it was Tic Tacs.

By 2014, I couldn't open a pickle jar. Caroline started opening them for me without saying anything, which somehow felt worse than if she'd made a joke about it.

By 2019, I'd developed what the VA doctor called "early occupational osteoarthritis" in both hands, particularly the knuckles of my right thumb and first two fingers. He looked at my x-rays for about 90 seconds and shrugged.

"It's the job," he said. "And it's age. It'll get worse. Take Tylenol. Try not to grip things too hard."

That was it.

I retired in August 2023. I thought retirement would help. No more bundles, no more cold mailbox doors, no more 6 hours a day of pinching and gripping. I thought my hands would rest and slowly come back.

They got worse.

There's a thing nobody warns you about with hand pain. It's not the pain. It's the way it follows you into every quiet moment of your day. Pouring coffee. Buttoning a shirt. Holding a fork. Turning a doorknob. Tying your shoes. Every single one of those things became a small negotiation, a calculation, a private little defeat.

I started wearing slip-on shoes. I bought button-up shirts with snaps instead. I switched from a regular toothbrush to one of those big rubber-handled ones for kids with disabilities. I started drinking my coffee out of a mug with a fat handle.

Caroline noticed everything and said nothing. That's the kind of woman she is.

The wallet showed up on October 17, 2024.

I sat at my kitchen table that afternoon with that wallet open in front of me and I tried to call the number on the back of Robert Lassiter's library card. Wrong number. I tried Information. No listing. I drove out to the address on his license, all the way past Presque Isle, and the house was for sale, empty, with weeds in the gravel driveway.

I came home and put the wallet on the kitchen counter and stared at it for an hour.

The next morning I walked the wallet down to the police station on West 38th Street. The desk officer was a kid maybe 26 years old, and he took the wallet from me with both hands, the way you'd take a casserole dish from your grandmother, and he said, "Sir, this is the second wallet anyone has turned in to me this week. The other one was empty. There was almost $50 in this one. I just want you to know that's not nothing."

I drove home and Caroline asked me how it went and I started crying at the kitchen sink, with the water still running, holding a plate I'd been about to wash.

I cried because in 9 weeks it was going to be Christmas Eve. And every Christmas Eve since Hazel was born, I had sat with her on my lap in the living room and helped her sign her name to the cards we gave Caroline and Megan and Travis. Hazel would hold the pen and I would hold her hand and we would do the H together, then the A, then the Z, then the E, then the L, very slowly, very carefully. It was our thing.

And I knew, standing there at that sink, that I was not going to be able to do it that year. Because my right hand had gotten so bad over the summer that I couldn't sign my own name on a check anymore without my fingers locking up halfway through. Caroline had been writing the checks for 5 months.

I had been hiding it from Megan. I had been hiding it from Hazel. I had been hiding it from myself.

That night I went into my workshop in the garage, where I keep all of my dad's old tools that I inherited when he passed in 2008, and I sat on the workbench stool and I looked at his hands' worth of wrenches and chisels and hand planes, and I felt, for the first time since I'd retired, like an old man.

Not a 62 year old man. An old man. The kind my dad turned into in his last few years, the kind who watches his hands betray him in slow motion and pretends not to notice.

I sat in that workshop until close to 1 in the morning. Caroline finally came out in her bathrobe and she didn't say anything, she just sat down on the other stool and put her hand on my back, and we sat like that for a while.

The thing that changed everything didn't change for another 11 days.

His name is Walter Krzyzewski. He was on my route from 1998 to 2012, in the green house with the white shutters on Wagner Avenue. He'd been a foreman at Erie Forge for 41 years, and his hands looked like they'd been carved out of a fence post. He'd come out to the mailbox in November in a t-shirt, no coat, and hand me a coffee he'd made me on his percolator, in a Steelers mug, and we'd stand there for 4 or 5 minutes talking about the Pirates or the Bills or whatever his wife Joanne was making for dinner.

I ran into Walter at Wegmans on October 28th. He was in the produce section, holding two avocados, turning them over in his hands and squeezing them gently. I almost didn't recognize him because the man I remembered moved like every joint in his body had been welded.

He turned and saw me and yelled my name across three aisles.

"Donny! Donald! Come here, get over here, I haven't seen you in a thousand years!"

I walked over and he grabbed both my hands in his and shook them, hard, like a man who was glad to see me. I felt my right thumb knuckle pop and I winced before I could stop myself.

He looked at me.

"Aw hell, Donny. Your hands."

I tried to wave it off. I told him it was the job, the years, you know how it is.

He looked at me for a long second and then he said, "Step over here a minute. By the lemons. I want to tell you something."

I followed him to the lemons.

"You remember how I was when you used to come up the porch?"

I remembered. He used to need a full 8 seconds to get his hand around the door handle. I remembered him telling me once that he couldn't grip a fork at dinner anymore and Joanne had to cut his meat.

"My hands were finished," he said. "Finished, Donny. I couldn't button a shirt. I couldn't shake a hand without it hurting for an hour after. I'd been to three doctors and they all told me the same thing. It's the job. It's the age. It's the years. Take ibuprofen, try to live with it, see you in a year."

He held up his hands and made fists, then opened them, then made fists again.

"I'm 74 years old. I just squeezed two avocados to check if they were ripe. Did you see me do that?"

I had seen him do that.

"My daughter in law sent me something," he said. "Last winter. She'd been reading something. Some research her sister had been into. About a fruit they use in India, some old plant from over there, and what it does inside your joints. Not the pain part. The deeper part."

I'm going to be honest with you. The minute he said the word "fruit" I felt myself shut down. Because I'm 62 years old, I've worked for the federal government for three decades, I've raised a daughter and now I have a granddaughter, and I do not have time for berry juice nonsense from somebody's daughter in law.

But it was Walter. And Walter wasn't selling me anything. He was holding two avocados in his hands at Wegmans and telling me what had happened to his.

"Just hear me out for a minute," he said. "Because I know what your face is doing right now. I had the same face when Marcy told me about it. I told her to stop trying to sell her father in law on hippie crap. But she said, 'Walter, just read it. Just read what's actually happening inside a joint when it stops working. Then decide.'"

So I let him talk.

What Walter explained to me in that grocery store, leaning on the lemon display, was something nobody at the VA had ever bothered to explain to me. And I'm going to do my best to tell it to you the way he told me, because it's the part of this story that matters.

He said that when a joint hurts, what most people think is happening is that the cartilage is worn out and the bones are grinding and that's the pain. And that's part of it. But it's not the whole story. The bigger story, he said, was what was going on with the soft tissue around the joint, and inside the joint, in the fluid itself.

He said there's a kind of slow, low-grade fire that gets going in the tissue around aging joints. Not the kind of fire that flares up and goes away, like a sprain. The kind that just smolders, day after day, year after year, quietly chewing on everything. The lining. The cartilage. The little structures inside the joint that are supposed to keep it slick and easy to move.

He said the fire is fed by something called oxidative stress, which is just a fancy way of saying the cells in those tissues are getting worn out faster than they can repair themselves. Like rust on a bumper. And once the rust gets going, the inflammation gets going, and once the inflammation gets going, the rust accelerates, and the joint just spirals downward year after year.

He said Tylenol does nothing about any of that. Tylenol just blocks the pain signal. The fire keeps burning. The rust keeps spreading.

What he'd been taking for almost a year, he said, was something different. It wasn't a painkiller. It didn't numb anything. What it did, based on what his daughter in law's research said and what he could feel in his own hands, was support the body's own ability to put a damper on that smoldering fire. To help the tissues handle the oxidative stress instead of being chewed up by it. To help the joint do what it was already trying to do for itself.

And he said, very specifically, "Donny, it doesn't fix anything. I'm not telling you it fixed me. I'm telling you that I think it gave my body what it needed to start handling itself a little better. And my hands started feeling like my hands again."

He pulled out his phone right there by the lemons and he showed me the bottle.

It was Alevia. Alevia Amla.

He told me he took 2 capsules a day with his coffee in the morning. He told me Joanne had started taking it too. He told me his brother in law in Buffalo had started taking it. He told me the bottle lasted a month and he kept a backup in the cabinet next to his blood pressure pills.

"And the best part," he said, "the part Marcy made sure I knew. If you take it for the full thing and you don't feel a difference, they give you your money back. 90 days. You just send it back. You don't even have to be nice about it."

I drove home that night with a bag of apples and a pound of ground turkey and I sat in the driveway for about 15 minutes before I went inside.

Then I got out my phone and I looked up what Walter had told me. Not to check if he was lying. Walter doesn't lie. To check if it was real.

What I found was that the fruit he was talking about, amla, also called Indian gooseberry, has been used in their traditional medicine system over there for something like 2,000 years. It's not new. It's not somebody's biohacker invention. It's older than the Roman Empire.

And what I read, in plain language, was that amla is one of the most antioxidant-rich foods anybody has ever measured. It's loaded with vitamin C, but more importantly, it's loaded with a whole family of polyphenols and tannins that the research community has been quietly studying for decades.

The thing those compounds appear to do, which is what Walter was trying to tell me, is help the body manage oxidative stress in tissues. Including the tissues around joints. And researchers have looked at amla's role in supporting healthy inflammatory responses, the kind that smolder in aging joints and connective tissue.

I'm not a doctor. I'm a retired mailman. I'm telling you what I read and what I came to understand.

What amla seems to do, based on what's actually supported in the research, is work with what your body is already doing. It supports the antioxidant systems your cells already have. It's associated with healthier markers of inflammation. It's linked to better outcomes for the kind of slow tissue damage that builds up over decades of use.

It's not a painkiller. It's not blocking a signal. It's giving the tissues themselves a little more of what they need to keep handling their job.

And the more I read, the more one phrase kept coming back to me. The fire and the rust. That's what Walter had said. The slow fire that nobody talks about, smoldering in the joint, feeding the rust that everybody thinks is just "wear and tear." Tylenol doesn't touch that fire. Ibuprofen doesn't touch that fire. None of the things my VA doctor had ever suggested touched that fire.

But here was something that might, at the cellular level, give my body a fighting chance against it.

I ordered Alevia Amla that night, sitting on the edge of my bed in my reading glasses, at 11:47 PM. Caroline was already asleep. I used the same credit card I'd used to pay for my reading glasses 6 years ago. Two clicks. 90 day guarantee. Free shipping.

The bottle showed up 5 days later in my mailbox. Which, given my career, felt like a small private joke between me and the universe.

I started taking it the morning it arrived. 2 capsules with my coffee. Caroline asked what I was doing and I told her the truth. I'd run into Walter Krzyzewski at Wegmans and he'd told me a story and I'd done my homework and I was going to try it.

She didn't laugh at me. She didn't roll her eyes. She said, "Good. I've been worried about you, Donald."

That was the first time in 2 years that anybody in my house had said the word "worried" out loud about my hands. Including me.

The first week, I didn't feel anything. I told myself that was fine. Walter had said it was a slow build, that for him the first real moment of "wait, something's different" came around 3 weeks in. I kept taking it.

The second week, I noticed I'd buttoned my own flannel shirt one morning without thinking about it. I stood in front of the bathroom mirror and looked down at the buttons and tried to remember when I'd last done that. I couldn't remember.

The third week, Caroline asked me to open a jar of pickles. I went to hand it back to her out of habit. She said, "No, Donny, you try first." I twisted the lid. It opened.

She stared at me. I stared at her. Then she walked over and kissed me on the forehead and walked back to the sink.

By the fifth week, I was carrying coffee with my right hand again. Not just a mug. The full carafe. From the kitchen to the dining room. Without setting it down halfway.

By week 7, I was working in my dad's workshop again. I'd avoided it for about a year because the wrenches and the chisels all required a grip my hands couldn't give. I started small. I tightened a hinge on the back gate. I sanded down a rough spot on the kitchen drawer that had been catching for two years. I oiled the squeaky one on the bedroom door that Caroline had asked me about three Christmases ago.

I want to be careful here. I want to tell you what I felt, not what I want you to think I felt.

I did not become a 20 year old man. I'm 62. My hands are still 62 year old hands that worked for 31 winters in Erie, Pennsylvania. There are still mornings where my thumb is stiff and I have to roll it open like an old hinge.

But there is something happening underneath the surface. Something my hands seem to recognize. The fire that Walter described, the slow burning rust, it feels like somebody turned the temperature down.

I sleep through the night. I used to wake up at 3 in the morning with my right hand throbbing, and I'd get up and pace the kitchen and try not to wake Caroline. I haven't done that in almost two months.

I grip the wheel of my truck normally. Not with a death grip to compensate, not with my whole palm wrapped around the bottom of it like a man who's afraid of dropping it. Just normally.

I shook the hand of my new neighbor last Sunday and I didn't flinch when he squeezed.

And on December 24th, on Christmas Eve, Hazel sat on my lap on the couch with a stack of red cards and a black pen, and we did the H together, and the A, and the Z, and the E, and the L.

I did most of it. She steadied my hand.

Caroline watched us from the kitchen doorway with a dish towel in her hand. She didn't say anything. She didn't need to.

When Hazel was done, she looked up at me and she said, "Grandpa, your hand isn't shaky anymore."

I told her she was right. I told her Grandpa was working on it.

She kissed the back of my hand, the one with the worst knuckles, the right thumb, the one that had given out on me at the kitchen sink in October.

And I sat there on the couch and I thought about Robert E. Lassiter, the man whose wallet I'd found in my mailbox 9 weeks earlier, and the little Post-it note inside that wallet in a kid's handwriting. "Grandpa, I will bring this back. I promise."

Some grandsons borrow your wallet for a school project and bring it back.

And some things you thought you'd lost for good, you find a way to bring back yourself.

I'm telling you this because I know somebody is reading it who has been hiding their hands the way I hid mine. Pretending the jar didn't need to be opened. Pretending you didn't want to sign that card. Pretending the workshop wasn't worth going into anymore. Pretending it's just age.

It might be age. It might be the job. It might be the years.

But underneath the age and the job and the years, there's a slow fire that nobody talked to you about, and there might be something quiet and old and from the other side of the world that can help your body do what it's been trying to do for itself the whole time.

Alevia Amla is one bottle a month. 60 capsules. Two a day with breakfast. They make it in the USA. The guarantee is 90 days, full money back, no fight, no argument. If it doesn't do anything for you, you send it back, and you're out the cost of nothing.

I sat in my car in the church parking lot on a Sunday and let my own granddaughter get baptized without me inside.

I could see the doors from where I was parked. White doors. Wreath still up from Easter. My daughter Tanya's van was three spaces down. Everybody I loved was on the other side of those doors, and I was out in the lot with both hands on the wheel because I did not trust them to hold anything smaller than a wheel right then.

My name is Loretta. I am 58 years old. And I want to tell you about the day I missed Nia's baptism, because it was the day I finally stopped lying to myself.

I have cooked in the same school cafeteria in Tupelo, Mississippi for 31 years.

Thirty one years of getting there at 5:30 in the morning. Thirty one years of biscuits and green beans and 400 trays. I fed two generations of this town. Kids I cooked for now bring me their own kids in the checkout line at the Piggly Wiggly, and they still call me Miss Loretta.

I was proud of my body for a long time. It could stand on concrete for eight hours. It could carry a stockpot with soup in it. It could do a double on state testing week and still make it to Wednesday night service.

So when it started to quit on me, I did what I imagine you would do.

I made excuses for it.

It started small. Around 2 or 3 in the afternoon I would get this shaky, sweaty, hollowed out feeling. Like somebody pulled a plug in the bottom of me and everything drained out at once. My hands would tremble. My thoughts would go loose. I would have to sit down on an upturned bucket in the back by the walk in cooler and eat a handful of anything sweet just to feel like myself again.

I told myself it was the heat.

Cafeterias are hot. Everybody knows that.

Then it started coming earlier. And harder. And the sweet snack that used to bring me back would bring me back for maybe an hour, and then drop me even lower than before, like the floor had a floor under it.

I went to the doctor. Of course I did.

He looked at my numbers and used the word "borderline." Said my fasting sugar was creeping. Said to cut back on carbs, lose a little weight, come back in six months. He was kind about it. He was also out of the room in about nine minutes.

So I cut back. Lord, did I cut back.

I gave up the biscuits I made for a living. I gave up sweet tea, which in Mississippi is close to giving up water. I bought the little books that count everything. I walked the track at the middle school on Saturday mornings when my knees let me.

And the crashes kept coming.

That is the part nobody tells you. You do everything right and the thing still has a hold of you. And after a while you start to believe the problem is you. That you are lazy. That you are weak. That you are just one of those people who cannot get it together.

I carried that shame around like a second apron.

Now let me tell you about the parking lot.

Tanya's baby, my Nia, was getting baptized on a Sunday morning in April. Eleven o'clock service. I had a dress pressed and hanging on the bathroom door for a week. I had cooked for the lunch after. Two pans of my macaroni, a ham, greens, the whole thing was sitting in Tanya's kitchen ready to go.

I was so happy that morning. I want you to know that. I was happy walking out my door.

But I had barely eaten, because I was nervous, and because I was still trying to be good about my sugar, and by the time I got to the church and parked, it hit me.

2:40 is a lie. It hit at 10:40 in the morning that day. Way early. Way harder than usual.

The lot tilted. My hands went slick and shaky on the wheel. My heart was going like I had run there. And this fog came down over me so thick I could not have told you my own middle name.

I sat there and I cried.

Not because I was sad about the fog. Because I knew, sitting there, that if I walked into that sanctuary shaking and sweating and gray in the face, I would take the light off my granddaughter. Everybody would turn and look at Miss Loretta and start whispering and fussing, and it would become about me.

So I stayed in the car.

I watched the doors. I heard the organ. I sat in that parking lot and let the most important morning of my baby's little life happen without me in the room, because my own body had become something I was ashamed to bring inside.

That was the bottom.

Tanya came out looking for me after. Found me in the car. She did not fuss. She just opened the door and got in the passenger seat and held my hand and said, "Mama, what is going on with you."

And for the first time, I told her the truth. All of it. The shaking. The fog. The crashes. The shame. How I had done everything the doctor said and it did not work and I had stopped believing there was any answer for me.

She listened. Then she said something that stuck with me.

She said, "Mama, you always say the food is the problem. But you eat less than anybody I know. Maybe the food was never the problem."

I did not know it yet, but she was closer to the truth than any doctor had been in six years.

Now I have to tell you about Casey.

Casey rents the other side of my duplex. She is maybe 34, a pediatric nurse over at the hospital, works these long shifts and comes home in her scrubs looking wrung out. Sweet girl. We wave. She grows tomatoes in five gallon buckets on the little slab out back because that duplex does not have a real yard to speak of.

About a week after the baptism, I was sitting on my back step feeling low, and Casey came out in her scrubs to water those buckets before her shift.

She could tell something was wrong. Nurses can tell. She came and sat on the step next to me and asked, and I do not know why but I told her too. Maybe because she was a stranger to my life. Maybe because she was not going to look at me the way family looks at you.

I told her about the crashes. The shaking. The 2 in the afternoon plug getting pulled.

And Casey did not say "cut back on carbs." She did not use the word "borderline."

She said, "Miss Loretta, can I tell you how somebody explained this to me one time, in a way that finally made sense?"

I said go ahead, baby.

And she said something I have thought about every single day since.

She said, "It is not really about how much sugar you eat. It is about how fast the food you eat turns into sugar in your blood."

She picked up her watering can and set it down, like she was lining up her thoughts.

"Your body has this whole process," she said, "that is supposed to control the speed. Food comes in, and the process breaks it down slow, so the sugar trickles into your blood a little at a time. When that is working right, your body keeps up easy and you never even feel it. You never crash. You never shake."

"But that process is fragile. Years of stress wear it down. Processed food wears it down. Getting older wears it down. A little bit at a time, year after year."

"And when it gets worn down enough, the food you eat stops trickling in slow. It comes in fast. Way faster than your body was ever built to handle. That is the spike. And when your body slams the door on that spike, that is the crash. That is the shaking. That is the plug getting pulled at 2 in the afternoon."

I sat there on that step with my mouth open.

Because I had spent six years believing I was eating wrong. And this young woman was telling me the food was never really the problem. The thing that controls the speed of the food had worn down. And every year I fought it with smaller and smaller plates, the speed problem underneath kept getting worse.

"That is why cutting back only takes you so far," Casey said. "You can eat almost nothing and still crash, because it was never really about the amount. It was about the speed. And nobody is checking the speed."

I want to stop right here and say something to you directly, whoever you are reading this.

If you have been blaming yourself, please hear me.

If you have cut back and cut back and still get that shaky, sweaty, foggy drop in the afternoon. If you have been told you are "borderline" and sent home with a pamphlet. If you have started to believe that you are just weak, or lazy, or one of those people who cannot get it together.

Maybe the food was never the problem. Maybe it is the speed. And maybe nobody ever told you, because a nine minute appointment does not have time to explain speed.

I asked Casey what in the world you even do about a thing like that.

And this is where she told me about the pomegranate.

Now, I about laughed. A fruit? I had cut out fruit trying to fix this. I told her that.

She said, "Not the fruit like you are thinking. And not the juice either, that is all sugar. I mean the extract they pull out of the peel. The part you would throw away."

She told me the peel is where all the good stuff hides. There are these compounds in it called punicalagins. Hard word. She had me say it twice. Punicalagins.

And she said researchers have looked at those punicalagins for the way they help support that exact process, the one that controls how fast the food breaks down into sugar.

"When that process gets a little more support," she said, "the sugar can go back to trickling in slower, more like it did when you were younger. The spikes can ease off. The crashes can soften. Same food. Your body just handles it more like it used to."

She said the peel extract is also one of the strongest antioxidants ever measured in a food. And that matters, she said, because it is that same wear and tear, that same kind of rust from stress and years, that broke the speed process down in the first place. So you are helping the pathway and easing the thing that wore it down. Both at once.

She told me the piece that made me trust her most.

She said most pomegranate products on the shelf are junk. They will stamp "pomegranate" on the bottle and standardize the cheap way, to something called ellagic acid, which does not prove there is any real peel chemistry in there at all. She said the punicalagins from the peel are the part that actually does the work, and most companies skip them because the peel is harder to work with.

"If you ever try one," she said, "make sure it is real peel extract, standardized to punicalagins. Not juice. Not ellagic acid. The peel."

Now let me answer the thing you are thinking, because I thought it too.

"If this was real, my doctor would have told me."

I sat with that one a long time. But here is what I landed on. My doctor had nine minutes. He had a chart with a fasting number on it and a schedule packed full of other people just like me. He is not a bad man. He just does not have time to explain the speed of food to a cafeteria cook, and he gets paid to manage numbers, not to talk about the peel of a fruit. Sometimes the person who finally explains it to you is not in a white coat. Sometimes she is watering tomatoes in scrubs on the step next to yours.

I found the one Casey was talking about. It is called Alevia's Pomegranate.

It is an organic concentrated extract made from the peel, standardized to those punicalagins she kept talking about. Not juice. Not the cheap ellagic acid version. The real thing. It is made right here in the USA. Two little capsules a day. That is the whole job.

I did not expect much. I have been let down before. I ordered it mostly so I could tell Casey I tried.

Let me tell you what actually happened.

The first week, honestly, I did not notice a thing. I want to be straight with you about that, because anybody who promises you week one is selling you something. I just took my two capsules with my coffee and went to work.

Somewhere in the second week, something was different, and it took me a minute to even name it.

The 2 in the afternoon plug did not get pulled.

I kept waiting for it. I sat down on my bucket by the cooler out of habit, braced for the drop, and it just did not come the way it always came. It was softer. Like a dimmer switch instead of somebody yanking the cord out of the wall.

By the third week I stopped carrying the little sweet snacks in my apron pocket.

I had carried those things for years. Little emergency candies for when the floor fell out. And I reached for the pocket one afternoon and realized I had not touched them in days.

By about week five, my daughter noticed before I said one word to her.

Tanya came by on a Sunday and I was on my feet in my own kitchen, cooking for the whole family, moving around, talking, laughing. And she stood in the doorway and looked at me a second too long.

She said, "Mama. You are not gray."

I did not even know I had been gray. But she had watched it on me for years, that gray, washed out look I would get by afternoon, and it was gone off my face and she saw it before I did.

I am not going to sit here and tell you my numbers or make it sound like a miracle. It was not a lightning bolt. It was quieter than that. It was a plug that stopped getting pulled. It was a pocket I stopped needing to fill. It was standing in my own kitchen without bracing for the floor to drop.

It was getting to be myself in the afternoon again.

There is a picture on my phone I look at sometimes.

Nia got dedicated again, sort of, at a little family thing this summer at Tanya's house. Nothing churchy, just cake and everybody in the backyard. And there is a picture somebody took of me holding that baby up in the air, both my hands, steady as anything, both of us laughing.

I was not in a parking lot for that one. I was in the middle of it, right where a grandmother belongs.

I keep thinking about all the years I blamed myself. All the smaller plates. All the shame I wore like an apron I could not take off. And nobody, not once, told me it might not be about the amount. That it might be about the speed. That there might be something that helps support the very thing that wore down underneath all of it.

I am not a doctor. Casey is a nurse but she was not being my nurse on that step, she was just being my neighbor. I am a cafeteria cook telling you what happened to me.

But if you are the one sitting in the parking lot. If you are the one who cut back and cut back and still crashes. If you have started to believe the problem is just you.

Please hear me. Maybe it was never you.

Alevia's Pomegranate comes with a 90 day money back guarantee. Try it for up to 90 days, and if it is not for you, send the bottle back and they will refund you. That is the whole risk. A few weeks of two little capsules with your morning coffee, and if your body does not answer the way mine did, you send it back and you are out nothing but the trying.

I only wish somebody had put it on the step next to me six years ago.

I saw the back of my own head in an elevator mirror at St. Luke's in April and I got off on the wrong floor just so I wouldn't have to look at it again.

There was a man in the elevator with me. A visitor, not staff. He was holding a bouquet of grocery store carnations wrapped in plastic and he was reading something on his phone. He didn't see anything.

But I saw everything.

The mirror was one of those long ones that wrap around the corner of the elevator, and I had turned to press 4, and there it was. My whole scalp.

Not a thinning. Not a widening part. My scalp. Pink and shining under the fluorescent light like the crown of a doll that had lost half its hair.

I pressed 2 instead. I got out at admin. I walked to the stairwell and I took the stairs the rest of the way up, and I have taken the stairs at St. Luke's every day since.

My name is Loretta. I'm 56 years old. I've been a hospice case manager in Duluth, Minnesota for 23 years.

I've sat with more dying people than I can count. I've held hands with wives who were about to become widows. I've told grown men that their father had 3 days left, and then told them again the next week when the father was still hanging on.

I know what real suffering looks like.

So when I tell you I stood in a stairwell at my job and cried about my hair, I need you to know I understand how that sounds.

My daughter Karin lives in St. Paul with her husband and two kids. She calls on Sundays. My mother is 82 and still lives in her own house in Superior, Wisconsin, right across the bridge. My sister Marjorie lives up in Ely, about 2 hours north, on the edge of the Boundary Waters. She retired from the Forest Service 3 years ago and I don't see her as much as I want to.

I've been divorced 8 years. His name was Eugene. He works at the port. We were fine and then we weren't and now we're neither.

I share a little townhouse near Lester Park with a rescue cat named Roscoe and a lot of unfinished projects. That's the shape of my life. A schedule, a route, a Sunday call, and the lake.

My hair used to be my thing.

That sounds vain to say out loud but it's true. It was the color my mother's used to be. A dark, warm brown with a natural wave that fell right past my shoulders. My whole life people had touched it in stores. Reached out and lifted it and asked me what I used on it. I used almost nothing. That was the joke.

I stopped noticing when it changed. It happened slow. It happens slow for a lot of women my age and I want to say that out loud because I spent a year thinking I was the only one.

First it was the shower drain. I'd been clearing it every couple weeks for as long as I could remember. Then it was every week. Then it was every 3 days and I stopped counting because I didn't want to know.

Then it was my pillow.

I started finding hairs on my pillow in the morning. Not a hair. Hairs. A little dark scatter of them across the white cotton every single morning. I'd sweep them off with my hand before I made the bed. I'd pretend I hadn't seen them.

Then it was the towel.

I started keeping a black hand towel by the sink because after I brushed my hair the white one looked like I'd been shedding a dog on it.

Then it was the ponytail.

The ponytail I've worn to work my whole adult life started feeling different in my hand. Thinner. Less. Like the elastic wanted to slip off because there wasn't enough there to hold it.

I switched my part from the left to the right because the right side still had some coverage. Then I switched it back a month later because now the right side didn't either. I bought one of those powders you're supposed to shake on your scalp to hide it. It stained the collar of my navy work cardigan and I threw it out in the parking lot at Menards so no one at home would see it in the trash.

I stopped washing my hair as often because every wash meant more loss. I stopped brushing it in front of the mirror because I couldn't watch the strands come out on the bristles.

I started wearing a wide black headband to work.

I told my coworker Denise it was because my ears were cold. It was July.

The thing about hospice work is you learn to notice what people are protecting. A widow who keeps her husband's reading glasses on the kitchen counter for a year. A daughter who won't sit in her father's chair. A man who won't take off his wedding ring even though the finger under it has gone gray.

I know how to see the small things people do to hold onto themselves.

I just couldn't see what I was doing to hold onto me.

My doctor told me it was probably my age. My thyroid was fine, my iron was fine, my hormones were "in the range for a woman your age." She said the words genetic and postmenopausal and shrugged in a way that was supposed to be gentle. She said some women lose their hair as they get older and there wasn't really much to do about it.

That's a hard thing to hear at 56 in a fluorescent room while you're still wearing your work badge.

I tried the shampoo aisle. I tried the pills at Walgreens with the little pink bottle. I tried the biotin gummies my daughter sent me from Target. I tried a scalp serum I ordered at 1 AM after crying in the bathroom that I dropped 42 dollars on and used exactly twice.

Nothing did anything.

By March I had started keeping my hair in a low bun with the bun pulled forward so it would hide the crown of my head from behind. I had cancelled a dentist appointment because I didn't want to lie back in a chair with a bright light overhead where the hygienist could see my part from above. I had asked my daughter to take our Christmas photo from the front instead of the side.

I hadn't told anyone.

Not my sister. Not my daughter. Not my best friend Ellen who I've known since nursing prerequisites at UMD.

I was pretending.

I was 56 years old and I was pretending.

My mother turned 82 on the second Saturday in May. We do the same thing every year. Perkins in Superior, 12:30 PM, the corner booth by the window that looks out at the parking lot. My mother orders the potato pancakes with a side of applesauce and a decaf coffee she barely drinks. My sister drives down from Ely. My daughter drives up from St. Paul with the grandkids if the weather holds.

That year the weather held.

I pulled into the parking lot 10 minutes early. Marjorie's truck was already there. My sister is always 15 minutes early to everything, always has been since we were kids, and I love her for it and it also drives me a little crazy.

I walked in.

She was already at the booth. She stood up when she saw me and I stopped in the middle of the walkway between the tables like someone had pulled the brake on me.

Her hair.

I'm going to try to explain this the way I saw it.

My sister is 63. She has always looked older than me even though she's 7 years my senior. When we were younger it was because she was outside for a living, working trailheads, doing search and rescue in the winter, running a chainsaw for 30 years. Her hands looked like a man's hands. Her face was weathered in the way beautiful things get weathered, and her hair had started to thin at the temples when she was 55, and by the time she retired at 60 she had a short pixie cut that she trimmed herself at her kitchen sink because she said there wasn't enough left up there to bother a stylist about.

I hadn't seen her in person since Thanksgiving.

The woman standing in front of me at Perkins on that Saturday in May had hair to her shoulders.

Not thick like a magazine ad. But there. Present. Filled in through the crown where the light used to shine through when she leaned over her plate. Grown out at the temples where the two little bare patches used to be. Enough of it that she'd pinned one side back with a small tortoise shell clip like she used to wear in the 80s.

I hugged her and I said "your hair" and she laughed and said "yeah, I know, isn't that something."

And I sat down and I didn't taste my food.

I got through lunch. I sang happy birthday. I helped my mother out of the booth and to her car. I told my sister I'd see her back at the house because we were all going over to help mom hang a new porch light.

I drove the 3 miles to my mother's place in a fog.

Marjorie was in the driveway when I pulled up. She was leaning against the tailgate of her truck. She had her hands in the pockets of her jean jacket. She looked at me over the roof of my car and she said "you want to talk about it."

Not a question.

That's my sister.

We sat on the porch swing at our mother's house while my daughter and the grandkids were inside setting up the ladder. I could hear my mother telling Karin where to find the extra bulbs. The lake was 4 blocks away and you could hear a gull sometimes and a boat horn from the harbor.

I told her about the pillow. The towel. The powder. The headband in July. The Christmas photo. The dentist appointment I cancelled.

I told her about the doctor with the shrug.

She said it wasn't happening to her hair anymore.

She said she'd been at it for close to a year and she wanted to tell me and hadn't because she didn't want to sound like every ad she'd ever scrolled past on Facebook. She said the piece that had finally made her try it wasn't a promise about her hair.

It was a study Diane had shown her on her phone about something called oxidative stress.

I want to explain this the way she explained it to me on the porch swing because it made sense in a way nothing else ever had.

Marjorie said think about rust.

She said think about a car that sat in a barn for 20 years. The metal underneath is fine. It's the right metal, same as when it was new. But something in the air, over time, does something to it that nobody planned for. It scales up. It roughens. And the paint on top starts to lift, and the trim starts to weaken, and after long enough the car looks the way it does not because the metal is bad but because the surface has been slowly oxidized.

She said your body does that too. From the inside.

She said the doctors call it oxidative stress and they call the process itself oxidation, and it's the same word. It's rust.

And the tissue that gets rusted first is the tissue with the most delicate blood supply. The small vessels. The capillaries that feed the places that don't get a lot of flow to begin with. The tips of the fingers. The lining of the arteries. The back of the eyes.

The scalp.

She said the follicles that grow your hair are fed by the tiniest little vessels in your body. Smaller than you can imagine. And when the vessels get rusted, the follicles don't get what they need. They don't die exactly. They just get quiet. They shrink. They put out a thinner strand. Then a shorter one. Then nothing at all for a while. And the whole system slows down not because the follicle is broken but because the environment around it has gotten too rusty for it to do its job.

She said all those pills and shampoos and gummies I'd tried had been trying to feed a follicle that couldn't hear them.

Because the mailbox was rusted shut.

I sat there on the porch swing with my hand over my mouth.

She said what she'd been taking was pomegranate.

Week 3: Same. I told myself I would give it the full 90 days because I was not going to be the woman who quit at 3 weeks and then wondered.

Week 4: My daughter called on a Sunday and said "mom, did you get your hair cut" and I laughed because I hadn't been to a stylist in months. I looked at myself in the bathroom mirror after we hung up. Something looked different at my temples. I couldn't say what.

Week 5: The hairs on the pillow were fewer. Not gone. Fewer. I counted them one morning. There were 6. There used to be more than I could count.

Week 6: I took my headband off at work on a Tuesday and I forgot to put it back on and it was 3 in the afternoon before I noticed. Denise didn't say anything. But she looked at me a beat too long over the top of her monitor.

Week 7: My mother called and said "Retta, is your hair growing back."

Week 10: I put it in a ponytail one morning without thinking. And the ponytail felt like a ponytail again. Not a wisp. A ponytail.

I want to tell you that's when it hit me. But it hit me in pieces over the next month.

The powder went in the trash for real this time.

The headband I kept, because it turns out I did like it as an accessory. But not to hide anything.

I made the dentist appointment. I let the hygienist see my part from above and I didn't think about it once.

My daughter took a photo of me on a boat in August with the sun behind me and I sent it to Marjorie without cropping it. Marjorie sent back a photo of her own hair pinned up with the same tortoise shell clip she'd worn at Perkins.

She wrote "same team."

I'm not telling you this because my hair is the point. I'm telling you this because I lost something I didn't know how to talk about, and I got it back, and the getting it back changed more than my hair.

I stopped hiding.

That's the part.

There is something that happens when your body starts giving you back small pieces of what it used to do. You realize how much energy you were spending on the hiding. On the compensating. On the not-mirror-glancing and the not-Christmas-photo and the not-ponytail. And when the reason to hide goes away, all that energy comes back to you. And you don't know what to do with it at first, and then you remember.

If you're a woman my age and something similar has been happening to you, and you have been quietly hiding it the way I was quietly hiding mine, I want to tell you a few things.

There you will be
Sponsored
I always imagined meeting my mate would be the best moment of my life. I was right about it being unforgettable. I was wrong about everything else.
It started, as most disasters in my life do, with me being completely unprepared.
***
The packhouse kitchen smelled like lye soap and yesterday's dinner, and my knees had gone numb on the stone floor twenty minutes ago. I shifted my weight, wrung out the rag, and kept scrubbing.
Five a.m. The kitchen had to be done before the house woke up.
This was my life. Had been since I was twelve, when the Night Shade Pack took me in after the death of my parents. Dad died first, working himself into the ground trying to keep us fed, his body just giving out one Tuesday morning like a light switch flipping off. Mom lasted three more months. The healers called it illness. I called it what it was–she missed him so much she followed him.
I didn't blame her for it. I tried very hard not to blame her for it.
The pack separated me and my twin sister, Lana, a month after the funeral. Standard procedure for orphaned Omegas with no next of kin was being reassigned to work within the ranks. Lana was blonde and blue-eyed and so pleasant to look upon that the Braxton family–Beta rank and filthy rich–took one look at her and decided she had no business being a maid. They took her in as their daughter.
I wasn't so lucky.
That was five years ago and I had scrubbed approximately eighteen thousand square feet of the pack house's floors since then, by my rough estimate. Somewhere around year three, I made a decision. 
I was going to get into Greymoor Academy, and I was going to get out.
And three weeks ago, I received the Lycan Queen's scholarship, against all odds. Burning my fingers with the midnight candle. Dragging my near dead exhausted body after work to the attic to study with less than four hours of sleep daily. It paid off, and even if Alpha Dante Hayes wasn't pleased when he found out I took the exams after he'd expressly told me Omega maids didn't get to dream of grand futures and forbade me from taking the test, he couldn't refuse my summons from Greymoor. It would be a direct disrespect to the Queen.
But what he could do was triple my chores and make it nearly impossible to attend school. 
But clearly, he had underestimated how determined I was to change the trajectory of my life. 
Greymoor Academy was the kind of school that took future Alphas and sharpened them into leaders, future Betas and taught them how to counsel. Gammas, how to enforce. Girls from good bloodlines went there to marry up. Bloodline mattered more than brains within those walls. But if you could graduate at the top of your class, the most powerful packs in the world would come looking for you. Real careers. Real money. A real life completely unlike the one I was enduring. 
That was my plan. Graduate as the top student and change my life.
In twelve hours, I would be eighteen. In twelve hours, one of two things was going to happen. Either I would find my mate and he would be my ticket out of this life or I wouldn't, and Greymoor would be. Either way, everything changed in twelve hours.
The kitchen door swung open.
I didn't look up. Looking up was something you learned not to do as a maid.
Unhurried footsteps crossed the kitchen. The toe of an expensive boot stopped six inches from my hand. The boot glided over and pressed over my fingers, hard. 
I winced, sinking my teeth into my bottom lip as I sat back on my heels.
Cole Hayes, son of Alpha Dante Hayes, and future Alpha of the Night Shade Pack, looked down at me with the perpetual sneer he saved for things he'd found on the bottom of that expensive boot.
He had been doing this since we were children. The bullying, the derogatory comments that started when I was thirteen, stress-eating through my parent's death anniversary and not holding it together very well. Fatso. Ugly. Pig. Oink, oink.
Anorexia came at fifteen. By the time the Head Maid found out what I was doing to myself, the severity of the damage was so great that even three years later, even if I was now perfectly healthy, I still hadn't gotten my monthly cycle and I couldn't shift. 
Cole didn't know that last part. Nobody knew except Lana. In Ashbourne, being wolfless was worse than being a rogue. It didn't matter that I did have a wolf, but just couldn't shift. It all fell under the category of wolfless. If Alpha Hayes found out, my pack membership would be stripped and I would have nothing. Not the packhouse. Not the scholarship. Not even the floor I was currently kneeling on.
It was a secret I guarded with my life. Lana finding out had been as a result of my fifteen year old naive self who still regarded her twin as her best friend crying to her about it. She had mocked me for it.
Well, at least, she didn't tell anyone.
Cole lifted the glass from the counter. "Congratulations on the scholarship, Fatso. Though, I wouldn't get too excited. Your mother was an Omega maid. Her mother was an Omega maid. The misfortune mustn't be as hard to scrub free from your dirty blood as it must be to scrub out these floors."
He lifted his boot off my throbbing fingers and kicked the bucket violently, causing the contents to splash over my skin. "Start over," he said and walked out.
I sat there on the wet floor in the dripping silence of the empty kitchen, water running down my face, and I did not cry. I had made a rule about that years ago. Not in this kitchen, not on this floor, not where any of them could walk back in and see it.
I reached for the rag.
Twelve hours, I told myself.
I started over.
***
Lana was waiting at the packhouse gates under the light drizzle as I rushed out to catch the bus to the Academy.
She leaned against her sleek black Bentley in white heeled boots, a cropped jacket and a short leather skirt. 
Lana had always been stunning. Her blonde hair sat perfectly smooth, the perfect bone structure, the mile-long model legs and baby blues that made boys and girls alike forget themselves. She was perfect, in the ways I could never be.
Regina's theory was that Lana came out first and simply took things we should've shared.
I thought she was probably accurate, considering I looked like a hot mess.
I had sandy brown hair that woke up every morning with a completely different personality, electric blue eyes that Jenny once called too intense to be pretty, which actually makes them better, and a body that I had spent years at war with and was only now beginning to negotiate a peace treaty with.
I understood Lana's need to pretend I didn't exist, but it didn't make it sting any less.
"Happy birthday," she said.
There was a time, during our childhood, when those words from her would have meant something. We used to say them together, pressed against each other in our parents' bed.
"Happy birthday," I replied.
She looked me over. The Greymoor sweatshirt I had on because I couldn't afford anything else. The baggy pants. The bag on my shoulder packed with the six textbooks I'd saved four months to buy. My unruly, frizzy hair.
"You actually got the scholarship," she murmured.
"I did."
Something moved through her expression. It looked like resentment. "I'll be there, too."
I nodded. All of Ashbourne's elite would be there, and Lana Braxton–no longer Lana Adams–was one of the elite.
"Don't approach me at school. I have a position to maintain." Her eyes lingered on my worn out sneakers. "You understand that I can't be associated with a common maid. I can't have your dirt and skunk following me around."
She slunk into the car without waiting for a response, like she couldn't spend one more second being seen with me. And as she sped past, her tires sprayed a fresh wave of muddied water against my clothes.
Maisie
I arrived at school late, soaking wet through my clothes and shivering like a drowned rat. The drizzle had become rain approximately forty five seconds after I left the packhouse, because the universe often liked to shit in my face. 
I missed the bus. I missed orientation. I missed the tour. I walked four blocks in the wrong direction before a janitor took pity on me and pointed me toward the lecture hall, and by the time I found it, the period was nearly over and every single seat was taken. 
"Ah, Ms. Adams," said Professor Halven, peering over wired-rimmed glasses. "Late again, I see. Swept up in yet another hurricane. I don't suppose it's too much to hope that you left that particular habit behind in high school." 
Laughter rang through the hall as my teeth clattered, "S-sorry, M-Mr. Halven."
He ignored me, facing the class once more. "And now, your questions." 
I started for the back, embarrassment flushing my cheeks red as my shoes squeaked loudly. 
More laughter. 
If the ground would be kind enough to open up and swallow me whole.
This was recoverable. The first day was always the worst day, and everyone would forget this by next week. Hopefully.
They wouldn't. Half of this room had known me since high school, and the other half would hear stories by noon. Ashbourne was a Pack town. Everyone knew everyone, which meant everyone knew Maisie Adams: the clumsy Omega maid who walked into walls, tripped over flat surfaces, and had once, memorably, knocked an entire refreshment table into Alpha Dante's son, Cole Hayes, at the harvest festival.
So much for fresh starts.
A hand shot up from the left. Jenny Park, one of my two best friends, waved at the empty seat beside her and I slid into it and exhaled.
"Maisie," she whispered, honey-brown eyes wide. "What happened to you?" 
"What didn't?" I sighed tiredly.
Regina wordlessly pulled her boyfriend, Nick's soccer jacket off his shoulders and draped it over mine. Nick, to his credit, only winked at me.
Regina Braxton was Lana's stepsister. The Braxton family's daughter. She had grown up in the same house as my twin, watched exactly how Lana spoke about me and had once stood up for me during a Pack event when Lana's friends thought it was a good idea to test my resistance to scalding hot tea.
We've been thick as thieves since then.
"Happy birthday, May," she said with a half-giggly smile.
"Is it?" I mumbled sourly, snuggling deeply into the jacket.
My ears perked up as Darby Foreman said loudly enough to carry across the hall, "What actually happens when a mate bond is rejected?"
Professor Halven's stare flattened. "I'm positive that is not a part of the syllabus, Ms. Foreman." 
Laughter echoed in the hall, but Darby wouldn't be deterred. "Just last fall, there was a case of a girl dying in Ashbrook because she got rejected. Many of us turn eighteen this year and would like to know how to avoid that fate. This is a werewolf academy, after all. One lecture on it wouldn't hurt." 
There were many more agreeing nods this time. I found myself leaning forward despite myself.
Professor Halven seemed mildly irritated, but he set down his notes. "Most of you have been told a romantic story. The Moon Goddess selects two wolves and binds their souls." He pauses. "That part is true. What isn't is that it can be broken with a tantrum and three convenient words. I Reject You."
Another round of laughter. But Halven didn't laugh.
"When one wolf rejects another, the words do not sever the bond." His gaze swept across us, heavily. "They wound it. The wolf experiences rejection as spiritual mutilation. The Goddess forged that tie. When one side attempts to tear away from it, the backlash is, in the same way, divine."
"But I read that accepting the rejection ends it," a boy said.
Professor Halvern's smile was thin. "Nonsensical fiction."
Murmurs broke across the hall.
"The bond remains. The rejected wolf suffers most. Physically, emotionally, and the result is always catastrophic, with one of two endings. Death. Or insanity."
Another girl, Tanya, raised her hand. "Then how does one completely sever the bond before the pain kills them?" 
"You cannot. There is only one authority on this continent who can dissolve the Goddess-ordained bond."
We all knew who.
The Lycan Queen.
"A living descendant of the Goddess's first bloodline, the Queen's abilities stretches far beyond our imagination, and one of many is being able to override the tether." He gestured with flourish. "But she does not grant dissolution lightly. There must be a petition from both parties. A hearing. Only if the reason stands strong enough, will she break the bond. But even that may take weeks. Enough time to shatter a person completely." 
He stepped off the podium. "Which is why the law against rejection was passed by the first king. It remains frowned upon by society and punishable by banishment." His grey eyes refocused on Claire. "Now, if that would be all, class."
I sat very still for a moment, the weight of it settling somewhere uncomfortable in my chest.
Death. Or insanity.
I shivered.
***
The hallways were packed with students, first years and seniors alike. Fliers were going about for invitations to the mixer next week. I couldn't go, not with all of the chores I had to tend.
"Of course, they go here," Regina sighed wistfully. "I would pay a hefty sum to see what's packed underneath. For observational purposes, of course."
Jenny snorted, but her voice was equally dreamy. "Pretty sure you have to be one of them to even get noticed. I would right about sell my left kidney to mate with one of them."
I turned to the sight of four Lycans males crossing the hallway with an air of superiority that even the most powerful Alpha in Ashbourne couldn't duplicate if he wanted to.
The world simply bent the rules for and around them. The crowd of first years and seniors alike parted, unbidden, and stared unabashedly. You either wanted to fuck them or be them.
They were made different. Some said it was because they were the Moon Goddess's direct descendants. Others were convinced they were simply gods descended from above to preside over us.
The latter might seem a little obnoxious until you discovered they were all, indeed, royals. Nobility. But that wasn't all. You only had to look at them to understand.
They were so beautiful, it was unfair. They were like Greek gods wading through a room of plain mortals like us. Over six foot five inches tall. Tanned, flawless skins, thick ridges of proportioned muscles that made you think of all the things you could eat off their bodies. 
Eyes that glowed like the sun. An aura that crushed and screamed danger. You could never mistake a Lycan for a Werewolf. The difference was too vast to compare and bordered on rude. And it didn't make it any easier that they were better at everything.
Hotter. Faster. Stronger. Larger. More lethal. Where Werewolves were fierce, Lycans were deadly. They had the tendency to kill first and ask later. So, naturally, no one fucked with or talked to them. Not that they ever mingled with our kind.
In the whole world, there were fewer than twenty Lycans left. They were a dying-out race and that made them that much more special and highly sought after. Hence, having four of them in a small town like Ashbourne was like experiencing comets fall from the skies once in a million years. 
Even worse, they were all enrolled in the Academy. I thought it was strange, but everyone else only seemed concerned with drooling.
I looked away.
I knew better than to swoon like every other female. I was an Omega. Lycans were only attracted to strength, intelligence, and beauty. They rarely glanced at us, and in the event that they did, it was always an Alpha blooded female.
Never someone like me.
I shuddered again, the cold seeping deeper into my bones. "If we don't get somewhere warm, I just might turn into a fucking popsicle–" 
My wolf who had been quietly humming since I woke up suddenly surged forward with a force that knocked the breath out of me.
I stopped walking.
Jenny said something. I didn't hear it.
The scent hit me a half-second later.
Something sweet and deep and completely, devastatingly right. It bypassed every rational thought I had and went straight to the part of me that was a wolf before it was anything else. My body turned toward it before my brain authorised the movement.
And I walked directly into a wall.
The impact sent me straight to the marble floor. My bag split, books flying everywhere, cellphone skidding somewhere under someone's boot. I sat there blinking for a full, stupid second, hair in my face, hands flat on cold stone.
Then I looked up.
Dark green eyes.
Almost black, actually. The kind of green that existed at the bottom of very deep water. Blonde hair was trimmed shorter on the sides, and the longer pieces on top were messy in that, "I just rolled out of bed" kind of way. A jaw that had a cleft in it. Dark denim jeans that hugged powerful thighs. A black t-shirt that showed off thick muscular arms and matching dark boots.
Cole Hayes looked down at me.
He was standing with Tucker Reeves and Reid Calloway, the Beta's and Gamma's son, and Lana was at his side, his fingers stroking her bare stomach. 
They'd been together since they were fourteen.
Everyone knew they'd end up mated and create beautiful, blonde, cruel babies together. It was inevitable. The Braxtons were the most powerful family after the Hayes and had been pushing for Regina to be Luna, but Regina was a wild, uncontrollable card and would never be told what to do with her life.
Lana, however, was ambitious and had been working to be Luna since before she ever understood what the word meant. 
But Cole's nostrils flared. He blinked, as though confused.
He took one step toward me. One step away from Lana.
And the scent slammed into me again, so strong this time that my wolf threw herself at the surface of my mind with an urgency that was almost painful.
Goddess, please, not him. Anyone in the world who has ever existed or will exist. Not him.
My wolf didn't care that I hated Cole Hayes vehemently, or that he was the reason I hid behind baggy clothes. That he had made me hate my body so much, I stopped looking in the mirror and nearly killed myself.
She thought he was ours.
Cole crouched in front of me.
Realization crashed over Lana's face, panic and fear leaping into her eyes as he reached out, breathing hard, and touched my cheek, eyes heavy-lidded with such corrosive lust and hunger that I began trembling.
But at that moment, I could not control my synapses. My body wanted him like it needed warmth. I wanted things that I didn't yet know existed. I wanted to stake my claim on him. I wanted to bury my nose in his neck and run my tongue up and down his pulse. To arch my neck and let him mark me. 
His soft touch turned cruel, something like claws began digging into my chin. "Maisie Adams," he said softly. His gaze ran down my body. "The goddess must have lost her mind if she thought we belonged together. I'd sooner jam my dick through a grinder than stick it in your fat ass."
The hall quietened. He wasn't exactly being discreet.
My wolf whined petulantly, wanting me to throw myself into his arms, but his words had dropped like a cold bucket of water onto my head. I scrambled back, chest heaving as I fought the pull. 
Goddess, but it felt like I would die if he didn't touch me.
Someone grabbed my shoulder–Regina or Jenny maybe, pulling me up. "Stay away from her."
Stay away? How? My world was reconstructing around him. I could smell him and feel his heart beat pulsing with mine. My heart, my very body was aching for him.
But Cole smirked, rising to his feet as if completely unaffected. "By the next full moon, I will be the Alpha of the Night Shade Pack. I have no use for a maid, a weakling Omega like you who can't even shift."
My head went very quiet and my gaze swung to Lana's, stinging with betrayal.
She had told him.
And now, the entire hall knew it too. It rippled across the space in waves, whispers, gasps and mocking laughter. They called me a freak. Wolfless. A runt.
"The Pack needs a stronger Luna." He pulled Lana closer to him. "Lana Braxton is much more deserving of being my mate and would make a better Luna than you ever could."
I suddenly realized what was happening.
My heart began to slam against my ribcage like a battle ram.
He was going to reject me.
I suddenly recalled Professor Halven's words.
Goddess, I'm going to die. And if I don't, I might go insane. And in the event that I somehow survived both, I would be faced with the stigma of being rejected for the rest of my life.
Because no he-wolf wanted to be stuck with another man's reject.
I tried to speak, but I didn't get a chance.
"I, Cole Hayes, future Alpha of the Night Shade pack, reject you, Maisie Adams, as my mate and future Luna of my pack," he declared coldly.
Agony split through my chest like a blade of fire. I screamed, loud, raw and guttural. My wolf howled in pain. It was like nothing I'd ever heard before and it split my head in two as she wept for him. It tore into me like a knife being plunged deep to cut my heart right out, piece by piece.
They said I howled like a banshee, cried like a child, threw up and collapsed like a ragged doll in my own vomit.
All I knew was pain.

The Blood Pressure Journal

I almost didn't go to my granddaughter's piano recital.

She's 7 years old. Her name is Amaya. She has been practicing the same Beethoven piece for 4 months on the upright in her mother's living room, the one with the sticky middle C, and she was going to play it in front of 60 people in the auditorium at Springhill Elementary on a Thursday night in March, and her grandmother almost stayed home.

I sat in my bedroom in my best blue dress with my purse on my lap and I told my husband Cornell to go on without me. He turned around in the doorway with his tie half knotted and he said, "Loretta. What are you doing."

I said, "My pressure is up. I can feel it. I don't want to make a scene."

He looked at me for a long time. Then he said, "Loretta. She's going to look for you in that crowd."

And I sat on the edge of the bed and I cried.

Because I was 63 years old and I was scared to sit in an auditorium full of people for 90 minutes because I was afraid my body was going to embarrass me in front of my own grandbaby.

My name is Loretta. I live in Mobile, Alabama, off Spring Hill Avenue, in the same little brick house Cornell and I bought in 1991 when our oldest was 4. I worked 31 years as a kindergarten teacher in the Mobile County school system. I retired in 2022. I have three children and 6 grandchildren and the youngest of them, Amaya, is the one who calls me on FaceTime every Sunday after church to show me her piano hands.

And on a Thursday night in March 2024, I almost missed her first recital because my blood pressure had been climbing for two years and the pills my doctor gave me weren't holding it down anymore.

Let me back up.

I was diagnosed with high blood pressure when I was 54. Doctor Whitfield at the clinic on Airport Boulevard, the one with the parking lot you can never find a spot in, he took my pressure twice on a Tuesday morning and he said, "Mrs. Loretta, your top number is 162. We need to put you on something."

I didn't argue. My mama died of a stroke at 71. My daddy had two heart attacks before he was 65. I knew what runs in our family. I took the lisinopril and I started walking three mornings a week and I cut back on the salt and I thought I was doing what I was supposed to do.

For a few years, it held. Numbers came down. Not great, but better. The doctor was happy.

Then about two years ago, somewhere around 61, it started creeping back. He upped the lisinopril. Added a water pill. The numbers came down for a minute and then crept back. He added a third medication, a calcium channel blocker, and the side effects started. My ankles swelled up like sausages by 4 in the afternoon. My head felt thick. I started getting dizzy when I stood up from the couch.

I'd go for my checkups and the cuff would beep and Cornell would be sitting in the chair across from me and I'd watch his face change when the numbers came up on the little screen. 156 over 94. 162 over 98. 168 over 101.

Doctor Whitfield would shake his head and adjust the prescription and say, "Loretta, sometimes the body just doesn't want to cooperate. We'll keep working on it."

Keep working on it. Like my pressure was a stubborn child in his classroom.

But the thing nobody talks about with blood pressure is what it does to you between the appointments. Not the numbers. The fear.

I started feeling it in my chest at random times. A heaviness. A pressure behind my eyes when I bent down to tie my shoes. I'd be at the grocery store reaching for a can of crushed tomatoes on the top shelf and a wave of something would come over me and I'd have to grab the cart handle and wait for it to pass.

I stopped going to the Thursday night Bible study at Mount Olive because the church is on the third floor of the family life center and the elevator is slow and I started worrying about getting stuck in it.

I stopped going to my sister Vernita's apartment because it's two flights up and by the time I got to her door I was breathing like I'd run a mile.

I started saying no to things. Not big things, at first. Just little things. The Saturday cookout at my brother in law's. The hair appointment with Miss Yvonne who I'd been seeing since 1998. My friend Patrice's birthday dinner at Wintzell's downtown.

I told everyone I was just tired. Cornell knew. He knew because he'd come home and find me sitting in the recliner in the dark with the TV off, just sitting there, listening to my own heart.

And then Amaya's recital came up.

My daughter Tanya called me three weeks ahead to remind me. She'd already called me two times before that. She knew, the way daughters know, that I'd been pulling back. She said, "Mama. Amaya is asking when you're coming. She wants to know what color dress you're wearing so she can match her ribbon."

I told her I'd be there. I bought the blue dress at Dillard's that weekend. I had my hair done on the Wednesday before. I planned it out the way you plan out a trip to a foreign country, every step, every parking lot, every bathroom, every chair.
