There you will be
Sponsored
I always imagined meeting my mate would be the best moment of my life. I was right about it being unforgettable. I was wrong about everything else.
It started, as most disasters in my life do, with me being completely unprepared.
***
The packhouse kitchen smelled like lye soap and yesterday's dinner, and my knees had gone numb on the stone floor twenty minutes ago. I shifted my weight, wrung out the rag, and kept scrubbing.
Five a.m. The kitchen had to be done before the house woke up.
This was my life. Had been since I was twelve, when the Night Shade Pack took me in after the death of my parents. Dad died first, working himself into the ground trying to keep us fed, his body just giving out one Tuesday morning like a light switch flipping off. Mom lasted three more months. The healers called it illness. I called it what it was–she missed him so much she followed him.
I didn't blame her for it. I tried very hard not to blame her for it.
The pack separated me and my twin sister, Lana, a month after the funeral. Standard procedure for orphaned Omegas with no next of kin was being reassigned to work within the ranks. Lana was blonde and blue-eyed and so pleasant to look upon that the Braxton family–Beta rank and filthy rich–took one look at her and decided she had no business being a maid. They took her in as their daughter.
I wasn't so lucky.
That was five years ago and I had scrubbed approximately eighteen thousand square feet of the pack house's floors since then, by my rough estimate. Somewhere around year three, I made a decision. 
I was going to get into Greymoor Academy, and I was going to get out.
And three weeks ago, I received the Lycan Queen's scholarship, against all odds. Burning my fingers with the midnight candle. Dragging my near dead exhausted body after work to the attic to study with less than four hours of sleep daily. It paid off, and even if Alpha Dante Hayes wasn't pleased when he found out I took the exams after he'd expressly told me Omega maids didn't get to dream of grand futures and forbade me from taking the test, he couldn't refuse my summons from Greymoor. It would be a direct disrespect to the Queen.
But what he could do was triple my chores and make it nearly impossible to attend school. 
But clearly, he had underestimated how determined I was to change the trajectory of my life. 
Greymoor Academy was the kind of school that took future Alphas and sharpened them into leaders, future Betas and taught them how to counsel. Gammas, how to enforce. Girls from good bloodlines went there to marry up. Bloodline mattered more than brains within those walls. But if you could graduate at the top of your class, the most powerful packs in the world would come looking for you. Real careers. Real money. A real life completely unlike the one I was enduring. 
That was my plan. Graduate as the top student and change my life.
In twelve hours, I would be eighteen. In twelve hours, one of two things was going to happen. Either I would find my mate and he would be my ticket out of this life or I wouldn't, and Greymoor would be. Either way, everything changed in twelve hours.
The kitchen door swung open.
I didn't look up. Looking up was something you learned not to do as a maid.
Unhurried footsteps crossed the kitchen. The toe of an expensive boot stopped six inches from my hand. The boot glided over and pressed over my fingers, hard. 
I winced, sinking my teeth into my bottom lip as I sat back on my heels.
Cole Hayes, son of Alpha Dante Hayes, and future Alpha of the Night Shade Pack, looked down at me with the perpetual sneer he saved for things he'd found on the bottom of that expensive boot.
He had been doing this since we were children. The bullying, the derogatory comments that started when I was thirteen, stress-eating through my parent's death anniversary and not holding it together very well. Fatso. Ugly. Pig. Oink, oink.
Anorexia came at fifteen. By the time the Head Maid found out what I was doing to myself, the severity of the damage was so great that even three years later, even if I was now perfectly healthy, I still hadn't gotten my monthly cycle and I couldn't shift. 
Cole didn't know that last part. Nobody knew except Lana. In Ashbourne, being wolfless was worse than being a rogue. It didn't matter that I did have a wolf, but just couldn't shift. It all fell under the category of wolfless. If Alpha Hayes found out, my pack membership would be stripped and I would have nothing. Not the packhouse. Not the scholarship. Not even the floor I was currently kneeling on.
It was a secret I guarded with my life. Lana finding out had been as a result of my fifteen year old naive self who still regarded her twin as her best friend crying to her about it. She had mocked me for it.
Well, at least, she didn't tell anyone.
Cole lifted the glass from the counter. "Congratulations on the scholarship, Fatso. Though, I wouldn't get too excited. Your mother was an Omega maid. Her mother was an Omega maid. The misfortune mustn't be as hard to scrub free from your dirty blood as it must be to scrub out these floors."
He lifted his boot off my throbbing fingers and kicked the bucket violently, causing the contents to splash over my skin. "Start over," he said and walked out.
I sat there on the wet floor in the dripping silence of the empty kitchen, water running down my face, and I did not cry. I had made a rule about that years ago. Not in this kitchen, not on this floor, not where any of them could walk back in and see it.
I reached for the rag.
Twelve hours, I told myself.
I started over.
***
Lana was waiting at the packhouse gates under the light drizzle as I rushed out to catch the bus to the Academy.
She leaned against her sleek black Bentley in white heeled boots, a cropped jacket and a short leather skirt. 
Lana had always been stunning. Her blonde hair sat perfectly smooth, the perfect bone structure, the mile-long model legs and baby blues that made boys and girls alike forget themselves. She was perfect, in the ways I could never be.
Regina's theory was that Lana came out first and simply took things we should've shared.
I thought she was probably accurate, considering I looked like a hot mess.
I had sandy brown hair that woke up every morning with a completely different personality, electric blue eyes that Jenny once called too intense to be pretty, which actually makes them better, and a body that I had spent years at war with and was only now beginning to negotiate a peace treaty with.
I understood Lana's need to pretend I didn't exist, but it didn't make it sting any less.
"Happy birthday," she said.
There was a time, during our childhood, when those words from her would have meant something. We used to say them together, pressed against each other in our parents' bed.
"Happy birthday," I replied.
She looked me over. The Greymoor sweatshirt I had on because I couldn't afford anything else. The baggy pants. The bag on my shoulder packed with the six textbooks I'd saved four months to buy. My unruly, frizzy hair.
"You actually got the scholarship," she murmured.
"I did."
Something moved through her expression. It looked like resentment. "I'll be there, too."
I nodded. All of Ashbourne's elite would be there, and Lana Braxton–no longer Lana Adams–was one of the elite.
"Don't approach me at school. I have a position to maintain." Her eyes lingered on my worn out sneakers. "You understand that I can't be associated with a common maid. I can't have your dirt and skunk following me around."
She slunk into the car without waiting for a response, like she couldn't spend one more second being seen with me. And as she sped past, her tires sprayed a fresh wave of muddied water against my clothes.
Maisie
I arrived at school late, soaking wet through my clothes and shivering like a drowned rat. The drizzle had become rain approximately forty five seconds after I left the packhouse, because the universe often liked to shit in my face. 
I missed the bus. I missed orientation. I missed the tour. I walked four blocks in the wrong direction before a janitor took pity on me and pointed me toward the lecture hall, and by the time I found it, the period was nearly over and every single seat was taken. 
"Ah, Ms. Adams," said Professor Halven, peering over wired-rimmed glasses. "Late again, I see. Swept up in yet another hurricane. I don't suppose it's too much to hope that you left that particular habit behind in high school." 
Laughter rang through the hall as my teeth clattered, "S-sorry, M-Mr. Halven."
He ignored me, facing the class once more. "And now, your questions." 
I started for the back, embarrassment flushing my cheeks red as my shoes squeaked loudly. 
More laughter. 
If the ground would be kind enough to open up and swallow me whole.
This was recoverable. The first day was always the worst day, and everyone would forget this by next week. Hopefully.
They wouldn't. Half of this room had known me since high school, and the other half would hear stories by noon. Ashbourne was a Pack town. Everyone knew everyone, which meant everyone knew Maisie Adams: the clumsy Omega maid who walked into walls, tripped over flat surfaces, and had once, memorably, knocked an entire refreshment table into Alpha Dante's son, Cole Hayes, at the harvest festival.
So much for fresh starts.
A hand shot up from the left. Jenny Park, one of my two best friends, waved at the empty seat beside her and I slid into it and exhaled.
"Maisie," she whispered, honey-brown eyes wide. "What happened to you?" 
"What didn't?" I sighed tiredly.
Regina wordlessly pulled her boyfriend, Nick's soccer jacket off his shoulders and draped it over mine. Nick, to his credit, only winked at me.
Regina Braxton was Lana's stepsister. The Braxton family's daughter. She had grown up in the same house as my twin, watched exactly how Lana spoke about me and had once stood up for me during a Pack event when Lana's friends thought it was a good idea to test my resistance to scalding hot tea.
We've been thick as thieves since then.
"Happy birthday, May," she said with a half-giggly smile.
"Is it?" I mumbled sourly, snuggling deeply into the jacket.
My ears perked up as Darby Foreman said loudly enough to carry across the hall, "What actually happens when a mate bond is rejected?"
Professor Halven's stare flattened. "I'm positive that is not a part of the syllabus, Ms. Foreman." 
Laughter echoed in the hall, but Darby wouldn't be deterred. "Just last fall, there was a case of a girl dying in Ashbrook because she got rejected. Many of us turn eighteen this year and would like to know how to avoid that fate. This is a werewolf academy, after all. One lecture on it wouldn't hurt." 
There were many more agreeing nods this time. I found myself leaning forward despite myself.
Professor Halven seemed mildly irritated, but he set down his notes. "Most of you have been told a romantic story. The Moon Goddess selects two wolves and binds their souls." He pauses. "That part is true. What isn't is that it can be broken with a tantrum and three convenient words. I Reject You."
Another round of laughter. But Halven didn't laugh.
"When one wolf rejects another, the words do not sever the bond." His gaze swept across us, heavily. "They wound it. The wolf experiences rejection as spiritual mutilation. The Goddess forged that tie. When one side attempts to tear away from it, the backlash is, in the same way, divine."
"But I read that accepting the rejection ends it," a boy said.
Professor Halvern's smile was thin. "Nonsensical fiction."
Murmurs broke across the hall.
"The bond remains. The rejected wolf suffers most. Physically, emotionally, and the result is always catastrophic, with one of two endings. Death. Or insanity."
Another girl, Tanya, raised her hand. "Then how does one completely sever the bond before the pain kills them?" 
"You cannot. There is only one authority on this continent who can dissolve the Goddess-ordained bond."
We all knew who.
The Lycan Queen.
"A living descendant of the Goddess's first bloodline, the Queen's abilities stretches far beyond our imagination, and one of many is being able to override the tether." He gestured with flourish. "But she does not grant dissolution lightly. There must be a petition from both parties. A hearing. Only if the reason stands strong enough, will she break the bond. But even that may take weeks. Enough time to shatter a person completely." 
He stepped off the podium. "Which is why the law against rejection was passed by the first king. It remains frowned upon by society and punishable by banishment." His grey eyes refocused on Claire. "Now, if that would be all, class."
I sat very still for a moment, the weight of it settling somewhere uncomfortable in my chest.
Death. Or insanity.
I shivered.
***
The hallways were packed with students, first years and seniors alike. Fliers were going about for invitations to the mixer next week. I couldn't go, not with all of the chores I had to tend.
"Of course, they go here," Regina sighed wistfully. "I would pay a hefty sum to see what's packed underneath. For observational purposes, of course."
Jenny snorted, but her voice was equally dreamy. "Pretty sure you have to be one of them to even get noticed. I would right about sell my left kidney to mate with one of them."
I turned to the sight of four Lycans males crossing the hallway with an air of superiority that even the most powerful Alpha in Ashbourne couldn't duplicate if he wanted to.
The world simply bent the rules for and around them. The crowd of first years and seniors alike parted, unbidden, and stared unabashedly. You either wanted to fuck them or be them.
They were made different. Some said it was because they were the Moon Goddess's direct descendants. Others were convinced they were simply gods descended from above to preside over us.
The latter might seem a little obnoxious until you discovered they were all, indeed, royals. Nobility. But that wasn't all. You only had to look at them to understand.
They were so beautiful, it was unfair. They were like Greek gods wading through a room of plain mortals like us. Over six foot five inches tall. Tanned, flawless skins, thick ridges of proportioned muscles that made you think of all the things you could eat off their bodies. 
Eyes that glowed like the sun. An aura that crushed and screamed danger. You could never mistake a Lycan for a Werewolf. The difference was too vast to compare and bordered on rude. And it didn't make it any easier that they were better at everything.
Hotter. Faster. Stronger. Larger. More lethal. Where Werewolves were fierce, Lycans were deadly. They had the tendency to kill first and ask later. So, naturally, no one fucked with or talked to them. Not that they ever mingled with our kind.
In the whole world, there were fewer than twenty Lycans left. They were a dying-out race and that made them that much more special and highly sought after. Hence, having four of them in a small town like Ashbourne was like experiencing comets fall from the skies once in a million years. 
Even worse, they were all enrolled in the Academy. I thought it was strange, but everyone else only seemed concerned with drooling.
I looked away.
I knew better than to swoon like every other female. I was an Omega. Lycans were only attracted to strength, intelligence, and beauty. They rarely glanced at us, and in the event that they did, it was always an Alpha blooded female.
Never someone like me.
I shuddered again, the cold seeping deeper into my bones. "If we don't get somewhere warm, I just might turn into a fucking popsicle–" 
My wolf who had been quietly humming since I woke up suddenly surged forward with a force that knocked the breath out of me.
I stopped walking.
Jenny said something. I didn't hear it.
The scent hit me a half-second later.
Something sweet and deep and completely, devastatingly right. It bypassed every rational thought I had and went straight to the part of me that was a wolf before it was anything else. My body turned toward it before my brain authorised the movement.
And I walked directly into a wall.
The impact sent me straight to the marble floor. My bag split, books flying everywhere, cellphone skidding somewhere under someone's boot. I sat there blinking for a full, stupid second, hair in my face, hands flat on cold stone.
Then I looked up.
Dark green eyes.
Almost black, actually. The kind of green that existed at the bottom of very deep water. Blonde hair was trimmed shorter on the sides, and the longer pieces on top were messy in that, "I just rolled out of bed" kind of way. A jaw that had a cleft in it. Dark denim jeans that hugged powerful thighs. A black t-shirt that showed off thick muscular arms and matching dark boots.
Cole Hayes looked down at me.
He was standing with Tucker Reeves and Reid Calloway, the Beta's and Gamma's son, and Lana was at his side, his fingers stroking her bare stomach. 
They'd been together since they were fourteen.
Everyone knew they'd end up mated and create beautiful, blonde, cruel babies together. It was inevitable. The Braxtons were the most powerful family after the Hayes and had been pushing for Regina to be Luna, but Regina was a wild, uncontrollable card and would never be told what to do with her life.
Lana, however, was ambitious and had been working to be Luna since before she ever understood what the word meant. 
But Cole's nostrils flared. He blinked, as though confused.
He took one step toward me. One step away from Lana.
And the scent slammed into me again, so strong this time that my wolf threw herself at the surface of my mind with an urgency that was almost painful.
Goddess, please, not him. Anyone in the world who has ever existed or will exist. Not him.
My wolf didn't care that I hated Cole Hayes vehemently, or that he was the reason I hid behind baggy clothes. That he had made me hate my body so much, I stopped looking in the mirror and nearly killed myself.
She thought he was ours.
Cole crouched in front of me.
Realization crashed over Lana's face, panic and fear leaping into her eyes as he reached out, breathing hard, and touched my cheek, eyes heavy-lidded with such corrosive lust and hunger that I began trembling.
But at that moment, I could not control my synapses. My body wanted him like it needed warmth. I wanted things that I didn't yet know existed. I wanted to stake my claim on him. I wanted to bury my nose in his neck and run my tongue up and down his pulse. To arch my neck and let him mark me. 
His soft touch turned cruel, something like claws began digging into my chin. "Maisie Adams," he said softly. His gaze ran down my body. "The goddess must have lost her mind if she thought we belonged together. I'd sooner jam my dick through a grinder than stick it in your fat ass."
The hall quietened. He wasn't exactly being discreet.
My wolf whined petulantly, wanting me to throw myself into his arms, but his words had dropped like a cold bucket of water onto my head. I scrambled back, chest heaving as I fought the pull. 
Goddess, but it felt like I would die if he didn't touch me.
Someone grabbed my shoulder–Regina or Jenny maybe, pulling me up. "Stay away from her."
Stay away? How? My world was reconstructing around him. I could smell him and feel his heart beat pulsing with mine. My heart, my very body was aching for him.
But Cole smirked, rising to his feet as if completely unaffected. "By the next full moon, I will be the Alpha of the Night Shade Pack. I have no use for a maid, a weakling Omega like you who can't even shift."
My head went very quiet and my gaze swung to Lana's, stinging with betrayal.
She had told him.
And now, the entire hall knew it too. It rippled across the space in waves, whispers, gasps and mocking laughter. They called me a freak. Wolfless. A runt.
"The Pack needs a stronger Luna." He pulled Lana closer to him. "Lana Braxton is much more deserving of being my mate and would make a better Luna than you ever could."
I suddenly realized what was happening.
My heart began to slam against my ribcage like a battle ram.
He was going to reject me.
I suddenly recalled Professor Halven's words.
Goddess, I'm going to die. And if I don't, I might go insane. And in the event that I somehow survived both, I would be faced with the stigma of being rejected for the rest of my life.
Because no he-wolf wanted to be stuck with another man's reject.
I tried to speak, but I didn't get a chance.
"I, Cole Hayes, future Alpha of the Night Shade pack, reject you, Maisie Adams, as my mate and future Luna of my pack," he declared coldly.
Agony split through my chest like a blade of fire. I screamed, loud, raw and guttural. My wolf howled in pain. It was like nothing I'd ever heard before and it split my head in two as she wept for him. It tore into me like a knife being plunged deep to cut my heart right out, piece by piece.
They said I howled like a banshee, cried like a child, threw up and collapsed like a ragged doll in my own vomit.
All I knew was pain.

🔥 He threw me away as unworthy. I survived, raised his triplets, and built a life without him. 👑
Chapter 1.
CHAPTER ONE

Aria's POV

 
There is an old saying that the man you meet at nineteen will change your life forever. He will be your greatest love… or he will be the one who breaks you the most.
 
I didn't believe it until I met Kael, the absolute love of my life. To the world, he was Kael Darkriver, the powerful Alpha of the Crimsonclaw Pack, a man feared and respected. But to me… he was just Kael, and he was everything I ever wanted in a man.
 
He was the man who used to sneak away from pack meetings to sit beside me by the river, who knew every strange thought in my head and never once thought I was weird. He was the only person who truly saw me.
 
I was always an odd duck, misunderstood by everyone but Kael. He understood me, he knew me, he loved me. With him, I felt like I belonged, and because of that I never cared what anyone thought about secretly fooling around with the alpha. 
 
I was ready to go through every miserable day with the pack, swallowing their snide remarks and sneering as long as I ended up in the warm embrace of Kael's arms at night under the moon where we would lie on the grass and talk for hours about everything and nothing. We may not be bonded mates, but we had a very strong bond.
 
Whatever everyone had to say didn't matter, I was the love of Kael's life, he was my peace, and one day I was going to become his mate, his Luna. And they would have no choice but to accept me.
 
“What are you doing?” Rowan's voice disrupted my train of thought. “You've been smiling at that mirror for hours, the blood moon is already almost here. 
 
I blinked and looked at him through the mirror. My older brother leaned against the doorframe with his arms crossed, his dark brows pulled together in amusement.
 
“A girl always needs to look good, you know. Especially when you have an eventful evening to look forward to… but I don't expect you to understand.” I teased and rolled my eyes.
 
“Eww... Please spare me the details of your forbidden romance with the Alpha. You have two minutes or I'll leave you, chop chop.” he said, walking away.
 
I stuck my tongue out at his back then quickly wriggled into my dress, a long black off-shoulder gown and I paired it with silver shoes.
 
“Legal Advisor,” Rowan called dramatically from the hallway. “Let’s go before the ceremony ends without you.”
 
“Okay, okay, I'm coming.” I hurriedly packed my purse as I ran after him.
 
Tonight was important — not only was it the Blood Moon gathering, but it was also my first official event as legal advisor to the pack.
 
Kael had just appointed me legal advisor to the pack, and despite the fact that many people protested the decision and some elders had argued against it openly, Kael stood firm in his decision. He knew  I was capable, he knew it was my dream, and he helped me get it. Just like always, it had been the two of us against the world.
 
The sacred grove was already filled with the rest of the pack when we arrived. The air buzzed with tension, and everything glowed red from the reflection of the blood moon that hung heavy in the sky, making the shadows look darker.
 
“What's going on?” I whispered to Rowan who also had a confused look.
 
In front of the pack, Kael stood there with the pack elders.
 
My heartbeat quickened the moment I saw him. Even in the red moonlight he stood out, tall and commanding. But something about him looked different tonight…and my stomach clenched in an anxiety I couldn't explain.
 
My eyes strayed to the figure behind him and landed on her. 
 
Selene Vale.
 
She stood a few paces behind Kael on an elevated platform, dressed in white so stark it seemed to glow under the crimson moonlight like fresh snow stained with red.
 
Why was she standing there? My stomach twisted tightly. And why hadn't Kael looked at me once since we arrived? What the hell was happening, somebody say something already.
 
Unease crept slowly through my chest as Elder Darius raised his staff and struck it against the ground, and sound echoed through the grove like thunder, so loudly that the groove fell silent.
 
“Wolves of the Crimsonclaw Pack,” he announced, his voice echoing throughout the grove. “Tonight is more than the celebration for the Blood Moon. Many years ago, the Moon Goddess delivered a prophecy to this pack. A prophecy foretelling the arrival of the Alpha’s true Luna.”
 
What stupid prophecy was he talking about, I was going to be the alpha's chosen mate, so what in fucks name was going on here.
 
My fingers clenched at my sides as Elder Darius turned.
 
Not toward me but toward Selene.
 
“Tonight,” he announced, his voice rising like a final judgment, “the prophecy has been fulfilled.”
 
For a moment, the world seemed to tilt upside down as gaps exploded through the clearing, followed by the sounds of bodies dropping to the floor as wolves began dropping to one knee around me.
 
But I couldn't move, I could barely breathe as I watched Selene step forward and slip her hand into Kael’s.
 
The sight hit me like a physical blow and before I realized what I was doing, I stepped forward.
 
“Elder Darius,” I said, and every head turned to me.
 
“Aria…” Rowan’s hand closed quickly around my arm, but it was too late.
 
“How can you be so certain?” I asked. My voice sounded calm, but inside me something was breaking.
 
“Prophecies are not simple riddles,” I continued. “You taught us that yourself, didn't you? You cannot choose a Luna simply based on a howl.”
 
Darius’ eyes hardened. “Be careful, child.”
 
“I am being careful,” I replied quickly. “Blood and sound are not proof of destiny. What evidence do we have beyond…”
 
“Enough.” Kael’s voice cut through the night like a blade.
 
I turned to him instantly, my heart still filled with hope. There was no way he actually believed this, he loves me.
 
I searched his face, looking for anything that told me he was still the man who loved me and I was still the one he loved.
 
Tell them this is madness… I pleaded silently. Tell them you wouldn't marry a woman just because of a prophecy.
 
But his eyes were cold and distant and he barely looked in my direction.
 
“The elder has spoken,” he said evenly. “The Moon Goddess has spoken.”
 
Something inside my chest shattered and a bead of tears formed in my eye but I wiped it off almost immediately.
 
Selene lowered her gaze modestly, but I saw a small smile curved at the corner of her lips.
 
“I accept,” she said softly. “I will serve as Luna for the pack… and for my Alpha. I will give you strong, pure-blooded heirs.”
 
My Alpha? Her words were like daggers stabbing through my heart.
 
Kael nodded once, looking down at her.
 
“Kael, what if this is a mistake—” Rowan stepped forward, anger flashing across his face.
 
“It is not,” Elder Darius snapped sharply. “The Thornlocks would do well to remember their place.”
 
And in that moment, everything became clear.
 
This wasn’t fate or destiny or a prophecy. This was politics and about choosing a powerful lineage for the Alpha. And I was the wrong choice.
 
They walked away from me, ignoring me like I was nothing more than a nuisance, and turned to face the pack.
 
I heard Kael and Selene howl towards the moon and then the pack followed them, howling together in unison, but I could barely hear it, the sound of my heartbeat banging loudly in my chest and my thoughts filling my head drowning out everything else.
 
How is this happening? Was Kael pretending all along? Where was this prophecy coming from all of a sudden? Did he know about it all this while? Had I been played for a fool?
 
Rowan’s hand touched my shoulder gently and I flinched, coming back to reality. The blood moon had passed already and the groove was almost empty now.
 
“Are you okay?” Rowan asked, and I nodded automatically. But of course I wasn't okay, my joy had turned to ashes in my mouth, my world was crumbling before my very eyes and there was nothing I could do about it. I was helpless, and the one person who used to fight all my battles was the demon I was fighting this time.
 
“Can I have a moment?” Kael asked, walking towards us.
 
Rowan frowned at him. “I don't think this is the right—”
 
“It’s okay, I'll be fine.” I said softly, cutting him off, and he studied my face.
 
“Are you sure Aria?” He asked and I nodded.
 
He turned and walked to one corner of the grove to give us some privacy.
 
Karl stood in front of me, looking down at me with a cold expression that speared through my chest. We should have been running off to our secret spot now, holding each other and talking about the future, but everything has fallen apart.
 
For a moment, neither of us spoke, and I searched his face, looking for a hint.
 
There was pain buried under the coldness. I could see it no matter how hard he tried to hide, because I knew him so well. But there was also a strong resolve that told me that there was nothing I could say or do to change his mind.
 
“We can’t be seen together anymore,” He whispered, his voice hollow. “We had plans, but fate had other plans and we can't fight against destiny.”
 
The words felt like ice sliding into my chest, and anger flickered in me.
 
‘‘Do you actually believe that bullshit?”
 
“It's traditional and as alpha I can't do anything about it and neither can you!” He said , raising his voice at me.
 
As if I were the problem, as if it was all my fault that he chose to be with someone else over me. I was the collateral damage in all this, and he didn't even care.
 
He sighed and rubbed his forehead tiredly.
“It's nobody's fault, it's just unfortunate we couldn't work out… Stay well Aria.”
 
Unfortunate? 

My heart twisted painfully. That's all he could say? Unfortunate? No, I was the unfortunate one. I was just the foolish girl who dreamed of being Luna, while he was still an Alpha who had his pack and his Luna. 
 
I watched him walk away and vanish into the night without even as much as a backward glance.

Chapter 2
CHAPTER TWO

Aria's POV

 
 
The walk home that night felt longer than any journey I had ever taken. Rowan stayed beside me the entire time, silent but watchful, like a guardian shadow.
 
I could feel his worry as he watched me, angry, heartbroken and ashamed as I stumbled into the house. My vision blurred from tears that refused to stop falling and my makeup was a hot mess smeared across my face, but I didn't care enough to wipe it away.
 
My heart felt hollow, as if someone had reached into my chest and scooped everything out, leaving only an aching emptiness behind.
 
I entered my room, and the moment my body touched the mattress, the quiet tears turned into loud sobs, and I had to bury my face into the pillow to muffle the sound. The pain inside me felt unbearable and I could still hear Kael’s voice echo in my mind.
 
“It’s unfortunate we couldn’t work out.”
 
Unfortunate. 

That word kept ringing in my head. It felt like the past year of my life had been nothing more than an inconvenience. As if the love I believed in had never existed at all.
 
I cried until my throat burned and my chest ached, and my eyes could barely stay open, but before I drifted off to sleep, I whispered a small prayer.
 
Please… don’t let me wake up tomorrow.
 
Unfortunately, my prayer went unanswered and I woke up the next morning.
 
The next few days passed like a blur. I didn't leave the house for days, hell I couldn't even leave the bed. Sometimes I stared at the ceiling for hours, my thoughts drifting in painful circles. Other times I cried until my head throbbed and my body felt too heavy to move.
 
It wasn't just that I felt betrayed, it felt as if my heart had shattered into a thousand sharp pieces inside my chest. Every memory of Kael felt like poison now, and it felt like my soul, my whole world had cracked. I refused to eat or shower for two days straight, all I did was cry, drink water when Rowan forced a glass into my hands… and then cry again.
 
By the third day, Rowan finally lost his patience. I heard him moving around the kitchen, and a while later, he pushed open my bedroom door and walked in with a bowl of pudding and sat beside me on the bed, nudging my shoulder gently. 
 
“Sit up.”
 
“I’m not hungry,” I muttered weakly.
 
“I didn’t ask if you were.”
 
“Go away.” I groaned, but he ignored me and dipped the spoon into the pudding and held it in front of my mouth.
 
“You can cry all you want,” he said quietly. “You can curse Kael and curse the Moon Goddess if it helps. But you are not going to starve yourself to death over that idiot.”
 
My throat tightened, and I suddenly realised that I wasn't alone in this. Rowan must have been heartbroken seeing me slowly starve myself to death these past few days.
 
The food tasted like water and raw egg in my mouth, but I ate it anyway.
 
It took five days before I finally stepped outside, and when I did, I could feel stares on me everywhere I went.
 
Of course they stared. I was Aria Thornlock, the girl who was foolish enough to love the Alpha.
 
I pretended not to hear the whispers and words they said behind my back, I tried to tell myself that their words didn't matter and I was stronger than this, until I ran into her… Selene.
 
When her eyes met mine, her lips curved slowly into a cruel smile.
 
“Aria,” she said sweetly.
 
I tried to walk past her but her hand shot out and grabbed my arm.
 
“Are you okay?” she asked, tilting her head slightly. “I noticed you seemed very… upset the night I was made Luna.” Her voice dripped with mock concern and a bit of condescension that I tried to ignore.
 
“I’m fine.” I said, forcing a smile and trying to pull my arm free but she tightened her grip.

“Aria… what’s wrong?”
 
The fear in my voice was evident. “I’m… pregnant.”
 
Lisa stared at me with confusion. Her voice softened. “Is that… bad news?”
 
A flood of emotions hit me, fear, heartbreak, protectiveness, the ghost of Kael’s touch, the memory of his warmth, and the pain of his betrayal.
 
“I’m alone,” I whispered. “I have no one.” Tears poured out of my eyes again.
 
Lisa took my trembling hands, squeezing them in hers. “You have me, I’m here for you, I promise.” She embraced me gently, stroking my hair until I quieted down.
 
Weeks passed, and Lisa took care of me with quiet patience, making sure I ate and rested.
 
Then the next full moon came, and Lisa returned from her shift to find me chained to the radiator, my body contorting, my eyes glowing silver. My body twisted painfully as Nyra fought to shift.
 
Lisa stared in stunned silence, frozen at the door. 
 
“You’re… a werewolf,” she whispered, staring at me in awe.
 
When I finally returned to my human form, exhausted and terrified, Lisa wrapped me in a blanket and sat with me on the kitchen floor.
 
“I’ve read about your kind,” she said quietly. “People talk, hunters talk. I believed it, but… I never thought I’d meet one.”
 
My whole body was still shaking with a mix of panic, fear and shame. “Please don’t tell anyone. I mean absolutely no one can know,” I begged.
 
She squeezed my hand. “Your secret is safe with me.”
 
Lisa wrapped her arm around me and placed my head on her shoulder. And for the first time since exile… I believed in someone other than myself..
 
After a long silence, I whispered the words that had been growing inside me. “I’ve decided to keep my baby. I won't abandon my child,” I said softly. “Not the way I was abandoned.”
 
A small, fragile life was growing inside me, and I made a quiet promise at that moment.
 
“I will protect you,” I whispered. “Even if it costs me my life.”

I sat in the driveway of my own house for 22 minutes at my granddaughter Nevaeh's first birthday party.

The balloons were on the mailbox. Pink ones, and a silver one shaped like a number 1 that kept catching the wind and twisting. I could hear music from inside. I could see my daughter's silhouette through the living room window, carrying something, moving fast the way she always does when she's hosting.

And I couldn't get out of the car.

Not because I didn't want to. Not because I was scared of anything. But because 4 weeks earlier, I'd crashed so hard at my sister Valerie's Easter dinner that I'd had to lie down on her couch for an hour while the kids hunted eggs in the yard. I could hear them laughing through the window. I could hear my name being called. And I couldn't lift my head off the throw pillow.

That was Easter.

This was Nevaeh's first birthday. Her first. The one with the photos. The one that goes in the album.

And I was sitting in my own daughter's driveway, in a car that still smelled like the restaurant we'd grabbed lunch at, gripping the steering wheel, trying to negotiate with my own body.

Just get through the door. Just get through the door. That's all.

My name is Claudette Williams. I'm 63 years old and I've lived in Shreveport, Louisiana my whole life. I raised 2 kids mostly on my own after my ex-husband relocated for work and decided the relocation was permanent. I worked 28 years as a school administrator for the Caddo Parish school district. I am not a woman who sits in driveways.

But there I sat.

Let me back up. Because none of this started with Nevaeh's birthday. It started a long time before that, slow enough that I almost didn't notice it happening.

I've always had what my mother called a "sweet tooth the size of Texas." Growing up in her kitchen, there was always something on the counter. Peach cobbler. Bread pudding with vanilla sauce. Her sweet potato pie that I have tried, for 40 years, to replicate and can't.

I didn't worry about any of it when I was younger. You don't. You eat what's in front of you and you run around and your body handles it and nobody thinks twice.

But somewhere in my mid-50s, things changed.

It started with tiredness. Not the tired-because-you-didn't-sleep tired. A different kind. The kind that shows up about an hour after you eat lunch and sits on your chest like a sandbag. I'd be at my desk and I'd feel this wave come over me, this heavy, foggy, almost dizzy feeling, and I'd have to prop my elbows on the desk and just breathe through it.

I mentioned it to my doctor at my annual. She asked about my sleep. I said my sleep was fine. She nodded and wrote something down.

A year later I mentioned it again. She asked if I was under stress. I was. I'm always under some kind of stress. I'm a 60-year-old Black woman who raised 2 kids alone in Louisiana. Stress is just Tuesday. She nodded and wrote something down.

A year after that, she ran some labs and had a conversation with me I wasn't quite ready for.

My fasting blood sugar had been creeping up for years. She used a phrase I'd heard before but always thought applied to other people. Pre-diabetic range.

She said it gently, the way doctors do when they're trying not to alarm you. Cut back on the carbs. Try to walk more. Come back in 6 months.

I walked out of that office and sat in the parking lot for a minute, which was apparently becoming a habit I hadn't noticed yet. I didn't cry. I just sat there and thought: I knew something was off. I've known for years. And I kept being told it was stress and sleep and getting older. Nobody said anything was actually wrong until now.

I went home and I did what she said. I cut back on bread. I stopped putting sugar in my coffee. I walked the neighborhood 4 times a week for the next 3 months.

At 6 months, my numbers had barely moved.

I went back. She said I was doing the right things. She said to keep going. She talked about medication.

I wasn't ready for medication. Not yet. I've watched people in my family go down that road and I've seen where it leads. My mother was on 3 medications at 68. My aunt Dottie was on 5 at 72, and she'd spend half an hour at the kitchen table every Sunday morning sorting her pill organizer like it was a part-time job. I wasn't ready to start that chapter.

So I tried more things. I tried the cinnamon supplements they sell at the pharmacy. I tried apple cider vinegar, which, I have to tell you, is one of the more unpleasant things I've put in my body. I tried cutting out rice and then mourning the loss of rice for approximately 3 weeks. I lost maybe 4 pounds.

The crashes kept coming.

That's what I want you to understand. It wasn't just that my numbers were off. It was the feeling. The crashes. The way my body would go from fine to completely useless within an hour of eating. It wasn't dramatic. I wasn't passing out. But I was disappearing, kind of. Going somewhere foggy and unreachable, and having to wait for it to pass.

I missed a grandkids' school play because of it. I missed the first part of my coworker Patricia's retirement party. I left early from Thanksgiving because after the meal I could barely keep my eyes open and couldn't drive myself home.

These are small things. I know they sound small. But they added up in a way that started to feel like I was watching my own life from a distance. Like I was always slightly behind the glass.

And then came Easter Sunday at Valerie's house.

My sister Valerie lives in Bossier City, about 20 minutes across the bridge. She does Easter the way my mother used to do Easter, which means it starts in the morning and ends when you physically cannot eat another thing. Ham, potato salad, green bean casserole, deviled eggs, macaroni and cheese, sweet potato pie, and a yellow cake with the icing so thick it holds the shape of the spatula.

I ate what I ate. It was Easter. There were 17 people in that house and I wasn't going to be the one with the sad little plate of iceberg lettuce.

About an hour after we sat down, I felt it coming. The heaviness. The fog. The sandbag on my chest.

I tried to push through. I went outside with the kids for a little while. I helped Valerie carry dishes to the kitchen. But by 2 PM I was on her couch with a throw pillow under my head, listening to my grandchildren laughing and my family talking and a baseball game coming from the back bedroom, and I could not make myself get up.

My daughter Keisha came and checked on me. I told her I was fine, just tired.

She knew I wasn't fine.

I drove home at 4:30 and I didn't talk about it to anyone. Not Keisha, not Valerie. I just put it in the place where I was putting all of it and I tried not to think about it too hard.

But I thought about it.

I thought about it right up until I was sitting in my daughter's driveway on a Saturday afternoon in June with a pink balloon on the mailbox and Nevaeh's birthday happening on the other side of that door.

I made myself go in.

Keisha saw my face when I walked through the door. She pulled me aside into the kitchen while her husband Robert was busy lighting candles and the kids were chasing each other around the yard. She looked at me for a second and then she hugged me without saying anything.

When she pulled back she said, "Mama. You have to try this thing Auntie Val told me about."

I said, "Keisha, if this is another apple cider vinegar situation—"

She laughed. Said, "No, Mama. It's pomegranate."

I said, "Pomegranate."

She said, "I know how that sounds. Just listen."

So I listened.

She told me that Valerie had started taking a pomegranate extract supplement a few months back. That Valerie had mentioned it almost in passing, the way Valerie mentions things she doesn't want to make a big deal out of, which means it's actually a big deal.

Apparently Valerie had been having her own version of what I was having. The afternoon lows. The crashes. She hadn't told me because she knew I'd worry. But she'd started taking this pomegranate extract and she'd noticed something. Not dramatic. But real. The crashes were easing. She wasn't white-knuckling her way through the afternoon anymore.

Now, my first thought was: Valerie just had a good couple of months and is giving pomegranate the credit.

I'm a school administrator. I've heard a lot of stories. I don't take them at face value.

But I went home that night after Nevaeh's birthday, and I sat at my kitchen table with my reading glasses on and I started looking into it. Not because I was convinced. Because I was desperate enough to look.

What I found surprised me.

Your body has a process that controls how fast the food you eat turns into sugar.

Food comes in. Your body breaks it down. Sugar enters your blood. When that process is running the way it's supposed to, the sugar comes in gradually. Your body keeps pace. You stay level. You feel normal.

But that system doesn't stay perfect forever.

Stress wears it down. Processed food wears it down. And just plain aging wears it down. A little bit at a time, year after year, until the pathway that used to control the speed can't quite do it the way it used to. Now food turns into sugar faster than your body is built to handle. That's the spike. And then your body overcompensates. That's the crash.

It's not just about what you eat. The food you've always eaten hasn't changed. Your body's ability to manage it has been slowly worn down. And that's a different problem than a different diet can solve.

What I read about pomegranate was that it contains compounds called punicalagins. They're found mainly in the peel of the pomegranate, which is why you wouldn't get them just from eating the fruit. What researchers have been studying is how these punicalagins interact with the body's process for breaking down carbohydrates into sugar.

Specifically, they seem to support the pathway that controls how fast that breakdown happens.

When that pathway gets better support, the sugar from your food comes in more gradually. More like a slow tide than a wave. Your body has time to respond. The spikes don't have to be so sharp. And when the spikes ease, the crashes ease too.

It's not forcing anything. It's not overriding anything. It's more like giving your body back a tool it already had but has been slowly losing its grip on.

Pomegranate also ranks among the highest antioxidant foods ever measured. And that matters because the same oxidative stress that wears down the carbohydrate pathway is also the stress that keeps those wear-and-tear effects going year after year. More antioxidant activity means less of that ongoing damage to the system.

I found research on this. Not anecdotes. Actual clinical research. A large analysis that looked at dozens of studies and found that pomegranate supplementation was associated with meaningful support for fasting blood sugar levels and for the way the body responds to insulin. The effects were most consistent in people who already had elevated blood sugar to begin with. Which, as of my last lab appointment, was exactly me.

I sat with all of that for about a week.

Then I ordered a bottle.

I want to be honest with you about the first few weeks because it wasn't some dramatic overnight story.

Week 1, I didn't feel much. I was skeptical enough that I was looking for reasons to write it off.

Week 2, I noticed I was making it further into the afternoon without that heavy, foggy feeling showing up. I thought maybe I'd just had a better week. Slept better. Eaten lighter.

Week 3, I had my daughter's family over for a Sunday dinner. I made chicken, rice, cornbread, a peach cobbler. The kind of meal that, 6 months ago, would have put me on the couch by 4 PM.

I did the dishes after dinner.

I want you to understand what I mean when I say that. I did the dishes. I loaded the dishwasher, I wiped down the counters, I sat on the back porch with Keisha and Robert while the kids ran around in the yard, and I watched the sun go down. I wasn't fighting anything. I wasn't white-knuckling through an afternoon fog. I was just there. Present. In my own backyard. In my own life.

Keisha noticed. She didn't say anything for a while. Then she said, "Mama, you seem good tonight."

I said, "I think I might be."

That was around week 3.

By week 6 I had another check-in with my doctor. She ran labs. My fasting number had moved in the right direction. Not a dramatic shift. But a real one. The kind that made her pause for a second before saying anything.

She asked what I'd changed.

I told her about the pomegranate supplement.

She did the thing doctors do when they're not sure what to say about something, which is give a sort of careful nod and say "well, keep doing what you're doing." I'll take that.

More than the numbers, though, what I kept coming back to was the feeling.

Not feeling like I was managing a condition. Not feeling like I was in a constant negotiation with my own body every time I sat down to eat. Just feeling like myself. Like the version of me that showed up fully, that didn't have to ration her energy or plan her afternoons around the possibility of crashing.

The version of me that could walk into a birthday party instead of sitting outside in the driveway.

I thought about Nevaeh a lot during those weeks. About the birthday party I almost didn't walk into. About the Easter Sunday on the couch. About all the edges of things I'd been missing, all the moments I'd been watching from behind the glass.

I didn't want to watch anymore.

I want to tell you about one more thing before I get to the close.

A few weeks into taking the supplement, I called Valerie.

I told her what I'd found in my own research. I told her about the pathway, about the punicalagins, about the way the system was supposed to work and how it gets worn down. I half expected her to tell me I was overcomplicating it the way she sometimes does when I go deep on something.

Instead she got quiet for a second.

Then she said, "Claudette. That's exactly what it felt like. Like my body just started keeping up again."

Keeping up.

That was the phrase. That's the whole thing, right there. Not some dramatic transformation. Not a miracle. Just your body keeping up again. The way it used to. The way it's supposed to.

If any of this sounds like your life, even pieces of it, I want you to know about Alevia Pomegranate.

I tugged at the scrap of black lace riding up my hip. This outfit wasn’t clothes, it was a prayer. A tiny, see-through prayer.
I caught my reflection in the cracked dressing room mirror and barely recognized the girl staring back. The silver wig was cold and synthetic against my neck.
"We’re getting that money, Bri. I swear," I said.
Brianna looked at me, her eyes rimmed with red, "Gianna, you don't have to do this. You’ve already done enough for us. You shouldn't have to be in here, looking like this. We'll find another way."
"There is no other way, and you know it," I snapped, then immediately softened. I grabbed her hands. They were ice cold, "I am not letting anything happen to any of us. I'd rather stand out there in front of a thousand strangers than spend one second wondering where Cole Mercer took you. If this is what it takes to keep all of us safe, then I'm doing it. End of story."
The door swung open, Mama D came in with a smile. She looked us up and down, her eyes lingering on the way the black straps dug into my skin. She hated this as much as we did.
"Are you ready, girls. It’s go time," she said, waving a hand dripping in fake gold rings, "We’ve got a private party in the Gold Room. These aren't your usual local creeps. These guys are fancy. Suits that cost more than your lives, clean fingernails, the whole deal. They’ll throw heavy cash if you make them feel like kings. Don't blow it."
I swallowed hard and reached for the black lace mask on the vanity. I tied the silk ribbons behind my head, feeling a tiny bit of relief as the fabric hid my eyes and nose. If I couldn't see them clearly, maybe they couldn't see the real me.
Walking into the private room felt like stepping into a freezer. It was dark, filled the smell of top-shelf bourbon and the kind of cologne that lingers in your throat. Three men sat on the leather U-shaped couch. They were leaning in, talking in low voices.
"It’s a simple wire," one was saying, "We move the first billion through the offshore accounts in Cyprus by morning."
First billion.
The word made my head spin. I was here risking everything for a few grand, and they were talking about money that didn't even sound real.
The music started, I stepped into the center of the rug, moving my hips, not like Bri and Tasha were moving. Instead, I used the only thing I knew: my training.
I rose onto the tips of my toes, my calves flexing, I moved my hips in a slow circle, every muscle in my stomach rippling with a control that only years of the barre could give you.
I arched my back until my silver hair nearly swept the floor, my ribs expanding as I took a shaky breath.
I could feel their eyes on me. The room went dead silent. The talk of billions stopped. I arched my back, sliding my hands down my sides, trying to look like I enjoyed the way their eyes tracked my every move.
The man in the center slowly sat straight. He didn't say a word. He just lifted one hand and curled two fingers, beckoning me closer.
As, I got closer, the details hit me. He was wearing a dark charcoal suit that fit his broad shoulders perfectly, no tie, just a crisp white shirt unbuttoned at the top.
I stood between his knees, my body swaying to the beat. I looked up, and for a second, I forgot to breathe.
He was... beautiful, like, scary beautiful. He had a jawline so sharp that it looked unreal. But it was his eyes that trapped me, a light, piercing brown, like clover honey held up to a flame.
I stepped even closer, my bare thigh brushing against the expensive wool of his suit trousers. I arched my back again, my spine supple as a whip, and let my arms flow upward, before I brought them down to graze my own collarbone.
I was using every bit of my ballet training, the control, the lines, the way I knew exactly how to shift my weight to make my hips sway just right.
Slowly, he reached out. His hand was large, his fingers long and tanned covered in tattoos. He started to reach for my waist, his palm open as if he wanted to pull me onto his lap.
I didn't think. I just reacted.
I caught his wrist with one hand and pushed it back toward his chest. I didn't break eye contact. I just gave a tiny, slow shake of my head.
Look, but don't touch, I'm not that kind of girl. I'm just here for the cash.
I expected him to get angry. I expected him to snap or call Mama D to complain. Men like this weren't used to being told "no," especially not in a room they paid for.
Instead, a slow, lopsided smile spread across his face. It transformed his face from a cold statue into something human, something even more dangerous because of how charming it was.
He didn't try again. He just leaned back into the leather couch, crossing one leg over the other, watching me with a look that said he was suddenly very, very interested in the girl behind the mask.
I slowly turned my back to him, arching my spine until I could see him over my shoulder. I moved my hips in a slow circle, the black lace of my thong barely covering anything.
I heard a soft rustle of fabric.
I turned back around, my silver hair stuck to my glittery skin. He was reaching into the inner pocket of his suit jacket.
He pulled out a thick wad of cash. It was all hundred-dollar bills, crisp and new.
He didn't just throw it at me. He didn't tuck it into the table. Instead, he held the money between two fingers and looked up at me. His light brown eyes were darker than before. He didn't say a word, but the way he tilted his head was a question.
Can I?
My heart was thumping so hard I thought it would burst through my ribs. Slowly, I stepped even closer, until my stomach was inches from his face. I didn't nod, but I didn't move away.
He leaned in. I felt his hot breath on my skin, his hand came forward, and he didn't just tuck the money in. He took his time.
His fingers slid under the strap, grazing the skin of my hip. He let his knuckles drag against me, pressing a little too hard, a little too long. The friction sent a literal shock through my system, an electric spark that started at my hip and shot straight to my core.
I gasped, my back arching instinctively. It was a reaction to the heat of his touch. He knew exactly what he was doing. His thumb traced the edge of the lace, dipping just an inch lower than it needed to, claiming a piece of me that wasn't for sale.
He looked up at me from his seat, that lopsided, beautiful smile growing wider as he saw my chest heaving. He watched my reaction like it was a show created just for him.
"Good girl," he mouthed, though no sound came out.
He finally let go, but the skin where he’d touched me felt like it was on fire.

It was just the nerves of meeting the legendary Salvatore Capone's inner circle.

Two nights ago.
Five thousand dollars.
His hand at my waist.
His eyes on me.
My stomach turned into a block of ice. I felt sick. I felt naked, even in my dress.
“Mum…” my fingers tightened painfully around Jules’, “Who… who are those people?”

“Oh,” she said lightly, “That’s Salvatore’s sons. Adriano, Dante… and the one with the glasses is Raphael.”
Those eyes were the same ones that had watched me dance.
Watched me bend.
Watched me take his money.
The world tilted.
The man I stripped for.
The man who tipped me five thousand dollars like it meant nothing.
He was my soon-to-be stepbrother.
