Chapter 2
Raphael
Gold-digging whores.
I didn’t even have to look at them to know that’s exactly what they were. The smell of desperation always clung to women like them, no matter how much expensive perfume they sprayed on their wrists to hide it.
Hazel Kinsley. She was the widow of some pathetic senator who had managed to die and leave her with a mountain of debt and a name that wasn't worth the paper it was printed on. So, naturally, she did what people like her do best. She found a shark. She latched onto my father like a leech, hoping his shadow would be enough to hide her from the world.
My father, the great Don Salvatore Capone, was a joke. He couldn't even figure out how to be a father to his own blood, yet here he was, tripping over his own feet to play hero for a woman who probably didn't even know his favorite food. He was so eager to take care of her and her baggage. It was embarrassing.
And the worst part about all this was... Hazel was sitting in my mother’s chair.
That chair was sacred. Seeing this stranger—this parasite—sitting there felt like watching someone spit on a grave.
Right next to her sat the older one. Genevieve, or whatever forgettable name she had. She was trying to look small, trying to blend into the furniture, but I could see the way her eyes darted around, probably counting the silverware and figuring out how much she could hock it for.
And then there was the ten-year-old, Juliet. She was bouncing in her seat, looking at the chandelier like it was made of diamonds.
I didn't want them here. I didn't want their noise, their cheap problems, or their fake smiles. This was my home and my father had just opened the gates for a bunch of nobodies.
Every time Hazel laughed, I felt a pulse of pure, dignified hatred in my neck. She looked far too comfortable. Her hands were small and soft, the hands of someone who had never worked a day in her life, someone who had spent her husband’s money until the well ran dry.
Now she was here to drink ours.
I leaned back, taking a slow drag of my cigarete, letting the smoke cloud the space between us. I wanted her to feel unwelcome. I wanted her to feel like an intruder, because that’s exactly what she was.
"So, Gianna," Claire said. As the Donna and my sister-in-law, she was basically the queen of our home, and she sounded way too friendly for a table full of people who looked like they wanted to commit a felony, "You’re in college, right? What are you actually studying?"
I expected her to say something useless. Art history. Philosophy. Something that required zero brain cells.
"Tell them, honey. It's very advanced," her mother added.
Gianna, her name was Gianna...
"I'm studying Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning," she said, "Mostly deep neural networks."
I didn't move, but my head tilted just a fraction of a millimeter.
My brain did a quick scan. AI and ML? Deep neural networks? That was the language I used to build the back-end systems that moved our money across the globe.
I finally shifted my gaze, letting it settle on her for the first time. Long, light brown hair. Green eyes that seemed to be fighting to stay calm.
My memory is a filing cabinet of faces, names, and patterns, I don't forget things.
And looking at her, a warning light flickered in the back of my mind.
She looked familiar. It was vague, but I’d seen those eyes before.
Green eyes were a rare find. My brain doesn't make mistakes, and it was telling me right now that this wasn't the first time our paths had crossed.
I didn't know where I had seen her, but the more I stared, the more my skin prickled. I leaned back, my eyes narrowing behind my glasses. I’d figure it out.
"That is incredible," Maddie said. My other sister-in-law's face lit up with that genuine, annoying warmth she always had, "That’s complicated stuff. We actually have a genius in the family who works with that kind of tech all the time. Raphael, you have to talk to Gianna!"
I felt the trap snap shut around me. What the fvck, Mads? Adriano was looking at me from across the table, a smug look on his face. He knew I hated being forced to interact with the help, and that’s all these women were to me.
I took one last pull of my cigarete and crushed it out in the crystal ashtray.
"It's interesting work," I finally muttered as I adjusted my glasses, "You'll need a good server cluster..." I just said.
Most students just play with toy datasets. They don't have the compute power for anything real.
I expected her to look away, to be intimidated by the coldness in my tone. Most people were.
Instead, she leaned forward, "Oh! Are you… building models?" she asked, "For what kind of application?"
I felt a strange, sharp prickle at the base of my skull. I didn't answer her. I couldn't. Because if I told her what I used my models for, I’d have to kill her before the dessert was served.
"Papà Salvatore, do I get my own room?" the little one, Julia, chirped.
Of course. There it was. The real reason these parasites had crawled out of the woodwork and into our dining room.
They weren't looking for a family, they were looking for real estate. They were already measuring the bedrooms, picking out which corners of our legacy they could claim for themselves.
The transparency of it was disgusting
Adriano choked on his wine, and the dinner turned into the train wreck I knew it was always going to be.
--- ---
I tossed my glasses onto the dresser. I didn't actually need the prescription, my vision was perfect but when you spend eighteen hours a day dissecting code and staring at glowing monitors, blue-light protection becomes a necessity, not a choice.
I valued my efficiency too much to let my eyes fail me.
During the day, I had a legit tech firm to run, but at night? At night, I ran the Chicago Outfit. I did it all from behind a screen, digitally controlling everything. It took hours of staring at the glass, moving numbers, and watching data streams.
My job was simple: keep us getting richer and keep ruining the lives of anyone who got in our way.
I could drain a bank account before the owner even finished typing their password. If I wanted to, I could erase a person’s entire existence, social security, credit history, birth certificate with a few clicks.
And right now, my only job was to figure out which one of these parasitic women was trying to bleed my family dry. We don’t do "new beginnings" in this house, and we definitely don't do "happy families." We do assets and liabilities.
And these women looked like the kind of liabilities that needed to be liquidated.
I started with the most obvious target. The one leading this little gold-digging expedition.
The mother.
Hazel Kinsley.
I wanted to see the exact moment she decided my father was her winning lottery ticket.
By the time I was done with her, she wouldn't just be out of our house, she’d be wishing she’d never even heard the name Capone.
The click of the lock was the only warning I got.
"Raphael."
My father’s voice cut through the silence in my room. I didn't even have to look to know he’d stopped dead in his tracks the second his eyes hit the surveillance photos on my laptop of his girlfriend. I closed my eyes for a split second, a cold, sharp sigh escaping my lips as I felt my patience thinning.
I turned my head slowly, expecting to see him standing there alone, probably looking for another round of excuses for his pathetic dinner choices or his sudden need for a soulmate.
Instead, I found him flanked by Vincenzo.
My oldest brother. The Don.
Vincenzo stood there with his arms crossed. He was the one man in this world whose orders were absolute, the final authority I couldn't ignore, no matter how much I wanted to.
Seeing them together made the situation clear, whatever my father was about to ask. He brought the Don along to make sure I understood whatever this was, it wasn't a favor or a request. It was a mandate. An order.
"Yeah?" I asked, my voice flat and monotone, matching the cold glow of the screen. I didn't even bother to minimize the windows.
My father stepped further into the room, his eyes landing on the data-heavy screens and the high-res photos of Hazel Kinsley I had pinned to the desktop.
He didn't look angry, he looked like he’d expected exactly this.
He gestured toward the screen with a flicking motion of his hand, "That," he said, his voice dropping into that low, serious tone he used when business was on the line, "That is exactly why I’m here, Raphael. I knew you’d already be digging. I knew you’d be trying to find a reason to tear this apart before it started."
I kept my gaze locked on Vincenzo, "What, I’m not even allowed to run a basic background check anymore? I already sat through the dinner. I endured the disrespect to my mother's table and listened to your little sob story. Is there something else you need from my schedule, or can I get back to actual work?"
"Raphael," my father repeated, "I saw that look in your eyes at dinner. I know how your mind works. You see a new variable, and you want to solve it. You want to dig."
My head snapped towards him, a muscle in my jaw twitching.
He stepped closer, "I’m telling you right now, let it go. Hazel and her girls are not a project. They aren't a threat to be analyzed. I want you to respect their privacy. That means no deep dives, no hacking their bank statements, and absolutely no background checks. You stay out of their digital lives."
I raised an eyebrow, "You’re asking me to be blind, Dad? In this house?"
"It’s not a request," my father snapped, his jaw tightening.
Vincenzo finally moved. He took a single step forward, and the temperature seemed to drop. He didn't have to raise his voice, the authority he carried was enough to crush the lungs of a lesser man.
"It’s my order as well, Raphael," Vincenzo said, "You will stand down on this. If I find out you’ve been sniffing around their history or running their names through your servers, I’ll take it as a direct middle finger to me. They’re under my protection now. Am I making myself clear?"
I felt the burn of frustration in my chest. My instincts were screaming at me that something was wrong, that those rare green eyes were a puzzle I needed to solve but I was a Capone. I understood the chain of command.
"Crystal," I bit out.
"Good," Vincenzo said, giving me a single, stiff nod. "Go on a hunt. Do your thing. Go burn off that energy on some real enemies. Just leave those women out of it."
The second the words left his mouth, the rage boiled over. I didn't even think, I just grabbed my laptop and hurled it across the room with everything I had. It hit the hardwood floor, snapping into two pieces, the screen flickering one last time before going dark.
Vincenzo gave his head a shake before leaving. But my dad stopped. He walked over, and placed a hand on my shoulder. He gave it one squeeze before turning and leaving me alone.
I stood up and shoved my chair back, the screech of metal against the floor echoing my mood. I walked over to the closet and ripped off the charcoal suit, tossing the expensive fabric onto the floor like it was trash, and replaced it with a black muscle-fit shirt that clung to my chest and shoulders. Next came the heavy, black tactical trousers, military grade, built for movement and utility.
I slid my customized handguns into their holsters and tucked my knives into their hidden sheaths. Every blade was sharp enough to split a hair, every weapon was a part of me. I rolled my shoulders and cracked my neck.
My phone vibrated. A single text glowed on the screen: Is the hunt on for tonight?
Yeah, I typed back.
I slid the phone into my pocket. I needed the hunt. I needed the clarity of the chase to wash away the irritation of the dinner and the weight of Vincenzo’s order felt like a collar around my neck, and I hated the way it pulled.
I headed down to the garage. The heavy steel doors slid open, and rows of supercars sat under the glow of LED strips. Ferrars, Lamborghins, custom-built monsters that could outrun a helicopter.
My eyes landed on my favorite, the Ducati Panigalle V4. It was a blacked-out demon of a bike. I grabbed my helmet, pulled it over my head, and the world went quiet, just the sound of my own breathing.
I kicked the engine over, and the bike roared to life, a deep, aggressive growl that vibrated through the floor and up my spine. I hit the throttle, and the garage door couldn't open fast enough. I blurred out into the night.
The party was at The Void. That was the name of our massive, black-stone mansion tucked so deep into the woods that the law couldn't find it even if they had a map.
It was a place where things disappeared
I pulled up in the driveway, the bass from the music was so loud I could feel it in my teeth. The house was glowing, lights spilling out onto the lawn where hundreds of people were already losing their minds. This was a typical mob party, expensive booze, dangerous men, and women looking for a way in.
The second I cut the engine and pulled off my helmet, everything changed.
"Yo, RC!" someone shouted over the music.
"Holy shit, Raphael is here!"
I felt the eyes on me immediately. People cleared a path as I walked toward the entrance. I was aggravated. I was pissed. I wanted to be invisible, but when your last name is Capone, you’re a sun that everyone wants to burn in.
"Raphael!"
A group of girls drifted toward me. One of them, a blonde with lips plumped to perfection, leaned into my space, her hand brushing my bicep.
"Raphael, baby, you look like you want to kill someone," she purred, her eyes scanning my tactical gear.
I didn't push her away. I didn't even look at her. I wasn't mad at them, they were just playing the game they were born to play. I was mad at the glitch in my head. I was mad that I was being told to play nice with parasites.
"Move," I ordered.
She didn't look offended, she looked thrilled. That was the problem with people like this. They loved the edge of the knife until it actually started to cut.
I needed to drown out the sound of my father’s voice. I needed to forget the Don’s orders. But most of all, I needed to figure out why I felt like the hunt tonight wasn't going to be enough to fix my head.
I pulled out my phone. My thumb hovered over the screen for a second before I dialed.
"Enzo," I said, my voice cutting through the bass of the party.
"Yes, boss?" Enzo answered immediately.
"You remember the girl from the Gold Room two nights ago?" I asked.
I didn't need to describe her, he knew which one had my attention.
"The dancer? Yeah, I remember."
I didn't care what it cost. I didn't care who she was. I just needed to clear my head, and she was the only thing I’d seen in days that made my blood run hot for the right reasons.
"Find her," I ordered, "Get her to the Void. Now."
Chapter 3
Gianna
I was back at the Rose Garden, which was basically a fancy way of saying a place where girls got dressed up to be arm candy for guys with too much money.
"I’m telling you, Mama D, they aren’t humans," I groaned, throwing my head back so hard my ponytail nearly hit the floor. "They are like... six different flavors of Doom. It’s a Doom Buffet."
Mama D, the only woman I knew who could look scary while wearing a floral robe and holding a cigarete, blew a cloud of smoke toward the ceiling. She looked us over like a mother hen guarding a bunch of sparkly chicks, "They’re Capones, G."
"I saw more gvns today than I’ve seen in my entire life!" I said, waving my hands around, "And they don't even hide them. It’s like, 'Oh, pass the salt, and also, here is my Glock.' And the staring! Oh my god, the staring. They didn't just look at me; they stared at me like I’d personally broken into their house and stolen their favorite children."
Tasha laughed, her dark skin glowing under the vanity lights as she dusted gold shimmer over her collarbones, "Girl, at least they’re rich. If I’m going to be stared at by a man with a weapon, he better have a private jet and a designer suit."
"It’s not funny, Tash! One of them, Adriano looked like he wanted to snap his fork in half just because my mom breathed," I said, leaning over to grab a hair tie.
Jasmine was sitting right next to me, her dark hair pulled back as she carefully pinned a small, jeweled nose stud into place. She didn't look worried at all. She just glanced at me through the mirror with a tiny, wicked smile.
"I don't know, G," she teased, "Maybe they weren't trying to scare you. Maybe they just liked the view. You did wear that dress that makes your waist look like it doesn't exist."
"Their stares were hostile, Jas. Extremely hostile," I muttered, but my mind immediately drifted to the one brother who stared at me harder than everyone else.
Raphael.
I felt a cold shiver run down my spine just thinking about him. He was the one I was most afraid of. He sat there with those sharp glasses and those eyes that felt like they were scanning my hard drive. Every time he looked at me, my heart stopped. I was so sure, so absolutely positive, that he was going to stand up, point a finger at me, and tell everyone he’d seen me at the Gold Room.
I’d been so careful. The club had dim lights, and I wore that heavy mask and the wig. He probably didn't recognize me.
I took a shaky breath, feeling a wave of relief wash over me all over again. He hadn't said a word. He’d just looked at me like I was a bug he didn't feel like squashing yet. He definitely didn't recognize me. He couldn't have. If he knew his future stepsister was the same girl he’d watched on a stage, I’d be at the bottom of a lake by now.
"I just need to stay out of his way," I whispered to myself, grabbing my brush. "I’ll be fine. He’s never going to find out. There is no way."
"What are you mumbling about?" Tasha asked, nudging me.
"Nothing," I lied quickly, forcing a bright, fake smile, "Just hoping my luck holds out. I’m going to go help Mama D with the inventory in the back."
In the corner, Morgan was vibrating. She was the baby of our group, barely eighteen. Her straight, jet-black hair was pulled into a high, sleek ponytail, and she kept tugging at the hem of her tight dress. She looked like she was about to go to her first prom, except the prom was a high event gala or something with men twice her age.
"Are they... are they going to come here?" Morgan asked, "The Capones?"
I softened, reaching over to pat her hand, "No. They stay in their castles. This place is too 'low-rent' for them."
She’d been practicing her sultry walk in the hallway for three hours.
"You'll be fine," Bri said, walking over and putting a protective arm around Morgan’s shoulders, "Just remember, we look at them, but we don't see them. We’re just here for the paper."
Emma walked over, her eyes soft as she squeezed my hand. "G, you don’t have to go back to that house. You can stay here. Your mom... she can live her new life with them, but you don't have to be part of that."
I gave her a small, grateful smile. These girls were like my family. I met them when I was sixteen, five years ago, after I’d run away from a life that felt like it was crushing me.
They didn't ask questions, they just opened the door and took me in. It took my mother four months to track me down, and when she finally did, she tried to cut them out of my life like they were a disease. She thought she’d succeeded. She had no idea that not a single day had passed in five years where I hadn't talked to them.
Mama Denise ran the Rose Garden, but it wasn’t what people thought. These girls were escorts, they were the arm candy for the elite. They went to the galas, they danced at the high-class events, but they were strictly off-limits. Mama D was like a lioness, no one was allowed to touch her girls. Not ever.
I wasn't officially on the roster, but I was always here. Since I didn't have a real job, I made myself useful. These women were the ones who stepped up when my world was falling apart. They helped me pay for my mom’s spine surgery. They kept us afloat when Senator Kinsley—Jules’ father—died and left us drowning in mountains of debt.
Every time I needed a miracle, Mama D used her connections to make it happen.
So, yeah, I owed them everything. Helping out was the least I could do. Whether it was inventory, or filling in when they needed someone to look pretty at a party, I was there. They were my safety net.
"And leave my mother alone with those six giants from hell? No way," I said, wrinkling my nose, "I have to be there for Jules. Someone has to make sure she doesn't accidentally become a mobster."
"Which of you were at the Gold Room two nights ago?" Mama D asked, clapping her hands to get our attention. "There’s a black car idling at the curb for you. A private request."
My heart did a weird little stutter, a cold prickle of sweat hitting the back of my neck. "A request? From who?"
"High-end client," Mama D said, "He sent cash up front just to get the car moving. He’s at some estate out in the woods called The Void."
Tasha and Brianna shared a look, then turned to Mama D.
"We were all there, Mama," Tasha said, stepping forward while adjusting her earring. "Me, Bri, and G. But Gianna is off duty tonight. She isn't on the books for house calls."
"Yeah," Bri added, nodding toward me. "The guy probably saw one of us. Send Tasha or me. We’re already dressed and ready to go."
Mama D looked at the thick envelope of cash in her hand, then back at the girls, "Fine. Go on then. I’ve already vetted the guy, well, his people. They gave their word you’ll come back untouched. If he just wants a Gold Room girl, one of you will do."
I watched them head for the door, and suddenly my heart hammered against my ribs.
He was there. My stepbrother. What if... what if he did recognize me? What if he was the one who sent that car?
No. That was impossible. I wore a mask, a wig, and the lighting was garbage.
"You okay, G?" Mama D asked, noticing my pale face.
"I'm fine," I lied, "Just... tired. I should get going. I need to get back before mum notice I'm missing."
I gripped my coat, my knuckles white, and stayed hidden in the shadows until I heard the low rumble of the car engine fade away. Tasha and Brianna were gone. I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding, leaning my forehead against the cool metal of the lockers.
I was safe.
Then, the world exploded.
The heavy front doors of the club didn’t just open, they hit the wall so hard that I jumped, my heart leaping into my throat.
"Where’s my money, Denise?" a voice boomed.
I peered around the corner. It was Cole Mercer. The leader of the Lake Street Reapers. He walked in swinging a heavy aluminum baseball bat. Behind him, four of his guys followed.
Smash.
Cole swung the bat, shattering a shelf of glass bottles behind the bar. Shards of crystal flew everywhere, raining down.
"The week is up!" Cole yelled, his eyes wide and manic. He stepped up to a table and flipped it over with one hand, the wood splintering, "I’m tired of waiting. This place looks busy. You've got my cut, or I start breaking legs."
Mama D stepped forward, her face was cold though I could see her fingers trembling, "Cole, stop. You're scaring the girls."
"I don't give a damn about their feelings!" he snapped, bringing the bat down on a chair, snapping the legs like toothpicks.
He walked over to where the girls were huddled. He stopped in front of Morgan. She was shaking so hard she could barely stand, her eyes huge and wet with tears. Cole leaned in close. He reached out and tangled his dirty fingers in her sleek black hair, pulling her head back.
"You're the new one, right?" he sneered, "Maybe if Denise doesn't have the cash, I just take you instead. We can find a way for you to pay the debt."
"Get your hands off her!" I snapped, stepping forward before I could talk myself out of it.
Cole turned his head, a slow, ugly smile spreading across his face, "Ah, the little scientist. You got something for me, G?"
Mama D rushed to her desk and pulled out a thick envelope, "Here! It’s all I have right now, Cole. Take it and leave."
Cole snatched the envelope, counted it quickly, and spat on the floor. "Seven? You owe me ten, Denise. You’re short."
He raised the bat again, eyeing a massive floor-to-ceiling mirror.
"Wait!" I shouted. I reached into my bag, pulling out the three thousand from the tip I received two nights ago. I walked over and slammed the stack of bills onto the bar, "There. Three thousand. That makes ten. Now leave us alone."
Cole picked up the cash, thumbing through it with a greasy smirk. He looked at me, then at the terrified girls. He stepped away from Morgan, finally letting go of her hair.
"Next time, don't make me come down here and break your toys," Cole said, pointing the bat at Mama D’s chest. "Next week, I want twelve. Interest for making me wait. Don't be late, or I’ll burn this Garden to the ground with all of you inside."
He laughed, a dry, hacking sound, and signaled his men. They kicked over one last lamp on their way out, leaving us in the flickering darkness.
Morgan collapsed into a chair, sobbing into her hands. I stood there, staring at my empty bag, my hands finally stopping their shake only to turn cold as ice.
"You didn't have to do that, G," Mama D whispered, "That was for you. You needed that for your college tuition. Your future."
I swallowed the lump in my throat and shook my head, not letting myself regret it for even a second. I walked straight over to Morgan, who was still trembling like a leaf, and pulled her small frame against my chest. I held her tight, letting her hide her face in my shoulder.
"I’ll figure it out, Mama," I said.
I smoothed back Morgan’s hair, feeling her tears soak into my shirt.
"Don't worry about the tuition, okay? We’ve got each other’s back. Always. Money comes and goes, but we're family. We’ll find a way to fix this. I promise."
I meant it, but as I looked at the wreckage of the room, I knew I was in deep.
My bank account was officially at zero, and my stomach felt like it was tied in knots. I had nothing left, no safety net, no backup plan, just the crushing weight of everything falling apart at once.
Chapter 4
Raphael
I leaned against the cold brick wall of the mansion, my arms crossed, watching the show. Our soldiers were busy dragging in the trash, fifty men, all bound at the wrists, their faces covered in bruises and tears. They were lined up like cattle ready for the slaughter.
This was the Hunt for the night, and the air already smelled like sweat and fear.
Adriano walked in behind them, looking entirely too casual. He had his hands shoved deep in his pockets, his expensive coat fluttering as he moved.
"The cells downstairs were getting a bit crowded," he said, his voice light, almost bored. "So I brought you fifty of the worst. Traitors, rats, and the kind of scum that touches people who can’t fight back. They’re all yours. Do whatever you want with them."
I didn't say a word. I just watched, my mind already calculating the thrill of the hunt.
Luca walked over and crouched down in front of one man who was shaking so hard his teeth were chattering. The second the man’s eyes met Luca’s, a dark, wet stain spread across his trousers. He literally pissed himself just from a look.
That made Luca smile. It wasn’t a normal smile, it was the kind of jagged, hateful expression that made your skin crawl. He looked more alive in this basement than he ever did at a family dinner.
"Is that the one?" I asked, my voice flat.
Luca didn't look back at me. He just kept staring at the man, his eyes dark and empty. "Yeah," he whispered, "This is the piece of trash who... did those things to his own son."
Just then, the heavy metal door groaned open. Dante walked in, looking annoyed as he tried to peel some girl off his arm. She was clinging to his sleeve like her life depended on it, but he just shoved her back toward the hall telling her something sweet to hold her off. He straightened his collar and strolled over to us, looking at the row of trembling men.
"What did I miss?" Dante asked, checking his watch. "The party started without me?"
I looked at the fifty men, then at my brothers. The night was young, and I had fifty different ways to make sure these men regretted ever being born.
"Just getting ready to play," I said.
I reached for the weapon resting on the table. It wasn't something you could just buy, I had spent months in my lab building it, piece by piece. It was an electronic bow, sleek and matte black, looking more like a piece of high-tech surgical equipment than a weapon. It was light as a feather but strong enough to put a hole through a brick wall.
I picked up one of the arrows. I had designed these myself, too. They weren't just sharp sticks, they were smart.
The tips were made of a special metal that didn't just pierce skin, the moment they hit a target, they sent a massive electrical surge straight to the heart.
I’d programmed them to track heat, so once I locked on, there was no running away. If I fired, the arrow did the thinking for me. It didn't matter how fast these men ran or where they tried to hide in the dark. My arrows would find them, and the last thing they’d feel was a thousand volts of my own personal brand of justice.
"Take them to the back," I ordered.
I gestured toward the massive floor-to-ceiling glass walls that looked out into the blackness. Behind the mansion lay the heart of our estate, acres and acres of thick forest.
It was our own private playground, a kingdom of pain where the rules of the world didn't exist.
The soldiers started grabbing the men by their collars, dragging them toward the heavy steel doors.
"Make sure they understand the map," I added, a small, dark smirk playing on my lips, "There is no exit. The entire forest is wrapped in ten feet of electrified barbed wire. The only way out of those woods is back through this house. And to get through this house, they have to get past us."
I watched the realization hit the prisoners. Their eyes went wide as they looked at the dark treeline. It wasn't just a forest, it was a cage. A massive, beautiful, green cage. They could run until their lungs burned and their feet bled, but they would always be trapped inside our world.
"Give them a five-minute head start," I told Adriano, "I want them to feel like they have a chance. I want their hearts to be pumping fast. It makes the sensors on my arrows lock on much better."
The thrill of the hunt, the power of the tech, and the absolute control over fifty lives. To most people, this was a nightmare. To me, it was the only time I truly felt like a god.
The heavy stone back terrace was crowded with the kind of men who ruled the world from glass skyscrapers.
These weren't just random guys, they were the heirs, the CEOs, the sons of senators, they were the guys I’d gone to Ivy League schools with, the ones I traded stocks with, and the ones who sat across from me in high-stakes boardrooms.
"Raphael," a voice called out. It was Julian, the son of a tech mogul I’d helped take over a competitor last year. He adjusted the night-vision goggles on his head, a glass of expensive bourbon in his other hand, "I heard you updated the software on the perimeter sensors. Please tell me the 'no-kill zone' near the wire is gone. I want to see them hit the electricity this time."
I didn't even look up from my bow. "I fixed it, Julian. If they touch the fence, they’ll light up like a Christmas tree. Try not to miss this time."
A few of the guys laughed, these men weren't here for a gala or a charity auction. They were here for the high that only the Capones could provide. We had grown up together, gone to the same elite schools, and now we shared the same dark secrets.
"The entry f^e is paid?" I asked, not looking at them as I calibrated the touch-screen on my bow.
"Every cent, Raphael," one of them, a billionaire's son with a cruel glint in his eyes replied, "And the side bets are already at ten million for the first kill."
I looked out at the fifty shadows running into the treeline. My screen flickered to life, showing fifty small, pulsing heat signatures.
"The rules are simple," I said, my voice cutting through the excited deep voices of the men, "The forest is a closed loop. If they reach the wire, they die. If they stay still, they die. The only way they 'win' is if they make it back to the mansion basement before the sun comes up."
I paused, a cold, sharp smile stretching across my face.
"But I’ve never had a winner."
The men around me laughed, they gripped their weapons, high-end rifles and crossbows, waiting for my signal.
I’m the one who provided the playground for their darkest desires, the one who turned a boring Friday night into a hunt that would be whispered about in boardrooms for months.
"Five minutes are up," I whispered, flicking the safety off my bow, "The Void is open. Happy fvcking hunting, gentlemen."

Her own father shot her through the heart and killed her. 
All because she wanted freedom. That was all she had asked for in twenty-eight years of service as the best assassin.
He had taken her in as a child with nothing. Built her into the most dangerous instrument he had and aimed her at everything that needed to be destroyed. She killed for him.
She learned piano so she could sit beside his targets at concerts. She learned to cook so she could infiltrate their kitchens. She mastered hacking, marksmanship, combat, five languages, and field surgery.
She gave him everything. One mission more, he promised. Then she would finally be free.
So she completed it. Twelve guards, one drug lord. She killed them all. Bleeding in the silent plaza, she heard clapping. 
Amos Joyce, her godfather, stepped over the bodies in a perfect suit. "twenty-eight years," he said. "You worked so hard." 
"Yes, sir. Now it is time for me to leave," she said with a genuine smile on her face. He sighed. 
"Yeah, time to leave this world… my child!"
Before she could react to what he said, a gunshot rang out. 
The heat tore through her chest before her brain caught up. She looked down.
A dark stain bloomed from her heart and spread fast, unstoppable, absolute. Her legs gave out. She hit the flagstones on her knees and watched him draw the handkerchief from his pocket and wipe a trace of blood from his cheek with it. "Goodbye, Evelyn."
So, that was what twenty-eight years was worth. She wanted a life of her own, but her reward for loyalty was death. Or so she thought….
Nine hundred miles away, at the exact moment she closed her eyes for the last time, a twenty one-year-old actress named Evelyn Hawthorne was being held underwater from behind.
She was an excellent swimmer. Everyone agreed on that…..
She had gone into the water at a private villa party willingly and confidently, the way good swimmers go into water.
Someone had kept both hands on her efficiently, calmly, until the fighting stopped. The scratch marks along their arm told the real story. The alibi told a different one. The defibrillator fired.
The line stayed flat. They increased the power, fired again, a twitch, then another, then a rhythm, uncertain at first, steadying into something that would hold. The room breathed out. But the soul that opened its eyes in that hospital bed was not the one the doctors had been fighting to save. It was hers.
The first thing she did when she opened her eyes was take a hostage. She had no memory of where she was. The ceiling was wrong. The body was wrong, soft-armed and pale. A stranger's hands at the ends of her arms. Her instincts had no interest in that distinction.
She yanked the IV needle free, grabbed the nearest person by the hair, and pressed the sharp end against his carotid artery. "Don't move if you want to live," she rasped. The man she had pinned, Ethan Hawthorne, though she didn't know his name yet, went completely still, reflexively, correctly. The older man across the room raised both hands without being asked.
She scanned the room. Hospital, no guards, no weapons beyond the needle she was holding. Two men, no military bearing, no threat posture, but good instincts, both of them. And they were looking at her with an expression she was unaccustomed to receiving. It took her a moment to identify it. It was grief.
A door opened. Nurses, a doctor, the ordinary machinery of a medical response. A firm-handed older nurse marched over and guided her back onto the mattress before she'd fully processed a counter move. She let her. She needed time to assess. The doctor found nothing wrong with her head. Possible disorientation from oxygen deprivation, he said. Short-term memory disruption. The family should be patient and gentle. So she sat and let them be patient. She catalogued what she had. A name — Evelyn Hawthorne — and a face that stared back at her from the window glass like a stranger's reflection. Pale, wide-eyed, fragile in a way she had never been in any life she remembered. The older man was Richard Hawthorne, the father. The young man whose hair she'd pulled was Ethan, the brother. There was a mother who had fainted in the hallway and been put to bed in the next room. There was significant money, the quiet, embedded kind, that showed itself in the quality of everything around it.
She told them she had amnesia. It wasn't entirely a lie. She knew nothing about the life she had just inherited, and she was not ready to explain the one she had left behind. She used the phone carefully. One search, two words. Amos Joyce. Top result, California governor's race. The man credited with organizing the takedown of a major drug cartel had jumped five points in the polls overnight. His numbers were still climbing. There was a photo of him shaking hands with federal agents in front of a seized shipment. He was smiling. He was celebrating. Somewhere in the world she had just left behind, Amos Joyce was celebrating a mission that she had died completing — a mission he'd sent her on, knowing exactly what he was going to do when she finished it.
She set the phone down. She had no weapons, no money of her own, no connections in this life. The body she was occupying had soft hands, weak arms, and a public reputation that could be summarized by the comment she found in the first ten minutes of scrolling her social media. "I'm tired of hating on Evelyn Hawthorne every day. From now on, I'll just carve the insults on her tombstone." She had forty-thousand followers across all platforms combined, and the positive ones had been purchased by her family's PR budget. Amos Joyce was the governor-elect of California. He had resources she couldn't imagine from where she was sitting. But she had time, and she had every skill he had spent twenty-eight years forcing her to build.
She picked the phone back up and kept reading. The woman who had drowned Evelyn Hawthorne was named Cassidy Reed. She was an actress, a real one. Actual credits, actual fans, the kind of industry position that felt solid until you understood whose protection was underneath it. 
Her protector was a woman named Scarlett Vance, her superior, the daughter of a family so embedded in military and political infrastructure that her name appeared in no press coverage at all, which was itself a kind of power. Cassidy had held Evelyn Hawthorne underwater from behind, face hidden, hands steady, until the fighting stopped. She'd had reasons. Evelyn had witnessed something at the villa she shouldn't have. When the paramedics arrived and shocked Evelyn back to life, Cassidy had already confirmed with the right people that no one had seen anything. The kayak and wet suit were gone. The alibi held. But Evelyn Hawthorne had survived.
Scarlett’s response when Cassidy reported this was careful and unhurried. "Test her. If she has genuine amnesia, she's no threat. If not, let me know before she becomes one." Cassidy passed the message along and lit a cigarette. 
A watch was placed on her before she left the hospital. She didn't know that yet. What she knew was that she had nearly drowned, that the police report called it accidental, and that the woman at whose villa it happened had walked out of the hospital the moment the flatline became a pulse without looking back. She filed that away, and she kept reading.
She had one month before filming began, and she used every hour of it that she could take without attracting attention. She ran before the household woke up — four miles, then five, then six as the weeks progressed — and this body began to remember what bodies were capable of when asked seriously. 
The family's chef received a new meal plan: two eggs, half a pound of beef, a large glass of whole milk, and a high-protein salad at every main meal. Her mother and sister stared at the portions across the breakfast table as if she had developed a second personality, which, in the most literal sense available, she had. The family thought the original Evelyn was preparing for a television show. They were not wrong. They simply didn't understand what she was preparing for.
In the quiet hours, she worked on other things. Ethan's company had suffered a sophisticated cyber attack while she was still in the hospital. Someone on the inside had leaked defense protocols to an external actor and the damage was significant. 
She fixed it overnight from the computer system she'd had installed in her room. Patched the vulnerabilities, embedded a new defensive core that could write its own countermeasures in real time, and while she was already inside the architecture, cleaned up a constellation of legacy bugs that the tech department had been collectively afraid to touch for years because they couldn't predict the cascade failure risk. Ethan received a call from his tech director at five in the morning saying that the company's security system had apparently upgraded itself overnight and the app was running ten times faster. 
Meanwhile, she studied the other contestants. Kyle was the one to take seriously. Solo expeditions in the Amazon, months alone in the Gobi Desert, survival records that read like field operations reports rather than adventure travel. Maya Sutton was a decorated competitive athlete. Cody Nash moved through terrain the way people move through rooms. 
Any of the three of them, in a real survival situation, would be a resource. The mystery guest was Julian Donovan. He returned from studying abroad five days before filming launched, walking through the airport in sunglasses and a mask, an entourage of eight behind him. Security footage she found online showed him stopping in front of the promo poster for the show. 
He looked at each photo in turn. He stopped at hers for a moment that was longer than the others, though not long enough to draw conclusions from, and then moved on without a word. His manager was quoted in a fan account shortly after: "If you must do this show, stay as far from Evelyn Hawthorne as you can. She's a walking disaster." Julian's reported response was a slow smile. "She'll learn to stay out of my way." She read that, set the phone down, and thought about it. Interesting.

September sixteenth. The show launched at eight-o-clock in the evening, but the cameras started rolling that morning. 
The production crew collected every phone before they boarded the bus. She didn't argue. She had already studied everything she needed.
On the bus, the host made the introductions. Each of them waved at the camera. The comment section under her personal live channel — three-lakh viewers, most of them there to see her fail — sent a wave of vomiting emojis when she smiled.
She assessed the other contestants without appearing to. Kyle gave nothing away at all, a blank antisocial stillness that she found instantly reassuring because it was the posture of a man who didn't need anyone else and knew it. 
Maya and Kyle were barely containing excitement. Boone, in a blindingly orange jacket, was trying very hard not to be seen looking at her. Then the partition rose between the driver's cabin and the passenger section. 
The host and camera crew pulled on gas masks. A thick white mist hissed from the back of the bus. Everyone around her was unconscious within ninety seconds. She had taken a full breath the moment she saw the host reach for his mask. She had held it. She had let her body go completely limp and played dead while the production medics checked her pupils with a pen light and found nothing but a convincingly insensible actress. They tied her wrists, blindfolded her, and loaded her into a separate vehicle. She slowed her breathing, kept her face slack, and let the genuine thrill of anticipation rise through her chest. This show was already more interesting than she'd expected.
They untied her after they placed her. She heard the vehicle leave. She waited until the engine noise was fully absorbed by the trees. Then she opened her eyes and took inventory. One backpack, a pop-up tent, a lighter, disinfectant wipes, a water bladder, two protein bars — the barest possible start. She noted what she didn't have and began moving. 
Two million people were watching her personal live feed through cameras hidden in the trees and brush around her. She was aware of the cameras. She factored them in the way she factored in any variable she couldn't remove — as a constraint to work around, not a problem to solve. The operators were good at staying hidden. She'd seen enough surveillance equipment deployed in the field to recognize the signs of professional concealment. She gave them the acknowledgement of not acknowledging them and got to work.
The first thing she needed was water. She found a stream within the hour, small, clear, threading between smooth stones, fed from the mountain above. She checked the current, traced it downstream, found a bend with flat ground, and began setting up camp. She built the fire with controlled airflow and minimum smoke.
The viewers watching, she learned much later, couldn't quite reconcile what they were seeing. The actress who had been publicly mocked for years, the internet's favorite punching bag, the girl they'd shown up to watch fail — was moving through the wilderness like she'd been there her entire life. They kept watching.
She was already thinking about food. Her stomach had been growling for two hours when she found the solution. 
The rabbit burrow announced itself to anyone who knew how to listen. The grass along the approach path was worn thin and angled in a consistent direction. The tunnel entrance was oriented correctly — uphill, sheltered from the prevailing wind. The size and depth of the tracks told her she was working with an adult animal, healthy and well-fed. She pulled the drawstring from her jacket hood — three feet of strong cord — and tied it into a slip knot that required a very specific understanding of load distribution and release dynamics to get right. 
The kind of knowledge you accumulated after someone stood over you in the rain and made you restart from the beginning every time the tension was wrong.
She set the snare on the rabbit's uphill path home, propped it with a Y-shaped branch cut from the thicket, ran a trigger line back to a tree she climbed to wait in.
The viewers on her live feed had been drifting away for twenty minutes. She didn't move. Twenty minutes, thirty. The forest breathed around her. Then she heard footsteps and voices. Julian Donovan and Boone were walking directly through her setup, arguing about cryptids. The rabbit bolted from the noise they made straight down its path and directly into the snare. She yanked the rope from twelve feet up. The slip knot cinched clean around its hind legs. The animal dropped to the ground.
Aiden screamed. He launched himself off the earth with the full body commitment of a man who had decided something large and prehistoric had just attacked him, and he grabbed Julian around the shoulders with the grip of a drowning person finding something to hold. Julian's face went through five distinct expressions before settling on one that could most charitably be described as trapped. Trapped, and also developing a headache.
She slid down from the tree with the rabbit. "It's a rabbit," Julian said to no one in particular. Then, louder: "You can jump that high? You should have been an athlete." Aiden said he had tried but hadn't passed the exam. He said it with genuine earnestness.
She looked at the two of them and made the calculation. Three was harder to manage than one, but both of them had zero survivable options alone in this terrain, and she had already decided somewhere in the last few seconds that she was responsible for them whether she'd agreed to it or not. She kept the rabbit. She kept them, too.

They ate better that night than either of them had expected. The rabbit was gutted, rubbed down with Hawthorne Foods seasoning she'd brought in her pack — a brand partnership she had inherited from the original Evelyn, along with the contract, the deposit, and the complete online reputation — and roasted over a fire she built with controlled airflow and minimum smoke. Julian ate more than half of it without speaking for the first ten minutes. Aiden ate whatever Julian left and kept making small involuntary sounds of gratitude.
After dinner, Aiden fell asleep immediately. Julian held on longer, fighting exhaustion the way overtired people do when their nervous system can't distinguish between tired and threatened. His breathing was uneven, his eyelids working overtime. There had been a spider incident earlier in the day. He wouldn't tell her the details, but the effect on his nervous system was obvious. She gave him twenty minutes to sleep on his own. He didn't. She told him she could help. He covered the back of his neck with both hands immediately. "I'm afraid of pain," he said. "Have you been watching too many action movies?" she said. He considered this. “Probably.” She told him to lie down.
He lay with his head facing out of the shelter, eyes turned up. She squatted at the entrance and held her right hand above his face — index finger first, then middle, ring, pinky — a slow, continuous wave that she kept perfectly even. The kind of technique she'd used on injured teammates in the field who couldn't quiet their own thoughts enough to lose consciousness. You needed to be steady. You needed to clear your own head entirely while you did it, so there was nothing in the motion but the motion itself. Julian's eyes stayed open for ninety three seconds. Then they didn't. He was in deep, even sleep within two minutes.
The comment section, she was told later, went briefly and completely silent. And then the messages began flooding back in. “
What kind of actress knows how to do this?”
“ What is she?”
“ I need to know everything about this woman immediately.”
She adjusted the backpack she'd set beside him so Aiden's feet couldn't reach his head during the night. She added sticks to the fire and listened to the forest.
Three hours later, the drone arrived. She had been waiting for the drone. She had worked out within the first hours of the show that the production crew would send missions this way — midnight drops, dramatic timing, no warning, just the hum of rotors through dark trees. Supplies, task cards, a contained moment that the viewers would find thrilling. She had prepared for it the moment Aiden and Julian fell asleep. She rolled her jacket tight around a fist-sized stone she'd set aside that afternoon and waited by the fire.
When the drone hovered directly above the campsite and its camera found her face, she looked up at it and smiled. The production director, watching from the mobile command center, said afterward that the smile was immediately recognizable as the same one he'd seen before she robbed the squirrel. He lunged for the walkie-talkie. Too late.
She swung the jacket in a long, powerful arc overhead and released it. The weighted end hit the drone's rotors with the flat crack of a stone on water. The machine lurched sideways, tipping hard. She was already moving — three bounding steps, a foot planted against a tree trunk, launched upward, caught a branch at fifteen feet, bolted higher, and snatched the falling drone out of the air with both hands before it could strike the ground. The camera steadied. A completely calm face filled the operator's monitor. "Thanks for the drone," she said. "Don't mind if I do."
Aiden's voice woke Julian. Julian said later that he'd slept more soundly than he had in years. He lay on his back for a few seconds, registered the canvas above him, registered that he was in the wilderness, and then looked at the pile of components on the ground with the expression of a man encountering something that required a moment before responding. "You took it apart," he said. "The propellers can be sharpened into knives," she said without looking up from what she was working on. "The motor rods become tent supports, fishing spears, or grill skewers. The camera lens will concentrate sunlight for fire starting when the lighter runs out. The landing struts are grill material. The signal wire can be braided into a stronger rope. The battery housing is waterproof storage." He stared at her. "You knew they were going to send it," he said. She didn't answer.
He sat down across the fire from her. He was quiet for a long time. And during that quiet, she noticed the thing she had started noticing the night before. The cool, performative distance he carried as reflexively as other people carried keys was giving way to something more honest underneath. Something that looked like a man discovering that a problem he'd thought he understood was considerably more complex than he'd assumed. When he asked how she knew any of this, she told him, "Books.".
She went hunting because she was hungry and because she needed to think. She came back to camp with five quail tied to her belt, the snake hanging from one hand by its tail, a bag of eggs cushioned in her pack, and foraging pouches full enough to make a real meal.
Julian looked at everything she was carrying and did not speak for a moment. Then she handed him the snake reflexively, the way she would have passed equipment to a teammate. And he took it before he'd registered what it was. He looked at it, he looked at her, and then Julian Donovan — a man who had been composed on camera for the better part of a decade — screamed and flung it away from himself with full body revulsion, frantically wiping his hands on his pants, his voice loud enough to startle birds out of the canopy above. Aiden refused to come down from his rock for eight minutes.
"Does your agent have your voice insured?" she asked Julian when he'd managed to stop making sounds. "With a scream like that, you'll blow your vocal cords." "Why didn't you warn me?" he said. "I assumed it was obvious what I was holding," she said. "It's a headless snake," he said. She considered this. "Yes."
She built the grill from the drone — six landing struts, eight propeller blades repurposed as skewers, the whole structure over a fire pit she dug to manage airflow. The quail went on first. Quail eggs into the stainless steel bowl from the supply package, Mushrooms on separate skewers brushed with barbecue sauce. The snake for her, over the hottest part of the flame.
Julian ate two whole quail without speaking for the first ten minutes. Aiden ate everything else and kept producing small sounds of involuntary gratitude that he seemed unable to suppress. Neither of them mentioned the snake. She watched them from across the fire and thought: this is genuinely the strangest thing she had ever done. In twenty-eight years of covers, she had cooked for drug lords, arms dealers, and politicians in kitchens that cost more than most houses. She had always been performing a function — gathering intelligence, building access, making herself useful to someone who would eventually need to be taken apart. No one had ever looked at her food the way these two were looking at it. With uncomplicated happiness. With the straightforward gratitude of people who had simply been hungry and been fed.
Julian set down a finished quail bone and looked at her across the fire. "I had you completely wrong before this show," he said. "I know," she said. He held her gaze. The expression on his face was one she had started cataloging — the cool, practiced distance that came with his level of celebrity slowly giving way to something more genuine underneath. The look of someone who had encountered a significant discrepancy between their model of a situation and the actual data, and was deciding quietly, and without announcing it, to take the discrepancy seriously.
He came from money — the kind that showed itself not in what he spent but in the automatic expectation that the world would arrange itself appropriately around him. He had spent years under a degree of public scrutiny that would have hollowed most people out, and he had learned to operate within it with the self-containment of someone who decided early that exposure was more dangerous than distance. He was, in most observable ways, the opposite of Aiden, who generated noise and warmth and nervous chatter with the emotional transparency of someone who had never learned to hide anything because he'd never needed to.
Julian was watching her the way she watched targets — methodically, carefully, filing details rather than reacting to them. He had noticed the calluses on her hands. She had seen the moment he noticed. He hadn't said anything. He had kept eating and kept watching. And somewhere behind those watchful eyes, he was quietly running an inventory of everything since the show began. The squirrel, the snare, the drone, the hypnosis, the snake, the grill assembled from components no actor should have known how to repurpose. He was building a picture. He wasn't close to the actual answer yet. And the actual answer was one she had no intention of giving him. But he was the kind of person who kept looking until he found something. She added a stick to the fire and changed the subject. He let her.

The mission card called it the outfitter's cabin. The task: reach a remote structure before sunset. Persuade the owner to surrender a map and a fortune. Simple reality show theater. The kind of challenge designed to feel difficult while being safely contained. The kind of thing she would have worked out in thirty seconds on any mission briefing. But she had already been working something else out.
"How do you think a place gets a name like the wilderness?" she said. Aiden and Julian looked at each other. "Boars," Julian said after a moment. "A lot of boars," she confirmed. "The name is the warning. The production crew scouted this forest and found animals that were actually dangerous. So they built the warning into the brief in a way that passes as atmosphere. We move in the afternoon window. We move efficiently. We make no noise after dark. The animals are real."
Aiden's pace picked up immediately. She was right about most of it. She was not right about the cabin.
The chemical stench hit her the moment she stepped through the door. Not decay, not old wood or mildew. Something sharper, specific. She knew that smell the way she knew the smell of cordite — involuntarily, permanently, coded into memory before conscious thought had a chance to process it. The smell of pharmaceutical precursors being cooked under inadequate ventilation. The pots and pans stacked under a military green tarp in the corner. The haphazard pile of containers along the far wall. The syringe she'd spotted in the grass outside before entering and kicked under a pile of fallen leaves before the cameras caught it.
This was an active drug production site. Not a historic one, not a cleaned-out shell of a former operation. The equipment under the tarp was recent. The chemical smell was current. The syringe she'd spotted in the grass outside had not been there long enough to rust. The production crew had done their location scout without understanding what they were standing in. They had brought seven contestants and a live feed broadcasting to two million viewers into the operational territory of a working criminal organization, and they had no idea. They had filed the location permits, arranged the hidden camera network, designed the treasure hunt, and walked entirely past the evidence of what the cabin was actually being used for. They were guests at a drug operation's main site, and the people who ran that operation would eventually come back to check on it.
She processed this in approximately three seconds. She stood in the doorway and looked like a girl who was simply surprised by a gruff man with a theatrical prop. Chase, locally sourced by the production crew, good stage presence, had been given instructions to be difficult and entertaining. He was doing his job. What was in the corner under the tarp was not part of anyone's job description.
Chase jabbed the handle at her. "Turn around and leave." She was thinking about the tarp, about the syringe, about the distance between this cabin and the nearest access road, and what kind of people chose this location for this purpose, and how far away they currently were. Chase jabbed the handle again. One problem at a time.
She shot forward — left hand on the end of the handle, right hand coming down in a short, sharp chop across Chase's wrist. The nerve pathway she'd struck sent a spike of numbness through his entire hand. His fingers opened. The handle hit the floor. Before his expression had finished registering surprise, it was in her hands. Chase stared. Julian stared. Aiden, in the doorway behind her, stared.
She looked down at the hardwood in her hands. Dense, well-made. The kind of material that didn't flex when you directed force through it correctly. "Persuade," she said calmly. "Fine." She gripped it with both hands, planted her feet, and drove her palms toward each other in opposite directions. The crack filled the cabin like a rifle shot. The handle broke into two clean halves. She set them both down on the floor.
The room was absolutely silent. The comment section, she was told later, recorded five seconds of dead air before anyone typed anything. What broke the silence was someone's attempt to describe what they just watched. She just — she just snapped it like a twig. What?
"Was that persuasive enough?" she said, looking at Chase. "Are you going to give us the supplies?" Chase gave them everything.
And she stood in the doorway holding a bottle of water that one of the show's actors had just handed her, thinking about the smell under the tarp and the number of people who would eventually come back to check on their operation.
Something was wrong with the production crew's signal. She noticed it in their movement first. Small tells — camera operators making eye contact with each other in the way people do when they've received instructions they aren't sharing. Two of them excused themselves from their area within twenty minutes of each other. A walkie-talkie crackled and was immediately muffled. Chase eventually explained what he'd been told. Two contestants, Maya Sutton and Cody Nash, had gone off course after disturbing a hornet's nest. Their personal tracking signals were offline. The production crew was mobilising a full search, and to cover the range required, they needed to move the satellite vehicle.
The satellite vehicle. Everything on the set ran through that truck — the live feed, the camera network, the GPS trackers, the entire remote monitoring system. The moment it moved beyond effective range of their sector, every camera in the area would lose its network connection. The broadcast would go dark. The viewers at home would see static and a message asking for their patience. They would be invisible. They would be unreachable. They would be entirely on their own.
She heard the diesel engine of the satellite truck turn over somewhere beyond the tree line. She processed what that meant before the sound had fully faded. No satellite feed meant no camera network. No camera network meant no live broadcast. No live broadcast meant no witnesses. It meant no one watching from the outside could see what happened next. It meant the production crew's search team, wherever they were in the forest, was operating in a communications dead zone that was about to get worse. It meant that if something went wrong in this cabin, the evidence of it would only exist if someone inside the cabin survived to report it.

She did not react. She kept her face steady and asked Chase to locate the remaining water bottles, because that was exactly what an actress on a reality show would ask in that moment. A girl worried about supplies. A girl who had no idea that the situation she was standing in had just undergone a fundamental change in character. Inside, she was counting the distance to the nearest road, the time between now and full dark, and the variables she still didn't have numbers for.
The feed had been stuttering for twenty-two minutes. The comment section, visible later in a compilation someone made from screenshots, had descended into a particular flavour of chaos.
 “Is the production crew's Wi-Fi powered by a hamster on a wheel?”
“Something's happening. Why isn't anyone saying anything?”
 “I'm switching between streams, and they're all going bad at the same time. Someone just knocked.”
 “Did anyone catch that?”
She heard the knock before anyone could say a word.
Three sharp raps on the wood. Not a contestant. Not a crew member coming to check on them. The knock was deliberate.Confident. Like whoever was outside already knew exactly who was inside.
And Evelyn knew that knock.
Her face changed.
She immediately warned everyone, “Stop. Don’t open it.”
Who was standing outside?
Had Amos Joyce found her?
And if he had…
How did he know Evelyn was still alive?
