My new 25-year-old neighbor was trying to seduce my 55-year-old husband. She'd just divorced a man twice her age, won his house in court, and moved in next door. I decided to teach her a lesson she'd never forget.

I taught her one. It just wasn't the one I planned.

Her name was Kayla. She moved in next door in April.

I know how that sounds. The jealous older wife, threatened by the young woman on the block. Trust me — I've been married thirty years. I don't get rattled by a pretty face. My husband Greg is 55. I'm 52. We built something real and I have never once worried about it.

Until Kayla.

She moved into the Hendersons' old place after their divorce. Won the house off a man twice her age — that was the story on the street, anyway. Showed up with a U-Haul, a spray tan, and a German Shepherd she walked three times a day in shorts that barely qualified as fabric.

I noticed her the first week because she waved at Greg while he was mowing. Not a neighbor wave. A wave. The kind where you hold eye contact two seconds too long and let your hand drift down slow.

Greg didn't wave back. He's not that guy. Thirty years and the man has never given me a reason.

But she kept going.

Week two, she was at our door with a plate of brownies. "Just wanted to introduce myself!" Looking past me the entire time. Scanning the house for Greg. He was in the garage. She knew that, because she'd seen his truck in the driveway.

Week three, she started asking him for help. The kitchen faucet. A shelf that needed mounting. The garbage disposal. Always something that required him to be inside her house, alone, while she stood too close and laughed at things that weren't funny.

I told my sister Denise about it on the phone one night.

"She's testing you," Denise said. "She wants to see how much you'll take before you snap."

"I'm not going to snap."

"Good. That's what she wants. She wants drama. Don't give it to her."

I didn't. I watched. I waited. I kept my mouth shut and paid attention.

Then came the pipe.

Tuesday night, after ten. Greg and I were watching TV and his phone buzzed. He frowned at the screen.

"Kayla says she's got a burst pipe. Water everywhere."

"Call her a plumber."

"It's ten o'clock, Connie."

"That's not our problem."

He looked at me. I looked at him. He's a good man — that's the thing about Greg. He can't hear that somebody needs help and just sit there. It's one of the reasons I married him. It's also the reason I wanted to kill him in that moment.

"I'll be twenty minutes."

He was gone for forty-five.

When he came back he didn't look at me. Went straight to the bathroom, washed his hands, came to bed without a word.

I waited until the lights were off.

"Was there a pipe?"

Long silence.

"There was a pipe. I fixed it."

"And?"

"And she came out of her bedroom in a towel. Said she wanted to change while I was working and forgot I was there."

"She forgot."

"Connie."

"She forgot that the man she texted at ten o'clock at night was standing in her kitchen. She forgot."

"I left. Immediately. Nothing happened."

I believed him. Greg doesn't lie — the man goes red trying to fib about eating the last of the ice cream.

But something cracked open in me that night. Not jealousy. Something older. Something territorial. I'd spent thirty years building a life with this man and some 25-year-old thought she could walk in and rearrange it because she had a tight body and no shame.

I didn't sleep. I lay in the dark and I built a plan.

Not a confrontation — confrontation is what she wanted. The hysterical older wife on her doorstep, making a scene, proving she had power. No. I wanted something cleaner. Something that would strip her bare in front of the entire block so everyone could see exactly who she was.

It took me three weeks.

I started by getting friendly, which was the hardest part. Smiling in the driveway. Complimenting her garden. Accepting her invitation for coffee one afternoon while Greg was at work — sitting in the kitchen where my husband had stood fixing her pipe, drinking her coffee, nodding in all the right places.

I learned three things about Kayla that afternoon. She was vain. She was careless. And she talked about men — other women's husbands, on this block — like items on a shelf she hadn't decided whether to pick up.

I used all three.

I won't go through every detail, because this story turns out not to be about Kayla. Short version: I organized a block party. Fourth of July weekend. Everyone on the street. I spent two weeks on it — the food, the decorations, the speakers in the Millers' driveway.

And two days before, I used Greg's phone to send Kayla a text.

Not from me. From Greg.

I sat on the edge of our bed and typed four sentences I knew he'd never write. Asked her to meet him at the side of the Millers' garage during the party — 8 PM, after dark — because he "couldn't stop thinking about what almost happened."

My hands were steady. Not nerves. Satisfaction.

Greg never sent that text. He never knew about it. I deleted it from his phone the moment it went. But Kayla didn't know that.

At 8:05 PM on the Fourth of July, Kayla came around the side of the Millers' garage in a dress that left very little to the imagination, expecting to find my husband alone.

Instead she found me, Deborah Miller, Joyce Kwan from across the street, and six other women from the block, standing in a semicircle with their arms crossed.

I didn't say anything cruel. I didn't need to.

"Kayla. I think you have the wrong house."

Her face went white. She looked at that semicircle — every wife on the street — and she understood. Not just that I'd set her up. That every woman there already knew. The faucet. The shelf. The disposal. The towel. All of it.

She didn't say a word. Turned around and walked home. The Shepherd was barking through the window. Fireworks starting up two streets over.

Joyce leaned in and whispered, "That is the most satisfying thing I have seen in twenty years on this street."

For about ten seconds, I felt it. The vindication. The righteousness. The wife who didn't just protect her own marriage but every marriage on the block.

Then I walked back to the party to find Greg.

His chair was empty.

The plate I'd made him was on the armrest, untouched. His beer on the ground beside it, warm, barely sipped.

I scanned the yard. Dave was at the grill. The Kwans were handing out sparklers. Everybody was there.

Except my husband.

I found him at home, on the back porch, in the old wicker chair. No beer. No phone. Just sitting in the dark with the fireworks going off over the neighbor's roof.

I sat down next to him.

"You okay?"

He didn't answer right away.

"Con, can I ask you something and you not take it wrong?"

"Okay."

"You've spent the last month getting ready for that woman." He wasn't angry. That was the worst part. "Planning. Setting things up. Getting your hair done for a block party."

"Greg—"

"When's the last time you got ready for me?"

I opened my mouth and nothing came out.

"I'm not — I'm not accusing you of anything. I'm just telling you what I noticed." He was quiet a second. "You used to smell like something. In the morning. I'd walk past the bathroom door and I'd know you were in there before I saw you. It was just — you. That was a thing in this house."

He turned and looked at me.

"I couldn't tell you when that stopped. But it's been a while."

The fireworks kept going. I sat there in the dark next to the man I'd just spent a month defending, and something dropped through the floor of my stomach.

Because he was right.

I hadn't stopped caring about my husband. I'd stopped arriving. Somewhere in the last three or four years I'd become a woman who got dressed instead of a woman who got ready, and I had not noticed the difference, and he had.

I'd spent a month running surveillance on a 25-year-old in a sundress to protect my marriage from a threat outside my house.

And the thing actually draining out of it had been happening in my own bathroom, every single morning, for years.

Some protector.

Here's the part I have to be honest about, because it's the part that actually matters.

I hadn't quit out of laziness. And I hadn't quit because I'd stopped wanting my husband to look at me.

I quit because it stopped working.

There are six bottles on my dresser. I counted them that night after Greg went to bed, sitting on the floor of my own bedroom like a lunatic. Six bottles in five years. Two of them still in the box.

Every one of them followed the exact same arc.

I'd stand at the counter. The girl in the black apron would spray the little paper strip and wave it and tell me to let it open up. And it would be gorgeous under those lights. I'd hand over the card — eighty dollars, a hundred and ten, a hundred and forty for the last one.

And every one of them was dead by lunch.

I said the same sentence to that girl every time. Different store, different year, same sentence:

"The last one just didn't last on me. I think it's my chemistry."

I apologized to a nineteen-year-old for my own skin. More than once.

You don't keep doing a thing that gives you nothing back. Not for five years. Eventually you stop reaching for the bottle, and then you stop noticing you've stopped, and then one night your husband tells you he can't remember the last time the bathroom smelled like you.

That's how it actually happens. It isn't neglect. It's attrition.

I called Denise the next night. Not about Kayla — I didn't even mention Kayla. I told her what Greg said on the porch. Word for word.

Long silence.

Then: "Connie. That's me. That was me four years ago."

"What?"

"All of it. The bottles I stopped touching. Buying a new one every year like this one's going to be different. Bill saying something offhand about how I used to wear perfume, and me sitting in the car afterward feeling like somebody'd read my diary."

"How'd you fix it?"

"I found out why it was happening. And Connie — I was so angry when I found out, because it took me about ten minutes on the internet, and not one person at any counter in twenty-five years had ever told me."

"Told you what?"

"Those bottles are mostly alcohol. Sixty to eighty percent. Most of what you paid a hundred and forty dollars for is alcohol."

"Why?"

"Because it's cheap, and because it projects. It throws the scent into the air hard for the first few minutes. Which is exactly the four minutes you're standing at that counter with your card out."

"And then?"

"And then it evaporates. That's all alcohol does. It's the entire nature of the stuff. And when it lifts off your skin it doesn't leave alone — it drags the perfume out with it. The florals first, then the middle, then whatever's underneath. So it isn't that your perfume faded, Con. It got carried off. By the ingredient that was most of the bottle."

I sat down at the kitchen table.

"There's a second half," she said, "and this is the part that made me want to put my head through a wall. Your skin makes less oil as you get older. Starts in your thirties, keeps going. And once the alcohol's gone, an alcohol fragrance needs your skin's own oil to hold onto."

"Less oil."

"Less oil, faster fade. Which means the exact same bottle that lasted you all day at 28 is gone by eleven at 52. It isn't in your head and it isn't your imagination."

"So when I stood at that counter and said 'I think it's my chemistry' —"

"You were half right. It is your age. But it's not a flaw in you. It's a flaw in a product that was never built for your skin in the first place. And they let you apologize for it, because the alternative is admitting the bottle's the problem."

Twenty-five years of women apologizing to salesgirls for their own bodies.

"So what do you use?"

"I stopped buying perfume," she said. "I bought a different format."

"Meaning what?"

"An oil. No alcohol in it at all. And everything inverts — oil doesn't evaporate off skin, it binds to it. And body heat, the thing that murders a spray by speeding evaporation up, does the opposite to an oil. Your own warmth opens it up and keeps releasing it. So instead of peaking at minute two and dying at lunch, it gets better across the day. And it brings its own oil, so dry skin stops being the problem it's been for a decade."

"Then why does nobody sell it?"

"Because it won't throw a cloud across a department store in the first ten minutes. It won't win at the counter. And the counter is the only place they measure."

I didn't order it on her say-so. I've been burned by six bottles.

My first instinct was Amazon. I typed "perfume oil" and the top result had four and a half stars and eleven thousand reviews and cost nineteen dollars.

I had my thumb on Buy Now, then scrolled to the ingredients.

Alcohol denat. Second ingredient.

It was a spray with a nicer word on the front.

I closed it and did what I do. I opened a spreadsheet at eleven at night and went through two dozen of them, the same way I'd gone through Kayla's weak points three weeks earlier — methodically, no gaps.

Most died immediately. "Perfume oil" that's alcohol-cut. Roll-ons that are ninety percent carrier and a drop of synthetic fragrance oil, no structure to them at all — they smell like one flat note for an hour and then like nothing. Things with no actual note breakdown published anywhere, which always means there's a reason they won't publish it.

One met every criterion.

Genuinely oil-based. Zero alcohol. Seven botanical oils. A real note structure — jasmine, blackcurrant and pink pepper on top, peony and rose through the middle, warm amber underneath. Vegan, cruelty-free, dermatologist-tested. Pheromone-infused, which I rolled my eyes at and will come back to.

Nearly five thousand women had reviewed it. Four point eight stars. And I read a lot of them, because I no longer take anybody's word for anything.

They all said the same three things in the same order. It smells beautiful. It lasted all day. Somebody asked me about it.

Goda For Her.

Twenty-nine dollars. Buy one get one free.

I sat there with six bottles on my dresser behind me that had cost me somewhere north of six hundred dollars, and I ordered a twenty-nine dollar oil at half past eleven at night.

Day one. It came in a small black and gold bottle. A dropper, not a spray — which annoyed me for exactly one day and now I understand completely. Two drops. Wrists, neck, behind the ears. That's the entire application.

Jasmine first, and it's real jasmine — green and soft and alive, not the powdery thing that smells like a linen closet. Then peony and rose came up underneath, and it wasn't sweet. It was grown. And a warm amber settled under all of it like it had been sitting there waiting.

I put it on at seven in the morning and I forgot about it, which I want you to understand is not a thing that had happened to me in twenty years. I never forgot about perfume. I was always checking.

At 9:40 that night I was taking my earrings off and I caught it on my own wrist.

I keep 3 paper fans in the top drawer of my desk at Parkview Magnet High School and I have used every last one of them in the past 2 years to hide something my body will not stop doing to me in front of teenagers.

They're the kind of fans they hand out at Baptist funerals in the summer. Cardboard. A wooden stick stapled to the back. A picture of Jesus on one side and the name of the funeral home on the other. Mount Pleasant Baptist. Superior Funeral Chapel. My cousin's home going in 2021. My auntie's home going in 2023. I have been to too many funerals in the past 5 years and I have kept every single fan.

They live in my drawer under the pack of Post-its and the little bag of jolly ranchers I keep for the students.

I use one about 4 times a day.

Not to be cute. Not because I like the picture of Jesus. Because if I don't get air on my face and neck the moment I feel the wave come up my chest, I will sweat through whatever I'm wearing in 90 seconds and every parent standing at the counter in the front office will see it happen.

The move is quick. I open the drawer, pull out the fan, hold it low near my collarbone, flick my wrist 5 or 6 times, breathe through my mouth, put it back. Nobody who isn't looking for it sees it.

I have gotten so good at the church fan trick that I could probably teach a class on it.

I never wanted to be an expert at this.

My name is Alma. I'm 54 years old. I have been the executive secretary at Parkview Magnet High School in Little Rock, Arkansas for 19 years. Before that I was 5 years at Little Rock Central. Before that I was 8 years at a law office on Main Street doing intake.

I run the front office. I know where every teacher is at every hour of every day. I know which kids in the freshman class have older siblings who came through here. I know which parents are going through divorces and which ones are not to be seated together at open house. I know the alarm codes for 4 different rooms and the combination of the safe in the finance closet and the direct cell number of every school board member in Pulaski County.

I am the woman who knows.

That was the identity I built. That was who I was.

I was not supposed to be the woman who has to duck into a supply closet at 10:47 AM to press a damp paper towel to the back of her neck.

My husband Reggie is 57. He retired from the post office 2 years ago after 32 years on the same route in Southwest Little Rock. Now he fixes small engines out of our garage on Arch Street for cash and drives our daughter Camille's kids to karate on Wednesdays. Camille is 32. She teaches 5th grade in North Little Rock. Her twins are 8.

I have sung in that choir. I have taught Sunday school in the basement. I have served lemonade at 4 vacation Bible schools. I know every deacon's wife by name and every deacon's wife knows what I take in my coffee.

I have never in my life been the kind of woman who hides.

The flashes started when I was 51. They started small. A little wave. A little warmth. Nothing worth mentioning. My doctor said it was normal for a woman my age and told me to dress in layers and gave me a pamphlet.

By the time I was 52 they were bigger. I was waking up at 2:30 in the morning with the sheets soaked through and I was changing my nightgown in the dark so I wouldn't wake Reggie. I bought a little battery fan for my nightstand. I bought sheets with the moisture wicking. I bought a cooling pillow that cost 68 dollars off Amazon and didn't work.

By the time I was 53 they were bigger during the day than at night.

I was sitting at my desk at Parkview one morning in September, back to school night was in 4 hours, I had a stack of enrollment forms to file. It was 9:15 AM. The building was cool. My blouse was navy silk. And out of nowhere the wave came up my chest and hit my throat and my whole face went hot like someone had opened an oven in front of me.

I sat there gripping the arms of my chair.

By the time it passed I had sweat clean through my blouse under both arms and down the middle of my back. I could feel my bra clinging to my skin. I could feel my hair damp at the nape of my neck.

Miss Cheryl, the assistant principal, was walking by on her way to the copier. She said "Alma, honey, you okay."

I said I was fine. I smiled.

I went into the supply closet after she passed and I closed the door and I pressed my forehead against the cool metal of the shelving unit and I stood there for 4 minutes until I could breathe again.

That was the day I started buying blazers a size too big.

You would not believe the things I bought in the year after that.

A little pack of blotting papers for makeup that I used on my chest. A silk scarf that I told myself was for style. Our backyard had been neglected for years because Marvin worked Saturdays and I'd never wanted to set anything up out there if he wasn't going to be in it with me.

So when he retired, I started planning.

I'd bought a fire pit. A nice one, the kind with the propane line you can hook up to a tank. I'd planted three pots of knockout roses by the back fence. I'd put a little birdbath out there. I'd been pricing patio sets for 6 months. Marvin and I had picked one out together in February. A nice 6 piece set. Cushions in a soft green that I'd matched to the throw pillows on the porch. A glass top table that could seat 4 comfortably and 6 if everybody scooted in.

He insisted on paying for it himself. $1,247 with tax. He showed me the receipt at the kitchen table the night he ordered it. He was smiling. He said, "Diane. This summer is going to be good."

It came on a Friday in March. A semi truck pulled up in the cul-de-sac and the driver and his helper rolled the three big boxes off the lift gate and stacked them on our driveway and got the signature and drove away.

Marvin came out and looked at the boxes.

He stood there in the driveway in his blue Carhartt jacket with his hands on his hips for about 4 minutes.

I was watching from the kitchen window.

He went back inside.

The boxes stayed on the driveway.

Day 2, I asked him at breakfast if he wanted me to help him bring them around back. He said, "Diane. I got it. Don't worry about it. I'll knock it out this weekend."

The weekend came. The weekend went. The boxes stayed on the driveway.

Day 4, a Monday. He came out of the bathroom at 6:15 in the morning gripping the doorframe with his whole hand. Just standing there. I was making coffee in the kitchen and I saw him in the hallway, frozen, with one hand on the doorframe and his face all twisted up.

I started toward him. He saw me coming and he made himself let go and he made himself walk. He walked into the kitchen like nothing had happened. He poured himself coffee. He sat at the table.

I said, "Marvin."

He said, "Don't, Diane."

I said his name again.

He said, "I said don't."

He has not been a man you push when he says don't. That is a thing I have known about him since 1989. I let it go.

Day 7. A Thursday. He went out to the boxes at 9 in the morning with a box cutter. I made myself stay inside. I watched from the kitchen window the way a woman watches when she is trying not to be seen watching.

He cut open the first box.

He pulled out the table base. The instructions. A little plastic bag of bolts.

He squatted down to look at the instructions. He could not get back up.

He could not get back up.

He had to roll over onto one knee and use the cardboard box to push himself up to standing. And when he got to standing, he stood there for a long time just breathing.

I cried at the kitchen sink with the water running so he could not hear me.

He pushed the pieces back into the box. He took the instructions inside. He laid down on the couch and watched Fox News with the volume too loud and he did not look at me for the rest of the day.

Day 8. He didn't go outside. He stayed in the recliner.

Day 9. He didn't go outside.

Day 10. He didn't go outside.

Day 11 was a Monday.

Loan was walking her dog. A little fluffy white thing named Biscuit. She always walks Biscuit at 7:15 in the morning when I'm coming out to get the paper. We wave to each other. We've waved to each other for 11 years, since she and her husband Tuấn moved in next door from Pensacola.

I have to tell you about Loan because she is the reason this whole story changes.

Loan is 64. She came to the United States in 1983 from a village outside of Da Nang. She works part time as a bookkeeper for a Vietnamese grocery store on Government Street. Her husband Tuấn is a shrimper and is gone for weeks at a time on the boat. She has three grown children, all of whom are doctors or pharmacists or engineers, scattered between Houston and Atlanta.

She is the kindest, most observant woman I have ever known.

She has never once asked me a question I didn't want to answer. She has also never once missed something that mattered.

That Monday morning, she stopped Biscuit at the end of our driveway. She looked at the boxes. She looked at me.

She said, "Diane. Marvin doing okay?"

That was the whole question.

In another life, with another neighbor, I would have lied. I would have said, "Oh, you know Marvin. He'll get to it. He's been busy." And she would have said, "Mhm," and moved on.

But Loan asked it in that way she asks things. With her head tilted just a little. With her hands stilled on the leash. Like she had all the time in the world for whatever answer I gave her and like there was no wrong answer.

I stood there in my robe holding the newspaper.

I started crying.

I cried right there in my own driveway in front of my neighbor at 7:17 in the morning.

She did not panic. She did not hug me. She just walked Biscuit up the driveway closer to me and stood there next to me until I could get my words back.

I told her about the boxes. I told her about Marvin gripping the doorframe. I told her about the squatting and not being able to get back up. I told her about retirement and the trip to the Outer Banks we were supposed to take and the fishing off Dauphin Island and the friends we were going to have over again.

I told her my husband was 60 and his knees were 90 and we had planned a life he could not get up to do.

She listened to all of it.

When I was done, she said, "Diane. Come to my house Wednesday morning. After Marvin goes to his appointment. I want to show you something."

That was it. That was the whole invitation.

I said okay.

She walked Biscuit back down the driveway and went home.

Marvin had a dentist appointment Wednesday at 9:30. I dropped him off and instead of going to the Publix like I'd planned, I drove home and I walked across our yard to Loan's front door.

Her house smelled like lemongrass and ginger and something baking. She had a pot of tea ready. She had two little plates with sliced mango on them. She had a small notebook with handwritten pages on the kitchen table.

She sat me down. She poured me tea. She did not rush.

She said, "Diane. My husband Tuấn is 67 years old. He is on a shrimp boat right now. He left Thursday. He will not be home until next Friday. He works 18 hour days when he is out there. He pulls nets. He bends. He kneels. He lifts. He stands on a wet deck in the dark."

She paused. She let that picture sit in the kitchen for a minute.

She said, "Three years ago Tuấn could not do this anymore. His knees were finished. His hands ached. He came home from a 10 day trip and he could not get out of bed for 2 days. He cried in our bedroom. He thought he had to retire. We did not have the money for him to retire."

I was sitting there with my tea.

She said, "My oldest daughter Phuong is a pharmacist in Houston. She came home for Tết that year. She watched her father struggle to get up off the floor after he played with his grandson. She did not say anything that visit. She went back to Houston. Two weeks later a box came in the mail."

She got up. She went to a cabinet in her kitchen. She opened it. She took out a bottle.

She set the bottle on the table between us.

It said Alevia on the label. The word Pomegranate underneath.

I had never heard of it.

She sat back down.

She is a woman who would not waste money on something that did not have evidence behind it. She is a woman who, when I asked her on the phone if this was a real thing or a scam, said, 'Mẹ. The research on this fruit is real. I would not have sent it if I did not believe it.'"

I put one in his coffee every morning for 6 weeks before I told him I was doing it. He thought he was just drinking coffee."

She laughed when she said that. A small laugh.

She said, "Week 4, he came home from a trip and he did not have to lay down for 2 days. He laid down for an afternoon. Week 6, he came home from a trip and the next morning he went out and mowed the yard. Week 8, I told him what I had been doing. I thought he was going to be angry."

She paused.

She said, "He cried at the table, Diane. My husband. A man who has not cried in 30 years. He cried at this table. Because he had thought he was finished. He had been telling himself the rest of his life was going to be about giving things up. And his body had started giving him things back."

She took a sip of her tea.

She said, "I want to tell you what is in it. I want to tell you why it works. I want you to understand. Because if you do not understand it, you will not believe it, and if you do not believe it, you will not give it to Marvin long enough for him to feel anything."

And what Loan told me at her kitchen table that Wednesday morning was the thing that nobody else in 4 years of doctors and physical therapy and orthopedic specialists had ever told me about my husband's body.

She said, "The joints in your husband's knees have a smooth lining inside them. That lining is what lets the bones in his knee slide against each other without pain. When he was 25, that lining ran smooth. He could squat and stand and kneel all day and not think about it."

She said, "Over the years, that lining gets worn down. By the work. By stress. By processed food. By all the things we put into our bodies that are not what bodies are built to handle. And as the lining gets worn down, the body starts producing what the researchers call inflammation. Like a slow fire. Inside the joint."

She said, "That fire is what makes the joint hurt. That fire is what makes it swell. That fire is what makes him grip the doorframe when he is trying to walk in the morning. The fire is not just a feeling. It is something happening inside his body that he cannot see."

She said, "Doctors give you pills for the pain. They give you pills for the swelling. They give you injections. None of those things put the fire out. They just turn the volume down on it for a few hours."

She said, "Diane. Tuấn was on that floor 3 years ago. I have spent 3 years thanking my daughter every single day. The least I can do is give a bottle to my friend who is on the same floor."

I went home with the bottle in my purse.

The next morning I made Marvin's coffee.

I want to tell you what happened over those 8 weeks, because I do not want you to think this was a miracle.

He was unpacking the boxes.

He said, "Diane."

I said, "Marvin. You were on the bathroom floor."

He said, "Okay."

That was the whole thing. Just okay.

He has been taking it himself, openly, for 5 months now. He puts one in his hand at the kitchen counter every morning and he swallows it with his coffee.

The call came on December 23rd. I was standing at the kitchen island wrapping the last of the grandkids' presents when the phone rang, and I already had a bow between my teeth so I said hello with my jaw half shut.

It was the cardiologist's office. Dr. Merten himself. Not the nurse.

He said Ron's name and then he said the phrase that has not left my head since. Widow-maker territory.

I set down the scissors.

The kitchen faucet was dripping. The radio was playing that Bing Crosby song about being home for Christmas. Ron was out in the driveway with the snowblower because we'd gotten 6 inches overnight and the wind was pushing more of it against the garage door every hour.

And a doctor 43 miles away in Eau Claire was telling me the numbers from Ron's last blood draw were the worst he'd seen in a year and the calcium score from the scan they'd done in November put him in a category that had a name I'd never wanted to hear anyone say out loud about my husband.

Widow-maker.

I don't remember what I said back. I remember pulling the bow out of my mouth. I remember the roll of snowman wrapping paper unspooling off the counter and rolling across the floor toward the dog. I remember watching Ron's silhouette through the window over the sink, his red plaid jacket against the white, his breath coming out in clouds, and thinking he doesn't know yet. He's out there thinking about the snow. He doesn't know what I just heard.

My name is Judy. Judith on my birth certificate but nobody except my mother ever called me that, and she's been gone 11 years.

I'm 58. I've driven Bus 14 for the Rice Lake Area School District for 23 years. Same route, more or less. Out past Moon Lake and around by the old feed mill and then the loop up County Road SS where the Amish family with the seven kids lives and then back into town. I know every dip in that road. I know which mailbox the beagle likes to chase from. I know which parents wave and which ones don't.

Ron and I have been married 34 years this coming June. He worked at the Flambeau River paper mill for 31 of those years before they cut his position in 2019 and he took an early buyout. Since then he's done handyman work around town. Fixing docks. Rebuilding shed floors. Small stuff. Enough to keep him moving. He's never been a sitter, Ron.

Or he wasn't.

That's the part that had been chewing at me for maybe 2 years before that phone call. Ron sitting.

Ron in the recliner at 6:47 PM after supper with the paper unopened on his lap and his eyes closed. Ron passing on ice fishing with his brother Dean the last two Saturdays of December. Ron not lacing up his boots for the Rice Lake Aquafest parade in July, the parade he'd walked in with the Kiwanis for 18 years running. Ron saying "next weekend" about the loose board on the back deck for so many next weekends I finally called Cody Halvorson to come fix it myself and paid him $85 to do a job Ron used to do in his sleep.

I told myself it was age. I told myself it was retirement adjustment. I told myself his back was bothering him from the paper mill years and that's why he wasn't moving as much.

I told myself a lot of things.

But you know what wives know. You know the exact temperature of your husband's tired. You know the difference between a man who worked hard today and a man who is dimming.

Ron had been dimming.

And now on December 23rd, with two grandkids arriving Christmas morning and a ham thawing in the fridge and Bing Crosby singing about the snow, a doctor was telling me the plumbing under my husband's chest was in a category with a name that meant the widow was the one left behind.

I hung up. I picked up the wrapping paper. I finished the last present. I put the bow on. I put the presents under the tree. I wiped my face and I went outside and I stood in the driveway in my house shoes in the snow and I told Ron the doctor called.

He looked at me over the top of the snowblower. Snow on his eyebrows. His nose bright red.

"What'd he say?"

I said, "He wants you in on the 27th."

I didn't say the word. I couldn't. Not with him standing there in the red plaid jacket he's had since 1998 and the wool cap our son Danny bought him for Father's Day the year Danny turned 12.

I said, "He wants to talk about your numbers."

Ron nodded. He was quiet a second. Then he said, "Okay, Jude." And he pulled the choke and started the snowblower back up and finished the driveway.

That was our Christmas.

I want to tell you about the years leading up to that phone call because I think a lot of women are living in the middle of them right now and don't know it.

Ron's cholesterol had been "high" since his mid 40s. His first prescription was in 2011. Simvastatin. 20 milligrams. It brought the total number down. Not by a huge amount. But enough for the doctor to say "good, keep going."

Every year, the number crept back up. Every year, the dose went up or the drug got swapped. Simvastatin became atorvastatin. 20 became 40. 40 became 80. Then they added something else. Ezetimibe I think it was. Then something else on top of that for the triglycerides.

By the time Ron was 58, he was on 4 medications and his numbers were still not where the doctor wanted them.

And by the time he was 61, he was tired all the time. His hands ached. He forgot the name of Dean's new dog three times in one Sunday dinner. He stopped playing cribbage with the guys at the American Legion because he said he couldn't focus on the count. He stopped fishing. He stopped fixing things. He gained 22 pounds and none of it was muscle.

I asked the doctor once, at a follow up, what could be causing all the tiredness. The doctor looked at Ron's chart on the computer and said "he's 61, Judy. It happens."

I remember driving home that day and thinking, my dad ran a service station until he was 74 and he wasn't tired like this. My uncle Sig cut his own firewood until he was 71. Something wasn't right about "it happens."

But what do you do with a feeling. You don't do anything. You go home. You make supper. You watch your husband fall asleep in the chair by 7:30.

You keep driving Bus 14. You keep waving at the Amish kids. You keep telling yourself next spring will be different, next summer will be better, once he catches up on sleep he'll bounce back.

Christmas morning came. The grandkids came. Everyone smiled. Ron sat in the good chair and held our granddaughter Lucy on his knee and read her the book about the reindeer. He looked like himself for about 40 minutes.

I watched him from the kitchen and I thought about the word the cardiologist used.

The 27th came. Ron went in. I couldn't go with him because I had a sub route that day and no one else could take it. He came home with a folder full of new prescriptions and a follow up scheduled for the third week of January.

He sat down at the kitchen table with the folder and he said, "They want to add a fifth pill. And they want to talk about a stent in the spring."

I sat down across from him.

He said, "I don't know, Jude."

That was the first time in 34 years of marriage that I heard my husband sound like a man who was scared.

I didn't sleep that night. Or the next. Or the next.

Two days after New Year's, I did something I hadn't done in maybe 6 winters. I got in the car after my morning route and I drove out to Snusa's Bait and Tackle on Highway 48. The plan in my head, which was more of a wish than a plan, was to rent an ice shanty for the weekend and get Ron out on Long Lake with Dean. Get him doing something. Get him out of the chair.

Snusa's is the kind of place that has been there since 1962 and looks it. Wood paneling. A wall of lures. A minnow tank in the back that hums. A coffee pot on a hot plate with a sign that says "one dollar, honor system, we know your face."

I walked in and shook the snow off my boots and the woman behind the counter looked up from a paperback and said, "Judy Ahlgren?"

I hadn't seen Ingrid Solberg in probably 6 years. Her husband Curt had passed in 2020 and after that she'd moved out to the lake to be closer to her sister and I'd lost track of her. She was in her mid 60s now, thick grey braid down her back, red flannel over a Green Bay Packers sweatshirt, reading glasses on a beaded chain around her neck.

We hugged. She made me a cup of coffee. She asked about my boys. I asked about her grandkids.

And then she looked at me and she said, "You look tired, honey. You okay?"

I don't know why. Maybe it was the coffee. Maybe it was because she'd lost Curt and she'd know the sound of what I was carrying. Maybe it was just that I hadn't said any of it out loud to anybody, not even to my sister Bev in Duluth, and it had been building up under my ribs since December 23rd.

I told her about the phone call. I told her about the widow maker. I told her about the fifth pill and the stent and Ron in the good chair and Ron not fishing and Ron not remembering Dean's dog's name.

Ingrid listened. She didn't interrupt once. When I was done she poured me more coffee and she was quiet for a minute.

Then she said, "You know my brother in law Verlan?"

I did, sort of. He was married to Ingrid's sister Marlys, who lived out past Ladysmith. Verlan had been a shift foreman at the paper mill in Park Falls for a lot of years. I remembered him from a wedding once. Big guy. Big laugh.

Ingrid said, "He was on the same road as Ron. Statins for 15 years. Kept adding pills. Kept feeling worse. His numbers wouldn't stay down no matter what they did. Last spring his cardiologist told him if things didn't change by summer they were going to do a procedure."

I said, "What happened?"

She said, "Marlys is the reader in the family. She's always been the one going down the rabbit hole. She got fed up. She spent about two months reading everything she could get her hands on about what actually goes wrong with cholesterol. Not the number. The actual problem underneath the number."

I set my coffee down.

Ingrid pulled her glasses up onto her nose and leaned on the counter.

She said, "What she came home with was that the number the doctor watches, the LDL number, that's not really the thing that's causing the trouble. Cholesterol isn't the villain. Your body makes it on purpose. It uses it for a hundred different things. Building cells. Making hormones. Repairing tissue."

She said, "The trouble starts when cholesterol gets damaged in the bloodstream. There's a word for it. Oxidized. When cholesterol gets oxidized, it changes. It becomes sticky. That's the stuff that gets stuck to the artery walls. That's the stuff that starts building up. Not regular cholesterol. Oxidized cholesterol."

She said, "And here's the part Marlys couldn't get past. The standard test doesn't tell you how much of it is oxidized. It just counts all of it together. Good and bad in one big number. If the number is high, they hand you a pill. But the pill just tells your body to make less cholesterol overall. It doesn't do a single thing about the oxidation that's turning it dangerous."

I said, "So the pill lowers the number but doesn't fix the actual problem."

Ingrid pointed at me. "That's exactly what Marlys said. And here's what she said next. If the real problem is oxidation, then your body is going to keep making more cholesterol to replace what's getting damaged. It's a cycle. The more oxidation, the more your body ramps up production trying to keep up with the loss. That's why Verlan's number kept creeping back up no matter what dose they put him on. His body was trying to solve a problem the pill wasn't touching."

I sat with that for a minute.

I thought about Ron. Fifteen years of pills. Numbers creeping. Doses climbing. Something new added every couple of years. And underneath all of it, the same conversation, the same folder full of prescriptions, the same slow dimming.

I said, "Okay. So what did Marlys find that helped?"

Ingrid smiled and she reached under the counter and she pulled out a little bottle. Dark green. Simple label. It said Alevia Amla.

She said, "This."

I said, "What is that."

She said, "It's a fruit. Grows in India. They've used it in their medicine for thousands of years. It's called amla. Indian gooseberry. What Marlys found in her reading was that this fruit has some of the highest antioxidant activity ever measured in a food. And there are specific compounds in it called emblicanins that are especially good at protecting cholesterol from getting oxidized in the first place."

She said, "That was the piece that made her order it. If oxidation is what makes cholesterol dangerous, and this fruit helps protect against that oxidation, then it wasn't trying to lower the number by shutting down production the way the pill did. It was working on the actual problem underneath. Less oxidation. Less sticky cholesterol. Less that ends up stuck in the arteries. And when less is getting stuck, your body doesn't have to keep overproducing to replace what's being lost."

I looked at the bottle. It was small. Nothing about it looked like it had any business fixing anything.

Ingrid said, "I know how it looks. Marlys was skeptical too. Verlan was more skeptical. He'd been on the pills so long he thought this was hippie stuff. But Marlys said if he wouldn't try it she was going to start slipping it in his oatmeal. So he took it."

I said, "And?"

She said, "It took a few weeks before he felt anything different. That's what Marlys told me. Around week 3 or 4 he told her his head felt clearer in the mornings. His hands didn't ache the same. He had energy back around 3 in the afternoon that he hadn't had in years. By week 6 he was doing yard work again. By the time his next appointment came around in May, his numbers had moved. Not a little. Enough that the cardiologist asked him what he'd changed."

She paused. She looked at me.

She said, "The stent conversation got tabled. He's still going in for regular check ins. Nothing's a magic bullet. But he's out on the ice this winter with his boys. He wasn't going to be. That's what I know."

I asked her if she took it too. She said she had for about 5 months, ever since Marlys told her about it, and she felt sharper. Less foggy. She said at 65 she'd take that.

I bought a bottle from her right there.

She rang me up and she said, "Judy. Whatever you do, don't take Ron off his medicine on your own. Talk to the doctor. But there's no rule that says he can't add something that supports his body while he figures the rest of it out."

I nodded. I thanked her. I hugged her again. I got in the car and I sat in the parking lot with the bottle in my hand and I cried for about 4 minutes.

Then I drove home.

I told Ron the truth. I told him where I'd been. I told him what Ingrid told me about Verlan. I told him what the compounds in the fruit did and why it wasn't the same thing his pills were doing. I told him I was going to take it too.

He looked at the bottle on the kitchen table. He looked at me.

He said, "You went all the way out to Snusa's for this?"

I said, "I went out there to rent you a shanty. This came with it."

He almost smiled. First real one since December 23rd.

He said, "Okay, Jude."

Two capsules a day. That's what the bottle said. Ron started the second Sunday of January.

The first two weeks were nothing. If I'm being honest. He took the capsules with his coffee. I took mine. Life kept going. Bus 14. Groceries. The follow up appointment with the cardiologist happened and they added the fifth pill and scheduled the stent talk for April.

But around week 3 something started. Ron was up before me one Saturday. That hadn't happened in probably 2 years. He was in the kitchen making eggs. He said his back didn't feel like it usually did in the morning. I didn't make a big deal of it. I just sat down and let him make me an egg too.

Week 4 he called Dean and they went out on Prairie Lake for perch. He was gone from 6 AM until 2 PM. He came home tired but it was the good tired. The kind he used to have after a mill shift. He ate a whole plate of leftovers and went back out to clean the fish in the garage.

Week 5 he fixed the loose board on the back deck. The one Cody Halvorson had fixed once already but had come loose again in the fall. Ron pulled his tools out of the bin they'd been in since summer. He was out there for maybe an hour. He came in with sawdust on his forearms and I nearly cried in the kitchen watching him wash his hands.

Week 6 was when it really shifted.

He said one morning over coffee, "Jude, my head feels different."

I said, "Different how."

He said, "Just clearer. Like I can find the words again. I don't know when I stopped being able to find the words. But I can find them now."

I put down my coffee. I said, "I know."

Because I could feel it too. I hadn't said anything but I'd been sleeping better. My afternoon slump on the bus route had shrunk. I'd stopped needing the second coffee at 2:15. I'd started noticing bird songs on the walk from the bus barn to my car in the parking lot. Little things.

By the time April came around and Ron went in for the appointment they'd scheduled to talk about the stent, his numbers had shifted. Not all the way. Not perfect. But enough that Dr. Merten sat back in his chair and asked him what had changed.

Ron told him. All of it. The bottle. Ingrid. Verlan. The whole story.

Dr. Merten was quiet a long time. Then he said, "Let's hold off on the procedure. Let's watch it another 3 months."

Ron came home and told me and we stood in the kitchen and held each other for a long time and didn't say anything.

It's now been 9 months since that phone call on December 23rd.

Ron is out on the ice this weekend with Dean and Dean's grandson. He drove himself. He packed his own gear. He got up at 4:47 AM to be on the lake by sunrise and he was whistling in the garage as he loaded the truck.

His most recent numbers have kept moving in the right direction. His cardiologist has taken him off one of the medications and is watching to see if a second one can come off in November. The stent conversation hasn't come back up.

I don't know what the next round of bloodwork will say. I don't know what next winter will look like. Nobody does. What I know is that the man out on the ice this morning is a man I was starting to lose, and I'm not losing him anymore.

That's what I have to say.

If you're reading this and you're a wife who has been watching her husband dim for years while the pill count goes up and the doctor keeps saying "he's getting older, Judy, it happens," I want you to know you're not imagining it. You're not dramatic. You're not overreacting. You are watching something real.

Your husband's doctor is watching the chart. You are watching the man. You are closer to the truth than the chart is.

If you're the husband reading this and you're the one in the chair, and you're the one who used to build things and fix things and go out on the ice and now you sit, and you tell your wife you're just tired but you know in your gut it's more than that, I want you to know something too. It's not too late. It wasn't too late for Ron. It wasn't too late for Verlan.

There's a fruit that has been used for 5,000 years in one of the oldest medical traditions in the world. Modern research has looked at compounds in it called emblicanins and what they do to help protect cholesterol from oxidation. That is the actual problem underneath the number. Not the number itself.

And a 90 day money back guarantee, which means if it doesn't do anything for you in 3 months, you send back what's left and you get your money back. No arguing. No forms. No small print. Just your money.

I'm not a doctor. I'm a school bus driver from Rice Lake, Wisconsin. I'm telling you what I saw with my own husband. I'm telling you what Ingrid told me about Verlan. You do what you want with it.

I've been walleye fishing with my brothers every opening day of the season for 23 years straight.

This year I stayed home.

The truck was packed. My tackle box was by the back door. Kevin and Denny were already up at Turtle Flambeau Flowage in the cabin we've rented from the same guy since 2003. His name is Ray. He's 78 now. He lets us stay for what he charged us the first year because he says we're the only ones who ever call him when it isn't fishing season just to check in.

Kevin called me at 4:47 in the afternoon on the day I was supposed to drive up.

He said, "Ronnie. Where are you."

I said, "Kev. I can't make it this year."

He said, "The hell do you mean you can't make it. You okay?"

I said, "Yeah. I'm okay. Something came up."

There was a long silence on the line. My oldest brother is not a man who fills a silence. He waits it out.

I said, "Barb's not feeling great. I gotta stay close."

Which was a lie.

Barb was standing 4 feet from me in the kitchen when I said it. She looked at me over her reading glasses. She didn't say anything either. She just kept peeling potatoes.

Kevin said, "Alright, Ronnie. You take care of Barb. We'll drink one for you."

He hung up.

I stood at the sink for a minute. Then I walked out to the garage where my truck was still packed. I stood there in the doorway. I looked at the tackle box on the passenger seat. The green Coleman cooler in the bed. The rain jacket folded on top of the cooler. Boots wedged behind the driver's seat.

And I felt my feet.

Or, more accurate, I felt what my feet felt like now. Which is nothing.

Which is cotton.

Which is like walking on a mattress covered in a wool blanket that someone else is wearing.

Which is like every step lands about 3 inches farther down than it should.

Which is what I've been feeling for going on 14 months. And getting worse.

I couldn't tell my brothers I was skipping the trip because I was scared of losing my footing on the boat ramp at Turtle Flambeau and going into the water at 6 in the morning in 42 degree air with a boat backing down the ramp behind me.

I couldn't tell my wife of 33 years I was skipping the trip because I couldn't feel my own feet.

I hadn't told anybody the truth about this for over a year.

That night, I sat in my recliner in my little brick house on Terrace Avenue in Marinette, Wisconsin, with the TV on to a Brewers game I wasn't watching, and I thought, this is how it starts. This is how a man ends up sitting in a chair for the rest of his life. You give up one thing. Then another. Then the chair is the only thing left.

My name is Ron. I'm 57 years old. I was a union electrician for 34 years out of the local here in Marinette. I did the work at the shipyard for about 12 of those years. Big commercial jobs. I retired 2 years ago on a full pension. Not because I wanted to. Because I couldn't grip a wire nut anymore without watching my own thumb to make sure it was turning.

My wife Barb is 55. She works part time at the clinic on Cleveland Avenue doing billing. We have one son, Tyler, 29, who lives outside of Green Bay with his wife and our little grandbaby Jack.

I have two brothers. Kevin is 61, oldest, retired auto glass installer, lives in De Pere. Denny is 52, the baby, does hospital maintenance for one of the big hospital systems in Milwaukee.

We've all lived in Wisconsin our whole lives. We were raised by my dad, who was also a union electrician, and my mom, who cleaned houses for the doctors on the north side of Marinette until she got sick in 2004.

The walleye trip is the one thing the three of us have always done. Ice out. Opening weekend. Same lake. Same cabin. Same brand of coffee. We eat brats for supper on Friday, walleye we caught for supper on Saturday, and pancakes on Sunday morning cooked by whoever was the worst fisherman that weekend. That's the rule. It's usually Kevin.

Missing it wasn't just missing a fishing trip. It was crossing a line. It was admitting that something was different now. Something was really different.

The feet thing started in the spring of last year. I remember because I was still doing the odd job for cash after my retirement, and I was up on a scissor lift running conduit in the ceiling of a warehouse over in Menominee, Michigan. I was standing on the platform and I couldn't figure out why my balance felt off. Kept swaying a little. Grabbed the rail. I thought maybe the lift was moving. It wasn't. It was me. I was moving.

I got off the lift that day and I didn't get back on it. I never told the guy I was working for why.

Over the next few months, the pins and needles started. Just at night at first. Laying in bed, both feet buzzing like there was a low current running through them. Then it started in the daytime. Then it moved from buzzing to burning. Some nights it was so bad Barb would find me at 2 in the morning sitting at the kitchen table with my feet in a pan of cold water.

Then the numbness started. That was worse than the burning in some ways. Because burning tells you something. Numbness tells you nothing. You just stop feeling parts of your body. And your body starts making mistakes because it can't tell you what it's doing.

I went to Dr. Meinhardt at the clinic. He ran the tests. Blood work. Nerve conduction study up at Bellin. He said it was peripheral neuropathy. He said, "Ron, we're not sure exactly what's causing it in your case. It could be a lot of things. Age. Genetics. All those years around industrial chemicals in the shipyard. Sometimes we just don't know."

He put me on gabapentin.

The gabapentin made my head feel like it was full of wet cardboard and did approximately nothing for my feet.

I went back. He upped the dose. Same story.

He said, "Ron, we can try Cymbalta. Some folks get relief from that."

I told him I didn't want another pill.

He said, "Ron, at this stage, that's kind of what we have."

I want to tell you something about Dr. Meinhardt. He is a good man. He is not the villain here. He does the best he can with what he was taught. But when your feet feel like cotton and the medicine they give you doesn't work and they don't have a better answer, you eventually stop going in. Because what's the point.

So I stopped going in.

I stopped telling Barb the truth about how bad it was getting.

I stopped taking the walk we used to take in the evenings down by the marina.

I stopped going bowling on Thursday nights with the guys from the hall.

I stopped a lot of things.

And I would have stopped the walleye trip and never told anybody why, if my brother Denny hadn't driven 4 hours to my house on a Sunday afternoon.

I want to tell you about that Sunday.

It was 6 days after I'd told Kevin I couldn't make the trip. I was on my porch. It was one of those late April afternoons in Wisconsin that finally feels like spring. Maybe 58 degrees. The redbud in the front yard was starting to come in. I was drinking a black coffee even though it was 3 in the afternoon because I don't know what else to do with my hands anymore.

I saw a red Ram 1500 pull up at the curb.

Denny got out.

He didn't wave. He didn't holler. He just walked up my walkway, climbed my three porch steps, sat down in the empty rocker next to mine, and set a paper Culver's bag on the little table between us.

He said, "I got you a butterburger. And a chocolate malt. Because Barb texted me you haven't been eating."

I did not know Barb had texted my brother anything.

I said, "Denny. What are you doing here."

He said, "I'm sitting on your porch."

I said, "You drove 4 hours to sit on my porch."

He said, "Yeah."

We sat there for a while. He ate his burger. I picked at mine. He drank his malt. I let mine melt.

After maybe 15 minutes of nothing, Denny said, "Kev told me you bailed on the trip. And Barb told me you've been sitting in the recliner every night not moving. And Diane told me she wanted to talk to you and would I please drive up here and sit with you until you called her."

Diane is Denny's wife. She's 51. She's been a home health aide in Milwaukee for 22 years. She goes into people's homes and helps them get out of bed and shower and eat and take their pills. Most of her patients are between 70 and 90. She has been doing this long enough that when she talks about somebody, she talks about them like she knew them her whole life. She's soft, but she's not stupid. And she has seen every kind of thing a body can do.

I said, "Diane wants to talk to me."

Denny said, "Ronnie. What's going on with your feet."

I looked at my brother.

He looked at me.

And I don't know why, but I told him. Everything. The lift in Menominee. The pan of cold water at 2 AM. The gabapentin that didn't work. The walk I stopped taking. The bowling I stopped. The stuff I hadn't told Barb. The reason I hadn't gone up to Turtle Flambeau. The boat ramp thing. The thing about how you give up one thing and then another and the chair is the only thing left.

I told my little brother the whole story I'd been carrying by myself for 14 months.

When I was done, he was quiet for a while.

Then he said, "Alright. Call Diane."

He handed me his phone. He'd already dialed her. It was ringing.

Diane picked up on the second ring.

She said, "Hi Ronnie."

I said, "Hi Diane."

She said, "Your brother tell you why he came up there."

I said, "He said you wanted to talk to me."

She said, "I do. I've got 3 patients right now with what you're describing. And I've had probably 40 or 50 more over the last 22 years. I know what it looks like, Ronnie. And I want to tell you something."

I said, "Okay."

She said, "The reason nothing your doctor has given you is working is because none of it is doing anything for what's actually going on."

She said, "The cells in your nerves need a lot of energy. More than most cells in your body. They're the most energy hungry cells you've got, because they've got to maintain that protective coating around them and they've got to fire those signals all day long."

She said, "That energy comes from little tiny power plants in every cell called mitochondria. Everybody's got them. When you're young they're running strong. As you get older, and especially if you've spent your whole working life around industrial stuff the way you have, they start to slow down. And when the mitochondria slow down, the cells in your nerves are usually the first to feel it. Because they need the most fuel. And they're the first to run out of it."

She said, "When your nerve cells don't have the energy they need, they can't maintain themselves. They can't manage the burning. They can't keep the signals clean. And you start feeling exactly what you've been feeling. Cotton feet. Pins and needles. Burning at night. Missing steps because the signal isn't getting through."

She said, "The gabapentin they gave you tries to quiet the pain signal. It doesn't do a thing for the cells. Your cells are still starving. That's why it stops working after a while, or barely works at all."

I sat there on my porch holding my brother's phone and I did not say anything.

Because for the first time in 14 months, somebody had told me what was going on. Not what to take. What was going on.

Diane said, "Ronnie. Are you still there."

I said, "Yeah. I'm here."

She said, "I want to tell you what I've been giving to my mama for the last 11 months. She's 79. She was where you are 2 years ago. She stopped going to the senior center. She stopped going to bingo on Wednesdays. She was sitting in her recliner in Green Bay just like you're sitting on your porch. Then I found something and I did the reading and I called my sister who's a nurse in Madison and she looked at it too, and we started my mama on it. And Ronnie, my mama is back at bingo. She's not the woman she was at 60. She's the woman she was at 74. And that's the woman I thought I'd lost."

She said, "It's a fruit. From India. It's called amla. Some people call it Indian gooseberry. They've used it over there for 5,000 years. What it does, based on what the research is showing, is help support your mitochondria. Not force anything. Support them. There's a pathway in your body called AMPK. Amla helps activate it, and when AMPK is more active, the mitochondria can start producing energy the way they used to. And when the mitochondria are supported, your nerve cells are usually the first ones to feel it. Because they're the ones that were starving the worst."

She said, "It also has one of the highest antioxidant profiles of any food they've ever measured. Which matters because a lot of what wears the mitochondria down in the first place is oxidative stress."

I said, "Where do you get it."

She said, "There's one company I trust. Alevia. Made right here in the States. 30 servings a bottle. Two capsules with breakfast. Free shipping. And here's what convinced me the first time. 90 day money back guarantee. If you take it for 90 days and you don't feel a lick of difference, you send back what you have and they refund your money. No questions. No arguing."

She said, "I want you to try it, Ronnie. My mama is the reason I'm still standing. You're the reason my Denny is still standing. And I don't want to lose you to a chair."

I did not say anything for a while.

Denny was looking down at his boots on the porch floor.

I said, "Send me the website, Diane."

She said, "Already texted it to Denny. He'll show you."

Denny showed me his phone.

alevia.com/amla/33

I ordered 3 bottles that afternoon at the kitchen table with Denny standing behind me watching me do it because he said, and I quote, "I'm not leaving until I see you put in the credit card number."

He stayed the night. Slept on our couch. Left the next morning. Kissed Barb on the cheek. Told me to keep him posted.

The box came on a Wednesday. 4 days later. Free shipping like Diane said.

I opened my first bottle on a Thursday morning with my breakfast.

Now let me tell you what happened. Because I know how this reads. And I want to be honest with you the way Denny made me be honest with him.

Week 1. Nothing. My feet still felt like cotton. I called Diane on Sunday night. She said, "Ronnie, this is your body. It's been doing what it's been doing for a year and a half. It's not going to fix in a week. Give it the time."

Week 2. Nothing I could point to. But I slept a little better. That's it. That's all I got that week.

Week 3. Something small. I was sitting on the porch at 8 in the evening. I had my socks off because the burning has always been worse in socks. I looked down at my feet and I noticed my right foot was tapping. Just a little. Little rhythm. I don't remember when my feet ever tapped last. Because you can't tap a foot you can't feel.

Week 4. I was in the kitchen. I dropped a spoon on the floor. I bent down to pick it up. I felt the linoleum through my sock. Actually felt it. Cool linoleum. That was the first time I'd felt the floor through my foot in maybe 8 months.

I stood there in the kitchen holding a spoon and I did not tell Barb what had just happened. Because I didn't want to jinx it.

Week 6. This was Diane's week. She had told me on the phone that her mama noticed the real change around week 6. And she was right.

Week 6, I woke up on a Tuesday morning and I did not have to sit on the edge of the bed for 3 minutes waiting for my feet to know they were feet before I stood up. I just stood up. And walked to the bathroom. And walked back.

Barb was still asleep. I sat down on the edge of the bed and I looked at my feet on the floor.

I said, quiet, to nobody, "There you are."

Week 8. I walked down to the marina. All the way down. Two blocks. Came all the way back. Didn't stop once. Barb walked with me. She was talking about our grandbaby the whole time and I don't think she realized what was happening until we were back at the porch and I sat down and she said, "Ron. You just walked down and back."

I said, "I know."

Week 10. I called Kevin.

I said, "Kev. I owe you an apology."

He said, "For what."

I said, "For lying to you the day I bailed on the trip. Barb wasn't sick. I was."

Kevin was quiet for a while.

Then he said, "Ronnie. I knew Barb wasn't sick. I've known you were something for a while. I was waiting for you to say something."

I told him. Everything. Diane. Denny. The porch. The amla. The feet.

He said, "Ronnie. Next year we're going back up to Ray's cabin. All three of us."

I said, "Yeah, Kev. We are."

Week 12. Barb and I drove up to Green Bay to see Tyler and our grandbaby Jack. Jack is 2. He wanted to walk around their backyard with his little wagon.

I walked around that whole backyard behind that little boy for 45 minutes. On grass. Uneven ground. Over a garden hose. Up onto a little concrete patio. Back off. Around a tree.

Every step, I felt where my foot was landing.

At one point Jack turned around and hollered, "Papa! Come on!"

I said, "I'm coming, buddy."

And I was. I was coming.

Tyler was watching from the back door. He came out to the yard afterward. He said, "Dad. You're moving good today."

I said, "Yeah. I've been feeling a little better lately."

He didn't push it. But I could tell he'd noticed.

Now. Here's what I want to say to whoever's reading this.

I'm not a doctor. I'm a retired union electrician who spent 14 months hiding from his own wife and brothers because he couldn't feel his feet and didn't want to talk about it.

What I can tell you is what Diane told me and what I've lived over 12 weeks. Alevia's Amla isn't a cure for anything. Diane was clear about that. What it does is support what your body was built to do. When your nerve cells are supported, they can go back to doing their job. And when they can do their job, feeling can start coming back. Little bit at a time.

If you're reading this on your porch on a Sunday afternoon and your feet feel like cotton, or your hands are tingling, or there's a burning at night nobody can explain to you, or if you're a wife whose husband stopped going bowling last year and won't say why, I want you to check into Alevia's Amla.
