Lena’s POV
Three days.
I’ve been staring at the email for three days, and I still haven’t decided.
Alex is asleep in his room, Blue curled up at the foot of his bed like always. It’s past midnight, and I should be sleeping, but instead I’m sitting at my kitchen table with my laptop open, reading the consultation request for the hundredth time.
“Detective Marcus Hale, Special Crimes Unit, Chicago PD.”
Marcus Hale. I know him. Senior detective at the Supernatural Crimes Unit. He really isn’t a threat to me.
Except it’s Chicago.
And Chicago means the possibility, however small, of running into Rylan.
I pull up my bank account on another tab. $847.32.
The email mentioned “competitive compensation for specialist consultation.” That’s code for serious money. Probably more than I’d make in a month of regular work.
But it’s not really about the money, is it?
I click back to the email, to the attachment I’ve opened and closed a dozen times. The crime scene photo. The symbol carved into the brick wall behind the victim.
The Brand of the Free.
My father’s symbol. The mark he was researching when he died.
My chest tightens. I’ve spent five years accepting the official story, single vehicle collision, rural highway, no witnesses, tragic accident. Five years telling myself that sometimes bad things just happen.
But I’ve never believed it. Not really.
My father was careful. Methodical. And he was close, so close to something important. I could see it in his eyes those last few weeks.
“I’m onto something, Lena,” he’d told me the week before he died. “Something that could change everything we know about rogue movements in the Great Lakes region.”
Then he was dead.
And now, five years later, someone is using his research. His symbols. Killing rogues in Chicago and marking them with the Brand of the Free.
This isn’t coincidence. This is connected to whatever my father found. Whatever got him killed.
My phone buzzes. Text from Sarah.
Sarah: Still up? Saw your light on.
Me: Can’t sleep. Work stuff.
Sarah: The Chicago thing?
Me: Yeah.
There’s a long pause. Then:
Sarah: You need to go back. Not for the money. For the truth. You’ve always known your father’s death wasn’t an accident. This is your chance to find out what really happened.
Me: What if I can’t handle what I find?
Sarah: You’re stronger than you think. And Alex deserves to know the truth about his grandfather. About his heritage.
Another pause.
Sarah: I’ll keep Alex safe. You know I will. Go find your answers, Lena. Go find out what they did to your father. And if you need help, real help, from people who understand, you know where to find me.
I stare at the message for a long time.
She’s right. I need to know what happened to my father. I need to know if his death and my exile are connected, if the same people who framed me are the ones who killed him.
I need the truth. Even if it destroys me.
I hit reply before I can change my mind.
Me: I’m taking the case. Watch Alex for me. I’ll be back in a few days.
***
The next morning, I drop Alex off at Sarah’s place at 6 AM. He’s still half-asleep, clutching his stuffed wolf.
“Mama has to work,” I tell him, smoothing his hair back. “I’ll be back soon.”
Sarah meets my eyes over his head. “I’ll keep him safe. You know I will.”
I kiss Alex’s forehead and force myself to leave before the guilt can paralyze me.
***
I don’t go straight to Chicago.
I drive to the outskirts of Milwaukee, to a part of town where nobody asks questions and cash is the only currency that matters.
The garage is tucked between a pawn shop and a boarded-up laundromat. No sign, no name, just a rusted metal door.
Twenty minutes later, I’m the owner of a fifteen-year-old Honda Civic with 180,000 miles on it and plates registered to someone who doesn’t exist. It costs me lot of my savings, but it’s worth it.
Because if I’m going back to Chicago, back to pack territory, I’m not doing it in a car that can be traced. I’m not giving anyone the chance to find me before I’m ready to be found.
I’m not that naïve girl anymore. I’m a survivor. And survivors don’t take unnecessary risks.
I transfer my bag to the new car and pull out onto the highway.
Chicago is three hours away. Three hours to build my armor back up, layer by layer, until I’m strong enough to face him.
***
It’s around the two-hour mark when I start to feel it.
The wolfsbane is wearing off.
I’ve been taking it for five years, a carefully measured dose every morning that keeps my wolf dormant. But I took my last dose yesterday morning, and it’s been over twenty-four hours.
I can feel it in my bones first, a restlessness that makes me want to pull over and run. Then it’s in my senses, the world suddenly sharper, colors more vivid, sounds more distinct. My wolf stirs.
Just a flicker of awareness, a presence I haven’t felt in so long I almost don’t recognize it. But it’s there, waking up slowly, confused and disoriented after five years of forced sleep.
“Where are we?”
The thought isn’t mine. It’s hers. My wolf, speaking for the first time in half a decade.
I grip the steering wheel harder, trying to push her back down, but it’s like trying to hold water in my hands
PACK TERRITORY, she whispers, desperate and hungry. HOME.
“No,” I say out loud. “Not home. Not anymore.”
But she doesn’t listen. She’s stretching, testing the boundaries of her prison, and I can feel her pushing against my control. Not aggressive. Just… present. Aware. Awake.
I forgot what it was like. Forgot the way she makes me feel more ALIVE, more connected to something primal and ancient.
Forgot how much I missed her.
The Chicago skyline appears on the horizon, and my wolf perks up.
PACK, she says again, and this time there’s certainty in her voice. ALPHA.
My heart stutters.
But she’s right. I can feel it now.
He’s here.
Rylan is here, somewhere in this city, and my wolf knows it.
She surges forward, sudden and powerful, and I nearly swerve off the road. My hands jerk on the wheel, my vision blurs, and for a terrifying moment I’m not sure who’s in control, me or her.
“Stop,” I gasp, pulling over onto the shoulder. “Stop, please, just…”
She retreats, but slowly, reluctantly. I can feel her confusion, her hurt.
I rest my forehead against the steering wheel, breathing hard.
This was a mistake. Coming here was a mistake. But I think about my father. About the symbol carved into that brick wall. About five years of questions I’ve been too afraid to ask.
I think about Sarah’s text: “You’re stronger now.”
I am stronger. I’ve survived five years alone. I can do this.
I can do all of it without falling apart.
I pull back onto the highway and keep driving
***
The SCU building looks like any other government office, glass, steel, flags fluttering in the wind. But the moment I step through the front doors, my skin prickles with the energy of pack territory.
I stop at the reception. “Detective Marcus Hale’s office?”
“Conference room B, third floor. Down the hall to the left.” She says without looking up.
The elevator ride up is too quiet. I watch my reflection in the brushed metal doors. Leather jacket zipped. Dark jeans. Combat boots. Armor in place.
Third floor. Down the hall to the left.
I stop at the door to conference room B, take a deep breath, then knock.
“Come in,” someone calls.
I open the door.
There are three people inside: two men I don’t recognize, and…
My breath stops.
He’s standing by the window, his back to me, but I’d know him anywhere. The shape of his shoulders, the way he holds himself, the scent that hits me like a physical blow, cedar and smoke and something uniquely HIM.
Rylan.
My wolf surges forward with a force that nearly drops me to my knees.
MATE. She howls. MATE…MATE.
I slam my control down so hard it hurts, forcing her back, locking her away even as she fights me with everything she has.
Rylan turns around.
Our eyes meet.
The bond hits me like a tsunami. Not gentle. Not the soft pull I remember from before. This is violent, overwhelming, a tidal wave that crashes over me and drags me under.
Every instinct I have is screaming at me to go to him. To close the distance. To let the bond snap back into place and fill the aching void that’s been eating me alive for five years.
But then I see his face.
He’s looking at me with that same professional mask he wore five years ago. The one he put on when he stood in front of the entire pack and rejected me. Cold. Controlled.
The memory slams into me, standing in the center of the pack circle while Rylan’s voice echoed: “I reject you as my mate. You are no longer welcome in this pack.”
The heat in my body turns to ice.
I slam my control down so hard my wolf yelps in pain. I lock everything away, the bond, the heat, the desperate longing. I wrap myself in armor, layer after layer of ice and steel and professional distance, until I can’t feel anything at all.
When I speak, my voice is perfectly steady. “Detective Hale.” I take his outstretched hand, shake it once, let go. “Thank you for the opportunity to consult on this case.”
If Marcus notices the tension in the room, he doesn’t show it. “We appreciate you making the trip on short notice. This is Detective Rylan Kane, lead investigator, and Detective James Chen.”
I don’t look at Rylan. Can’t look at him. If I do, the armor might crack.
“Detective Kane. Detective Chen.” My voice is cool, professional. “I understand you have crime scene photos for me to review?”
“Yes.” Marcus pulls a folder from the table. “Five victims over the past four weeks. All rogues, all killed with surgical precision.”
I take the folder, careful not to let my hands shake. “Walk me through the timeline.”
Marcus starts talking, dates, locations, victim profiles, and I focus on his words, on anything except the man standing three feet away from me.
I flip open the folder. Standard crime scene documentation. Body positioned on concrete, throat torn out, blood pooled around the victim.
Next photo. Another body, different location. Same precision.
Third photo. Fourth photo.
And then the fifth photo, and my breath catches.
The symbol.
It’s carved into the brick wall behind the victim, rough but deliberate, and I know it. I KNOW it.
The Brand of the Free.
My hands start to shake. I flip through the rest of the photos, four more crime scenes, four more symbols, each one a variation on the same ancient mark.
This isn’t random. This isn’t just a serial killer targeting rogues.
This is connected to my father. This is connected to his death.
“Ms. Voss?” Marcus’s voice sounds distant. “Are you alright?”
I force myself to breathe. Force my hands to steady.
“I’m fine.” My voice doesn’t sound like mine. Too flat. Too controlled. “These symbols…”
“Do you recognize them?” Rylan’s voice cuts through the room, low and careful.
I have to look at him now. Have to meet his eyes.
He’s watching me with an intensity that makes my chest ache. Not the cold professional mask anymore. Something that looks almost like concern.
I hate that I notice. Hate that some part of me still responds to that look.
“Yes.” The word comes out steady. Professional. “I know it.”
The room goes very quiet.
Marcus leans forward. “Can you tell us what it means?”
“It’s called the Brand of the Free,” I say, my voice perfectly calm even though my heart is racing. “It’s an ancient symbol used by rogue resistance movements. Wolves who rejected pack hierarchy and Alpha rule.”
“Your father was researching this,” Rylan says quietly. Not a question. A statement.
“Yes.” I close the folder, set it on the table. “He was documenting the history of rogue movements in the Great Lakes region when he died.”
“Died how?” He asks.
“Car accident.” The lie comes easily. I’ve been telling it for five years. “Single vehicle collision on a rural highway. No witnesses.”
But I don’t believe it anymore. Haven’t believed it for a long time.
My father didn’t die in an accident. He was killed because of what he knew.
And now someone is using his research, his symbols, to kill rogues in Chicago.
“I’ll take the case,” I hear myself say.
Marcus nods. “Excellent. We can set you up with a workspace here….”
“I have conditions.” I look at Marcus, not Rylan. Can’t look at Rylan. “I work directly with you, Detective Hale. I need my own workspace, access to all case files and evidence, and a guarantee that I can leave the moment this consultation is over.”
“Of course,” Marcus says. “Whatever you need.”
“When can I start?” I ask.
“Right now, if you’re ready.” He stands, gestures toward the door. “I’ll show you to your workspace.”
I nod, gather my bag, and follow him toward the door.
I don’t look back at Rylan.
I don’t let myself think about the way my wolf is still crying, still reaching for him, still believing in a bond that died five years ago.
I just focus on the symbols, on the case, on the work.
On my father’s voice in my memory: “Someone has to ask the questions, Lena. Someone has to remember.”
I’m remembering now, Dad.
And I’m going to find out what they did to you.
Even if it destroys me.

The first tremor hit at four in the morning. Marcus Bell was already awake. He had been waiting for it for ninety-two days lying in the dark twelve meters underground, in a building he had spent everything he owned converting into the only thing that mattered. He didn't need to check his phone. He knew exactly what the tremor meant. The war had started. He had been here before. He had survived the first apocalypse with nothing no shelter, no preparation, no warning. He had watched people die in ways he still couldn't talk about. And then, impossibly, he had woken up ninety-two days before it all began again. This time, he was ready. The question was whether ready was enough
The first thing Marcus Bell did was sit down and remember.
Not research he already had the information. What he needed was to organise it, to pull it out of a memory that had been compressed by ten years of subsequent trauma and scrambled by the physical shock of moving backward through time. He closed his eyes and worked through it methodically, the way he had learned to work through things in his previous life: start with what you know for certain, then move outward.
The Capital: more than forty nuclear warheads, from five countries. The missile defence systems intercepted most of them, but not enough. The southern districts took the first and largest impact August fifth, nine:thirty a.m., a crater where apartment blocks and morning commuters had been. That afternoon: two more in the west, close to the city centre. The following day: a fourth, east of the capital, positioned to drive fallout across the metropolitan area on the prevailing wind. Radioactive dust turning the August sky into grey winter.
The evacuation routes heading northwest and west, toward the railway stations and military camps, were where the broadcasts directed people. The last missiles of the war had followed the crowd north. The trains had not arrived.
Marcus Bell had known people on those trains. He did not spend time thinking about them.
The northeast was different. Old factory conversions, university campuses, media parks. Low population density, no major military installations, no railway junction. The kind of area that warhead planners overlooked.
He drew a circle on the map near the Fifth Ring Road and began calling real estate agents.
He found the building on his third viewing.
The agent was pitching the bathhouse across the road when the system appeared in his field of vision: "A suitable shelter location has been found: the power distribution building." Marcus Bell walked past the agent mid-sentence. The agent assumed he had not heard and followed him.
The power distribution building sat inside a walled courtyard. The outer wall was three meters of old red brick with wire mesh still intact at the top. Inside the courtyard: a tall metal water tower, a pump house beneath it, and the building itself three storeys of solid reinforced concrete, each floor over five meters high, built to house industrial transformer equipment at the level of structural integrity that industrial equipment demanded. The south wall had been demolished when the factory relocated its transformers, the bricks still piled in the yard, but that just meant Marcus Bell could walk inside and see the frame clearly. Heavy reinforced concrete. Floor slabs poured solid. Staircase wide enough to move machinery.
And below the courtyard, accessed through a steel door in the stairwell: an underground garage, five hundred square meters, dry, high-ceilinged, with narrow ventilation windows ringing the upper wall and a waterproofing job that had kept the floor dry for thirty years.
He went back to the agent the next day and told him to get better lease terms.
He signed the five-year lease at eight hundred and sixty thousand dollars per year and paid the first quarter before the ink dried. He transferred three hundred thousand dollars to Old Chuck as a renovation deposit the same afternoon, calling him from the car: "Get every worker you have and start in two days."
He called Zack Zhao that evening.
Zack Zhao was eight years younger, an electromechanical engineer who had been systematically swindled out of everything he owned by a business partner in his mid-twenties and had arrived at Marcus Bell's courtyard door with nothing except his skills and his stubbornness. Marcus Bell had lent him two hundred thousand dollars without asking for collateral, on the assessment that Zack Zhao was the kind of man who honoured his debts. He had been right. Zack Zhao repaid every dollar within two years, and he had framed the promissory note and hung it in his office as a reminder of who had believed in him when no one else would.
He now ran one of the city's technically sharpest security companies. Marcus Bell told him to come out and look at the building.
Zack Zhao arrived the following morning and spent half a day walking every centimeter of the property. Marcus Bell described what he needed: no blind spots, full perimeter coverage, automated drone patrol, motion sensors on the outer wall, three monitoring stations inside the building, and a wrist-mounted controller that could display the whole system on a single display. Zack Zhao called it something from a video game. Then he threw himself into it with the focused joy of an engineer given a problem worth solving.
He ordered four one automated security drones from his own company's best product line each one equipped with high-definition cameras and infrared sensors, capable of memorising its patrol route after a single flight and repeating it independently, with over four hours of flight time and the ability to track and follow moving targets automatically. Then thirty-six surveillance cameras, outdoor and indoor models, plus hidden cameras for the stairwell and kitchen. A sliding camera platform installed on the south wall that could extend a camera arm above the wall when needed. All of it integrated with a custom wrist controller.
Marcus Bell bought a hundred of the premium outdoor cameras without bargaining. Zack Zhao stared at him.
"You're not short of money," Zack Zhao observed.
"I'm not planning to be short of much for long," Marcus Bell said.
What Old Chuck's workers built over eight weeks was nothing that would have been recognised as an office renovation.
The outer courtyard wall received an interior concrete skin a second layer built against the original brick, steel beams packed between the two, the combined structure now thick enough to absorb a car collision. The iron gate was torn out and a custom steel replacement installed on sliding rails with a locking bar mechanism operated from the inside: immune to forced entry from the exterior, tested by the fabricator against vehicle collision.
Every window received double-layered bulletproof tempered glass, sealed behind aluminium louvers that locked shut, the entire assembly enclosed in steel grille cages that took any first impact before it reached the glass. The first-floor railings were custom-fabricated at a specialist plant. The south wall was rebuilt and lined with lead-coated metal sheeting sandwiched in a forty-centimeter composite skin, radiation-resistant and structurally dense.
In the underground garage: two sixteen-cubic-meter fuel tanks installed in the corner and sealed under poured concrete thirty-two tons of diesel, enough to run the generators for an extended period. The generators themselves were positioned and connected. A lithium battery array equivalent to twenty electric vehicles went onto the first floor; an identical array on the third. The roof was waterproofed and covered with solar panels inefficient in the radioactive-dust sky that was coming, but capable of delivering any amount of free electricity for as long as there was light.
The building received central air conditioning and a fresh air system with controllable pressure differentials when sealed, the internal air pressure could be raised above the outside, preventing external contamination from finding its way in through any gap the seals had missed.
The first floor was divided into a large preparation room and a dining room designed for fifty, with a semi-open commercial kitchen behind a long counter four stoves, industrial refrigerators and freezers, a cold storage room for frozen meat. The second floor was dormitory space: six four-person rooms and two two-person rooms, each with two computers, storage boxes, and a wardrobe. The third floor was Marcus Bell's studio, bedroom, and personal storage, plus the all-purpose workbench along the east wall. The basement held the workshop, the refining machine, three large warehouses, and a generator room.
The medicine room a space of less than fifty square meters held three refrigerated cabinets stocked with antibiotics, wound care supplies, anti-radiation drugs in both oral and injectable forms, and radiation treatments. Marcus Bell had annotated his post-apocalyptic supply map with additional pharmaceutical sources: hospitals, pharmacies, distribution warehouses. He knew, from experience, that medicine was one of the three hardest currencies in the post-apocalyptic world. He bought as much of it as he could before the world ended and trusted the map to help him find more afterward.
He stockpiled food in three separate locations. The logic was simple: if one location was breached, the other two still held. Most of the long-shelf-life food compressed military biscuits, canned goods, field rations, powdered milk, cocoa, sugar, salt went to the supply warehouses in the underground garage, behind sturdy walls and locked iron gates. Some went to the food storage room behind the kitchen. A reserve went to his personal warehouse on the third floor. Three locations. Three independent lines of failure before the food was gone.
He also sent Zack Zhao out to buy five off-road electric motorcycles, a Chevrolet Express passenger van, an off-road pickup campervan, and a medium-sized Ford flatbed truck. He drove the flatbed himself from the used-car lot, stopped to load spare tires, and parked everything in the yard under a tarpaulin shelter built from salvaged steel tube and two layers of canvas, anchored down so the shockwave from a detonation would not send the vehicles rolling across the yard.
The vehicles mattered for a specific reason Marcus Bell understood from his first life. After the apocalypse, petrol would become scarce within months refineries destroyed, distribution networks gone, the remaining stored fuel controlled by whoever had the weapons to hold it. Noise would matter equally: a conventional engine was audible for hundreds of meters in a quiet post-apocalyptic city, and in a world where radiation zombies were drawn to sound, noise was a targeting beacon. Electric vehicles were silent. Their fuel was electrical energy, which the shelter's generators and battery arrays could produce from diesel that Marcus Bell had buried in the ground. The five motorcycles had a hundred kilometers of range each. The farm tricycle had two hundred. In the ruins of the Capital, that was freedom of movement that no petrol vehicle could reliably match.
The post-apocalyptic supply map on the third floor was the last piece of the preparation architecture, and in some ways the most valuable thing in the building. Marcus Bell had spent hours annotating it over the weeks of construction, pulling from memory every resource location he had visited or heard reliable reports of in his first life: hospitals with intact pharmaceutical stores, police stations with armories that had been overlooked in the initial chaos, warehouses on the edges of the blast zones where the shelving was still intact, civil defence facilities whose locations were not publicly known, logistics hubs where food and medicine had been waiting for distribution when the bombs fell. He printed it in sections, laminated each sheet, and filed them in a waterproof folder in his personal storage on the third floor.
He had survived ten years of the post-apocalyptic Capital, in his first life, navigating that environment without this map, learning its geography through costly experience. Now he had a detailed, annotated reference built from ten years of that experience, compressed into laminated sheets and available to anyone who needed it.
Eight weeks. Eighty million dollars. The building that Old Chuck's workers had renovated looked, from the road, like an unusually well-built commercial studio conversion. From inside, it was a fortified survival structure designed to function as a community anchor for dozens of people across an extended period of apocalyptic conditions with the food, water, power, medical supplies, weapons, manufacturing capability, and intelligence infrastructure to make that possible.
The last item on the shelter's twelve-component checklist was the one that could not be solved with a phone call or a bank transfer.
Weapons.
A classmate studying in Europe pointed him toward an antique weapons forum the kind built around firearms whose patents had long expired, whose historical interest placed them in an enthusiast's grey zone, where knowledgeable people catalogued and sometimes reproduced century-old designs for the pleasure of the craft. Behind a ten-euro premium membership gate, Marcus Bell found complete manufacturing blueprints for dozens of classic designs, annotated by fabricators who had built functional versions and documented every deviation from the original specification.
He spent two weeks reading before he placed his order.
What he needed was not the most powerful firearm available. It was the most useful one useful specifically in a post-apocalyptic city where the ammunition supply would be whatever had survived the collapse of the civilian and military logistics networks. He already knew the answer from ten years of post-apocalyptic experience: the two most common rounds in the ruins of the Capital would be the seven.sixty twoxthirty nine millimeter AK cartridge used in the Type fifty six semi-automatic, the AK family, the most widely distributed militia weapons in the country and the NATO-standard round.
He needed firearms calibrated to those rounds.
He also needed suppressors. Not for stealth though stealth would matter but because firing an unsuppressed weapon in an enclosed space was physiologically damaging, and because the sound of a gunshot in the post-apocalyptic ruins carried for hundreds of meters and attracted exactly the kinds of things that it was better to avoid attracting. He needed night-vision compatibility. Not because he planned to fight at night, but because in the nuclear winter the sky would be grey all day and the effective daylight hours would be short, and a man who could only operate in full daylight was a man with half the operational time of someone who could not be stopped by darkness.
He also needed to think about range and use cases. In his previous life, the most common survival encounters in urban ruins had played out at distances between twenty and two hundred meters streets, corridors, collapsed buildings where sight lines were broken and cover was abundant. The Lee-Enfield's greatest attribute in this specific context was not historical reputation but calibre: seven.sixty twoxthirty nine AK rounds, the most common rifle cartridge in the ruins, available from militia armories, police stations, and civil defence supply caches across the city. He could source it locally, indefinitely. The ninety eight K's seven.sixty twoxfifty one NATO full-power round was less available but substantially more capable at range more energy, better penetration, more decisive stopping power. He had a thousand rounds in store and access to military caches already mapped.
The crossbows and melee weapons were equally deliberate. In a post-apocalyptic world where ammunition was finite and noise discipline was essential, silent-ranged weapons and close-quarters tools had a value that the pre-apocalyptic mind consistently underestimated. He ordered twenty mechanical crossbows with five hundred steel bolts, twenty quality full-tang blades, and a batch of reinforced entrenching tools the kind that could serve as both a digging instrument and a close-range weapon when nothing else was available.
A private German gunsmith located through the forum confirmed he could build to specification. The order went out through encrypted email. The shipment would travel through established smuggling routes via Southeast Asia Cambodia as a transit point, declared as a vintage motorcycle and arrive at a local logistics company's depot within four to six weeks.
Marcus Bell transferred the payment and went back to the forum.
He spent two more weeks reading blueprints. Not because he needed more weapons but because he needed to understand what he had ordered well enough to maintain and modify them, and because the forum contained something he had not expected: detailed analysis of post-battle weapon performance, written by people who had used these designs in actual conditions. He downloaded everything that was relevant and backed it up.
The crate arrived on an ordinary afternoon, exactly as promised.
Marcus Bell worked through the outer planks methodically with the crowbar. Under them: two large green polymer storage boxes, stacked, their surfaces marked with alphanumeric codes and a workshop logo he recognised from the forum. The combination was a six-digit code from an encrypted email he had memorised.
He entered it and lifted the lid.
The first box held the firearms in walnut cases trimmed with brass. The Mauser ninety eight K occupied the longest case dark wood and blued steel, museum-quality finish, the eight X optical scope mounted and zeroed on its rail, a suppressor threaded to the muzzle, a spare barrel and full maintenance kit in the side compartments. In the adjacent case: the Lee-Enfield, shorter, re-chambered to fire the common seven.sixty twoxthirty nine AK cartridge. A six X scope, a suppressor. The same careful craftsmanship, a man who built firearms because he understood them. Two smaller cases held the pistols: a .fourty five calibre Colt M NINETEEN ELEVEN with a tactical flashlight and four spare magazines, and a nine MM long-barrel version with a fifteen-round magazine, four spare magazines, and its own dedicated suppressor. Spare barrels, spare scopes, maintenance tools for all four weapons. Every component accounted for and documented.
He set the first box aside and opened the second.
The ammunition was arranged in internal compartments by calibre. A thousand rounds of NATO seven.sixty twoxfifty one for the ninety eight K. Two thousand rounds of seven.sixty twoxthirty nine for the Lee-Enfield. Five hundred .fourty five calibre half solid, half hollow-point and two thousand nine MM. In separate sealed tins: armour-piercing rounds and incendiary rounds for both rifles. And two hundred .fourty five pineapple rounds a fragmenting design that shattered on impact with soft targets, built specifically for large biological threats.
Marcus Bell checked the action on each weapon, seated the scopes, pressed the suppressors to confirm the thread fit. Everything had been made to the specification he had described in the encrypted emails. He locked the firearms in the weapon cabinet in the maintenance room and turned the handle.
The system notification appeared instantly: "Side mission: Weapon inventory in the maintenance room complete. All twelve branch tasks completed. Main Quest My Sanctuary Completed."
Three rewards. Simultaneously.
He ran the basic draws first: four in sequence, four pointers spinning simultaneously in the pale blue interface floating in his field of vision. A package of compressed biscuits sealed with a ten-year shelf life system-grade, which meant higher caloric density than anything commercially available, the kind of rations that a military-grade shelter would issue rather than the civilian equivalent. A sealed water bottle of unusual structural quality. Emergency gauze in red-cross packaging. And twenty rounds of nine MM hollow-point ammunition in a rectangular red plastic box, each round machined to a consistency that commercial mass-production rarely achieved.
He set them on the table and considered them. The ammunition was the most practically useful item in the batch not for its quantity but for what it implied about the system's understanding of what he would need. Twenty rounds of hollow-point nine MM, produced at a quality standard above anything commercially available. The system knew what it was equipping him for. He moved on.
The first intermediate draw produced six throwing knives in a leather case each blade balanced to a precision that went beyond what ordinary manufacturing could account for. The system flagged them as named equipment: a category Marcus Bell recognised from his first life, when certain post-apocalyptic craftspeople with specific evolved abilities had begun producing weapons with properties beyond the sum of their physical components. In the post-apocalyptic world he remembered, named equipment was extraordinarily scarce in a settlement of tens of thousands of people, the presence of a single craftsperson with the ability to produce it would attract intense competition from survivors eager to acquire anything they could make. He had not expected to hold any this early.
The second intermediate draw produced the sealed plastic injector with the fluorescent red fluid inside.
A bio-enhancing potion.
Marcus Bell set it on the desk and held it for a long time.
He knew what it was. In his previous life, it had taken two full years after the apocalypse for scientific teams at survivor settlements to synthesise the first generation of enhancement drugs a controlled application of what radiation and mutation had been doing to the population anyway, formalised into a deliverable product. A single basic-level injection increased a person's core physical attributes by twenty to fifty percent depending on underlying physique. Strength, endurance, nerve-reflex speed: all of them pushed beyond ordinary human maximums in a single session. For a small number of people with exceptional foundations, the improvement was substantially larger. For the rare few whose talent was recognised after injection, the drug was the beginning of a transformation that made them categorically different from ordinary survivors.
He already knew that he was one of those rare few. He had been, in his first life. But knowing it and experiencing it were different things, and this time he intended to go into the injection as calmly as the research recommended.
The drug worked better in a calm body. The research had demonstrated this clearly: elevated stress hormones at the point of injection degraded the uptake efficiency and reduced the attribute gains. He set it in the desk drawer. There was still a day of work to complete first.
He spent his remaining hundred bottle caps on the advanced lottery draw.
The result: "One primary material refining machine extracts basic common materials from various impurities; generates bottle caps." The machine materialised in the cleared corner of the underground workshop two meters wide, three meters long, a feed inlet at one end and a discharge outlet at the other. It was equipped with a storage compartment at the back, already connected to the power supply. Feed it scrap metal, demolition debris, organic matter: it sorted everything to standardised base components and returned them graded and purified. In the ruins of a city, where raw materials were everywhere but usable manufacturing feedstock was not, this machine was the difference between a workshop that could keep producing indefinitely and one that eventually ran out of what it needed.
Marcus Bell positioned it in the workshop, connected the power cable, and went up to the third floor to run the all-purpose workbench's first real test.
He placed a wrench from the tool rack on the scanning surface. Blue light swept the metal in thin parallel passes. The screen asked: Scan and save blueprints? He said yes. A white blueprint appeared in the display panel three craftable variants listed below it, iron and steel and aluminium, with the aluminium option highlighted as the only material currently loaded in the inventory tray. He clicked it.
The workbench vibrated. Twelve seconds of mechanical sound from inside the fabrication unit. Then the discharge bay opened and an aluminium wrench rose into the light every surface machined cleaner than the original it had been scanned from, the threads on the jaw sharper and more consistent.
He worked through the entire tool rack over the next two hours. Every common item scanned, blueprinted, permanently catalogued: wrenches of every size, clamps, brackets, pipe fittings, connectors, hinges, structural hardware. Each item that went into the library was another item the workshop could produce on demand, to a quality above hand fabrication, without Marcus Bell being physically present at the machine to make it.
He tried the ninety eight K. The workbench declined: "Item too complex. Workbench level insufficient. Intermediate-level upgrade requires five hundred bottle caps."
Zero bottle caps remaining.
He acknowledged the limitation without frustration. The upgrade would come later the refining machine would generate bottle caps as it processed materials, and system missions would continue issuing and paying out as long as the shelter was occupied and active. The workbench would eventually reach the level where it could blueprint firearms and produce them automatically. For now, what mattered was the shutdown sequence.
With three days left, the system issued its final pre-apocalypse mission: replenish supplies. Two bottle caps per ton of weight.
Marcus Bell rented the remaining ten warehouse units across the road. Eight he filled with metal ingots and processing materials dense, heavy, efficient generators of bottle caps per dollar spent, and the post-apocalyptic manufacturing feedstock the refining machine would need to produce materials faster than he could collect scrap. The last two he loaded with canned goods and compressed biscuits.
The news was accelerating. Domestically, things remained surface-stable. Internationally, the picture was deteriorating in the way that only Marcus Bell could read accurately: not as a developing situation, but as a countdown. He watched it with the specific detachment of a man who already knew the outcome and was no longer watching for information but for timing. Three days. He needed to make the most of each one.
On the penultimate day, he went to the suburbs.
From a used-car lot near the eastern ring road, he found a three-wheeled electric farm vehicle the heavy-duty kind, built for agricultural work, with a lithium battery upgrade already done and a semi-enclosed canopy. The range was close to two hundred kilometers. In a city where petrol would become scarce within weeks of the apocalypse and noise would attract every radiation zombie within earshot, a silent electric vehicle with that range was worth more than any petrol car.
He drove it back to the cultural park himself. He went back for a Chevrolet Express van and an off-road pickup campervan, hiring a driver for the van while he drove the campervan. Then the Ford flatbed truck, stopping on the way back to fill the bed with spare tires. Five off-road electric motorcycles, ordered from a flagship store, with ten spare battery packs compact, silent, a hundred kilometers of range per charge, the kind of transportation that left no trail of noise in a world where noise was fatal.
He covered everything in the yard under a salvaged-steel shed and double-layered it with canvas tarpaulin, the trucks anchored down so the shockwave from a nuclear detonation would not roll them across the yard.
On the last day, the birds were wrong.
He had been up since before dawn and had noticed it while checking the perimeter from the roof. Large flocks moving north too many, too consistent, not migration season. The formations were not the loose dispersal of birds going about their business but a directed movement, like something had told them simultaneously which direction was safer and how urgently to go. In the storm drains running along the road outside the park, swarms of rats were moving in the same direction visible through the drain grates, flowing steadily, dozens of them, small bodies moving with the focused efficiency of animals responding to a signal that had not yet been broadcast on any human frequency.
In his previous life, he had not noticed the animals on the last day. He had been asleep, in the apartment he had been renting at the time, and he had woken up to the first explosion with no warning and no preparation. Later, talking to survivors in the airport shelter, he had heard the same story repeated in different forms: people who had kept animals described their pets becoming frantic in the hours before the bombs, cats hiding behind furniture, dogs refusing to come out from under beds. The animals always knew. They had always evacuated before the humans understood what they were evacuating from.
Marcus Bell noticed it now, and the familiarity of it made the timing feel suddenly very real in a way that ninety-two days of countdown had not quite made it feel. The world was not ending in theory. It was ending today. He watched the rats for a moment, then went back to work.
He unbolted the solar panels from the roof mountings and carried them downstairs.
Marcus Bell moved through the building from top to bottom, sealing as he went.
The solar panels were inside, protected from the electromagnetic pulse and the shockwave. He had carried them down himself, one panel at a time, stacking them flat in the corridor of the second floor against the wall. The cameras every one of the thirty-six were each wrapped in its own electromagnetic shielding bag, individual sleeves of metallised fabric sealed with tape, protecting the circuitry inside from the initial pulse. The monitoring servers, backup drives, and communications equipment went to the underground garage, twelve meters below ground level, below the effective reach of the pulse from any detonation that was not landing directly on the building.
He paused at the server rack and spent thirty minutes backing up the internet data he had captured to every drive he owned. The data represented something the post-apocalyptic world would be desperate for and unable to reproduce a real-time record of the first day of World War III, showing which cities had been struck, which regions had been spared, which evacuation routes were already compromised before they were announced as compromised. In a world where the internet was gone and the only remaining information came from whoever you happened to meet, this archive was worth more than most of the physical supplies in the building. He sealed the drives in anti-static bags and stored them in three separate locations.
He checked the roof ventilation hatch. Steel door. Four locking bars seated in their brackets. Sealed.
Each floor, systematically, room by room: aluminium louvers shut and latched at both their upper and lower mounting points. Windows crisscrossed on the interior face with adhesive reinforcing tape pressed into a diagonal grid the method used in earthquake-zone construction, designed to hold a shattered pane in place under pressure so it did not spray inward as shrapnel. Every gap at the window frames sealed with a bead of silicone sealant pressed into place with a putty knife and run twice for certainty. Every door closed and tested in its frame, every gap at the threshold taped.
The laundry room and kitchen: ventilation grilles sealed with silicone. The rooftop access door: already sealed, locking bars already down, but he checked it again. The stairwell at every level: fire doors pulled shut and tested.
The underground entrance: wooden boarding fitted over the concrete ramp to prevent debris from the shockwave rolling into the passage. The steel roll-up gate cranked down to its stop. The roller shutter closed and its entire perimeter sealed with a continuous bead of silicone around the bottom edge, up both sides, across the top junction with the ceiling, every place where the outside world might find a way through.
The steel door at the bottom of the stairwell connecting the first floor to the basement: closed, locked from the basement side, the gap at the threshold sealed.
Generators: down. Battery power only. Two indicator lamps left running in the underground garage, providing the minimum light needed to navigate without drawing power from the main arrays. Every other light in the building off.
He walked through the building one final time, from the basement to the third floor and back, checking by feel and by the thin beam of a hand torch. No light escaping through any gap in the louvers. No air movement from any unsealed vent. No sound from outside.
The building was sealed.
He found the phone in his pocket and made the last call.
"Boss? I was about to go out to a job."
"Don't," Marcus Bell said. "Take tomorrow off and stay indoors. Tonight go to the supermarket. Fill what you can: food, water, daily necessities. Then come home and stay there."
A pause. "Is there a lockdown coming? I haven't seen anything."
"If you trust me," Marcus Bell said, "do this without asking for an explanation right now. One more thing whatever you hear on the broadcasts in the next few days, do not go north. If things become very bad and you can't stay where you are, find a way to reach the cultural park."
Three seconds of silence. The silence of a man who had learned, at some cost, when to ask questions and when to trust the person asking him to act.
"Understood," Zack Zhao said. "I trust you."
Marcus Bell put the phone down.
The box he had already sent to Zack Zhao was in transit emergency food, a flashlight, and the most important item: half the box filled with anti-radiation medication, both oral doses and injectable forms. In the first days and weeks after a nuclear blast, the difference between surviving radiation exposure and dying from it often came down to whether you had the right medication and took it in time. In his previous life, Marcus Bell had watched people die from radiation sickness who had survived everything else the bombs, the cold, the food shortage because they had no medication at all. Zack Zhao was a very intelligent person. If he had the medication and the warning and the food to sustain himself through the first phase, there was a real chance he would find his way through.
In his previous life, Zack Zhao had followed the evacuation broadcasts toward the railway stations. The last missiles of the war had found the trains on the tracks. He had been twenty-eight years old a man who had rebuilt himself from nothing through skill and stubbornness, who had repaid a two-hundred-thousand-dollar debt that most people in his position would have walked away from.
Whether he would act on the warning, whether the box would arrive in time, whether any of it would be enough none of that was within Marcus Bell's control. He had done what he could. He filed the uncertainty away and went downstairs to wait.
The tremor came before dawn. A single pulse through twelve meters of concrete barely perceptible, easily missed by someone not expecting it. Marcus Bell was on his feet and up the stairs before it finished.
He turned on the computer and found what he had always known he would find.
The news channels were mostly static. A handful had emergency broadcasts running anchors with controlled fear in their voices, delivering information that was already outdated by the time it reached the air. The internet was chaos: forums and news sites filling simultaneously with reports from dozens of cities, each one confirming in different words what Marcus Bell had known since May fifth. The war had started.
He opened his laminated supply maps and began marking with a pen. Every confirmed nuclear impact placed as a dot, cross-referenced against his own memory of where the warheads had fallen and verified against the incoming reports. Southern districts: first and largest. Coastal cities. Central transport hubs. Political and cultural centres. Each dot placed with precision, representing something that had already happened once, reproduced now in exact agreement with his memory from ten years in the future.
This was data, and data was what the ruins of the Capital would be starving for. Every survivor settlement that eventually formed in the post-apocalyptic city would face the same problem: they knew their immediate surroundings, they knew the rough outline of what had happened, but they did not know the detailed geography of destruction and survival across the wider region. Which areas had been struck. Which districts were intact enough to scavenge. Which routes were passable and which were still too radioactive to enter without dying. Marcus Bell was building the most comprehensive record of that geography that any survivor in the city would possess, from real-time data collected while the internet was still alive.
He compressed everything news footage, forum posts, news site archives, government announcements onto every backup drive he owned and filed them in the underground workshop in waterproof containers.
The second bomb struck the Capital in the early afternoon. He knew exactly when it was coming. He was at his desk when the building shook a pressure wave at this distance rather than a structural assault, the windows rattling in their taped frames, the indicator lamps swinging, every sealed door in the building groaning once before settling back. He checked every seal immediately, moving through the building at a walk, pressing his hand against the seals at each window, testing the door frames. Every seal held. Every door was seated. The water system was reading nominal. The power was reading nominal.
Thirty minutes later he was back at his desk, watching the internet reports continue to fill in the picture, until they stopped filling in anything until the internet died somewhere between the second and third impacts, quietly, without a closing message, in the way that everything essential dies in a catastrophe: mid-sentence, without announcement.
The third bomb followed in the evening. Another shake. Another check. Holding. The sky outside, visible through the narrowest gap he permitted himself at one corner of one louver on the third floor, had gone from the grey of an August afternoon to the grey of a sealed room radioactive dust settling over the city in a blanket that would not lift for months.
He closed the louver and went back downstairs.
Marcus Bell went to the kitchen and made instant noodles on the electric stove. He ate standing at the counter, tasting nothing, because he had not eaten in twenty-four hours and the next phase required a functional body. When he was done, he went back to the basement and lay down on the bunk.
The radio was still broadcasting the evacuation instructions in a loop from the bedside unit he had left running the same message repeating every forty minutes, the voice of a government that had already ceased to function in any meaningful sense, directing citizens toward evacuation routes that were already gone. He listened to it cycle twice before he turned it down to background level and stared at the concrete ceiling and waited for the next day.
On the second day after the bombs, the radio announced that the Capital had been abandoned. The government emergency plan had directed the remaining survivors toward rail evacuation north. The evacuation message cycled. Marcus Bell listened to it complete three loops, then turned the radio down.
Outside the sealed building, the sky was completely dark at midday. The radioactive dust that had settled in the hours following the impacts had formed a continuous atmospheric layer, blocking the sunlight that would normally reach the city in August. In his first life, Marcus Bell had seen this from the outside the way the dust turned the sky into a grey ceiling that leached all colour from the ruins below it, the way the light that filtered through had a flat, directionless quality that felt wrong in every small bone of the body, the way the first weeks of the nuclear winter had a particular psychological weight that he had not been prepared for and that had broken people who had survived everything else.
He had not been out in those first weeks last time. He had been underground, in a shelter that was running out of food, surrounded by people who were beginning to understand that the world outside was not going to be survivable in the way they had hoped. He remembered the specific quality of that fear very clearly.
He was not going to make those people wait for food this time.
He found the enhancement potion in the desk drawer. The sealed plastic injector, the red fluid catching the light.
In his previous life, the science of enhancement drug uptake had been studied carefully after the first generation of drugs became available. The researchers had determined with consistent evidence that a body in a calm physiological state low cortisol, regular respiration, relaxed muscle tissue absorbed the drug more completely and converted it into higher attribute increases than a stressed body under the same injection. The practical instruction was simple: control your breathing, lie flat, stay calm.
He sat in the chair at the workbench desk and regulated his breathing. Long slow exhale. Deliberate slow inhale. He felt the chair under him and the cool air of the sealed basement and the particular stillness of a building that had survived the first wave of everything without a crack.
He pressed the injector to his left arm and released the pressure mechanism.
The warmth arrived immediately from the injection point up his arm, across the shoulder, down his spine, radiating outward to his extremities in a slow building flood. His hands grew heavy. His vision narrowed to the middle distance and then closed.
He lay flat on the bunk, interlaced his fingers across his chest, and let his breathing slow until it stopped being a conscious act.
He slept for three days.He could see in the dark.
Not completely not daylight clarity but from the dim red pulse of the indicator lamps, he could see the computer chair across the room, the tool rack on the far wall, the individual implements on it. He could see the enhancement vial on the desk, five meters away, and read the barcode on its side without moving. He blinked and tested this moved his focus between the near and far ends of the room, checking whether the improvement was consistent or just an adaptation artefact from waking in darkness. It was consistent. Better in the near field than at distance, but the distance capability was also expanded beyond what it had been before the injection.
His night vision had improved in a way that could not be explained by three days of dark-adapted eyes. This was structural. Something in the architecture of his visual processing had changed.
He stood carefully and found his balance different lighter, more responsive, the contact between his feet and the concrete floor more precise, as if the nerve signals running from his feet to his brain and back had been routed through a faster channel. He walked across the room to the tool rack and back. The adjustment was not a learned compensation. It was already there, already natural, already the baseline.
He opened the shelter system.
Below the structural panels and mission interface, a new section had appeared: Shelter Characters. One entry. His own.
Marcus Bell Shelter Manager
Attributes Strength: four. Stamina: five. Agility: eight. Intelligence: five .
Talent Abilities: "Special Physique Increases enhancement potion injection effectiveness by fifty percent. Permits one additional injection at the same potion level." "Calm and Composed Doubled resistance to fear, tension, and anxiety. Reduced susceptibility to negative emotional states."
He looked at the agility score for a long time.
Eight. Nearly three times the baseline of an ordinary adult. In his previous life, the research teams that had mapped human enhancement had established what the attribute numbers meant in practical terms. Strength above ten was the threshold where internal energy began to manifest, where enhancement stopped being merely physical and became qualitatively different. People who reached that threshold underwent changes that made them a different category of human being entirely, with abilities that defied the normal mechanical limits of the human body. It was rare, exceptional, and sought after by every major settlement in the post-apocalyptic world.
Stamina governed wound recovery and environmental endurance. People with high stamina adapted faster to harsh conditions, healed from injuries more quickly, and could sustain output longer under physical stress without reaching the point of failure. In the post-apocalyptic world, where medical facilities were primitive and injuries were frequent, stamina was the attribute that kept people alive across months and years rather than days.
Intelligence produced compound improvements that were subtle at the individual level but decisive across time faster learning, stronger retention, better analysis of complex situations. The research teams in the major survivor cities had observed that the core of every scientific and technological operation was staffed almost entirely by high-intelligence new humans, whose ability to absorb and apply information at speed made them worth ten ordinary researchers in any given working session.
Agility at eight meant his nerve signals moved at close to three times normal speed. It meant his dynamic vision the capacity to track and correct against fast-moving targets was beyond what any unenhanced human could achieve through training alone. It meant that in the first second of any physical threat, before conscious thought had fully formed, his body would have already responded. Dodged. Moved. Counterattacked.
His Special Physique had amplified the injection by fifty percent. Without it, the agility score would have reached perhaps five or six meaningful, but not the outlier it was. With the Special Physique, he had landed at a level that placed him in the upper tier of what enhancement drugs could produce. The Special Physique also allowed one more basic-level injection. One more opportunity to push another attribute past its natural ceiling.
He filed that away. First things first.
He also looked at the structure of the Shelter Characters panel the way its column headers were designed for loyalty, skills, morale, and current assignment and understood what the system had been built for. It was not a single-survivor tracking system. It was a community management interface, waiting for a community to appear in it. The system that had guided him through ninety-two days of preparation had not been preparing him to survive alone in a very well-equipped basement. It had been preparing him to manage something larger.
He took out the post-apocalyptic supply map and spread it flat on the workbench.
The pentagon blast door at the bottom of the pedestrian passage. The civil defence facility beyond it capacity two to three hundred people, government-maintained, restocked by Lt. Lee's team in the weeks before the apocalypse. The passages marked on the laminated floor plans connect that facility to the residential communities of Eastfield to the east and Westgate to the west. Arrows on the maps pointing down corridors that Marcus Bell had not yet walked, toward spaces he had not yet seen, potentially occupied by people who had made it underground before the bombs fell and who had been sitting in the dark since, eating through whatever they had managed to grab in fifteen minutes of panic and rationing it as carefully as frightened people in the dark were able to ration anything.
He looked at the shelter's dining room. Capacity: fifty. He looked at the dormitory floors. Capacity: thirty to forty. He looked at the medicine room. Capacity: enough antibiotics and anti-radiation treatment to sustain many people through the worst of the initial exposure period.
The shelter had been built for this. Not for him. For this.
That calculation the one that had sat underneath every dollar spent and every design decision made over ninety-two days was about to move from calculation into action. The shelter was ready. Now the question had to be answered in the world, not on paper.
The food in those facilities was running out.
That was not speculation. It was a calculation the civil defence stores divided by the number of people who could have reached the facilities, measured against the days since the bombs fell. The answer was not months. It was days.
He had survived before without any of this.
He needed to hold that clearly, because it was the core of everything he was about to do. In his first life, he had stumbled into the apocalypse without preparation, without resources, without a map or a weapon or an enhanced body or a system. He had survived by instinct and stubbornness and the particular grinding competence of someone who had been hurt enough times to stop being surprised by it. After ten years, he had become one of the most capable fighters in his region. He had led search teams with the highest survival rates in the airport settlement. He had mattered.
But he had never been positioned early enough to save anyone before they were already in crisis.
He had arrived into disasters already happening and done what he could with the time available. He had watched people die from radiation sickness who might have survived with the drugs in the medicine room one floor above him. He had watched groups starve who might have lasted another month with the food in the three warehouses below him. He had watched communities fracture and collapse for lack of the kind of organisation that a system specifically designed to build and manage communities might have provided, if anyone had had one before the world ended.
This time, he had built the infrastructure before the crisis.
The dining room for fifty people: waiting. The dormitory rooms with their paired computers and personal storage: waiting. The medicine room with its three refrigerated cabinets of antibiotics and anti-radiation drugs: waiting. The LAN servers loaded with ten thousand hours of films and music and games because he knew, from ten years in the dark, what it did to people when they had nothing to hold onto waiting.
He had not built any of it for himself.
The radiation counter was lower than it had been the day before.
He had been reading it twice daily since the bombs fell. The numbers had peaked in the immediate aftermath of the last strike and had been decreasing in small fractions since irregular, dependent on wind patterns and atmospheric settling, but consistently in the right direction. The northeast district was still lethal to anyone without a sealed protective suit and a breathing mask. But lethal was a threshold, not a fixed state. The number was moving toward survivable.
His calculation was this: the civil defence facilities in the surrounding communities Eastfield to the east, Westgate to the west had been rated for two to three hundred people each. The people who had reached them before the bombs fell had arrived with whatever they grabbed in the fifteen minutes between the broadcast and the first impact. Emergency stores supplemented by whatever the inhabitants had managed to carry. The facility stores covered weeks for a population of that size, not months.
The radiation would not fall to safe outdoor exposure levels for weeks at minimum. But the people inside those facilities did not have weeks of food. They had days.
The blast door at the bottom of the pedestrian passage was twelve meters underground, sealed from the fallout, already re-lubricated and maintained by Lt. Lee's team. The passage was navigable. The only barrier was the pentagon lock the five-pointed star insertion port that required a specialised tool wheel Marcus Bell did not yet have.
He had never thought of the pentagon tool wheel as a problem he could not solve. His master key could open mechanical locks any mechanical lock manufactured before March twenty twenty five. The blast door's pentagon insertion port was not a conventional keyhole. It was a different mechanism entirely, designed for a different kind of tool. The master key could not transform itself into something with the torque-bearing capacity of the tool wheel. He had accepted that early and moved on.
But the tool wheel was in the system somewhere. The laminated booklet in the red metal box on the passage wall had described the facility's emergency equipment. Standard civil defence procedure required that every facility maintain its own operational tools, available to whoever reached it first in an emergency, precisely because the people who needed to operate the facility in a crisis could not be assumed to have arrived with the correct equipment from outside. That meant the tool wheel was in the passage, or in the guardhouse, or in the facility's emergency cache on the other side of the door.
The master key could open every door between him and the blast door. The maps showed him where to look. The passage was navigable and sealed from the radiation above ground.
He was not going to wait for the radiation to fall below the threshold for safe outdoor exposure. He was going to suit up and go underground.
Marcus Bell suited up. Mask sealed. Radiation counter: still falling. Seven days underground. Three nuclear shockwaves. Not a single system had failed. The shelter had worked. Every wall, every seal, every buried fuel tank exactly as designed. But a shelter built for fifty had only one name in it. Somewhere beneath him, past a blast door he hadn't yet opened, people who had survived the end of the world were running out of food. He turned the lock. The gate swung open. The ruins of the city waited. The apocalypse arrived exactly as Marcus Bell predicted. But the hardest part was never the bombs. Who had survived behind that blast door? Would they trust a stranger in a radiation suit? And when the food ran out how far would desperation go?
