Every recruit who had eaten freely lurched out of bed and staggered toward the stairs, their stomachs immediately staging a protest against sudden violent exercise after enormous quantities of spicy food. Some of them made it to the assembly point. Several made it only to the side of the road before their bodies announced, definitively, that tonight's game was over for them.
The recruits of Squad One and Squad Two, running on empty stomachs but otherwise fully functional, thought the same thought simultaneously: thank God for Wyatt Walker.
The game had a name and a reputation. Cat and Mouse. Every year, the company's new recruits got a head start and tried to hide on Greenstone Mountain while two full battalions of veterans hunted them down with training rifles. Every year, the new recruits were wiped out completely. They hid in the dark, got scared, got found, got tagged, and spent the rest of the night eliminated and embarrassed.
No recruit class in the history of the Iron Fist Regiment had ever done anything more interesting than survive a few hours longer than expected.
Captain Austin explained the rules with obvious enjoyment. Recruits are the mice. Veterans are the cats. Thirty-minute head start. Five miles northeast to Greenstone Mountain. After that, veterans with training rifles come in. Anyone tagged is eliminated. Game ends at morning roll call. No weapons for the recruits. No prize for last standing. Definite punishment for anyone who gets shot.
"Have you ever seen a mouse ask for a gun to fight a cat?" he said, when a recruit asked about weapons. "You'll be lucky just to hide."
Wyatt was calculating while Austin was still talking. The whistle had blown when the assembly started. The speech was eating into their thirty minutes. He broke from the formation the moment Austin finished and started sprinting, shouting over his shoulder: "Blackwood started the clock when the whistle blew! We have less than twenty-five minutes! Go!"
The formation dissolved. Everyone ran.
The system unlocked the third mission before he reached the mountain: Lead at least thirty recruits to complete the game and break the Iron Fist Regiment's record. Reward: Elite-level Fighting Technique — issued in advance. If the mission fails, you lose the skill permanently.
A wave of pain hit him like a spike through the skull — combat knowledge downloading at high speed, enormous and overwhelming. He sucked air through his teeth and kept running. When it cleared a few seconds later, he could see fighting differently — angles of attack, follow-through, counters and transitions all clicking into place with the kind of fluency that usually takes years of training to build.
He also had a tactical problem. He had roughly forty recruits on the mountain with him — the ones who had made it, who were not currently doubled over on the roadside from the chili — and they were facing two full veteran battalions with no weapons, no equipment, no darkness experience, and no plan beyond hiding and hoping.
Cole climbed a tree and scouted below. "Vets are coming," he called down quietly. "They're spreading around the base of the mountain, not coming up. They're forming a perimeter."
"Exactly what I thought," Wyatt said.
He stood up. Everyone looked at him.
"If they're spreading around the base," Wyatt said, "their strength is distributed thin. A circle has no heavy point — everyone covers a little bit of everything. If we mass our force and hit one concentrated spot, even veterans can't hold that."
The objections came immediately. They had no weapons. They had training rifles on the other side. Anything they tried would get them tagged.
"We hit them before they raise their rifles," Wyatt said. "We move first. We go hard and we don't let up."
Brock was on his feet. Clay was on his feet. Then the rest of them — one by one, then several at once, climbing out of their hiding positions, deciding that being hunted was worse than being the hunter. Even Blake, who had been holding a private grudge against Wyatt since the first day, stood up and fixed his eyes on the tree line below with something fierce and decided in his face.
They hit the first veteran squad from a boulder above a ravine. Three men, moving casually through the dark, completely confident in the overwhelming numbers advantage that was supposed to make this exercise trivial. Wyatt and Brock dropped on two of them before they could react. The fight was immediate and complicated — bodies tangled together, no room for a clean shot, the veterans' weapons useless while grappling in close. Cole came in sideways and drove his shoulder into the third man's gut, dropping him backward. Blake grabbed the falling training rifle before it hit the dirt and fired.
Three veterans eliminated. One training rifle acquired. The counterattack had a weapon now.
The recruits stripped everything they could carry — rifles, ammunition, field rations, radio equipment — and disappeared back into the dark.
The first confused radio reports started reaching the command post. Foley's team is down. Ambushed by recruits. The First Battalion Commander's face went dark. His veterans — his experienced, trained, multiple-deployment veterans — had been taken out by untrained recruits who were not supposed to have weapons. Something was very wrong with this picture.
He gave new orders: stop small-group patrols. Increase group sizes. Sweep systematically. No more exposure.
Meanwhile, Wyatt's force was growing. A Squad Two sergeant named Keller got lured into a clearing by three recruits in captured camouflage who claimed to have spotted more targets and needed help. The moment Keller's seven-man squad stopped moving in the clearing, the three decoys hit the ground, and volleys of training fire came from multiple directions simultaneously. Eight targets, exposed, caught flat-footed. When the smoke cleared, every veteran in the squad had been tagged.
Keller sat up and looked at Wyatt with what was, despite everything, a certain amount of admiration. "Wyatt Walker, Brock Kowalski, you two are ruthless." He handed over his rifle without further argument.
By three in the morning, Wyatt's force had forty-three members and an arsenal of captured equipment. They were rested, fed on looted rations, and in significantly better shape than the veterans who had been running search patterns for hours. Two full battalions had lost the initiative. They were being directed around Greenstone Mountain by a man on his fourth day in the army.
Then Wyatt looked at the distant glow of the temporary command post at the base of the mountain. The headquarters. The nerve center. The place where Austin Hayes and the battalion commanders were running the whole operation from the safety of a command post that had never in the history of this exercise needed to defend itself.
Why not take the command post?
He had one last move to make before the assault. A veteran named Fly was lying on the ground with his team, technically uneliminated — Wyatt had deliberately not fired the training round to tag him, had even told his men to let these guys keep some of their pride. Fly, calculating, not unreasonably, that an uneliminated soldier was allowed to use his radio, called the command post and reported Wyatt's apparent plan: heading for the summit, planning to descend the back side to the regiment. All units should redirect to the summit immediately.
The command post redirected. The veterans on the mountain rushed toward the summit.
Wyatt stepped out of the shadows with his squad and fired on Fly's team. He stomped the radio under his boot.
"You used us," one of the veterans said.
"If you'd treated us as equals," Wyatt replied, "you wouldn't even have to ask."
The road to the base of the mountain was clear. Forty-nine recruits moved through the dark toward the command post that was now, for the first time in the history of this training exercise, almost entirely unprotected.
The command post was quiet. No ambush. No last-minute defense. The area was deserted except for the people who were supposed to be there — the battalion commanders, a skeleton crew, and Austin Hayes.
Blake was next to Wyatt when they crouched in the dark outside the tent, close enough to hear the voices inside. "We're really doing this," Blake said quietly. It wasn't quite a question.
"Those vets have been pushing us around for three days," Wyatt said. "It's about time."
He sent Blake and Brock to sweep the flanks first — ten men each, checking for ambushes. If they hit trouble, they were to fight hard and draw fire, giving the main group time to pull back. Either way, the recruits won — if the assault succeeded, they won. If it triggered an ambush and Blake and Brock's small teams were captured, the larger group waited out the clock in safety. The clock ran until morning. Recruits who had not been eliminated by morning had completed the game.
There was no scenario in which the recruits lost.
Blake stared at him. He had not spoken to Wyatt without hostility since day one. The hostility was gone now. "Whatever beef we had was just company drama," he said. "Right now, it's us against them. He's the commander. I'll follow his orders." He gathered his men and went.
The flanks were clear. Brock's all-clear signal came back. Forty-nine recruits moved into the command post in under two minutes.
Austin Hayes looked up from his command table at the ring of muddy, exhausted, grinning new recruits. He looked at Wyatt. And then, slowly, he started to smile — not the cold predator's smile from the first day, but something more genuine than that, something with actual respect in it.
"Even though your men 'killed' me tonight in my own command post," he said, "I have to admit I'm impressed. Really impressed." He leaned forward. "That veteran's report — the one that sent us all toward the summit — you set that up deliberately, didn't you? You let him keep his radio on purpose."
"Yes, Captain."
Austin slapped his thigh. "I knew something was off about that report. I just couldn't figure it out in time." He shook his head. "One step behind."
It was Blake who delivered the final piece. He stepped forward and told them about the fallback plan — the scouting teams sent first, the arranged signal to draw fire if an ambush was waiting, the main group positioned to melt back into the dark and simply wait for morning. There was no version of events in which the recruits had not already won.
The First Battalion Commander whispered something that required a moment before words came back to him. The Second Battalion Commander — who had been cracking his knuckles and glaring when Wyatt first walked in — was nodding, all the hostility replaced by something else entirely.
"A rookie, in the army for less than four days," the First Commander said quietly, "comes up with a plan that perfect."
Austin used the command post's own comms equipment to send false orders to the veterans still sweeping the summit. Then he told Wyatt to take his people and go home as winners.
"Go on," he said. "Let the vets save a little face, and for God's sake, let us old guys save some of ours."
Forty-eight recruits turned as one and ran out of the tent. The second the last man cleared the door, the sound hit the night — a roar of released joy, forty-eight voices chanting Wyatt's name, sprinting toward the Iron Fist Regiment with everything they had left.
Inside the tent, Austin, the battalion commanders, and the skeleton crew stood there shaking their heads.
Austin pulled out his phone. It was almost dawn. He called Colonel Warren Croft and spent thirty minutes reporting the night's events in detail, singing this kid's praises without stopping, going through every piece of the counterattack from the stolen rifles to the false intel to the command post seizure. He didn't hang up until the sky started going pale at the edges.
The next day, Austin tested Wyatt in front of the entire barrack. There was one thing he was sure that Wyatt would not have done - memorize the army manual.
He screamed at Wyatt to recite it in front of everyone. Wyatt had only glanced at the manual once. The punishment is Ten lashes of whip, the Sergeant declared.
The voice inside Wyatt’s head said: New Power Unlocked. Photographic Memory.
The entire regulations manual Wyatt had glanced at the night before was now locked behind his eyes. Wyatt recited the first half of the book from memory. Every word. Every article. Without a single error.
The room went silent.
The seargeant said one word: "Unreal."
On the second night, one of the best athletes in the company was hiding in a bathroom stall with a lit cigarette — a clear barracks violation. Wyatt found him. Instead of reporting him, he turned the faucets on loud, buying time. Austin arrived on patrol and smelled the smoke immediately.
The next morning, Austin produced the carton on the parade ground. He lit twelve cigarettes at once and told the offending recruit to smoke his fill. What followed was the kind of training moment that stays with a soldier for the rest of his life — not because it built character, but because the lesson could never be forgotten.
Wyatt, for the crime of having tried to warn his friend, got ten laps of duck-walking around the parade ground, shouting "Hooray for the Captain" with every step. His legs went from burning to numb to burning again. He finished all ten laps.
"I am sorry I dragged you into this," his friend said.
Wyatt shrugged it off. "We are on the same team. Forget about it."
They were friends after that — in the way military friendships form. Fast, without ceremony, sealed by shared difficulty.
Two days later, the courage training began.
A Stryker armored vehicle. Twenty inches of clearance. A sergeant demonstrated without a long speech: he walked in front, let the vehicle come at speed, dropped and slid between the tracks at the last possible moment, and stood up on the other side. "All you have to do is lie still," he said. "Find your spot between the tracks, stay flat, and do not move."
Nobody raised their hand.
The sergeant's eyes moved across the formation and stopped on Wyatt. "You dared to challenge the captain on your first day. At least I know you are not a coward."
Wyatt took the helmet. He walked out in front of the vehicle. He lay down. He crossed his hands over his chest. He raised his arm to signal the driver. He had already calculated the geometry — his width, the track width, the clearance, the margin for error. The numbers said he was fine. He believed the numbers.
The machine rolled over him. He stood up. He handed the helmet back. The sergeant started clapping. The recruits joined him — the same recruits who had served a collective punishment partially because of Wyatt, clapping hard and genuine, unable to help it.
Then Wyatt asked to go again. This time he stood in front of the vehicle instead of lying down. The barrel got close. Five feet. Three feet. Twelve inches from his chest. At twelve inches, he dove. The machine rolled over him. He stood up on the other side.
The system unlocked a new mission before anyone could react.
Extreme Rescue. Intervene at the critical moment to protect a comrade and prevent a training accident. The targeted recruit will die. Proceed with extreme caution.
The word registered — die — and then it started.
An earnest recruit who had volunteered to go next had closed his eyes and raised his arm. The Stryker started moving. The grinding mechanical roar filled his skull and shorted out every rational instruction he had been given. His hands went up. He put his arms directly in the path of the tracks.
The driver could not stop in time. The sergeants were already shouting.
Wyatt was already running. He was out of the formation before the sergeants fully registered what was happening, closing the distance at a dead run, and he grabbed the recruit's collar an instant before the tracks would have crushed his arms. The recruit ended up on the ground, shaking so hard he could not stand.
That afternoon, Captain Austin pinned the Army Commendation Medal to Wyatt's chest. "In the history of the entire United States Army," Austin said, his voice carrying to every corner, "no one has ever earned an honor this high on their second day of service."
The mess hall erupted. Recruits who had been jealous of him, recruits who had barely known him for forty-eight hours, were on their feet chanting his name. The sound traveled through the walls and across the base. The fastest-decorated recruit in recorded American military history. Forty-eight hours in.
On the fourth day, the mess hall offered something rare: extra-spicy chili con carne. Every recruit loaded up their trays. But Wyatt looked at the veterans nearby. They were not eating. They were watching — with the kind of smile you wear when you already know how the story ends.
"Hold on," he told his squad. "Something about this feels wrong."
Squad One and Squad Two stopped eating. The other eight squads ate until they were full. At ten that night, an emergency assembly whistle blasted through the barracks. Every recruit who had eaten freely lurched out of bed, their stomachs staging a protest against violent exercise after massive quantities of spicy food. The recruits of Squad One and Squad Two ran on empty stomachs, fully functional, thinking the same thought simultaneously: thank God for Wyatt Walker.
The next mission was Cat and Mouse. Every year, recruits got a thirty-minute head start to hide on Greenstone Mountain while two full veteran battalions hunted them down. Every year, the recruits were wiped out completely. No recruit class in the history of the Iron Fist Regiment had ever done anything more interesting than survive a few extra hours.
Austin explained the rules with obvious enjoyment. No weapons. No equipment. "Have you ever seen a mouse ask for a gun to fight a cat? You will be lucky just to hide."
Wyatt was already calculating while Austin was still talking. He broke from the formation the moment Austin finished, shouting over his shoulder as he ran.
"The clock started when the whistle blew. We have less than twenty-five minutes. Go."
The system unlocked the next mission: lead at least thirty recruits to complete the game and break the Iron Fist Regiment's record. Reward: Elite-level Fighting Technique — issued in advance. Failure means losing the skill permanently.
Combat knowledge downloaded into him at high speed — angles of attack, follow-through, counters and transitions, the fluency that takes years to build. He sucked air through his teeth and kept running.
"Vets are coming," a scout called down from a tree. "They are spreading around the base of the mountain. Forming a perimeter."
"Exactly what I thought," Wyatt said. "A circle has no heavy point — everyone covers a little bit of everything. We mass our force and hit one concentrated spot. Hard. Before they can raise their rifles."
The objections came: no weapons, outnumbered, facing veterans with training rifles and years of experience. Wyatt did not negotiate. One by one, the recruits climbed out of their hiding positions and stood up. Even the sprinter — who had been running a private grudge against Wyatt since day one — stood up and fixed his eyes on the tree line below with something fierce and decided in his face.
What followed was a counterattack that no one who served at Iron Fist ever forgot.
Veteran squads went down before they knew what hit them. Weapons were stripped, equipment captured. Recruits lured patrols into killing grounds using captured camouflage and false radio reports. By three in the morning, forty-three recruits had an arsenal of captured rifles, more rations than they needed, and the initiative — two full battalions were now being directed around a mountain by a man on his fourth day in the army.
Then Wyatt looked at the glow of the command post at the base of the mountain. The nerve center. The place that had never once needed to defend itself.
He let one veteran keep his radio on purpose — and let the man use it, reporting false intel that sent every veteran on the mountain rushing for the summit. The moment the road cleared, forty-nine recruits moved through the dark toward a command post that was, for the first time in the exercise's history, almost entirely unprotected.
Austin looked up at the ring of muddy, exhausted, grinning new recruits. He looked at Wyatt. Then, slowly, he started to smile — not the cold predator's smile from the first day. Something with actual respect in it.
"That veteran's report — the one that sent everyone to the summit," Austin said. "You let him keep his radio on purpose."
"Yes, Captain."
Austin slapped his thigh. "I was one step behind." He shook his head. "One step behind a soldier on his fourth day." He told Wyatt to take his people and go home as winners. "Let the vets save a little face, and for God's sake, let us old guys save some of ours."
Forty-nine recruits turned and ran. The second the last man cleared the door, a roar of released joy hit the night — forty-nine voices chanting Wyatt's name, sprinting toward the base with everything they had left.
Austin pulled out his phone. He called Colonel Croft and spent thirty minutes going through every piece of the counterattack without pausing — the stolen rifles, the false intel, the command post seizure — singing this kid's praises the entire way. He did not hang up until the sky started going pale at the edges.
"Donovan."
"General, it is Warren Croft. Iron Fist Regiment." A pause — the pause of a man trying to find the right words. "General. What kind of monster did you send me? His skills are off the charts, but it is not just his skills. His tactics. His leadership. He is the whole package. If he stays here much longer, he is going to turn my entire regiment upside down. I am begging you, sir — take him back."
Donovan stared across the empty grounds.
"He has got my daughter wrapped around his finger, and now he has got Warren Croft singing his praises," he muttered. "I really underestimated him. But that is impossible — the background check said he was just some lazy, good-for-nothing punk."
He typed a message to his deputy: Extremely Urgent. Cancel all non-essential meetings. Push every project timeline forward. I am going to the Iron Fist Regiment.
What Donovan found at Iron Fist changed his calculus permanently.
A recruit who had embarrassed two battalions of veterans on his fourth day. Who had memorized the entire regulations manual without being asked. Who had, in thirty-one days, broken every training record the regiment had on the books.
On the thirty-second day, Donovan opened the wooden box. Inside, on velvet lining, sat a set of sergeant's stripes. The man who had ordered Wyatt's destruction now placed the highest early-service rank in the history of the Southeast Military Region onto the shoulders of the man he had tried to break.
"I am taking you to a new unit," Donovan said. "Amphibious operations. Codenamed the Dagger Regiment. That is your new home."
Wyatt looked at the stripes. Then at Donovan.
"You were the one behind the targeting," he said. Not a question.
"No comment," Donovan said.
He confiscated Wyatt's phone for the drive south — to prevent him calling the girl who had been leaving him voice messages for three months. Thirty-one days of her playing voice notes on repeat in her bedroom, alone. Her own father keeping them apart. Wyatt knew something was off. He just could not figure out how high the interference went, or why.
The Dagger Regiment made Iron Fist look like a vacation.
Wyatt arrived with the four men he had built something with at Iron Fist — the sprinter who had tried to block him on day one, the martial artist he had taken down in four moves, the triathlete, and the recruit he had pulled from the path of a Stryker. They went straight into Dagger selection, no rest, no preparation, competing against soldiers from infantry, artillery, and military police who had trained their entire careers for this moment.
Wyatt passed. Then he made Dagger his.
Not by outranking anyone. Not by pulling authority. The same way he had always done it — one impossible thing at a time, each one witnessed, each one adding to something the veterans could not explain away. The Dagger Regiment was the sharpest unit in the three hundred eighty-sixth Brigade. By the time Wyatt had been there long enough to matter, everyone in the regiment knew what the sharp end of Dagger actually looked like.
His platoon. His people. They went everywhere together — into the deep-sea operations training, the urban exercises, the classified drills that did not appear in any training log. He had a sniper on his team: a female soldier with more precision under pressure than anyone in the regiment, who proved it by taking down the Recon Company's best fighter in a single move in a live training session.
When the Red Blue Exercise was announced, the room went quiet.
One against six. The Dagger Regiment alone, facing every other unit in the three hundred eighty-sixth Brigade. The Red Force Commander — a tactical genius named Alistair Finch — had spent weeks preparing the trap. He had fortified San Diego. He had placed decoy command posts throughout the city. He had set ambushes at every predictable point of entry.
He had not prepared for Wyatt.
The Reinforced Platoon infiltrated his perimeter in stolen construction-worker disguises, slipped through checkpoints using improvised cover stories, and neutralized Red Force patrols one team at a time. They stripped uniforms. They captured radio equipment. They disappeared back into the city and reappeared somewhere new before anyone could track them.
The Red Force Commander was inside the Dagger Regiment headquarters — their own base turned against them. The windows were nano-crystal steel. Standard rounds could not breach it. Even a Gatling gun had failed to crack the material in testing.
Wyatt's plan: two snipers, four consecutive hits stacked on a single point. Nobody had ever practiced it. Nobody had ever attempted it.
One of the platoon's men volunteered as bait — deliberate capture, to draw the Commander into view. He knew what it meant. He went anyway.
A single gunshot cracked through the night. Inside the conference room, the Red Force Commander moved toward the window. The curtain shifted.
Wyatt fired.
His sniper fired immediately after. Two more in rapid succession. Four rounds stacked on a target the size of a human palm, through steel rated to stop everything.
The glass shattered.
The Red Force Commander was out of the exercise.
Blue Force won.
In the aftermath, Colonel Sterling Price — the man who had built the Dagger Regiment — made an announcement no one in that room was ready to hear.
The Dagger Regiment was being disbanded.
Orders from the top. The restructuring was final. In seven hours, the unit ceased to exist.
But from the rubble of that announcement came something else. Wyatt and his platoon — all six of them — had been selected for Red Cell evaluation. Special Forces. The unit that accepted fewer soldiers per year than any other program in the American military.
For the first time since waking up in a stranger's body, in a stranger's life, Wyatt Walker had a clear path to everything he had been building toward.
Wyatt was on his way to becoming the finest soldier in the military. All he had to do was survive selection.
Before any of them could leave — before the orders were signed, before the future could begin — Colonel Price stopped them.
The farewell oath.
He wanted it done individually. He wanted Wyatt first.
Wyatt stepped forward. The Colonel raised his right fist. And across the hall, outside the conference room, two people were standing in the corridor. Listening.
He had no idea they were there.
But Wyatt had seen one thing. That very morning, a vehicle arrived one base.  And the person inside was a woman. Wyass asked Commander Finch  who it was.
Finch looked worried for a moment. Then he recovered his composure. "She is with the Army Performing Arts Troupe," Finch replied, his voice quick and steady. "She came by to brief me on the year-end gala. Why? Is there a problem?"
Wyatt turned on his heel and walked away.
The elevator doors closed.
The moment they did, Finch's mask shattered.
What were the odds of Wyatt catching a glimpse of her?
He straightened. He had to report this to General Donovan immediately.
"You did the right thing, Finch," he said. "We cannot let those two recognize each other yet."
Wyatt had no idea that Claire, the girl for whom he joined the army, was in the same base as he was. He had not seen her in Three months.
Why is Claire at the base? Why is the Finch hiding the truth from Wyatt? What is General Donovan’s plan? Will Wyatt become the supersoldier he is capable of being?

Dr. James Anderson - Oncologist
Sponsored
I am going to say something every caregiver watching their person waste away on palliative chemotherapy needs to hear.

Your husband is not dying of liver cancer.

He is dying of Sorafenib.

The drug your oncologist prescribed to give him more time is the drug that is filling his belly with fluid, turning his skin yellow, destroying his appetite, collapsing his immune system, and making him beg you to help him to the bathroom because his legs will not carry him there.

I know because I am a board certified medical oncologist trained at one of the top cancer hospitals in Europe. I have prescribed Sorafenib to over a thousand patients. And then I watched it do the same thing to my own father.

The median survival benefit of Sorafenib for Stage 4 liver cancer is 2.8 months.

That is the number they do not put on the brochure.

Read every word of what comes next. Before you sign off on the next round.

My name is Dr. James Anderson. I'm 38 years old. Board certified medical oncologist. I did my advanced training in oncology in Heidelberg, Germany, at one of the top cancer research hospitals in Europe.

I have treated over a thousand patients with liver cancer, pancreatic cancer, gastric cancer, and colorectal cancer. I have sat across from families and told them "we have treatment options" while knowing that those options would buy their loved one a few months at the cost of everything that made those months worth living.

That is the deal. And until my father was the one in the chair, I never questioned whether the deal was worth taking.

Let me tell you about my father.

Joseph Anderson. 63 years old. Born and raised in west Texas. Hands like a man who built things his whole life because that's exactly what he was. A mechanical engineer by trade but an everything-builder by nature. He built our back porch with cedar beams he cut himself. He rebuilt the engine of a 1972 Ford pickup in our garage when I was twelve. He could look at a broken pipe, a cracked foundation, a seized motor, and tell you within five minutes what was wrong and how to fix it.

He never went to college. He learned everything by doing it. He used to tell me, "James, you read about the world. I touch it."

My mother Lily is the opposite of my father in every way that makes a marriage work. She is soft where he is solid. Quiet where he is loud. She raised me while running a small graphic design business from the spare bedroom. She made logos for churches and flyers for local restaurants and birthday invitations for neighbors' kids. She answered the phone with "Lily's Designs" in a voice so warm that people would call just to hear her say it.

They have been married for 41 years. They go to First Baptist on Sunday mornings. They hold hands during the sermon. My father opens the car door for my mother every single time, even when his knees started hurting three years ago and bending down to reach the handle made him wince.

That is who Joseph and Lily Anderson are. A respected father, a loving mother, and a son who went all the way to Germany to learn how to save people's lives and then came home and almost failed to save the life that mattered most.

My father was diagnosed with Stage 4 hepatocellular carcinoma — liver cancer — in March of 2024.

He had been having what he called "indigestion" for about six months. Bloating after meals. A dull ache under his right ribs that he blamed on a pulled muscle from working on the truck. He lost about fifteen pounds without trying, which my mother noticed before he did because she was the one buying his jeans.

He didn't go to the doctor until Lily made him. She told me later that she had to threaten to call me in Germany before he agreed.

The scan found a 4.2 centimeter mass in the right lobe of his liver. Two smaller lesions in the left lobe. And three spots on his lungs.

Stage 4. Metastatic.

His oncologist in Abilene — a good doctor, a careful doctor — laid out the standard playbook.

Sorafenib. That's the first-line drug for advanced liver cancer. A targeted therapy pill that tries to cut off blood supply to the tumor. Take it twice a day, every day, indefinitely.

The side effects of Sorafenib read like a list of punishments.

Severe diarrhea. Hand-foot syndrome, which means the skin on your palms and soles blisters and peels until walking and gripping become agony. Unrelenting fatigue. Nausea. Loss of appetite. And the one that matters most for this story — liver toxicity.

The drug you take for liver cancer actively damages the healthy liver tissue you have left.

I knew this. I had prescribed Sorafenib to hundreds of patients. I knew the pharmacology. I knew the clinical trials. I knew the median overall survival improvement was approximately 2.8 months compared to placebo.

2.8 months.

That's the number they don't put on the brochure.

My father started Sorafenib in April. I flew home from Heidelberg for three weeks to be there when treatment began.

The first two weeks were manageable. Dad was tired. His appetite dropped. But he was still Dad. He was still getting up at 6 AM. Still making coffee for Mom. Still walking out to the truck to check something he'd been working on even though he couldn't work on it anymore.

By week four the diarrhea started.

Not the kind you take Imodium for.

The kind where you're in the bathroom eight times a day. The kind where you stop eating anything that isn't white rice and toast because everything else comes straight through. The kind where a 63-year-old man who built things with his hands for a living has to ask his wife to help him to the bathroom because his legs are too weak to get there alone.

My mother never complained. Not once. She just held his arm and walked him there and waited outside the door and walked him back.

By week six, the ascites started. That's the medical term for massive fluid buildup in the abdomen. My father's belly, which had always been flat and strong, started swelling. Within two weeks he looked like he was nine months pregnant. He couldn't bend over. He couldn't tie his shoes. He couldn't sit in a chair without the pressure pushing up against his lungs.

They drained him at the hospital. Pulled 5 liters of fluid out of his abdomen in one session. My mother watched. She told me later she had to leave the room when the fluid started filling the collection bottles because it was dark yellow and she couldn't stop thinking that it had been inside her husband.

The fluid came back in nine days.

By week eight, the jaundice appeared. My father's skin turned the color of old parchment. His eyes turned yellow. His urine turned the color of iced tea. Every morning my mother would look at him across the breakfast table and try to find the face of the man she married inside the yellow stranger sitting across from her.

I was back in Germany by then. My mother would FaceTime me every night. She'd angle the phone so I could see Dad in his recliner. He'd wave at me. Sometimes he'd smile. Most nights he was asleep before she hung up.

One night she forgot to end the call. I could hear her in the kitchen. She was crying. Quietly. Into a dish towel. The way mothers cry when they don't want anyone to hear.

I booked a flight home that night.

When I walked into their house three days later, I barely recognized my father.

He had lost 28 pounds. His arms were thin. His face was hollowed. His belly was round and hard and enormous from the fluid. He was sitting in his recliner with a blanket over his legs even though it was May in Texas and 85 degrees outside.

He looked up at me. He didn't smile. He didn't wave.

He said, "Sit down, James."

I sat.

My mother was standing in the kitchen doorway. She knew what was coming. She had heard him rehearse it the night before while he thought she was asleep.

My father said, "I'm done."

I didn't say anything.

He said, "I know what you're going to tell me. You're going to tell me there are other drugs. Second-line options. Maybe a clinical trial. You're going to tell me that we should keep fighting."

I started to open my mouth.

He held up his hand.

"James. I'm your father. I changed your diapers. I taught you to ride a bike. I drove you to every baseball game you ever played. And I am telling you right now, as your father, that I do not want to die in a hospital chair with chemicals in my veins and my wife watching me shrink."

He stopped. His voice cracked.

"I want to die the way I lived. In my house. In my chair. With your mother next to me and my hands in my lap and my dignity still somewhere inside me."

I looked at my mother. She was holding the dish towel. She wasn't crying. She had already cried. Her face was still.

I looked back at my father.

I said, "Okay, Dad."

That is the moment I stopped being Dr. James Anderson the oncologist and became James the son. Just a man sitting across from his father who was dying and who had just told him to stop trying to fix it.

I helped my mother make dinner that night. We ate together — the three of us — at the same kitchen table where I had done my homework as a kid. Dad ate half a bowl of soup. It was the most he'd eaten in two weeks.

After dinner, my mother went to bed. She kissed Dad's forehead on the way past. He touched her hand as she walked by.

Then it was just the two of us.

I should have gone to sleep. I should have respected his decision and started the process of accepting it.

Instead, I sat down at that same kitchen table at 11 PM with my laptop and I did what I've been trained to do for eleven years.

I went looking for answers.

Not in the oncology databases I use at work. Not in the pharmaceutical pipelines. Not in the clinical trial registries.

I went to the NIH public database. The raw research. The population studies. The data that nobody builds treatment protocols from because there's no drug company funding it.

I was looking for anything. Any compound. Any population. Any anomaly that might protect my father's liver from the damage the Sorafenib had already done while supporting the immune system his body would need for whatever time he had left.

I didn't expect to find anything.

At 2 AM I found something that made me close the laptop, open it again, read it three times, and then sit in my father's kitchen with my hands shaking.

It was a population health study from the Caribbean. Buried in a 200-page report.

A village. 347 people. Researchers had gone there during the COVID pandemic because the village had recorded zero COVID deaths. That alone was unusual enough to send a team.

But when the researchers dug into the village's historical medical records, they found something that had nothing to do with COVID.

Zero cancer deaths in the previous decade.

Not low cancer rates. Zero. In 347 people over ten years.

They tested the blood of every adult in the village. Full panels. Comprehensive metabolic workups. Immune markers. Everything.

Two things stood out.

First, their white blood cell counts were extraordinary. Natural killer cell activity — the immune cells that patrol for and destroy abnormal cells — was functioning at levels the researchers had never documented in a general population.

Second, they all had elevated blood concentrations of a specific class of compounds called annonaceous acetogenins.

Acetogenins are found in the leaves of the soursop tree. A tropical fruit tree that grows across the Caribbean, South America, and parts of West Africa.

These compounds do something very specific at the cellular level. They block the production of ATP — the fundamental energy molecule that every cell in your body runs on — inside abnormal cells. Think of ATP as the electricity that keeps a cell alive. Acetogenins cut the power line. Without ATP, the abnormal cell starves and shuts down.

But here is what made me sit in that kitchen with my hands shaking.

The researchers had also tested the villagers' liver panels.

ALT and AST — the two enzymes that spike in your bloodstream when liver cells are damaged or dying — were at levels that would make any hepatologist cry with relief. Near-perfect liver function scores across an entire adult population, many of whom drank regularly and had dietary habits that would normally produce significant liver stress.

Their bilirubin levels — the compound that causes jaundice when the liver can't filter it out — were consistently in the low-normal range. Across the board.

These people were not genetically exceptional. They were not living some pure isolated existence. They ate what they ate. They drank what they drank.

The one variable that separated them from the rest of the world was that they consumed fermented soursop leaf water every single day. Passed down from their grandparents.

Not raw soursop fruit. Not a capsule from Amazon. Not a tea that you boil for thirty minutes.

Cold-fermented soursop leaves. Fermented for a full year. In traditional vessels. At ambient temperature. No heat. No chemical extraction.

365 days of fermentation.

That is the preparation that produces the 2% acetogenin concentration the researchers found in the villagers' blood. Commercial soursop products from the American market test at 0.3% to 0.5% when you send them to an independent lab. Most of them have no meaningful fermentation at all.

The difference is not incremental. It is the difference between a compound that does nothing and a compound that does everything.

I read the study three times.

Then I read something that made me close the laptop and press my palms into my eyes.

The researchers had submitted their findings for further study. Requested funding to explore the hepatoprotective — liver-protecting — properties of fermented soursop in cancer patients.

The FDA denied the funding.

The report was uploaded. The paper was filed. And nobody in American oncology ever cited it.

I sat in my father's kitchen at 3 AM and I thought about eleven years of medical training. Eleven years of conferences. Eleven years of pharmaceutical sales dinners and industry-funded research grants and drug-company-sponsored symposiums.

Nobody had ever shown me this data.

Not because the data was bad.

Because you cannot patent a soursop leaf. You cannot patent a fermentation process that Caribbean grandmothers have been using for a hundred years. And if you cannot patent it, you cannot protect the profits. And if you cannot protect the profits, you cannot fund the marketing. And if you cannot fund the marketing, it never reaches the oncologist's desk.

Sorafenib — the drug that was destroying my father's liver while it fought his cancer — generates approximately $1.2 billion in global revenue annually.

A soursop leaf grows on a tree.

You do the math.

But I am not an activist. I am an oncologist. And I needed to know if this compound could actually do what the data suggested before I gave it to my father.

I spent the next 72 hours reading everything I could find on acetogenins and liver cancer.

What I found confirmed what the Caribbean study suggested.

Clinical studies on soursop leaf extract showed significant, dose-dependent reduction in both AST and ALT levels. Those are the exact liver damage markers that had been climbing on my father's blood work every two weeks since he started Sorafenib.

The extract reduced total bilirubin — the compound turning my father yellow — back toward normal range in subjects whose livers were under toxic pharmaceutical stress.

In laboratory studies using HepG2 liver cancer cells — the standard cell line used to test compounds against liver cancer — the isolated acetogenin compound annonacin showed an IC50 value of 2.89 micrograms per milliliter. That means it took an extremely small concentration to kill half the cancer cells in the dish. For context, many approved chemotherapy drugs require concentrations ten to fifty times higher to achieve the same result.

And the mechanism was elegant.

Acetogenins don't carpet-bomb the body the way Sorafenib does. They target a specific enzyme complex inside the cell — the same complex the cell needs to produce ATP. In healthy cells, this creates a small, manageable dip in energy. The healthy cell compensates and recovers.

In cancer cells — which demand far more ATP than normal cells because they're dividing rapidly — the blockade is catastrophic. The cell can't produce enough energy to sustain itself. It starves. It shuts down.

The tumor gets hit at the cellular level while the surrounding healthy liver tissue is largely spared.

And in one specific animal study, subjects that received soursop leaf extract alongside Sorafenib showed significant reversal of the liver damage the drug had caused. Their AST, ALT, and bilirubin levels dropped back down. The drug was still fighting the tumor. The extract was protecting the liver from the drug.

Both working. At the same time. In the same body.

I sat back in my chair at 5 AM. Through the window I could see the sky turning gray-blue over my parents' backyard. My father's half-finished truck was sitting in the driveway. The cedar porch he built was lit up by the motion light because a cat had walked across the yard.

My mother's coffee maker turned on automatically. 5:15 AM. Same time every morning for forty years.

And I knew.

I knew I was going to give this to my father.

But I also knew from eleven years of oncology that the form of the compound matters as much as the compound itself.

I ordered nine soursop products over the next 48 hours. Every format I could find.

The first was a raw soursop capsule from Amazon. PureLeaf brand. Hard gelatin. My father put it on his tongue and his whole body seized. The chemo had destroyed his swallowing reflex. Between the Sorafenib and the ascites, his stomach was a war zone. The capsule triggered immediate nausea. He spit it into the sink.

The second was a liquid tincture. VitalSour. Twenty-two dollars. The dropper hit his tongue and he was over the toilet for ten minutes. The alcohol-based solvent was so harsh it felt like pouring acid on his already-inflamed gut lining.

The third was a powder I mixed into applesauce. He gagged on the first spoonful. The bitter plant compounds triggered his gag reflex so hard that my mother had to hold his head while he dry-heaved over the kitchen sink.

I tried seven more brands over two weeks. Capsules. Tinctures. Powders. Teas.

Every single one failed.

Not because the compounds weren't real. Because the delivery was wrong.

My father's digestive system had been systematically destroyed by four months of Sorafenib. His taste buds registered everything as metallic. His stomach lining was inflamed. His swallowing reflex was compromised. His gag response fired at anything that registered as medicinal.

I was trying to deliver a real compound through a body that rejected everything I put into it.

Nine brands. Eleven bottles. Every format on the American market.

All failures.

Then I found SimplySours.

They sent a Certificate of Analysis. ISO 17025 certified independent lab. Zero heavy metals. Zero pesticides. Zero synthetic additives. Full 365-day cold fermentation confirmed by batch records with timestamps. Heritage Caribbean trees in volcanic soil. Leaf-only extraction — leaves contain ten times the acetogenin concentration of the fruit. 2% verified annonacin.

And the format was different from everything else I had tried.

They had developed a pectin-bound gummy.

Pectin is natural fruit fiber. When you bind the fermented soursop extract into a pectin matrix, two things happen.

First, it strips away the harsh, bitter plant compounds that trigger nausea and gag reflexes in chemo-damaged patients. The neurotoxic alkaloids — the harsh compounds found in raw soursop that have been linked to movement disorders in people who consume unprocessed soursop daily — are naturally filtered out during the pectin-binding process.

Second, the pectin creates a slow-release delivery mechanism. Liquid drops hit the bloodstream in a single thirty-minute spike that the kidneys flush before it does anything useful. Capsules sit in a damaged gut that can't dissolve them — I had literally found intact capsules passing through patients' systems whole.

Pectin dissolves at a controlled, steady rate. It creates a continuous twelve-hour release of acetogenins into the bloodstream instead of a thirty-minute spike.

And because the brain recognizes pectin as food — not medicine — the gag reflex doesn't fire.

No choking. No gagging. No vomiting. No fighting.

Five seconds. Chew and swallow.

I gave my father his first SimplySours gummy on a Saturday morning at the kitchen table.

My mother was making eggs. My father was sitting in his usual spot. His skin was still yellow. His belly was still swollen. He hadn't eaten a full meal in three weeks.

I put the gummy in front of him.

He looked at it. Then he looked at me.

"What is this?"

"Just try it, Dad."

He picked it up. Put it in his mouth. Chewed slowly.

His eyebrows went up. Not a grimace. Not a gag. He actually looked surprised.

"Tastes like fruit."

"I know."

"That's it?"

"That's it."

My mother watched from the stove. She didn't say anything. She just watched.

The next morning, same thing. One gummy. Five seconds. No fight.

I stayed in Abilene for six weeks.

Here is what I documented.

Week one. Nothing dramatic. Dad was still Dad. Still tired. Still yellow. Still spending most of the day in his recliner with the blanket over his legs.

But on day five he slept through the night. All the way through. No 3 AM wake-up soaked in sweat. No restless shifting. He woke up at 6:15 and told my mother he hadn't slept like that in four months.

She wrote it down on the notepad she kept by the coffee maker. She had been tracking everything since the diagnosis.

Week two. His appetite shifted. Not a recovery. A crack in the wall. He ate half a plate of scrambled eggs. Then toast. Then, on a Thursday, he asked my mother if she would make her chicken soup. The one she makes from scratch. The one he hadn't asked for since before the diagnosis.

She made it. He ate a full bowl. His first full meal in over a month.

My mother stood at the stove and didn't turn around for about three minutes. I could see her shoulders shaking. The good kind.

Week three. I drew his blood and sent it to the lab.

His ALT had dropped from 187 to 94.

His AST had dropped from 203 to 112.

His total bilirubin had dropped from 4.2 to 2.1.

All three numbers moving in the same direction. Down.

The yellow in his skin started to fade. Not gone. But fading. His eyes looked less like old newspaper and more like his eyes.

My mother noticed before I told her the numbers. She said, "James, your father looks more like himself today."

Week four. Dad walked to the mailbox.

That doesn't sound like anything. But you need to understand that my father hadn't walked further than the bathroom in six weeks. The ascites had made every step feel like carrying a bag of sand strapped to his stomach. His legs were swollen. His balance was compromised.

He walked to the mailbox. Got the mail. Walked back. Sat down in his chair breathing hard.

Then he looked at me and smiled.

Not the brave smile he had been putting on for my mother for months. A real smile. The one I remember from when he would finish building something and step back to look at it.

Week five. The ascites started to recede. Not gone. But the pressure was easing. His belly was still round but no longer rock-hard. He could bend forward enough to reach his shoes.

Week six. Full blood panel.

ALT: 52. Normal range.

AST: 64. Nearly normal.

Bilirubin: 1.4. The jaundice was fading. My mother could see his actual skin color for the first time in three months.

And his white blood cell count — the number that determines whether your immune system can fight — had climbed from 2,400 to 5,100.

His oncologist in Abilene looked at the labs and then looked at me.

He said, "James. What changed?"

I told him.

He got quiet for a long time. Then he said, "Whatever you're doing, keep doing it."

That was eight months ago.

My father is still here.

He is not cured. I want to be honest about that. Stage 4 metastatic liver cancer does not get cured by a gummy or by anything else. The spots on his lungs are still there. The lesions in his liver are still there.

But they are stable. Not growing. Not spreading. Sitting exactly where they were eight months ago.

And the man sitting in the recliner today is not the same man I found when I flew home in May.

Last month my father went out to the driveway and opened the hood of his 1972 Ford truck. He stood there for about twenty minutes looking at the engine. He didn't fix anything. He just looked at it. Then he turned around, saw me watching from the porch, and said, "Give me another month. I'll have this thing running."

Last Sunday he went to church. First time in five months. He held my mother's hand during the sermon. She leaned her head on his shoulder.

Last Tuesday he ate dinner at the table — pot roast, mashed potatoes, green beans — cleared his whole plate, and asked for seconds.

My mother looked at me across the table while he was reaching for the serving dish. Her eyes were full. She mouthed two words at me.

"Thank you."

I couldn't answer. My throat was too tight.

I pulled the heavy coat out of the closet on a Sunday afternoon in November and just stood there in the hallway holding it.

It still smelled like last Christmas.

Like the cinnamon broom we'd had on the porch and the cold air from the back deck and a little bit of my grandson's hair, because he'd worn it as a cape running around the yard the day after Christmas when I was too sick to chase him.

I held that coat up to my face and I cried.

Because I knew what was coming.

It was the 2nd week of November. And in about 4 weeks, like clockwork, I was going to be flat on my back on the couch watching my family eat Christmas dinner in the other room without me.

Again.

My name is Patricia. Most folks call me Patty. I'm 57. I've taught kindergarten at the same elementary school in Bloomington, Indiana for 31 years, and I've been married to my husband Glen for 33 of those.

We have 2 kids. Our daughter Whitney lives in Indianapolis with her husband and our grandson Caleb, who's 6. Our son Marcus is a paramedic in Fort Wayne. He's not married yet, though he's been seeing a sweet girl named Hannah for almost a year now and I have my hopes.

I love my life.

I really do.

I love my kindergarteners. I love that I still get a little flutter on the first day of school in August even after 31 years of it. I love walking into my classroom on a Monday morning with the smell of crayons and that pink soap they use in the bathrooms and seeing 22 little faces light up because Miss Patty is back.

But every year, the same thing happens.

Every single year.

Around the 2nd week of December, one of my babies comes in with a runny nose. Maybe two of them. Maybe the whole class is hacking like a tuberculosis ward. And by Friday I feel that scratch in the back of my throat. And by Saturday I'm running a low grade fever. And by Sunday I'm wrapped in a blanket on the couch with a box of Kleenex and a bottle of Robitussin and my voice gone for the next 3 weeks.

I miss the Christmas concert.

I miss the cookie exchange at Sandra's house.

I miss our church's living nativity, which Glen has volunteered for as a shepherd every December for 18 years and which I have not seen him in once because I am always, always sick.

Last year was the worst.

Last year Whitney and Caleb were supposed to come down from Indianapolis on the 23rd. We were going to do a big Christmas Eve dinner, prime rib and Glen's mother's recipe for scalloped potatoes and the cranberry mold my grandmother used to make. Marcus was driving in from Fort Wayne. Hannah was coming with him for the first time. I'd ironed the Christmas tablecloth and pulled out my mother's china and bought place cards and written everyone's name in the gold pen I save for special occasions.

I came down with it on December 19th.

By Christmas Eve I had a fever of 102 and could not stand up without the room tilting sideways.

Glen had to host without me.

He carved the prime rib. He poured the wine. He sat at the head of the table while my whole family ate the meal I had spent 3 weeks planning and I sat in our bedroom in a sweat soaked nightgown listening to them laugh through the wall.

Hannah came back to say hi to me at one point. Sweet girl. She stood in the doorway because I told her not to come in and she said, "Mrs. Patricia, the dinner is just beautiful. Glen said you did everything. I can't wait to meet you for real next time."

Next time.

I'd waited a whole year to meet that girl.

And I met her through a bedroom doorway in a nightgown that needed to be washed.

I cried so hard after she left that Glen had to come in and sit on the edge of the bed and hold my hand for a while before he could go back out and pretend everything was fine.

That was last year.

And here it was, November 9th of this year, and I was standing in the hallway holding a coat that smelled like a Christmas I'd watched from a bedroom doorway.

I knew it was coming.

I knew it.

And I felt the same helpless dread I'd felt every November for I don't know how many years now.

This had been going on for a long time. Longer than the last 4 or 5 December collapses. I'd been the teacher who catches everything for my entire career. The flu in 2014 that put me in bed for 11 days. The bronchitis in 2017 that turned into walking pneumonia and had me on prednisone for a month. The strep in 2019 that I got from Aiden Murphy and gave to Glen and Whitney and almost the in laws.

My doctor, Dr. Hadley, would shrug when I'd ask her about it.

She'd say, "Patty, you're around 22 little petri dishes 8 hours a day. You're going to get sick. That's the job. Wash your hands, get your flu shot, get plenty of sleep, and let's keep doing what we're doing."

Wash my hands.

I washed my hands until my knuckles were cracked and bleeding by Halloween every year.

Plenty of sleep. I was in bed at 9:30 every night during the school year. Lights out. Phone face down.

Flu shot. Got it every September at the Walgreens on College Mall Road. Hadn't missed one in 20 years.

None of it mattered.

I'd take Airborne. I'd take Emergen-C until my urine was neon yellow. I'd drink so much green tea my hands shook. I'd take elderberry syrup. I'd take vitamin C. I'd take zinc lozenges that tasted like a battery.

I still got sick.

Every. Single. December.

I'd come to accept it as my cross to bear. The cost of doing this job. I'd told myself that I'd just have to be the kind of grandma who watched Christmas through a doorway from now until I retired.

And then.

Then.

About 3 weeks before that Sunday in November, we got a new substitute at school.

Her name was Ms. Lorraine.

She was probably in her mid 60s. Salt and pepper hair pulled back in a low bun. The kind of woman who looked like she'd been a teacher in another life, which it turned out she had been. She'd retired from teaching 5th grade in Terre Haute and moved to Bloomington to be closer to her daughter, and she was subbing a few days a week just to stay in the game.

She came in to cover the room next to mine for almost 2 full weeks while Mrs. Banks was out for a knee surgery.

I'd see her in the break room.

She'd be the only one in there sometimes, eating a sandwich she'd brought from home and reading a book.

She looked healthy.

That's what struck me. She had this color in her face, this sort of brightness in her eyes that you don't see on a lot of women our age. She wasn't dragging the way I always was by 2 in the afternoon. She wasn't blowing her nose. She wasn't coughing. The kids in Mrs. Banks's room had been hacking up a lung for a week and Ms. Lorraine was just chugging along like she was made of something different.

I asked her about it on a Wednesday in late October.

I was making my third cup of coffee at the Keurig and she was sitting at the little break room table and I just blurted it out.

"How are you not sick yet?"

She looked up from her book and smiled.

She said, "Honey, I haven't been sick in almost 4 years."

I almost dropped my coffee.

I said, "Are you serious?"

She set her book down and she folded her hands on the table and she said, "Sit down, Patty. Let me tell you what I do."

I sat down.

She told me she'd been a teacher for 38 years, same as me, and that for the first 34 of those, she'd gotten sick the way I got sick. Every winter. Every flu season. Every time a kid sneezed in her general direction in late November. She'd had the bronchitis years. She'd had the pneumonia year. She'd had the year she lost her voice for 6 weeks and her principal made her wear a button that said I CAN HEAR YOU, I JUST CAN'T TALK.

Then her sister, who lived in Seattle, started sending her a bottle every couple months of a garlic extract.

That was it.

That's what she said.

I think I made a face. Because she laughed.

She said, "I know, I know. I made the same face. Garlic. Like I was going to keep vampires off me. But Patty, let me tell you what it actually does."

She told me that there's a compound in garlic called allicin. It forms when fresh garlic is crushed. And allicin is one of those compounds your body recognizes and uses, particularly when it comes to supporting the front line of your immune system. The defenders that show up first when anything tries to take hold inside you.

She said when allicin is in your system on a regular basis, those front line defenders have what they need to do their job. And that can show up as fewer sick days. Faster recovery when something does get through. The kind of steady, quiet resilience that lets a 64 year old substitute teacher walk through a flu ward of 5th graders for 2 weeks and not so much as get a tickle in her throat.

Now I'm a kindergarten teacher in Indiana.

I am not a scientist. I am not the kind of woman who reads PubMed on her lunch break. I went to a small Christian college in the late 80s and I took one biology class and I cried through the dissection unit.

But what Ms. Lorraine said started making sense to me.

I'd been throwing everything at the wall for 30 years. Vitamin C. Echinacea. Elderberry. Probiotics. The expensive immune support powders from the health food store on Walnut Street. And not one of those things had stopped a December.

What if my body just needed something different?

What if the front line had been short on what it needed all this time, and I'd been pouring water on a fire that needed something else entirely?

I asked her what brand she took.

She told me. She wrote it down on a Post It from her bag and slid it across the table to me.

It said: ALEVIA. GARLIC EXTRACT.

I asked her about the smell.

Because here's the thing. I had been a kindergarten teacher for 31 years. I get hugged 40 times a day. I lean in close to read with 22 little ones. The last thing I needed was to be the teacher who smelled like an Italian restaurant.

She laughed.

She said, "Patty, I have hugged hundreds of children in the last 4 years. I have read books shoulder to shoulder with every grade level. There is no smell. None. They formulate it specifically so you don't get garlic breath or body odor. I would have stopped taking it years ago if it did that. I'd have rather been sick."

I went home that night and I told Glen.

I sat at the kitchen island and I told him every word Ms. Lorraine had said.

Glen poured himself a glass of iced tea and he listened.

When I was done, he said, "Patty, you have tried every immune support thing on the shelf at Kroger for 20 years. None of it has worked. If a substitute teacher who hasn't been sick in 4 years tells you what she takes, I think you should order it. What's it going to do, not work? You're already used to that."

I laughed.

For the first time in I don't know how long, I laughed about being sick.

I went into my office that night and I sat at the computer with my reading glasses on and I looked up Alevia.

I read for about 2 hours.

I read about the company. I read about how they make the extract. I read about why their garlic is different from what you'd get at the grocery store.

And I learned some things that honestly surprised me.

The garlic in the produce section at the Kroger, the cloves and the heads, those have been sitting in warehouses and trucks for weeks. Sometimes months. And the active compounds in them have broken down by the time they hit your kitchen counter. Most of it is flavor at that point. Not function.

The minced garlic in the jar in your fridge door? Basically inert. It tastes like garlic. There's almost nothing alive in it.

And here's the one that really got me.

Heat destroys allicin almost instantly.

So every time you sauté garlic in olive oil. Every clove you toss in a pot of spaghetti sauce. Every roasted head you mash onto bread with butter. The active compound is gone before the meal hits the table.

I had been cooking with garlic for 33 years thinking I was getting some benefit out of it.

I wasn't.

To get a meaningful dose from raw garlic, you'd have to eat enormous amounts of freshly crushed cloves every single day. The kind of amount that would have my kindergarteners refusing to sit next to me at circle time and Glen sleeping in the guest room.

That's where the extract comes in.

A real garlic extract, the kind Alevia makes, is processed in a way that preserves the allicin so your body can actually use it. Cold processed. Standardized. Concentrated. So every capsule has the same amount, every single time.

And, importantly to me, formulated to be odorless. No smell on the breath. No smell on the skin. Nothing.

Made in the United States in an FDA registered facility. Third party tested for purity.

And here was the part that closed it for me.

They offer a 90 day money back guarantee. You try it for 90 days. If it doesn't work for you, you ship the bottle back and they refund every penny.

90 days.

That would carry me from mid November all the way through February.

Through December.

Through the whole danger zone.

If I tried it and I still got sick the same way I always got sick, I could just send it back and be out nothing.

I ordered it that night.

It came on a Tuesday.

I took my first 2 capsules on Wednesday morning with my coffee, sitting at my kitchen table looking out at the bird feeder.

I want to tell you what happened next.

Because I am writing this in February. From my kitchen table. In a clean robe. With my voice. With color in my face.

Week 1, nothing dramatic. I took 2 capsules every morning. I went to work. I taught my babies. I came home. Nothing felt different.

Week 2, I noticed I was sleeping better. Not in any dramatic way. Just sleeping the way I used to sleep when I was in my 40s. Falling asleep faster. Waking up at the same time I'd been waking up, but feeling like I'd actually rested.

Week 3, the first kid in my class came in with a cough.

Mason Whitaker. Sweet little guy. Father runs a heating and cooling business. He came in on a Monday morning hacking like a chimney.

By Wednesday, half the class had it.

By Friday, Mrs. Devereaux next door was out sick. So was the music teacher.

I was waiting.

I was waiting for that scratch in the back of my throat. That little tickle.

It didn't come.

Week 4, the whole school was a mess. Half the teachers were out. They'd had to call in subs from 3 districts over. The principal sent home a letter about how flu season had hit early.

I felt fine.

Week 5, my old friend Sandra called me. She'd had it for a week and a half. She was on her second round of antibiotics. She said, "Patty, please tell me you're not getting this thing. It is brutal."

I told her I wasn't.

She didn't believe me.

I had to tell her about Alevia on the phone for 40 minutes.

She ordered it that night.

Week 6 was Thanksgiving.

I cooked.

I cooked the whole meal. Turkey, dressing, the casseroles, the pies, all of it. Glen kept trying to take things from me and tell me to sit down and I kept swatting him away.

Whitney brought Caleb down from Indianapolis. Marcus brought Hannah. We had 11 people around the table and I sat at the foot of it across from Glen and I looked at all of them and I had to excuse myself for a minute to go cry in the bathroom.

Hannah followed me in.

She knocked on the door and she said, "Mrs. Patricia, are you okay?"

I opened the door and I let her in and I hugged her properly for the first time.

She is going to be my daughter in law one day. I am telling you that right now.

December came.

I sat in the pew on Christmas Eve and watched Glen be a shepherd in the living nativity.

After 18 years of marriage.

For the first time.

I watched my husband stand in a bathrobe and a fake beard out in front of the church under a string of white lights and I cried so hard the woman behind me handed me a tissue.

Glen looked up and saw me and gave me a little wave with the staff he was holding.

I never thought I’d see him again.As I step off the bus, the scorching sun beats down on me. The heat here is unbearable, with not even the slightest breeze to offer relief. I already miss the places I've come to call home over the years. Grabbing my suitcase from the driver—who’s been eyeing me with a mix of disinterest and impatience—I flash him a polite smile, take my bag, and turn away without another glance.
The bus station is smaller than I remember. I push through the crowd, scanning the faces around me, searching for my aunt.
I’ve moved around more times than I can count—first with my mother, and then, after she passed away, with my aunt, who took me in along with her mate and daughter. Constantly relocating wasn’t a choice; it was a necessity. Someone was always after me.
My aunt was insistent that I return to this town, though I still don’t understand why. This place holds nothing but bad memories for me—especially since he is here. I refuse to say his name. He abandoned my mother and me when I was just ten years old. I watched her heart break a little more each day, while he never once looked back. He was too caught up in his pack, too in love with his own life to remember the daughter he left behind.
So why did my aunt want me back here? She and my cousin Eleanor have settled in this place, but I made it clear—I would only return if it was a matter of life and death. And now, I’m back, trapped in a town that will no doubt become my personal hell.
“Sierra, OVER HERE!”
I hear her before I see her. Turning to my left, I spot my aunt waving frantically, bouncing on her toes to get my attention. I force a smile and start making my way toward her.
As I walk, my senses sharpen. I can feel the weight of several eyes on me, curious and assessing. This town is a werewolf town. There are humans here, but my aunt told me they’re aware of the supernatural. Two packs live on the outskirts of town, sitting on opposite ends. One of them is his pack. And from what I’ve heard, they roam freely here.
This is going to be interesting—a panther shifter living in the middle of werewolf territory.
“Auntie,” I greet her with a smile, stepping closer.
She groans at the word, her expression shifting immediately. “Sierra, you know I hate being called that.”
I chuckle. “Sorry, Raven.” I pull her into a hug, feeling some of the tension ease from my body.
“How was the trip?” she asks, taking my bag from me as we head toward the exit.
“It was fine. First a plane ride, then a twelve-hour bus ride. There were a few stops along the way, so I got to stretch my legs. But I didn’t mind—I’m used to it. I also made sure no one was following me,” I add, glancing over my shoulder.
That’s when I notice the bus driver handing off his keys to another driver. Both of them are staring right at me.
I sigh.
“If one more person keeps staring, I swear I’ll rip their throats out,” Aria growls in my mind. She’s my panther counterpart—always on edge, always ready for a fight. My mother was a panther shifter, just like me, just like Raven and Eleanor.
“Why is everyone staring at me?” I mutter, uneasy. Aria steps forward in my mind, scanning the area through my eyes.
Raven smirks. “Well, it’s not every day a stunning twenty-year-old woman rolls into town.”
I snort. “Yeah, right. There must be plenty of girls here. But you know what I mean.”
I catch two elderly women watching me. The moment I meet their eyes, they quickly look away—but one of them seems to be mind-linking someone.
“I bet she’s telling her Alpha that someone new is here,” Aria muses, stretching lazily before retreating to the back of my mind.
Raven studies me, lowering her voice. “Be careful when Aria comes forward. Your eyes shift color slightly.”
I nod. “We’ll talk more in the car.”
We exit the bus station and head toward the parking lot, Raven leading the way to her small Toyota.
Just as we approach, a black Mustang screeches to a stop right in front of her car. Raven groans. “One Alpha too many,” she mutters under her breath. “Be nice, Sierra.”
The driver steps out first, his gaze flicking to me before he opens the rear door. Two young men climb out, looking to be around my age.
Then it hits me.
A familiar scent—one I haven’t smelled in years.
I stiffen as a low growl escapes me before I can stop it.
I know that scent.
He’s not my father. But he smells just like him.
Which means...
He must be his son.

Chapter 2
Sierra
I have a brother—or at least, someone who seems to be my age.
"You must be Raven’s niece, Sierra. My name is Dane. I’m the Beta of the Dark Valley Pack, and this here is Caleb, our Gamma. We wanted to introduce ourselves," Dane said.
I stared at him, unimpressed. His Alpha was either too busy or just didn’t care enough to find out who I was.
"Yeah, that’s me. Now, can you move your car so we can leave?" I said through clenched teeth.
Raven looked like she wanted to slap me but managed to restrain herself. "Sierra," she warned.
"My apologies, we didn’t realize this was your car," Dane said, clearly lying. Raven had been living here for months, and they had to know. "Cruz, could you move the car to a parking spot, please?"
The driver, Cruz, nodded, got back into the car, and drove it into a space on the opposite side of Raven’s vehicle.
"Better?" Dane asked with a smug smile.
"Yeah, I guess," I said with a hint of irritation. "Raven, can we go now? I’ve been awake for over twenty-four hours, and I’m exhausted." I let out a fake yawn for emphasis.
Raven smirked, knowing full well I was just trying to get out of this conversation.
"Of course, Sierra. Beta, Gamma, was there anything else you needed?" she asked while placing my bag in the back seat and loading my suitcase into the trunk.
Both men looked at me, and I noticed Caleb seemed to be mind-linking someone.
"He’s linking the Alpha," Aria, my wolf, murmured from the back of my mind. She had been watching everything unfold through my eyes, clearly amused.
After a few seconds, Dane turned back to us, his expression unreadable. "No, nothing else. Oh, actually—one thing. We’ll be stopping by the café later to pick up the cakes we ordered for the ceremony."
"No problem. They’ll be ready by the time you come to collect them. I hope the new Alpha has a great welcome-home party," Raven said.
"Oh, he will," Dane replied with a cocky grin.
I shuddered, my thoughts immediately going to all the crude things he could be implying. But then he caught me off guard.
"You two should come," he said.
Raven glanced at them before shaking her head. "I don’t think so. Sierra needs to rest after her long journey," she said.
I knew exactly why she was acting this way, and my blood boiled. I knew who would be at that party.
"Well, the invitation stands," Dane said.
Caleb looked at me carefully. "You should come to the packhouse—"
"I don’t think so," I cut him off before he could finish. "You both know my father is part of your pack. I will not—no, I will never—step foot in your packhouse. So why don’t you two go do whatever it is you need to do before I throw up all over those nice shoes of yours?" I snapped.
I turned to open the car door but hesitated for a second, looking back at Caleb. "Oh, and do me a favor—say hi to my father. I doubt he’ll show his face anytime soon, especially since it’s been ten years since he last saw me. So enjoy your little party, but don’t ever come near me again."
Without another word, I climbed into the car and slammed the door shut.
"Stupid wolves," I muttered under my breath.
I sat there, waiting for Raven to get in. Glancing through the window, I saw the three of them standing there, speechless from my outburst.
I hated that man. I never wanted to see the person who abandoned me.
"I apologize for Sierra," Raven said as she walked to the car, opening the driver’s side door.
Dane had recovered from my outburst and gave me a smug smile. "I hope she changes her mind. We don’t want any trouble," he said.
Without another word, the three of them turned and walked off.
Raven and I watched them go.
"Stupid wolves," I muttered again.
"Sierra, you need to be careful with what you say," Raven warned as she started the engine. We pulled out of the parking lot and onto the main road, driving in silence for a while.
Finally, I broke it. "Raven, why did you want me here?"

Chapter 3
Sierra
"Raven, why did you want me here?"
