The problem with that?
I did know why he left. And I knew exactly what had made him do it. Either Raven didn’t know, or she believed whatever lies he had told her.
Trying to change the subject, I asked, "Who’s the new Alpha? Why are they throwing a welcome-home party for him?"
She hesitated before answering. "His name is Damon. He’s the Alpha’s son. He’s been away for the past few months, training with neighboring packs," she said. "Before he left, he came into the café every day. You’ll probably see him around soon enough."
I didn’t want to see anyone—especially not an Alpha.
I let the conversation drop and turned to stare out the window.
The town was surrounded by dense forest, but the houses were built close together. After a few minutes, Raven pulled into the driveway of a small terraced house. It looked normal enough. The houses were near the forest, making it easy for wolves to shift and run freely.
"We need to shift soon. It’s been too long," Aria murmured in my head.
As I stepped out of the car, I suddenly felt like someone was watching me.
"Aria, do you sense anyone?" I asked, keeping my back straight.
"I don’t know, but I don’t like it here," she admitted. "Something feels… off."
I agreed. There was something unsettling about this place.
Raven must have felt it too because she glanced behind me, her expression unreadable. "Let’s get you inside. I need to head to the café to close up," she said, grabbing my arm and leading me toward the house.
Once inside, I glanced around. The living room and kitchen were open-plan, and a staircase led upstairs.
Raven hesitated before locking the front door.
"Everything okay?" I asked, narrowing my eyes.
"Yeah… Let me show you to your room. You can shower and rest while I head to the café," she said quickly.
She led me upstairs, showing me my room—which had its own bathroom.
"I had this installed last week, knowing you’d be visiting. Now that you’re staying, it’ll be useful," she said with a smile.
I nodded. The room was small but cozy—a far cry from sleeping on the ground or in trees.
"I got everything you might need. If you need anything else, we can go shopping tomorrow. Also, do you want to work some shifts at the café?" she asked.
"Yeah, sure," I said, just as my stomach growled.
She chuckled. "I’ll make you some sandwiches. You should eat, then sleep."
I yawned. "Thanks, Raven."
As she left, I couldn’t shake the feeling that something was wrong.
I was too exhausted to dwell on it.
Within minutes of my head hitting the pillow, sleep pulled me under.

Raven

I roll my eyes. Stupid wolves.

Oh, hell.
She’s pissed.

The car ride back to the pack house is quiet. It’s a long drive from town, and our driver is stuck behind another vehicle.
Kieran stares out the window, lost in thought.
I mind-link my father. “Hey, Dad, we’re on our way back with the cakes. There’s something you need to know. Sierra is back.”
“Yeah, I heard,” my father replies gruffly. “Kieran went to see her. I take it that didn’t go well? I told him to give her a few days to settle in.”
I sigh. “‘Didn’t go well’ is an understatement. She was furious. He wants the three of us to meet in your office to talk about it.”
My father is silent for a beat before responding. “We need to talk. I think you should be there for all of this—you’ll be Alpha soon.”
“Alright. We’ll be there in twenty minutes.”
I stick to Kieran’s request and don’t mention to my father that Sierra is my mate.
When we finally arrive at the pack house, we step out of the SUV.
Caleb, my soon-to-be Gamma, is waiting nearby. I know why—his mate, Eleanor, nearly got herself ripped apart for disrespecting me. From the look on his face, he already knows.
“Sorry about Eleanor, Alpha,” he says immediately. “She was just protecting her mother.”
I nod. “I’ll apologize to her later.”
He gives me a strange look. “You shouldn’t have to apologize. She’s still adjusting to our ways here. They lost their pack years ago and have been moving around ever since,” he explains, his gaze shifting past me to Kieran. “He shouldn’t have gone there,” he mutters. “I know most of what happened—Eleanor told me. It’s bad.”
I stare at him, taken aback. “I’ll find out more when we talk to my father,” I say before shutting off the mind-link.
Caleb nods and heads toward his house, where Eleanor is waiting. He probably misses her. Eleanor had mentioned wanting to tell Sierra something, but she wasn’t sure how her cousin would react—especially when it came to the subject of mates.
There has to be a reason why she despises the idea of having one.
A low growl rumbles in my head—my wolf, Cruz. “She’ll come around. We just need to take things slow with her.”
I freeze. My wolf has been obsessed with finding our mate for years, but he’s never been this patient before. Normally, he’s possessive and restless. But now, he just wants what’s best for Sierra—even if that means taking our time.
“What’s gotten into you? You’ve been quiet since you told me Sierra was our mate,” I ask him.
Cruz is silent for a moment before sighing. “I’m being careful with her. Seeing her father after all these years made her angry. And her panther… she’s powerful. Her emotions fuel her strength, and I think her panther has her own feelings about this entire situation. We need to figure out what happened.”
I nod. “You’re right, Cruz. Let’s find out exactly what we’re dealing with.”
He chuckles before settling in the back of my mind, alert but waiting. Waiting to learn more about our mate.

I almost called 911 when I found out the guy across from me was supposed to die in Beijing.

He didn't know I was watching him. For eleven minutes he held a glass of Macallan without taking a sip. His hands were shaking. Not from nerves. Something worse.

It was 2 AM. Emirates first class. Somewhere over the Arabian Sea. The bar was supposed to be empty at that hour. He was the only one there when I walked in.

No bags. No carry-on. Nothing in the overhead. Just a leather case, a phone he kept refreshing every few seconds, and a second phone in his jacket pocket that he never answered.

Every seat in his row was empty. All of them. Purchased. I asked the attendant if the flight was half-booked. She shook her head. "He bought them."

A man who buys out first class doesn't fly commercial. He flies private. Unless private is how they track you. Unless your name on a manifest is the thing that gets you killed. Unless someone already tried — on a flight to Beijing that a small plane flew into twelve hours after he got off the booking.

Something is happening right now that the people at the top already know about. He was one of them. And he said the rest of us have no idea what's coming.

Let me back up.

I was standing outside the bathroom at the front of the plane. The one in the back had a line four deep and my daughter Lily — she's four — was doing the little dance where you know you've got about ninety seconds before a disaster. So I picked her up and walked to the front.

First class. I had no business being up there. My company booked us business class for a work trip in London because the only economy seats left had a 19-hour layover in Istanbul. First time in my life I've sat above row 34. But the front bathroom was closer and Lily wasn't going to make it.

The wifi kept cutting in and out. That junk signal you get over the ocean where a page loads half way and freezes. I was standing there on my phone, waiting for Lily, when a headline loaded about two-thirds of the way.

BEIJING — Small aircraft crashes into CITIC Tower.

I tapped it. Nothing else loaded. Just the image — a hole in the side of a 109-story building and people running below. Then the wifi dropped.

"Jesus," I said. Out loud. To nobody. "A plane just hit a building in Beijing."

That's when I heard him.

"That wasn't for CITIC."

Four words. From the bar area, maybe ten feet away. I hadn't even seen him sitting there. Thobe under a navy sport coat. Shoes that were made by hand. A watch I couldn't name but knew cost more than my car. Sitting alone at the counter with a glass of whisky he hadn't touched and both phones in front of him — one face-up, one face-down.

I looked at him. He wasn't looking at me. He was staring at his own phone. Refreshing the same page over and over. Like he was waiting for the same story from a different source. Or a different version of it.

Before I could say anything, a flight attendant showed up. Polite but firm. The kind of voice where you know she's been trained to handle it without making a scene.

"Sir, this section has been privately reserved. I'm going to have to ask you to —"

He raised one hand. Didn't look up. Just a slow wave. Like brushing something away.

Then Lily came out of the bathroom. Hair messed up. Pajama pants with little strawberries on them. She grabbed my leg and looked around at the bar like she'd walked into a spaceship.

He looked at her. Then at me.

"She's yours?"

"Yeah."

Something in his face changed. Not a smile. Something behind it. Like a lock turning open.

He looked at the attendant. "It's fine. Get him a drink."

She brought me a gin and tonic. I sat down three seats from him. Lily climbed into my lap and fell asleep in two minutes. Just folded into my chest the way she does.

We didn't talk right away. I held my daughter and he held his glass and the plane hummed under us. The cabin was blue and dark. Felt like we were the only two people awake in the world.

I kept trying to reload the Beijing story. The wifi was dead. Just that one frozen image — the hole in the glass, the dust, people running.

"It won't load out here," he said. Still not looking at me. "They'll have it scrubbed by the time we land anyway."

"Scrubbed?"

"The footage. The video. China will take it all down. They've already started. Police on the ground are telling people to delete what they filmed." He said it the way you'd talk about the weather. Like it was just how things work.

"How do you know that?"

A few seconds of nothing. He took his first sip. Then:

"I was booked on a flight to Beijing this morning. I changed it twelve hours ago."

I felt my chest drop.

"Why?"

"Because somebody I trust told me not to get on."

I should've picked up my daughter and gone back to my seat.

But I didn't. Because you don't sit three feet from a man who dodged a plane crash by half a day — because someone whispered in his ear — and just walk away. Not when your four-year-old is asleep on your chest and you can feel the floor shifting under you.

He was running. And he'd made up his mind to tell me why.

He never gave me his name. Not that night. Not ever. But things came out in pieces over the next two hours. Between long pauses. Between drinks he'd order and not finish. Between looks at his phone that told me he was tracking something I couldn't see.

He was from the Emirates. His family was tied to the oil and gas world at a level where you don't have a job title — you have a seat. Over twenty years in and around the systems that keep the Gulf running. Aramco. ADNOC. The rooms where they decide how much oil the rest of the world gets.

He said it the way someone tells you they used to work at the post office.

His wife and three kids had been in Zurich for three weeks. He used the word "sent." Not visiting. Not on a trip. Sent.

I asked him what was going on. No games. My daughter was asleep in my arms and a man who dodged a plane crash was sitting three seats away at 2 AM over the ocean. I didn't want riddles.

He looked at Lily. Then at me.

"Your president said it on camera nine days ago. At the G7. Word for word. 'We run out of reserves at about four weeks.' He said it would be 'bedlam.' Those are his words. Not mine."

I stared at him.

"Did you hear him say that? Did anyone you know? Or did it get buried under the next headline before anyone could think about what it meant?"

I hadn't heard it. I'll say that right now. The president said the word "bedlam" about the oil supply on live TV and I had no idea.

"Four weeks," he said again. "That was nine days ago."

He told me the news has been showing us the safe version of the story. The tanker stuff. The prices. The deal. All real — but it's just the top layer. The part they're allowed to show.

"My country left OPEC on May 1st," he said. "After fifty-nine years. You know what that means?"

I didn't.

"It means we looked at what's coming and decided we're keeping ours. We have the oil. We have the capacity. And we pulled out so we could save our own supply instead of feeding it into a system that's about to fall apart."

He let that hang.

"When the country with the fourth-largest oil reserves on earth looks at the road ahead and says 'we're not sharing anymore' — that's the signal. That's the only one you need."

He told me the people at his level aren't worried about gas prices. They figured that part out months ago. What they're doing right now — quietly, with no cameras, no press — is buying water.

"Not overseas," he said. "In your country. Right now. Bill Gates is the largest private farmland owner in the United States. Two hundred and seventy-five thousand acres in nineteen states. When you buy land at that scale you're not buying dirt. You're buying the water under it. Every well. Every drop."

He tapped the counter.

"Jeff Bezos. Over a hundred and fifty thousand acres in Texas. Michael Burry — the man who called the 2008 crash before anyone — said publicly that his biggest bet after the housing market was farmland with water on it. BlackRock listed water as a top priority. They started trading water on the stock exchange in 2020. Like oil. Like gold."

He opened his leather case. Just enough for me to see the top page. Stamps. Seals. Legal text I couldn't read. He closed it.

"The richest people in your country are not buying stocks right now. They're buying access to the one thing you can't live three days without. And not one of them is talking about it."

I asked him why water. We have water. I pay sixty bucks a month for it. It comes out of the tap.

He almost smiled.

"Where do you think it comes from?"

"The city. Pipes. The plant."

"And what runs the plant?"

I didn't answer.

"Power," he said. "Gas makes the power. Power runs the pumps. Pumps push the water. You turn on your kitchen sink and you think you're turning on water. You're not. You're turning on gas. It goes through six steps before it hits your glass. You just can't see any of them."

He told me where he's from, they don't get to pretend.

The Gulf — Saudi, Emirates, Kuwait, Bahrain — has no freshwater. None. No rivers. No lakes. Nothing. A hundred million people in that part of the world drink water that comes from machines. Big plants on the coast that suck in ocean water, strip the salt out, and push out something you can drink.

Every one of those machines runs on power.

"We have forty-five days of water saved up," he said. "That's it. The whole country. Kuwait is worse. Bahrain is worse. A drone hit a water plant in Bahrain in March — one drone, one plant — and a whole region lost clean water for twelve hours. Not low flow. Not a warning. Nothing came out of the tap."

He said the richest families in the Gulf — the ones who sit at tables the news doesn't know about — started moving within the first week after the Strait got shut down. Not their money. Themselves.

"We learned this in February," he said. "Oil you can find more of. You can drill. You can ship it the long way around. But water — when the machines stop — there is no backup in the desert."

He looked at me.

"Your country is the same. You just have a longer pipe."

I told him we're nothing alike. We have the Great Lakes. Rivers everywhere. Rain every week.

"You have more freshwater than almost anyone," he said. "But you can't get to it. Not without power. Your water runs through the same setup ours does. Electric pumps. Treatment plants. Pressure systems. Take the power out and the pressure drops within hours. Within a day the taps go dry. You could live right next to Lake Michigan and die of thirst looking at it."

I felt sick.

"How long do we have?"

"Your president told you. Four weeks. Nine days ago. And the hub in Oklahoma where your country prices all its oil — Cushing — has dropped to twenty million barrels. That's less than two days' worth. They call it 'tank bottoms.' Below that, there's not enough crude in the tanks to push it through the pipes."

He leaned back.

"But here's the part they'll never say out loud. It won't get to zero. They won't let it. Because zero means they lose too. What happens before zero — and this is what your news won't show you — is controls."

"You lived through 2020," he said.

I nodded.

"Then you already know what controls look like. They told you two weeks. It turned into two years. They shut your job. Shut your school. Told you where to stand and how far apart. Picked which places got to stay open and which ones didn't. You did what they said. Everyone did."

He stared at the counter.

"That was a test run. And it worked. They proved people would listen. They proved the whole system could lock down and the people at the top could keep running while everyone else sat at home."

He looked at me.

"Energy lockdowns will be the same thing. Same playbook. But worse. Because in 2020 you still had power. You still had water. Your kids still took baths. The lights stayed on. The thing under all of it — the gas, the pumps — it kept going. You never thought about it."

He told me what it's going to look like.

"First they'll call it saving energy. Use less power. Turn off your AC. Cut your driving. They'll make it sound like everyone's doing their part."

He paused.

"Then it stops being a choice. Rolling blackouts. Your power goes out for four hours. Then eight. Then twelve. Not because there's not enough — because they're saving what's left for the things that matter to them. The military. The government buildings. The data centers. The systems that keep the people at the top running."

He said it like he was reading from a list. No anger. Just facts.

"Your street goes dark so a server farm stays on. Your family boils water on a camp stove so a building in DC keeps the lights on. That's how it works. That's how it works in every country I've seen go through this."

He looked at Lily. Still asleep on my chest.

"Then the taps slow down. Not because the water ran out. Because the pumps that push the water need power. And your power just got cut. Your city puts out a notice. 'Use less water.' Then another one. 'Boil all tap water.' Then one morning you turn the handle and nothing comes out."

Nothing for ten seconds.

"And at that point you do whatever they tell you. That's not a guess. That's not my take. That is what happens when someone else decides if your kids get to drink. You don't hold a sign. You don't make a call. You show up where they say. You take what they give you. And you say thank you. Because the only other choice is watching your son ask why his mouth is dry and knowing you had three weeks to fix it and you didn't."

Lily shifted in my arms. Her hair was stuck to my shirt. She smelled like the lavender shampoo Jess uses on her.

"How far is the nearest creek from your house?" he asked.

I'd never once thought about that.

"There's a pond behind my son's school. And a creek through the park about ten minutes away. I've driven past it every Saturday for six years."

"If the power went out Tuesday — no warning, just dark — how long does the water in your house last?"

Case of Dasani in the garage. Brita in the fridge. A day. Maybe less with two kids.

"The creek," he said. "Brown water. Algae on top. Bugs. You'd walk right past it. You'd never let your daughter near it. But everything your family needs to live is right there. Thirty feet from your son's baseball field. It's been there his whole life."

He said the gap between the families at the top and a family like mine isn't money. Isn't who you know.

"It's access. Being able to turn dirty water into clean water. Without power. Without a pump. Without asking anyone."

He told me there's something else the news won't touch. Something they're working hard to keep quiet.

"There's a tool," he said. "Military. Built decades ago for soldiers overseas. Hollow-fiber filtration. You can scoop water out of a ditch, a creek, a puddle — run it through this thing — and drink it clean on the other side. Bacteria gone. Parasites gone. No power. No batteries. Nothing. Just the filter and gravity."

He said every family at his level has them. Every one. Two per person. Home and car.

"The people at the top don't want the public to know this exists. Because this is the one thing that makes a normal family free. Free from the grid. Free from the system. If every family in your country had one of these, the lockdowns don't work. You can't control people through water if every household can walk to the nearest creek and drink clean."

He said some countries have already started blocking access to military-grade filters. That the specs have been pulled from public records in certain places. That the window to get them won't stay open much longer.

"It's the same reason they don't want you growing your own food. Collecting your own rain. Going off the grid. When a family can take care of itself — the system has nothing to hold over them. And this filter — this one piece of gear — gives every family in America the most important kind of freedom there is. Clean water without asking anyone."

I told him it sounds like a bunker. A shipping container buried in the yard.

He stopped me.

"The people I come from don't build bunkers. That's TV. The families who've lived through a real collapse — who come from places that fell apart — they do one thing first. Before the gold. Before the cash. Before anything."

"What?"

"They lock down water. A hollow-fiber unit that doesn't need power or pipes or a plug. Four hundred gallons per filter. No batteries. Works on gravity alone. Small enough for your coat pocket. Your daughter could hold it in one hand."

I asked how much. I was thinking thousands.

He told me.

I looked at Lily. Looked back at him.

"That's less than what I spent on groceries last Tuesday."

"I know," he said.

He reached into his jacket. Pulled out the second phone. The burner. Typed something with his thumb.

My phone buzzed on the counter.

A link. No message.

"Same one my clients use. Point-one micron hollow fiber. Gets rid of 99.999999% of bacteria and 99.999% of parasites from any freshwater source. No power. Lifetime warranty."

I looked at it. Looked at him.

He looked down at Lily. Asleep. Strawberry pajamas. Hair stuck to my shirt.

"You're standing in the front of a plane you don't belong in, holding your daughter, and you have no idea what's coming. In three weeks — when the blackouts start and the taps slow down — you'll have either done something or you won't."

He picked up his case. Both phones.

"Two per person. Don't forget the car."

He walked back to his row — all the empty seats — and didn't look at me again.

We landed in Dallas at 6:14 AM. Lily woke up when the wheels hit and asked for pancakes. I carried her through the airport and didn't open the link.

I thought it was crazy. Rich man on a plane telling scary stories about oil and water. I told myself money makes people like that. Told myself I was dumb for sitting there.

Drove home. Made pancakes. Cody came down in his baseball jersey. Jess poured coffee. Normal Saturday.

Then I turned on the TV.

Beijing crash. CITIC Tower. 109 stories. Footage gone from the internet. Police making people delete photos. China saying nothing. Word for word what he told me.

I opened my laptop.

Trump's G7 quote — real. Found the video. "We run out of reserves at about four weeks. It would be bedlam." He said it on camera. I watched it three times. I never heard about it until a stranger told me at 2 AM on a plane.

The SPR — real. On the government's own website. 331 million barrels. Lowest since 1983. Nine million drained in a single week.

Cushing — real. Twenty million barrels. Tank bottoms. Less than two days of what we use. Three articles calling it a crisis. Not one on the front page.

The UAE leaving OPEC — real. May 1st. After fifty-nine years. Keeping their supply. Found it on Reuters, Al Jazeera, BBC. Nobody in my life had said a word about it.

Bill Gates — real. 275,000 acres in 19 states. Biggest private farmland owner in the country. The water rights go with the land.

Michael Burry — real. Said on the record that his biggest move after calling the housing crash was buying farmland with water on it.

Water on the stock exchange — real. Started trading like oil and gold in 2020.

The Gulf — real. A hundred million people drinking from machines. Iran hit a water plant in Bahrain. Forty-five days of reserves for an entire country.

Every single thing he said was sitting right there on my screen. All public. All real. Not one word on my nightly news. Not once.

I closed the laptop and sat there staring at the wall.

1 AM. House dark. Cody asleep. Lily in bed with her star nightlight. Jess breathing slow next to me.

I went to the kitchen table. Phone in hand. Link still sitting in my texts.

I thought about the creek behind the park. Brown. Slow. Smells like wet dirt in the summer. I've driven past it every Saturday for six years and never looked at it once.

I thought about the Dasani in the garage. Eighteen bottles. Less than a day for four people.

I thought about what he said about the pumps. About how everything between that creek and my kitchen sink is just power. And nobody thinks about power until it's gone.

I thought about the blackouts. How they don't turn it off everywhere. Just your street. Just the places that don't matter to the people making calls.

I ordered four at 1:47 AM. Two for me. Two for Jess. Went back and got two more for the kids' bags.

The whole thing cost less than dinner at Applebee's.

Saturday morning I drove to the creek.

Brought one unit. Parked in the same lot we park in for Cody's games. Walked thirty feet to the water. Scooped from the shallows — brown, gritty, something green floating on top. Water you'd yell at your kid for going near.

Put the filter in. Drew it through.

Clear. Clean. No taste. No smell.

I stood in that parking lot and thought about every parent who pulls in here on Saturdays. Every dad with a bat bag. Every mom with a cooler. Not one of them knows they're standing next to a year of clean water for their whole family. They drive past it every week. They'll never think about it until the tap stops.

And by then they'll all be in the same line — waiting for someone to hand them a bottle and tell them what to do next.

I wasn't going to post this.

He didn't tell me what he told me so I could put it online. He said it because I was there. Because my daughter was asleep in my arms. Because I looked like the kind of person who wouldn't do a thing about it — and I think he wanted to be wrong.

But I have two kids. And my neighbor has three. And my sister in Ohio has twins. And not one of them knows what I heard at 35,000 feet.

So I'm posting the link. I don't make money from this. I don't sell these. I sell strip malls in Texas. I got lucky enough to be standing in the wrong bathroom line on the right plane.

The auto-pay for the boat came out of my checking account on the 3rd of every month for the last 34 months.

Three hundred and forty dollars.

For 34 months.

That's $11,560 for a boat that's been sitting under a blue tarp in our side yard, next to the propane tank, growing a small colony of wasps under the bow.

My husband Bernard doesn't know I've been paying it.

He thinks we let it go two years ago. He thinks the finance company took it back. He thinks the tarp is covering a chest freezer.

It's not. It's covering a 19-foot Lund Impact XS that we picked out together on his second-to-last day at UPPCO before he retired.

I've been paying that boat payment out of the tips I make at the salon. Twenty-dollar tips. Sometimes a folded fifty at Christmas. I put them in an envelope in my glovebox and once a month I deposit the envelope at the credit union drive-through and pray my auto-pay clears.

I couldn't tell you why I've been doing this except that the day we bought that boat was the last day I saw my husband happy.

And I wasn't ready to let that day be the last one.

My name is Colleen. I'm 62 years old. I've been cutting hair in Escanaba, Michigan for 38 years, and I work three chairs down from where I started, at a salon on Ludington Street called Cutting Edge that's had the same green awning since 1994.

My husband Bernard is 63. He retired three years ago in August from Upper Peninsula Power Company after 38 years on the poles. He climbed them in blizzards. He climbed them in ice storms. He climbed them in July when the black flies were biting through his coveralls. He came home more than once with frostbite on his cheekbones.

For 38 years he did that job. And when I say his knees were shot, I mean shot in a way you can't fix with ice and Tylenol.

The retirement plan was the boat.

We are Yoopers. In Escanaba, if you don't fish, I don't know what you do. Bernard grew up fishing Little Bay de Noc with his dad and his uncle Wayne. When his dad passed in 2013, Bernard fished with just Wayne. When Wayne passed in 2019, Bernard fished alone.

The plan was that once he retired he'd fish every day the weather let him. He'd take the boat out on the bay at 5:30 in the morning. He'd bring home walleye and I'd cook them in butter with sliced almonds the way my mother taught me. We'd have the grandkids up in the summer and Bernard would take them out and teach them what his dad taught him.

That was the plan.

Here's what actually happened.

The week Bernard retired, he tried to climb into the boat at the launch off M-35 and his right knee buckled so hard he had to sit down on the trailer fender for 20 minutes before he could stand up again. He got in eventually. He caught 6 walleye that day. He came home smiling.

But it took him an hour and 12 minutes to get out of the boat when he came back to the launch.

I know because he told me. He didn't call for help. He didn't want another fisherman to see him. He sat in the boat at his own trailer and waited until the parking lot cleared out, and then he pulled himself up by the console and stepped over the gunwale one leg at a time like he was climbing over a fence in slow motion.

He drove home. He unhooked the trailer. He put the boat in the side yard. And he came in and sat down in his chair and didn't say anything for the whole night.

He went out 3 more times that first summer. Each one was worse than the last. By September he'd stopped talking about the bay.

The doctor said knee replacement. Both knees. Bernard said not yet.

I understand why he said not yet. His brother Ronnie got a knee replacement in 2016 and had a blood clot that put him in the hospital in Marquette for 11 days. Bernard watched Ronnie limp for a year afterward and said, "I'll live with what I got."

So we lived with it.

He tried a glucosamine chondroitin from Meijer. Nothing.

He tried turmeric. Nothing.

He tried a copper knee sleeve his cousin recommended. Nothing.

He tried CBD gummies my daughter mailed him from Traverse City. He said they made him sleepy but the knees still hurt.

He got a cortisone shot in October of that first year. It helped for about 5 weeks. He got another one 4 months later and it didn't do much of anything. The orthopedic in Marquette said he couldn't keep doing them forever.

So Bernard stopped trying.

That's the part I want you to understand. He didn't just have bad knees. He stopped trying.

A man who climbed a 40-foot pole in a snowstorm at 3:47 in the morning to get power back to St. Francis Hospital in 1994 stopped trying to walk down to the mailbox.

He sat in his chair. He watched hunting shows. He watched fishing shows, which is worse. He'd watch a man on the Fox Sports channel catching walleye on Mille Lacs and he'd get this look on his face like somebody was reading his will out loud.

I'd come home from the salon at 6 in the evening and find him in the exact same position I left him in at 8:30 in the morning. Same coffee cup. Same throw blanket. Same view of the same corner of the same room.

The tarp in the side yard was slowly caving in from the snow.

I couldn't call the finance company.

I don't know how to explain it any better than that. I just couldn't do it. Signing the paperwork to let that boat go felt like signing something else, and I couldn't put my name on it.

So I started using the tips.

The turning point came in June.

Bernard's cousin Kirby has a fish camp on Little Bay de Noc, about 40 minutes north on County Road 513. Every year for as long as I've known Bernard, the men in his family have gone up there for a long weekend in June. His dad went. His uncle Wayne went. His brother Ronnie went. Bernard went every single year from age 14 until age 60.

Kirby called on a Wednesday night. Bernard put him on speaker.

"You coming up this year, Bernie?"

Bernard was quiet for a second.

Then he said, "I don't think so this year, Kirb."

Kirby said, "You said that last year."

Bernard said, "I know."

Kirby said, "You gonna come next year?"

And Bernard didn't answer.

He just sat there in his chair, and Kirby waited on the line, and I stood in the kitchen with a wooden spoon in my hand and a pot of chicken and dumplings I'd stopped stirring, and eventually Kirby said, "Alright, Bern. I love ya. Call me if it changes."

Bernard hung up the phone and put his hand over his eyes.

He didn't cry. Bernard doesn't cry. His father didn't cry when his mother died. His grandfather didn't cry when his brother died in Korea. Bernards don't cry.

But he put his hand over his eyes for a long time.

And I stood in the kitchen and I knew he was giving up.

I knew it the way you know a customer has been drinking before she sits in your chair, or the way you know a marriage is over before either spouse says the word. You know because you've been paying attention.

I stirred the dumplings.

And I thought about the tarp in the side yard and the $340 leaving my checking account on the 3rd of the next month, and I felt something in me get very quiet.

I had two choices. I could stop paying the boat and let it go, and Bernard could sit in that chair until he couldn't get out of it, and one day I'd bury him and drive past Kirby's camp on 513 and cry.

Or I could figure something out.

I don't know why I thought I could figure something out. I'm a hairdresser. I don't have any credentials. I don't have any special knowledge. I cut and colored hair for 38 years and raised two kids and made pasties every Christmas Eve.

But I had a chair every day. And people talk in that chair.

Eileen has been my Tuesday-morning 9:15 for 14 years. She's 67. She gets a wash and set every other Tuesday and a permanent wave every 4 months. Her husband Sigurd is a retired welder from the shipyard down in Marinette. Sig is 71 and until 2 years ago he could barely get out of a kitchen chair.

I didn't know this until Eileen sat down that particular Tuesday, two weeks after Kirby's phone call, and asked how Bernard was doing.

I looked at her in the mirror.

And instead of saying "good" the way I usually do, I said, "He's not doing good, Eileen. He hasn't been in that boat in almost two years."

Eileen was quiet while I combed her out.

Then she said, "Sig couldn't get up off the couch in 2022. You remember that?"

I remembered. Sig had missed the Delta County Fair for the first time in his adult life. Eileen had come in for her permanent wave the week after and cried into her cape.

"He's back at the shop now," she said. "Three days a week. He rebuilt the transmission on our grandson's Ranger last month."

I stopped combing.

"How?"

Eileen said, "My sister-in-law Maureen sent him something."

I want to be careful here about how I tell this part, because I don't want you to think Eileen sold me on anything. She didn't. She was talking about her husband. I was the one asking questions.

Eileen said Maureen's daughter is a nurse in a rehabilitation clinic outside of Green Bay. He told Maureen's daughter he'd been taking something for a couple of months before the surgery. Something with a fruit called amla.

Maureen's daughter looked it up.

She told Maureen. Maureen told Eileen. Eileen ordered a bottle for Sig.

Two months later Sig was up.

Here is what I understood by the time I went inside.

The problem in Bernard's knees wasn't just wear and tear. That's what I'd been told for years. That's what the orthopedic said. That's what every article in the AARP magazine said. Wear and tear.

But wear and tear is a description. It's not a cause.

The actual cause, or one of them anyway, is that the cells inside our joints need energy to maintain themselves. To keep the cartilage smooth. To keep the fluid where it belongs. To manage the low-level inflammation that happens every day in every joint of every human alive.

That energy is made by tiny structures inside every cell called mitochondria. You may have heard of them from a middle-school science class. The powerhouse of the cell. That's what they called them in 1978 when I was in Mrs. Aikens's class.

Well. As we age, and as we spend 38 years climbing power poles in the freezing cold, our mitochondria don't work the way they used to. They lose efficiency. They put out less energy.

And when the cells in your joints aren't getting the energy they need, they can't do their maintenance work. Cartilage doesn't stay smooth. The joint environment gets inflamed. Everything hurts.

I read this and I thought about Bernard's chair.

I thought about the glucosamine that didn't work. And the turmeric that didn't work. And the copper sleeves and the CBD and the cortisone.

Something Maureen's daughter had explained to Eileen finally landed for me. She'd said it was like sending a construction crew to a job site with all their lumber and nails and tools but no electricity. They can't run the saw. They can't run the drill. They can't do the work. It doesn't matter how much lumber you send.

Bernard's joints had been getting lumber for years. Glucosamine. Turmeric. Copper. They just didn't have any power to do anything with it.

Amla, from what I read, is different because of what it does to a pathway called AMPK.

I'm not a scientist. I'm going to explain this the way I understood it sitting in my Buick.

AMPK is like a switch inside your cells. When it's on, the cells make more energy and manage themselves better. When it's off, or working poorly, they don't. Amla is one of the few things that seems to reliably turn that switch on. It supports your mitochondria at the source instead of just throwing more raw material at cells that can't use it.

The active compounds in amla are called emblicanins. They're antioxidants but they also do something antioxidants don't usually do. They seem to signal to the cell to work better.

That was the piece I hadn't heard before.

Every supplement Bernard had tried was trying to add something to his joints. Amla was trying to help the cells in his joints do their own job again.

I said, "Sig fixed a transmission last month."

I didn't say anything.

He came back inside and had a beer.

Just a little. Bernards don't cry a lot.
