I don't give a f*ck if this upsets you. I'm going to say something nobody watching their kidney numbers slide wants to hear.

I hooked people up to the dialysis machine for 22 years. On October 19th, 2024, my own nephrologist scheduled me for the surgery they do right before they put you on it.

I was 58 years old.

I've been a dialysis nurse for 22 years. I've connected more patients to that machine than I could ever count. I've held their hands through the cramping. I've watched them go gray and cold on the table while the machine pulled the fluid off. I've wheeled them out after and told them they did great.

And on a Tuesday last October, a surgeon drew a purple line down my own forearm with a marker to show me where they'd cut to build the access. The fistula. The one I'd watched get placed in a thousand other arms.

Dialysis runs north of ninety thousand dollars a year. I'd spent two decades watching insurance fight my patients over every session.

They let me keep working. I'm still on the floor most days. But I'll never strap another patient into that chair without remembering the purple line a surgeon drew on my own arm, because everything I'd been trained to do and everything I'd handed my patients on their way out the door hadn't saved me.

I'm writing this because I know exactly what the doctors I work with will say when they see it. I don't care.

If you're over 50 and your kidney numbers are slipping, or someone you love is watching foam in the toilet every morning and getting told to wait and see, please read the whole thing.

I know it's long. I know you're scrolling. I know you've got things to do.

Fifteen months ago I would have given anything for someone who'd seen what I've seen to sit me down and tell me what I'm about to tell you.

Nobody did.

I first saw my own numbers slip six years ago at 52. eGFR of 68. A little protein flagged in my urine.

The report surprised me and it didn't. My father spent the last four years of his life tethered to the machine three days a week. He died at 64 the year I turned 41. My mother's blood pressure quietly took her kidneys over a decade before she passed. I'd watched the pattern in my own family, and I'd spent my whole career in the room while people who looked exactly like my father slid toward the chair.

So I did everything the doctors told me.

I went on the blood pressure pills. When my numbers kept slipping my nephrologist added a second one. I went on the renal diet the dietitian handed every patient. Low sodium. Low potassium. Low phosphorus. Careful with protein. I read every label in the grocery store. I weighed my food.

I walked every morning. I stopped drinking. I lost 20 pounds in the first year and kept it off. I did every single thing they put in front of me.

And every year my eGFR dropped anyway. 68. Then 60. Then 54. Then 48.

By last September I was following that renal diet to the letter and my number was still sliding.

Every visit my nephrologist looked at the chart and said the same word.

Stable.

Stable.

That word again.

I asked for a full panel last September because a hunch wouldn't leave me alone.

My eGFR had dropped to 31.

For anyone who doesn't live in this world, that's the range where the conversation stops being about diet and starts being about the machine. I'd sat in the room a hundred times while a nephrologist looked at a number like that and said we need to start planning access.

I asked one of the nephrologists I trust to really look at me. She did. She ordered an ultrasound of my kidneys and a 24 hour urine.

I scheduled them. And then I didn't want to know.

I want to tell you why.

Because sitting in the break room at 6 PM staring at my own number on the screen, I recognized something. I was doing exactly what my father had done. He'd been managed for years before the machine. His blood pressure had been controlled. His diet had been followed. His numbers had read stable right up until they didn't.

And he'd died at 64 in the same hospital system I'd built my career in.

I didn't chase the results because I already knew what they'd show. I didn't want to see it in writing. I told myself I had time.

I didn't.

Six weeks later my eGFR came back at 22.

The foam in my toilet bowl every morning was so thick it wouldn't flush on the first try. I'd been telling myself for a year it was just the cleaner.

My ankles were so swollen by the end of a shift I was buying shoes a half size up. I'd been blaming that on being on my feet for twelve hours.

I was up three and four times a night to pee. I'd been blaming that on getting older.

There was a taste in my mouth like I'd been sucking on a handful of coins. I'd been blaming that on the break room coffee.

The exhaustion hit me every afternoon like a wave and no amount of sleep touched it. I'd been blaming that on the shifts.

My eyes were puffy every single morning. I'd been blaming that on bad sleep.

Every one of those was a flag I'd watched in a thousand patients before their access surgery. And I'd explained every one of mine away.

My nephrologist looked at the 22, looked at the protein pouring out in my urine, and told me it was time to place the fistula. To get the arm ready before we needed it.

That was the Tuesday with the purple marker.

I went home and sat at my kitchen table after my husband had gone to bed, and I understood something I'd never let myself understand before.

Every drug I was on had been treating one number.

The blood pressure pills were forcing my vessels open.

The second pill was doing its own small thing.

The diet was lightening the load on filters that were already failing.

Not one of them had touched whatever was actually destroying those filters in the first place.

I've spent my whole life at the end of this road. I'd wheeled hundreds of people to that machine who looked exactly like my father, and exactly like me. Every one of them had followed the protocol. Every one of them had been told they were stable.

And it had failed me at 58.

I did something that night I hadn't done since nursing school.

I went and read the actual mechanism.

Not the diet handouts. Not the staging guidelines. How the damage actually happens.

I read for hours.

Your kidneys have a filtering system. It pulls the waste out of your blood and sends the clean blood back. It's been running in the background since the day you were born. You never had to think about it. Your urine was clear. Your energy was steady. That's how it worked when you were young.

But your blood is full of tiny unstable particles. Free radicals. From stress. From processed food. From sugar. From the toxins in modern life your grandparents never carried. From just getting older. Think of it as rust. Invisible rust, building up inside your kidneys, looking for something to attack.

And what it attacks is the filtering system itself. It scars it. Stiffens it. Clogs it. Wears it down a little more every single day.

And here's the part that stopped me cold.

Once those filters are damaged, they can't catch protein anymore. Protein is supposed to stay in your blood. It's the building block your body uses to repair itself. But damaged filters leak it out into your urine, and when it hits the water in the bowl it acts like soap. It foams. That foam every morning isn't nothing. It's the building blocks of your own body going down the drain.

And the damaged filters can't pull the waste out anymore either. So the waste backs up in your blood. That's the dark urine. The metallic taste. The puffy eyes. The swelling. The fog. The bone tired exhaustion sleep can't fix.

And it feeds on itself. More rust, more damage, less filtering, more waste, more rust. Round and round, worse every year. That's why my number was 60 one year and 48 the next and 22 by the time I finally looked. That's why the renal diet I followed perfectly never stopped the slide. It lightened the load. It never touched the rust.

None of it was hidden. It had been sitting in the same journals the doctors I work with read every month.

Everything I'd been handing people for 22 years was aimed at the wrong thing. We were managing the decline. Nobody was stopping what was driving it.

I closed the laptop and I couldn't sleep. Because I understood that I'd wheeled hundreds of people toward that machine following the exact protocol that had failed me, and every one of them still had the rust building in their filters, waiting for their own purple marker.

Two weeks later I was rooming a patient before her appointment. Taking her vitals. Pulling up her chart.

Her name was Leila. She'd been coming through our practice for three years. Her eGFR at intake had been 29 and dropping. Foam in her urine. Protein high. She'd been on the same road I was on.

Her eGFR that morning was 34. It had held or ticked up for three checks in a row. Her protein was down. Her nephrologist had stopped bringing up access surgery.

I looked at her across that little room and asked her what she was doing.

She was quiet for a moment. Then she said, 'My grandmother has been telling all of us for years. I never brought it up here because I didn't think anyone would take it seriously.'

I asked her what her grandmother had told her.

She wrote a name and an address on the back of an appointment card.

Gulnara. A town I'd never heard of out in the Central Valley. A house with a garden her grandmother had grown from seeds she'd carried over from her village in the mountains, in the old pomegranate country of the Caucasus.

I drove there the following Saturday.

I didn't tell my husband where I was going.

I didn't tell anyone at my clinic that a dialysis nurse with a fistula surgery on the calendar was driving almost four hours to sit with a 79 year old grandmother, because everything my training and my 22 years in that unit had taught me hadn't saved me.

I pulled into the driveway of a small house at 11:40 in the morning.

The garden along the front walk was unlike anything I'd seen. Herbs I didn't recognize. And by the door, a tree heavy with round, leathery, deep red fruit, splitting a little at the seams in the sun.

She was on the porch, sorting the fruit into a wooden bowl. Small woman. Thin. Late seventies. Moving like she was sixty. No cane. Clear, sharp eyes.

I introduced myself. Just as Denise. She looked up and asked me why I'd come.

I told her.

I told her I was a dialysis nurse. 22 years. That my own eGFR had crashed to 22. That they'd scheduled my fistula. That the diet and the pills I'd handed a thousand patients hadn't saved me. That my own father had died on the machine. That her granddaughter had told me about her.

She listened. She didn't interrupt.

When I finished she set the bowl down and said, 'Come inside.'

Her kitchen smelled like the fruit and something warm underneath it.

She poured me tea without asking.

She sat across from me and said, 'Your medicines are fighting the wrong battle. You already know this. That's why you're at my table.'

I did know it.

She reached into the bowl and set five split pomegranates on the table in front of me.

'This one is your foam. This one is your dark water. This one is your swelling. This one is your tiredness. This one is that taste in your mouth.'

She tapped each one.

'Every doctor treated these like different problems. A pill for the pressure. A diet for the diet. Wait and watch for the rest. It is not five problems. It is one. And you already know what it is.'

I nodded. I couldn't speak.

She said, 'Let me tell you what your body is actually doing. Your kidneys have a filter. It cleans your blood and sends it back. It has done this quietly your whole life. That is how it worked when you were young.'

She leaned forward.

'But your blood carries little broken things. From stress. From bad food. From sugar. From this modern life. From the years. Think of it as rust. It builds up inside the kidney, and it eats the filter. Scars it. Stiffens it. A little more every day.'

She sat back.

'And once the filter is eaten, it cannot hold your protein. So the protein leaks into your water, and it foams. And it cannot push your waste out, so the waste stays in you, and that is the dark water and the taste and the swelling and the tiredness. And here is what nobody told you. It gets worse on its own. More rust, more damage, less filter, more waste, more rust. That is why your number kept falling no matter how carefully you ate. The diet lightened the load. It never touched the rust.'

I told her I'd read all of it the week before.

I have eaten raw pork. Raw beef. Raw fish. Raw lamb. Meat that was still warm.
I have done this hundreds of times over thirty one years. Because it was my job.
My name is Rachel. I am seventy two years old. I was a parasitologist at the University of Connecticut for thirty one years. I studied intestinal parasites. How they enter. How they anchor. How they feed. How they hide. How they reproduce. How they survive.
I ate raw meat because you cannot study what you do not carry. In my field, controlled self-infection under medical supervision is standard practice. You need live specimens. You need to observe the full cycle inside a human host. Cell cultures do not replicate the gut environment. Animal models behave differently. To understand how an organism anchors, feeds, reproduces, and defends itself inside a living human body, you need a living human body.
I volunteered mine.
Let me tell you exactly what lives in raw pork and what it does inside you. Because this is the part that most people, including most doctors, do not know.
Raw pork can carry three primary parasitic organisms.
Trichinella spiralis. A roundworm. When you eat raw or undercooked pork containing Trichinella larvae, the larvae survive your stomach acid, enter your small intestine, and mature into adult worms within about two days. The adults mate inside your intestine. The females burrow into the intestinal wall and begin releasing live larvae, not eggs, live larvae, directly into your bloodstream. Those larvae travel through your blood to your muscle tissue, where they coil up inside individual muscle cells and form cysts. They can remain alive in your muscles for years. Decades.
Taenia solium. The pork tapeworm. When you ingest the cysticerci from raw pork, they attach to the wall of your small intestine using hooks and suckers built into their head. They grow. A single Taenia solium can reach twenty feet inside your intestine. It absorbs your digested food directly through its skin. It does not have its own digestive system. It does not need one. It is using yours. It releases segments filled with eggs that pass in your stool. A single tapeworm can live inside you for twenty five years.
Toxoplasma gondii. Not a worm. A microscopic protozoan. Pork is one of the primary transmission vectors. Once inside your body, Toxoplasma crosses into your bloodstream and forms cysts in your brain tissue and muscles. It alters neurotransmitter levels. Published research has linked chronic Toxoplasma infection to changes in behavior, reaction time, and cognitive function. Over sixty million Americans carry it without knowing.
I deliberately exposed myself to all three over my career. Under medical supervision. With pharmaceutical clearance protocols standing by.
Here is what I observed each time.
The first seventy two hours after eating raw pork, you feel nothing. The organisms are establishing. They are surviving stomach acid. They are migrating to their preferred tissue. They are not large enough or numerous enough to produce symptoms.
By day five to seven, the first signs appear. A subtle heaviness in the gut. Not pain. A fullness that was not there before. Like your intestine is aware that something new has arrived. Your bowel movements change in texture and frequency. Small changes. The kind you would not notice unless you were documenting every detail the way I was.
By day ten to fourteen, the bloating begins. The organisms are feeding now. They are anchored to your intestinal wall. They are consuming nutrients from your digested food before your body can absorb them. Your small intestine is where B12 is absorbed. Where iron is absorbed. Where zinc is absorbed. These are the first nutrients the organisms steal because they are the most bioavailable. Your brain needs all three to function. Names. Words. Memory. Focus. All of it runs on B12 and iron and zinc. When those levels drop, your brain does not crash. It dims. Slowly. One function at a time.
By week three to four, the secondary symptoms establish. Fatigue that does not match your sleep. Sugar cravings that feel less like wanting and more like your body demanding fuel. Brain fog. The kind where you walk into a room and forget what you came for. Where you reach for a word and it is not there. Your skin may change. Inflammatory responses. Eczema like patches. Your sleep may fracture. The three AM wake up that you blame on hormones or anxiety. It is not hormones. It is your immune system responding to organisms it can detect but cannot reach.
I documented all of this. Dozens of times. In my own body. Over three decades.
And each time I cleared the infection using pharmaceutical protocols. Ivermectin for the nematodes. Praziquantel for the cestodes. Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine for Toxoplasma.
Each time my symptoms resolved. My stool tests came back clean. My bloodwork returned to normal. I documented the clearance and moved on to the next research cycle.
Or so I believed.
What I did not know, and what I would not learn until a woman on a porch in Vermont told me, is that the pharmaceutical protocols were clearing the exposed organisms and leaving everything behind the biofilm completely untouched. Every clearance was partial. Every time I thought I was clean, a residual population was surviving behind the shield, silently feeding, silently reproducing, silently stealing the nutrients my brain needed to function.
For thirty one years.
By the time I retired at sixty nine, I had symptoms I attributed entirely to aging. Bloating every evening. Fatigue that did not match my sleep. Brain fog that was getting worse every year. Sugar cravings every afternoon. Skin patches on my forearms. Three AM wake ups. Fifteen pounds I could not lose.
I had every symptom I had observed and documented dozens of times in my own controlled infections. And I did not recognize them. Because I believed I was clear. Because the tests said I was clear. Because the tests catch twenty percent.
Here is what I know after three decades.
The organisms are inside you right now. That is not an opinion. It is data I collected in my laboratory over fifteen years. The CDC estimates over sixty million Americans carry Toxoplasma gondii alone. One organism out of hundreds.
The standard stool test your doctor would order catches roughly twenty percent of infections. I verified that number. In my lab. Repeatedly. Your doctor's test misses four out of five cases.
And here is the piece that defined the last five years of my life.
Every treatment fails at the same point.
Every one.
I documented this in my lab for over a decade. Every antiparasitic product, pharmaceutical and botanical, produces the same result. Two weeks of genuine improvement. Measurable reduction in parasite load. Real symptom relief. Then the organisms rebuild. The symptoms return. The infection comes back to baseline or worse.
I called it the two week wall.
I could not explain it. I published papers describing it. I presented the data at conferences. Nobody in my field could explain it either. The wall existed and nobody knew why.
When I retired in 2019, I decided I was going to find the answer.
Not in a journal. Not in another laboratory. I had spent thirty one years in laboratories and the answer was not there.
I was going to find it in the field.
I bought a used Honda CR-V. I packed a cooler and a suitcase and a notebook. And I drove across the United States for seven months testing every parasite solution I could find, on myself, in the real world, documented day by day.
My daughter Sarah thought I was having a breakdown. My sister thought I was grieving the career. My doctor told me to be careful.
I was not having a breakdown. I was running the experiment that thirty one years of academic parasitology had failed to run. I was going to test every solution Americans were using. Not in a petri dish. In my own body. And I was going to find the one that broke through the wall.
Here is what I tested. And here is what happened.
IVERMECTIN.
I started with what I knew best.
Pharmaceutical grade ivermectin. Not the veterinary paste from a feed store. Human pharmaceutical grade. 200 micrograms per kilogram body weight. I had administered this compound in clinical settings during my career. I understood the mechanism at the molecular level. It binds to glutamate gated chloride ion channels in the parasite's nerve and muscle cells. Forces the channels open permanently. Floods the cells with chloride ions. The parasite's nervous system shuts down. It cannot move. It cannot feed. It dies.
The mechanism is elegant. The Nobel Prize committee agreed in 2015 when they awarded it for this exact compound.
I took the first dose in a motel room in Scranton, Pennsylvania. I documented everything.
Days one through three. No perceptible change. Building tissue concentration. Expected.
Days four through seven. The first signs of response. My stomach, which had been bloated and distended every evening for years, was noticeably flatter. My head was clearing. I woke up on day six and for the first time in months I did not reach for coffee before I could form a coherent thought. The fog was thinning.
Days eight through fourteen. I felt like a different woman. The bloating was nearly gone. My brain was sharp in a way I had not felt since my fifties. I could read a journal article and follow every sentence. The sugar cravings that had been screaming at me every afternoon had gone quiet. My skin was calmer. I was sleeping seven hours straight for the first time in years.
I sat in a diner in Harrisburg on day twelve and I wrote in my notebook, "Is this the one?"
I wanted it to be. Ivermectin is well studied. The dosing is precise. The safety profile over forty years is excellent. If this was the answer, I could recommend it to anyone.
Day fifteen. The wall.
It hit overnight. I went to bed flat stomached and clear headed. I woke up distended and foggy. The bloating was worse than before I started. The fatigue crashed down like someone had pulled the power cable out of my body. The headaches started by noon. I pulled off the highway at a rest stop in Pennsylvania and sat in my car for two hours with my head on the steering wheel because I could not focus my eyes well enough to drive.
Day seventeen. I was back at baseline. Every symptom returned. As if the ivermectin had never happened.
I sat in that rest stop parking lot and I wrote one line in my notebook.
"Ivermectin kills exposed adults. One mechanism. One of four. The wall holds."
OIL OF OREGANO.
I drove to an herbalist in the Appalachian mountains of North Carolina who had been selling high concentration oregano oil for twenty years. She told me the carvacrol in oregano breaks the protective shield parasites build around themselves. She told me most products on Amazon are diluted to the point of uselessness. She sold me a bottle of wild oregano oil that she said was the strongest available in the country.
I took it at the dose she recommended. Five drops under the tongue twice daily.
The first two weeks were different from the ivermectin. The improvement was faster. By day four I could feel something shifting in my gut. The bloating dropped earlier than with ivermectin. My skin cleared slightly. The oregano was doing something the ivermectin had not done.
I believed the oregano was breaking the biofilm. In my lab I had studied biofilm disruption. Carvacrol does disrupt polysaccharide matrices. The herbalist was right about the mechanism.
But it only addressed the shield. It did not kill what was behind the shield. It did not reach the eggs. It did not remove the dead organisms.
Day sixteen. The wall.
Not as harsh as the ivermectin crash. But the symptoms returned. The bloating came back. The fog settled. The infection rebuilt.
One mechanism. Different mechanism than ivermectin. Same wall.
ETHIOPIAN BLACK SEED OIL.
I had been seeing these capsules everywhere on my drive south. Every gas station health shelf. Every pharmacy end cap. Every Instagram ad on my phone. Ethiopian highland black seed oil. The compound everyone was talking about was thymoquinone.
The marketing claimed that Ethiopian highland seeds contain up to 4.64 percent thymoquinone compared to half a percent in Egyptian or Indian varieties. At that concentration, the claim was that it dissolves biofilm. The fortress walls parasites build around themselves.
I drove to a shop in Atlanta that imported directly from Ethiopian highland farms. The owner was a young Ethiopian woman named Hanna. Her grandmother had used the oil in their village for stomach problems, skin infections, and parasites. She told me Americans had discovered it on TikTok about a year ago and she could not keep it in stock. She was selling two hundred bottles a week.
I bought the capsules. I took two before bed every night. I documented everything.
The thymoquinone is a legitimate compound. I had read the research papers. It does disrupt biofilm polysaccharide matrices. Similar mechanism to carvacrol in oregano but through a different biochemical pathway.
The first two weeks showed improvement. Different in character from the ivermectin. Where ivermectin had produced a sharp, clean improvement in cognition, the black seed oil produced a subtler shift. Bloating reduced more gradually. Gut activity increased. I was eliminating differently. Something was changing in the biofilm environment.
But thymoquinone alone, even at 4.64 percent, breaks the shield without killing what is behind it. The shield opens. The organisms are briefly exposed. But without wormwood or another antiparasitic compound hitting them the moment the shield drops, they simply rebuild the shield.
The women on TikTok who swear by it are not wrong about the compound. They are experiencing a partial disruption that feels like improvement because it is improvement. But the improvement cannot hold because the shield rebuilding outpaces the thymoquinone disruption.
Day seventeen. The wall.
Same pattern. Same rebuild. The infection came back.
I left Atlanta and drove north. I wrote in my notebook, "Black seed oil addresses biofilm. One mechanism. One of four. Insufficient alone. The wall holds."
WORMWOOD, CLOVE, AND BLACK WALNUT.
The standard herbal protocol. The Hulda Clark formula that every product on Amazon is some version of. I had tested this in my lab dozens of times. But I tested it again in my own body during the trip, using three different brands at three different dose levels.
Brand one. Standard dose. Two week improvement. Wall at day fifteen.
Brand two. Double dose. Slightly longer improvement window. Wall at day eighteen. Worse crash. More headaches.
Brand three. The most expensive product on Amazon with the highest concentration. Two week improvement. Wall at day sixteen.
The wormwood kills adults. The clove is supposed to handle eggs but the dose in commercial capsules is insufficient to penetrate the biofilm and reach the eggs embedded in the intestinal lining. The black walnut hits larvae. But without biofilm disruption, without egg penetration at therapeutic dose, without dead organism removal, the cycle restarts.
Three mechanisms. Still not four.
HOME RECIPES.
I tested them because Americans swear by them and I was being thorough. I spent three weeks in different parts of the country trying what people were actually doing in their kitchens.
Papaya seeds blended into a smoothie every morning for two weeks. I met a woman in a health food store in Asheville who told me she had been doing this for a year and her bloating was gone. She gave me her recipe. I followed it exactly. The papain enzyme in papaya seeds does have mild antiparasitic properties. I observed slight improvement in digestion. No measurable effect on parasite load. The wall did not apply because the product never produced enough initial improvement to crash from.
Diatomaceous earth in water. Three tablespoons daily. A man at a farmer's market in Tennessee told me his whole family took it. He said it shreds the parasites with its microscopic sharp edges. The theory is not entirely wrong, the silica structures are abrasive at a cellular level, but in the concentration you can safely ingest, the effect is negligible. What I experienced was significant gastric discomfort and no antiparasitic result worth documenting.
Raw garlic cloves on an empty stomach. Six cloves daily for ten days. I did this in a motel room in Kentucky and I can tell you that nobody came within fifteen feet of me for a week and a half. Garlic does have significant antimicrobial activity. Allicin disrupts bacterial and fungal cell membranes. I observed genuine improvement in bloating that I attributed to bacterial overgrowth reduction. But garlic alone addresses the fourth mechanism without touching the first three. The parasites themselves are unaffected.
Pumpkin seeds. A full cup daily, chewed thoroughly. Interesting result. The cucurbitins in pumpkin seeds produce a paralytic effect on certain organisms. I observed structures in my stool that suggested dead or dying parasites were detaching from the intestinal wall. The pumpkin seeds were doing something real. But they do not kill the organisms. They paralyze and release what is already dead or dying. Without something to do the killing first, the seeds have little to work with.
Turpentine on a sugar cube. Yes. People do this. There are Facebook groups dedicated to it. I tried it in a motel room in West Virginia with a bottle of water and a phone with 911 ready. One teaspoon on a sugar cube. The burning in my esophagus lasted four hours. No measurable antiparasitic effect. I wrote in my notebook, "Do not do this again."
Apple cider vinegar. Two tablespoons in water daily. Mild improvement in gut pH. No antiparasitic effect whatsoever. But the woman at the farm stand in Virginia who recommended it was lovely and I bought three jars of her pickles.
None of the home recipes broke the wall. None of them came close. Each one addressed a fragment of one mechanism at a concentration too low to produce a sustained result.
I was five months into the trip when I reached Vermont.
I had driven over eleven thousand miles. I had tested nine products and protocols on my own body. Every one had failed at the wall. But I was not discouraged because I had learned something valuable from every failure.
I now understood the four mechanisms individually. Ivermectin had shown me the adult killing mechanism. Oregano and black seed oil had shown me the biofilm. Pumpkin seeds had shown me the removal mechanism. Garlic had shown me the overgrowth. The wormwood formulas had confirmed the adult killing through a different pathway.
Each piece worked. Each piece was real. Each piece produced genuine, measurable improvement. But each piece alone was like trying to open a combination lock by getting one number right. You need all four numbers at the same time or the lock does not open.
I was sitting at a diner outside Burlington on a Tuesday afternoon. Late September. The leaves were just starting to turn. I had my notebook open on the counter and I was mapping the four mechanisms on a napkin, drawing arrows between them, trying to figure out if there was a combination protocol that could hit all four simultaneously.
The woman behind the counter was about fifty. She had been watching me write for half an hour. She refilled my coffee and she looked at my napkin and she said, "What are you working on?"
I gave her the short version. Parasitologist. Antiparasitic solutions. Testing them on the road.
She set the coffee pot down and she looked at me for a long moment.
"You should go see Margaret," she said.
"Who is Margaret?"
"She lives about thirty minutes north of here. A farm road off Route 15. White farmhouse. You can't miss it. She is a retired nurse. She has been helping people with what you are describing for as long as I can remember. My mother went to her in the 1990s. My sister went to her last year."
She wrote directions on the back of a receipt. I folded it and put it in my pocket.
I almost did not go. I was a parasitologist. I had spent my career in a university laboratory. The idea that a retired nurse in a farmhouse had solved a problem that thirty one years of academic research could not solve was, frankly, difficult to take seriously.
But I had driven eleven thousand miles. I had tested nine solutions. I had hit the wall nine times. And I had nothing left to test.
I drove out the next morning.
The road narrowed after about twenty minutes. Farmland on both sides. Cows. A white barn with a green roof. Then the farmhouse. Small. White clapboard. Blue shutters. A garden in the front that was still blooming despite the late season. And a woman sitting on the porch in a wooden rocking chair with a cup of tea in her hand.
She looked about eighty. Her hair was white and pulled back. Her face was lined in the way that faces line when they have spent decades listening carefully. She watched me pull into the driveway. She did not stand up. She did not wave. She just watched.
I walked to the porch. I introduced myself. I told her I was a parasitologist. I told her about my career. I told her about the trip. I told her about the two week wall and the nine products and the four mechanisms I had identified.
She listened without interrupting. She rocked slowly in her chair. When I finished she was quiet for a moment. Then she looked at me with eyes that had the steady patience of a woman who had heard a thousand versions of this story.
"How many of the four mechanisms did you address simultaneously?" she asked.
I paused.
"None. I tested them separately. One at a time."
She nodded.
“That is why the wall held. The four mechanisms are not sequential. They are concurrent. They must be addressed at the same time or the ones you did not address will rebuild the infection before the ones you did address can complete their work?”
She stood up from her rocking chair and held the screen door open.
"Come inside. I will make you tea. And I will show you what my grandmother figured out in 1923."
Her kitchen was small. Warm. A wooden table with a bowl of apples on it. Dried herbs hanging from the ceiling. She put a kettle on the stove and she took a yellowed recipe card from a drawer and set it on the table between us.
The card was handwritten in Hungarian. The ink was brown with age. Margaret translated it for me.
Nine ingredients. Each one targeting a different piece of the four mechanism cycle. Designed to work simultaneously. Designed so that no single mechanism has time to rebuild before the others reach it.
Wild organic wormwood for the adults. The wild strain, not cultivated. Up to ten times the active compound concentration that won the Nobel Prize in 2015.
Black walnut hull for the larvae.
Clove in liquid sublingual form for the eggs. Not capsules. Liquid that enters the bloodstream directly and reaches the intestinal wall at therapeutic concentration. This was the piece every Amazon product gets wrong. The clove is there on the label. But in capsule form, at commercial doses, dissolved in stomach acid, the eugenol never reaches the eggs embedded behind the biofilm in the intestinal lining.
Pumpkin seed for removal. I had already seen this mechanism work on my trip. Pumpkin seed paralyzes the dead organisms and physically escorts them out. No decomposition. No toxin flood. No crash.
Soursop leaf. A completely different killing mechanism than wormwood. Wormwood disrupts the nervous system. Soursop inhibits mitochondrial ATP production. Dual mechanism. Margaret's grandmother did not know the biochemistry. She knew that the two plants together worked better than either one alone. She figured out combination therapy a hundred years before modern pharmacology gave it a name.
Neem for the biofilm. I had already seen this work. The carvacrol cracks the shield open. Then the wormwood kills what was hiding behind it. Margaret's grandmother had been combining neem with wormwood since 1923. Hippocrates had been combining them since 400 BC.
Aged garlic for the bacterial and fungal overgrowth. The fourth mechanism. The one that ensures the gut environment does not simply reinvite new colonization after the parasites are cleared.
Margaret told me she had been using this formula for forty years. On thousands of women. On military families. On farmers. On people who came to her farmhouse from as far away as California because nothing else had worked.
She told me a younger woman she had mentored set up manufacturing three years ago. Small batches. Third party tested. Liquid sublingual form because a damaged gut cannot absorb capsules properly. Two drops under the tongue. Into the bloodstream in minutes. Bypasses the compromised gut entirely.
Wildroot Botanics. Organic Wormwood Drops.
I sat in Margaret's kitchen looking at a handwritten recipe card that was older than I was, written in a language I could not read, and I felt the same thing I imagine a physicist would feel if they found the missing equation written on a napkin in a diner.
The answer to the unsolved problem of my thirty one year career had been sitting in this farmhouse for four decades. Thirty minutes from a diner in Burlington. Written on a card from 1923.
I ordered Wildroot Botanics that night from my motel room.

Surviving every pharmaceutical clearance protocol because the pharmaceuticals never broke the shield to reach them.
I sat on the edge of my bathtub on day four looking at what I had produced and I felt something I had not felt in thirty one years of parasitology. Humility. I had studied these organisms my entire career. They had been inside me the whole time.
Week two. Bloating down. Cognition sharpening. Sugar cravings quiet. My stomach was flat by evening for the first time in years. I was sleeping through the night. The three AM wake ups I had blamed on hormones had stopped.
But I did not get excited. I had seen two good weeks nine times on this trip. I had written "Is this the one?" in diners in Pennsylvania and North Carolina and Georgia and every time the answer had been no. Two good weeks meant nothing to me anymore. Two good weeks was just the setup for the wall.
Week three. I watched for the wall the way you watch for a storm you know is coming.
Day fifteen. I woke up and checked myself. Stomach flat. Head clear. Energy present. No headaches. I wrote in my notebook, "Day 15. No wall."
Day sixteen. Same. No crash. No return of symptoms.
Day seventeen. I was sitting in my kitchen at home. Sarah had come over for dinner. I was telling her about a woman I had met at the diner in Burlington and I used the word "serendipity" in the middle of a sentence without reaching for it. A word that had been buried in the fog for months. It just appeared. Sarah looked at me and said, "Mom, your voice sounds different." I asked her what she meant. She said, "You sound like you're thinking at full speed again."
Day twenty one. No crash. No headaches. No fog. No bloating. No return.
I sat at my kitchen table on day twenty one and I looked at my notebook. I had been tracking data for five months across nine products. Every single one had crashed between day fourteen and day eighteen. Wildroot Botanics was at day twenty one with no signal of decline.
The wall had broken.
In five months of testing nine products, driving eleven thousand miles, spending thousands of dollars, and documenting every day in a notebook that was now almost full, I had never seen a single product get past day fourteen without the infection rebuilding.
Wildroot Botanics got past day twenty one. And the infection did not rebuild.
Week four. Material was still coming out. Deep biofilm colony. Organisms that had been anchored to my intestinal walls for decades. The pumpkin seed was pulling them out intact. No Herxheimer reaction. No toxin flood. No crash. Steady, gentle elimination. The way it is supposed to work when the dead organisms are actually leaving the body instead of rotting inside it.
Week six. I ran my own labs. Inflammatory markers down significantly. B12 up. Iron up. My body was absorbing nutrients properly for the first time in years. The sugar cravings had stopped completely. The bloating was gone. The brain fog that I had blamed on aging was gone because it was never aging. It was nutrient theft. Something had been eating the B12 and iron and zinc before my brain could use them.
The skin patches on my arms that I had treated with steroid cream for years faded to nothing in weeks. The inflammation driving them was gone because the source of the inflammation was gone.
Eleven pounds down without changing my diet.
Week eight. I called Sarah. I told her the trip was over. I told her I had found it.
She said, "Which one worked?"
I said, "None of the ones you can buy on Amazon. None of the pharmaceuticals. None of the TikTok products. The one that worked was in a farmhouse in Vermont. A formula from Hungary. 1923. Nine ingredients. Four mechanisms. All at once."
She said, "Mom, you drove across the country for seven months to find a bottle of drops in Vermont?"
I said, "I drove across the country for seven months because thirty one years of academic research could not solve this problem and a woman on a porch in Burlington could."

I am down nineteen pounds. My cognition is the sharpest it has been in over a decade. My sleep is deep and unbroken. My skin is clear. My gut works the way textbooks say a healthy gut should work.

I dumped chili on the Beta’s daughter in front of the whole cafeteria. Maybe it was reckless... but for once, I refused to bow. 🌶️⚡
Chapter 1
Chapter One: Bruises Before Breakfast
SMACK!!!
"That kitchen was supposed to be clean before I came home!" he roared.
The floor pressed cold against my cheek while my stepfather hit me for the second time that week. My body had not even finished recovering from the last beating, the one I had gotten because I had slept too late to cook breakfast.
His boot drove into my ribs. Something inside my left side cracked, sharp and bright enough to steal my breath.
Great. Another trip to the pack hospital. That would make more than one in the last two months.
"Get off your lazy ass," he snarled, "and have this kitchen spotless before I get back from training."
He stalked toward the back door, then paused only long enough to look at my mother. The look told her to leave me there and not help.
She obeyed.
I pushed myself upright inch by inch, one hand clamped over my side. Every breath scraped through me. When I finally managed to stand, I shuffled to the sink and turned on the water. Dishes first. Pain later.
I had overslept again because I had been up late finishing schoolwork.
My name is Talia Rivers. I am seventeen, female, and an Omega in the Black Summit Pack. At least, that is what my mother and stepfather have kept telling me my whole life.
My mother married him when I was two. I never knew my real father, and whenever I asked about him, she gave me the same thin answer: he had not cared about either one of us.
I am six feet tall and weigh one hundred fifty-five pounds, which makes me the tallest Omega female in the pack. I have never felt like the others. I am faster than most of them, stronger too, and I have never been good at bowing my head for high-ranking pack members just because they expected it.
Chestnut-auburn hair falls to the middle of my back, and my eyes are a pale green that people tend to stare at when they first meet me.
At the sink, my mother watched me struggle and smiled like she had been waiting for it.
"You should have finished your chores before bed," she said. "Now you have made Pierce angry again, and he has beaten your ass again this week. When are you going to learn?"
Disgust sat plain on her face.
I rinsed a plate harder than I needed to. "Maybe you should teach your daughter, Sabrina, to clean up after herself and her friends. I was awake half the night dealing with the living room they destroyed."
Her mouth tightened.
"You are never going to be anything except a low Omega," she said. "Do what you are told and keep your head down. Do you really believe your mate will accept you when you turn eighteen?"
She let out a cruel little laugh.
"He will take one look at you and reject you on sight. Then you will be trapped here for the rest of your life, alone, serving everyone."
I kept washing dishes and let the water cover what I wanted to say. Breakfast had to be ready before Pierce returned from training, and arguing with my mother had never saved me from anything.
I still did not know what I had ever done to her or to Pierce to deserve the way they treated me. Pierce was the pack Gamma, which meant the worst of it stayed hidden behind doors, especially inside our apartment in the packhouse.
Everything changed after my siblings, Brennan and Sabrina, were born. They had Gamma blood, so the pack treated them like royalty. Brennan most of all, since he was supposed to become Gamma after Pierce retired in a few years.
When the last dish was clean, I opened the fridge and took out bacon, eggs, and hash browns. Breakfast in that apartment was never small. I cooked a whole pack of bacon, a dozen eggs, an entire bag of hash browns, and half a loaf of bread for toast.
Brennan came into the kitchen while the food was nearly done. One glance at my face was enough. His eyes caught on the new bruises, and sympathy softened his expression.
"You made Dad mad again this morning?" he asked. "That is twice this week. You know how he gets about you doing every chore in this apartment, right, sis?"
"I know." I sighed and reached for another pan. "I slept too long because I had been up late with homework. Sabrina and her friends trashed the living room last night, and I did not get to my room until eleven."
"Next time she pulls that, or next time you are falling behind, tell me," Brennan said. "I will help."
He stepped close and gave me a sideways hug.
Pain flashed through my ribs, and I hissed before I could stop myself.
His face changed. "He broke another rib, sis?"
"Yeah." I forced the word out. "But I do not have time to go to the hospital before school and have it checked."
I grimaced as I lifted the iron skillet from the stove and lowered it into the sink.
Brennan and I had always been close, even with him being two and a half years younger than me. He had my back, and more than once, he had saved me from one of Pierce's beatings.
Sabrina was different. To her, I was a servant she could torment whenever she and her spoiled friends were bored. She was the little princess of the apartment, and whatever Sabrina wanted, Mommy and Daddy found a way to give her. She was seven months younger than Brennan.
"Breakfast is ready," I said. "I am going to wake Sabrina, then get ready for school."
Brennan stole a piece of bacon as I headed out of the kitchen, a smirk tugging at his mouth.
"Good luck with that, sis. You know she was up late last night."
"Not my problem," I called back in a singsong voice.
I walked down the hallway to Sabrina's room and knocked. Nothing. Of course.
When I opened the door, it looked as if a storm had ripped through the place and left only her room standing. Clothes and shoes covered the floor. Magazines lay scattered everywhere. Soda cans had tipped over on the carpet, leaving sticky stains behind.
Great. My whole afternoon would be swallowed by cleaning her room.
"Sabrina," I said, poking her in the back with one finger. "Time to get up for school."
She groaned and flung an arm around, trying to hit me without opening her eyes.
"Go away. Leave me alone," she mumbled, dragging the comforter over her head.
I crossed to the window and opened the curtains. Light spilled across the mess. Then I yanked the comforter off her.
"It is not my fault you stayed up late with your friends," I told her. "Get up. It is time for school. Unless you want to explain to your father why you missed school for the second time this month."
Another moan came from the bed, but she finally pushed herself upright. Her eyes found me, and a smirk curled across her face.
"No," she said. "I will tell Daddy you never woke me up, and then you will get another ass beating like last time."
She laughed as she walked toward the bathroom.
Little bitch.
The worst part was that Pierce would believe her. He always did. Then I would be the one getting hit again.
I was so tired of the beatings. In a few weeks, I would turn eighteen and get my wolf. After that, I could get the hell out of this pack and find somewhere safe, somewhere I would be treated like I mattered.
More than anything, I wanted to find my birth father. My mother refused to give me even the smallest useful detail, not his name, not the pack he belonged to, nothing.
That was fine. Nana knew. She had been waiting until I turned eighteen to tell me about him.
Nana and my mother had never been close, but Nana had spoiled me rotten every chance she got.
With Sabrina awake and getting ready, I went to my room, which was really the pantry, and grabbed my bookbag and shoes. Then I returned to the kitchen, washed the breakfast pans, and loaded the dirty dishes into the dishwasher.
Before I left, I said goodbye to my little brother, even though at fifteen he already towered over me.

Chapter 2
Chapter Two: Bruises Before the Bell
After I left the apartment, I took the stairs down.
Our family’s rooms are on the third floor of the packhouse. Alpha Zachary and his family occupy the fifth, while the Beta’s family has the fourth. Guests stay on the second floor, and the whole first floor is shared space: the dining hall, kitchen, theater, game room, and the common room where pack members gather whenever they want.
Ariana was already by the door when I reached the bottom.
The packhouse is also where the Omegas live and work. Ariana is one of them. At five-five, she stands a little shorter than I do, with long black hair, wide brown eyes, and the kind of face that always shows exactly what she is feeling.
“Come on,” she said, bouncing on her toes. “If we don’t leave right now, we’re going to be late.”
Thankfully, school is close. The high school sits just down the street, only about ten minutes from the packhouse on foot.
We had barely started walking before her attention snapped to my face. Her eyes narrowed at the fresh bruise I hadn’t had time to cover.
“Pierce was being a d**k again this morning?” she asked, worry tightening her voice.
I gave a dry little laugh. “When is he not being a d**k?”
Usually, I could hide the marks before anyone saw them. This morning had not given me enough time.
Ariana’s mouth pressed into a thin line. “When are you finally getting away from him?”
“As soon as I turn eighteen and get my wolf,” I said. Then, because hope was the only thing keeping me upright some days, I added, “Hopefully. I’m going to California to live with Nana.”
Black Summit Pack is a decent-sized pack, with about five hundred members. We are tucked into central Colorado along the Rockies, roughly an hour north of Denver. For our size, we are strong, mostly because Alpha Zachary insists that everyone train and stay ready in case rogues attack.
Lately, rogue attacks have been happening more often. At least once a week, someone tests our borders. So far, we have been able to hold them off, and no one in the pack has been lost.
Our territory includes the five-story packhouse, the training grounds, the training building, the warrior house, the school, and a shopping center with restaurants and stores. Pack homes spread out around it all. Some people work in those shops and restaurants; others commute into the city.
By the time Ariana and I reached school, Ryder was waiting near the trees outside.
He is Ariana’s cousin and one of the strongest up-and-coming warriors in Black Summit. At six-three, with a body that looked carved rather than built, shoulder-length blond hair, and dark blue eyes that could stop conversations, Ryder drew attention without even trying.
He had turned eighteen a couple of weeks ago, but he still hadn’t found his mate. Everyone knew he hoped it would be me when my birthday came. Ryder had been crushing on me since first grade, and he had never exactly been subtle about it.

Ryder went still.
A second later, his fingers caught my chin gently but firmly, turning my face toward the light. When he saw the bruise, a growl rumbled in his chest. Anger sharpened every line of his expression.
“One day, that bastard is going to get exactly what he’s earned,” he said. “Thinking he can put his hands on an Omega is bad enough. On a female Omega? That’s sick.” His gaze searched mine. “Do Alpha Zachary and Luna Marissa know about this?”
“No.” I pulled back, staring past his shoulder. “They don’t. It’s hard enough hiding it when he leaves marks where people can see them or when he breaks bones, especially when he keeps telling me to shut up about it. Healing takes forever without my wolf.”
Ryder’s anger softened into something sadder. He wrapped me in a careful hug, like he was afraid I might crack if he squeezed too hard.
“Soon,” he murmured. “You’ll be out of that apartment. You’ll get to live like a normal wolf for once.”
The three of us headed inside, splitting off toward our lockers.
Mine is down the hall from Caleb’s. As the future Alpha, he never stands alone for long. The school’s popular girls were already clustered around him like he was the center of gravity. My brother, Brennan, stood beside him too, since he is meant to become the next Gamma once he turns eighteen.
I gave Brennan a small nod and opened my locker.
Then Clementine’s voice sliced through the hallway.
“Ew. Brennan, seriously, how do you handle sharing an apartment with a gross Omega?” she asked him loudly. Clementine is the Beta’s daughter, and she never wastes a chance to remind people of it. “I can’t believe your dad still lets her stay with your family. She should learn where she belongs and line up with the rest of the disgusting Omegas.”
Brennan turned on her with a look of pure revulsion. A growl slipped from him before he spoke.
“Careful, Clementine,” he warned. “That’s my sister you’re talking about, and she’s a better person than you’ll ever be. Being an Omega doesn’t make her nasty.”
My chest warmed despite everything. I love when my brother defends me. He does it every time, just like Ariana, Ryder, and Mrs. Sharon, the head Omega.
Clementine tossed her hair, unimpressed. “Once I’m Luna, the Omegas are going to the old warehouse near the edge of the pack. Then they won’t pollute the packhouse just by existing.”
Caleb looked over at her and scoffed. “Who said you’re going to be my Luna? My mate becomes my Luna. No one else.”
Clementine and I have the same birthday, so she still has no way of knowing whether Caleb is actually her mate. For now, she is only his slutty girlfriend, the one who wears dresses so short they barely count as clothing and pushes her cleavage so high I swear her t**s are one deep breath away from escaping.

“We’ll find out,” he said, not exactly sounding thrilled.
The bell rang before anyone could say more, and I headed for first period.
History.
In that class, we study werewolf history and the laws that govern our kind. I actually love it. The differences between each law fascinate me, from blackmail to stealing another wolf’s mate to murder.
Unfortunately, Caleb and his crowd are in that class too. That means Clementine uses every chance she gets to make my life miserable. At school, she is one of my worst bullies, right up there with my sister and her little pack of followers.
I chose my usual seat near the window, where I could look out at the mountains when class became too much. Caleb, Clementine, and the others took over the back rows.
On her way past me, Clementine clipped my desk hard enough to send my books tumbling to the floor.
“Oops!” she sang. “My bad.”
She paused, then smirked.
“Not.”
Laughter broke out around the room. She moved a couple of desks behind me and slid closer to Caleb, while he only rolled his eyes.
“That is enough,” Mr. Palmer said from the front. He teaches history and has very little patience for drama. “Open your books to page ninety-eight.”
A wave of groans rolled through the class, but everyone obeyed.
I bent to collect my books and tried to pretend my face wasn’t burning.
A few minutes later, Clementine leaned forward until her breath brushed my ear.
“You really think you’re Miss Hot Shit, don’t you, Talia?” she whispered. “You’re nothing. A worthless Omega. You’ll be alone your whole life, because Omegas don’t deserve mates. You’re only useful as servants and for making more little Omegas to serve the rest of us.”
I kept my eyes on the page even though the words blurred.
I will never understand where she gets that kind of thinking. Her parents, Beta Raymond and his mate, Melanie, are kind people. Maybe Clementine is spoiled because she is the youngest and the only girl in a family of five. Her oldest brother, Rowan, will become the next Beta and is away at Beta training right now. Her other two brothers are Delta warriors, some of the best fighters in the pack.
Somehow, Clementine still turned into Clementine.
The rest of the morning moved quickly. That helped. None of my other morning classes had Clementine in them, so by the time lunch arrived, I could breathe again.
I went to the cafeteria to find Ariana and Ryder. After grabbing chili and fries, I carried my tray over to the table where my two best friends were already waiting.
For a little while, things felt normal.
We laughed. We joked. Ryder made some ridiculous comment that had Ariana nearly choking on her drink, and I almost forgot about the bruise on my face and the threat of going home later.
Then heat splashed over my head.
It ran down my hair, across my cheek, and soaked into my shirt. For one stunned second, I couldn’t move. The cafeteria went quiet in that awful way that happens right before people decide whether to laugh.
I turned.
Clementine stood behind me with an empty bowl dangling from her hand. A smug smile stretched across her face.
“Oops,” she said. “I must have tripped.” She laughed, bright and mean. “But Omegas should be used to being filthy all the time.”
Something inside me snapped.
I faced forward, picked up my own bowl of chili, rose from my seat, and dumped the whole thing over her head.
The cafeteria gasped as one body.
Then some of the Omegas started laughing. A few pulled out their phones and took pictures while chili dripped down Clementine’s furious face.
“Fuck you, cunt,” I said, my voice shaking but loud enough to carry. “At least I make chili look better than you do.”
Clementine trembled with rage. Then she screamed.
“FUCKING BITCH! WHO THE FUCK DO YOU THINK YOU ARE? YOU’RE NOBODY! JUST WAIT UNTIL YOUR STEPFATHER HEARS ABOUT THIS!”
My stomach dropped.
Oh, shit.
I was going to pay for that when I got home this afternoon.

Chapter 3
Chapter Three: No Way Out

“Without blinking.”
Clementine was still shrieking when Mrs. Fletcher, the principal, caught sight of the mess and stormed over.

Perfect. As if I wasn’t already dead enough.
We were marched to the office and dropped into the chairs outside Mrs. Foster’s door. Through the wall, Miss Cole’s voice carried as she called our parents. Clementine sat across from me, cheeks red, eyes locked on mine like she was trying to burn holes through my skull.

“Maybe your stepdad will actually finish it this time,” she said softly, sweetness dripping off every word. “Maybe he’ll kill you properly. You’re a useless Omega, and you don’t even deserve air.”
That was exactly the fear chewing through my stomach.
Nice knowing you, Black Summit Pack.
About thirty minutes crawled by before my mother, Pierce, Beta Raymond, and Raymond’s mate, Melanie, came through the school office doors. My mother and Pierce aimed matching glares at me. Raymond and Melanie rushed straight to Clementine, who had already switched on the fake tears.

My mouth fell open.
Across from me, Clementine smirked like she had just been handed a crown.
Mrs. Fletcher stepped out of her office and ushered the adults inside to discuss punishments. The door closed behind them. For an entire hour, I sat there with my arm throbbing and my anger getting hotter by the minute.

Rage shot through me so fast I was on my feet before I thought about moving. “That is complete bullshit. I was sitting there with my friends, minding my own business. That bitch started it, she gets to walk away, and I’m the only one being punished? That is so fucked up!”

Not toward home.
Toward the building where the pack kept the prison cells, the place where captured rogues were locked away after patrols and warriors dragged them in. I knew that building too well. Alpha Zachary had a torture room there, a place used to squeeze information out of rogues.
Pierce had taken me there several times when he decided I was out of control and needed extra discipline.
My back carried the proof. Too many scars to count, most of them from silver-laced whips dipped in wolfsbane.

Pierce knew me too well for that. Before I could reach for the door, he had mind-linked a couple of warriors and had them waiting beside the car to drag me out.

Her cell.
My cell.
That place had turned into my second home whenever Pierce got the itch to give me one of his severe beatings. I kept extra clothes there now, along with a blanket and a couple of books. Ariana was only allowed to bring my homework once a day. Mrs. Sharon brought two meals, usually bread and water, but she always found a way to sneak in something extra so I would not be too weak to stand, or to fight back if I got the chance.
The warriors nodded and clamped their hands around my arms.
Inside, the prison stank of piss, shit, and old blood. Under it all sat the worst smell.
Death.
A lot of rogues had died in that building because they had been stupid enough to attack us. The farther we went down the corridor, the heavier the air felt. New rogues shouted from behind bars as we passed.
“Come here, sweetheart!” one of them called. “I bet we could have some fun while we’re waiting.”

Pierce moved first. He stepped to the cell door, shoved a cattle prod through the bars, and shocked him.
The rogue howled and jerked backward.
“She is not here to entertain you,” Pierce snarled. “Sit down and shut the hell up, rogue, or I’ll drag you out and whip you again.”

“Get comfortable,” he growled. “I’ll be back after I take your mother home. You know what to do.”
I rolled my eyes, snapped my spine straight, and saluted him.

I lowered myself onto the narrow bed and waited for whatever punishment he had decided I deserved this time.

Chapter 4
Chapter Four: The Room Above

"Well?" she asked. "What do you think?"
I turned back to her, overwhelmed. "Luna, this is too much. I would have been fine with the Omegas."
Her smile warmed. "Sweetheart, I already know you are more than an Omega. Your aura is stronger than that. Stronger than an Alpha's, even. Something about you is extraordinary, and in two days, on your birthday, when you shift for the first time, we may finally understand it."
She paused near the door.
"In the meantime, I am going to speak to your mother and use my Luna command to make her confess who your father is. But for now, enjoy your day. Oh, and Alpha Sterling from Misty Mesa Pack will arrive the day after your birthday. He is coming to discuss the rogue problem with us. With luck, perhaps we can end it for good."

Chapter 5
Chapter Five: Dresses Before Dawn
Luna Marissa had barely finished showing me the bedroom before I found my way back downstairs. My brother and Caleb were already settled in the theater room with drinks, snacks, and the remote waiting for me.
Apparently, choosing the movie had become my job.
I did know movies. Whenever my mother and Pierce had not had chores lined up for me, I had watched them with Ariana and Ryder.
So I picked a romantic comedy.
Both boys complained like I had personally wounded them.
Ignoring the groans, I tucked myself into one of the big chairs with a blanket, popcorn, and a soda. A minute later, Celia came in, dropped into the seat beside me, and stole popcorn like she had bought it herself.
“What did you make them watch?” she asked, amused.
“Talia trapped us in a chick flick,” Caleb said, all dramatic suffering.
Celia tossed a kernel at him. “Still better than the horror movies and explosion-fests you two force on me every time.” Then she stuck her tongue out at her brother.
For all their whining, the guys were laughing hard before long. Caleb tried to pretend he was above it, but he failed. Brennan did not even bother pretending.
Celia leaned closer, practically buzzing. “Are you excited about tomorrow? Mom and I decided we’re getting you cute outfits. When you finally meet your mate, you are going to look amazing.”
I lifted one shoulder, uncomfortable with how much she wanted to give me. “I really don’t need a lot. Maybe a few shirts, since Pierce tore so many of mine. Nothing expensive.”
Her grin turned wicked. “Please. By the time we’re finished, the whole pack will be jealous of your closet. Almost as jealous as they are of mine.” She laughed at herself.
The rest of the afternoon slipped past in noise and comfort. More people drifted in, including Ariana and Ryder, and the room filled with laughter, movie quotes, and the smell of homemade pizza. Mrs. Sharon and the Omegas had made several of them, and for once, everything felt easy.
Then Clementine arrived and poisoned the air on contact.
She stood in the doorway like she owned the place, chin raised, eyes sharp with disgust. “Why is she here with those useless friends of hers?” she shrieked, pointing straight at me. “After what she did to me, she shouldn’t be allowed anywhere near this room.”
A collective eye roll moved through the room. Even Brennan and Caleb looked exhausted by her.
“Enough with the performance, Clementine,” Caleb said, his irritation plain. “Everyone knows you started it at school. You humiliated her in front of everybody. I’m done with your crap, and I’m done with you. I don’t want someone like you. We’re over.”
Her mouth fell open. For a second, she looked too stunned to speak. Then the anger rushed back. “You can’t be serious. We’re supposed to be a strong pack. The only way to become stronger is to get rid of the Omegas, or at least put them where they belong—as servants.”
Brennan’s expression hardened. “No. Omegas are not servants. They are pack. They help hold this place together, and they help keep us strong.”
Caleb nodded beside him, his jaw tight.
He pointed toward the hall. “Leave. You’re ruining everyone’s night, and none of us need that in here.”
Clementine spun away, but not before screaming over her shoulder, “This is not over, bitch!”
The door had barely cleared behind her before Celia, Ariana, and I burst out laughing.
Celia lifted her hand in a cheerful little wave at Clementine’s retreating back. “Bye-bye, witch.”
By the time we finally went upstairs, it was close to midnight. Celia, Ariana, and I climbed the steps linked arm in arm, laughing softly so we would not wake the entire house. We are having a small sleepover in my room, the kind of thing I had always wished for when I was younger and imagining what friends were supposed to feel like.
Celia glanced at my door, then at hers across the hall, and squealed. “I still can’t believe you’re right across from me!”
“I still can’t believe your parents gave me that room,” I said, and excitement made my voice lighter than usual.
We stayed awake for another hour even though we were all tired. Celia had brought magazines, so we sprawled across the bed and flipped through pages, planning the shopping trip like it was a mission.
Morning came too fast.
At seven, the mattress bounced under Celia’s weight as she jumped on the bed.
“Wake up, Sleeping Beauty!” she shouted. “It’s shopping day!”
I dragged a pillow over my head. “It is too early for that much happiness.”
“Nope. Get dressed and come downstairs. We’re eating breakfast in the dining room before we leave.” She was already halfway to the door when she said it.
After she left, Ariana pushed the blanket away from her face and blinked at me. “Is she always like this?”
I only shrugged. I was too sleepy to defend Celia or accuse her.
In the bathroom, I brushed my teeth, washed up, and twisted my hair into a messy bun. Then I dug through the dresser until I found a decent T-shirt and leggings, pulled them on, and finished with sneakers.
The dining room smelled like breakfast and fresh coffee. I filled a plate with fruit, sausage, and scrambled eggs from the buffet, then carried it to the head table.
“Alpha. Luna. Good morning,” I said, dipping my head to them both.
Alpha smiled at me. “Good morning, Talia. Did you sleep well?”
“Like a log,” I said, setting my plate beside Brennan. “Until a shrieking lunatic woke me up.” I glanced at Celia and laughed.
Everyone chuckled. Celia answered by throwing a strawberry at me.
Breakfast was easy and loud. We talked through the shopping options, and I learned that the pack center had plenty of good stores with beautiful clothes. Because of that, we would not have needed to drive the full hour to the mall.
Luna chose the mall anyway.
I was thrilled because I had never been to one before. At the same time, the thought of that many strangers made my stomach twist.
At nine, we headed outside to the two SUVs waiting in front of the house. Four warriors came with us as security, there to protect Luna and Celia.
Once we reached the mall, Celia and Luna took over completely. They pulled me from one high-end shop to the next, treating my closet like a problem they had personally sworn to solve.
They were happy, genuinely happy, choosing clothes for me. Everything they picked was current without being ridiculous, pretty without being impossible to wear. Luna paid attention to what would work for everyday life, while Celia kept adding things she claimed I absolutely needed.
In one store, Luna found a dark green satin dress that made me stop walking. It hung off the shoulders and had a sweetheart neckline, elegant without being loud. Best of all, the back rose high enough to hide the scars on my back.
By the time they were finished, exhaustion had settled into my bones. The warriors carried bags for us, several each, and I felt guilty every time I looked at the growing pile.
Somehow, I ended up with a dozen T-shirts, leggings, jeans, workout clothes, a few summer dresses, a couple of cocktail dresses, and the green gown. Celia added shoes, accessories, and makeup until I was sure my room would not have enough space.
When we climbed back into the SUV, I leaned forward between the seats. “Thank you, Luna. Thank you, Celia. This is way too much. I’ll pay you back when I have money.”
Luna looked back at me with a soft smile. “Don’t worry about that, Talia. Watching you enjoy it is the only repayment we want.”
Tears blurred my eyes before I could stop them. I reached over the seat and hugged her. “Thank you, Luna.”
Since I had been little, no one besides my Nana had done anything that kind for me.
Late afternoon had already settled in by the time we returned home, and all of us were starving. Thankfully, Mrs. Sharon had left sandwiches and snacks ready in the fridge.
I ate quickly, then hauled my bags upstairs. Putting everything away took hours. Shirts, dresses, jeans, makeup, shoes—each item had to find a place, and every time I touched something new, that strange grateful ache returned.
When I finally finished, I brushed my teeth and changed into the nightie I had gotten that day. I crawled into bed, and sleep caught me the instant my head touched the pillow.
My eighteenth birthday was tomorrow, and I fell asleep excited for it.

Chapter 6
Chapter Six: The First Shift
“Wake up. It’s time.”
The voice snapped through the dark so sharply that my eyes flew open. I pushed upright in bed, heart thudding, and searched the shadowed corners of my room. The clock read five in the morning. Outside the window, the world was still black.
“Who said that?” I whispered, already nervous.
A laugh brushed through my mind. “Me, silly.”
Oh, my Goddess.
My wolf.
Today is my eighteenth birthday.
“Are you really my wolf?” Excitement rushed through me so fast I could barely hold still. “What’s your name?”
“Yes, I am. My name is Whitefrost,” she answered, warm and certain inside my head. “I have been waiting a very long time to come forward. I know everything you have endured, Talia. The pain and heartbreak will not rule you anymore.”
“Whitefrost,” I breathed, smiling so hard my cheeks hurt. “I’m so happy you’re here. I can’t wait for tonight, when I finally shift into you.”
“We are not ordinary,” she said, her tone turning secretive. “You will understand after the shift. Everything you have been told until now is a lie. You are not the Omega your mother and Pierce claimed you were. You are far more than that. After tonight, they will bow to you.”
I wanted to believe every word.
I climbed out of bed, pulled on workout clothes, and headed for the training grounds. Late May air waited outside, cool but already carrying the promise of warmth. Yesterday, Alpha had told me I could begin training now that I was no longer on the Gamma floor. I did not need my mother’s permission, and I did not need Pierce’s either.
Delta Hayley was waiting to help me catch up with the wolves my age.
“Good morning, Delta.” I lowered my head respectfully.

“Then we start properly.” She stretched one leg out. “Warm up first. Since it’s your first day, we’ll keep the run to five miles.”
Five miles did not sound small to me, but I nodded and copied her movements.
For about twenty minutes, we stretched. Then we ran.
At the beginning, fear kept nipping at me. I expected my lungs to burn. I expected my legs to fail. Instead, I stayed beside Hayley as we circled the training grounds lap after lap before returning to the fighting circle.
Hayley stared at me like she was trying to solve a puzzle. “That was impressive. Especially for someone who has never trained.”
“That is because you have me now,” Whitefrost said, proud enough that I could feel it. “Wait until we shift tonight. They will all be surprised.”
“How surprised?” I asked her silently.
“You will see.”
