I saw the back of my own head in an elevator mirror at St. Luke's in April and I got off on the wrong floor just so I wouldn't have to look at it again.

There was a man in the elevator with me. A visitor, not staff. He was holding a bouquet of grocery store carnations wrapped in plastic and he was reading something on his phone. He didn't see anything.

But I saw everything.

The mirror was one of those long ones that wrap around the corner of the elevator, and I had turned to press 4, and there it was. My whole scalp.

Not a thinning. Not a widening part. My scalp. Pink and shining under the fluorescent light like the crown of a doll that had lost half its hair.

I pressed 2 instead. I got out at admin. I walked to the stairwell and I took the stairs the rest of the way up, and I have taken the stairs at St. Luke's every day since.

My name is Loretta. I'm 56 years old. I've been a hospice case manager in Duluth, Minnesota for 23 years.

I've sat with more dying people than I can count. I've held hands with wives who were about to become widows. I've told grown men that their father had 3 days left, and then told them again the next week when the father was still hanging on.

I know what real suffering looks like.

So when I tell you I stood in a stairwell at my job and cried about my hair, I need you to know I understand how that sounds.

My daughter Karin lives in St. Paul with her husband and two kids. She calls on Sundays. My mother is 82 and still lives in her own house in Superior, Wisconsin, right across the bridge. My sister Marjorie lives up in Ely, about 2 hours north, on the edge of the Boundary Waters. She retired from the Forest Service 3 years ago and I don't see her as much as I want to.

I've been divorced 8 years. His name was Eugene. He works at the port. We were fine and then we weren't and now we're neither.

I share a little townhouse near Lester Park with a rescue cat named Roscoe and a lot of unfinished projects. That's the shape of my life. A schedule, a route, a Sunday call, and the lake.

My hair used to be my thing.

That sounds vain to say out loud but it's true. It was the color my mother's used to be. A dark, warm brown with a natural wave that fell right past my shoulders. My whole life people had touched it in stores. Reached out and lifted it and asked me what I used on it. I used almost nothing. That was the joke.

I stopped noticing when it changed. It happened slow. It happens slow for a lot of women my age and I want to say that out loud because I spent a year thinking I was the only one.

First it was the shower drain. I'd been clearing it every couple weeks for as long as I could remember. Then it was every week. Then it was every 3 days and I stopped counting because I didn't want to know.

Then it was my pillow.

I started finding hairs on my pillow in the morning. Not a hair. Hairs. A little dark scatter of them across the white cotton every single morning. I'd sweep them off with my hand before I made the bed. I'd pretend I hadn't seen them.

Then it was the towel.

I started keeping a black hand towel by the sink because after I brushed my hair the white one looked like I'd been shedding a dog on it.

Then it was the ponytail.

The ponytail I've worn to work my whole adult life started feeling different in my hand. Thinner. Less. Like the elastic wanted to slip off because there wasn't enough there to hold it.

I switched my part from the left to the right because the right side still had some coverage. Then I switched it back a month later because now the right side didn't either. I bought one of those powders you're supposed to shake on your scalp to hide it. It stained the collar of my navy work cardigan and I threw it out in the parking lot at Menards so no one at home would see it in the trash.

I stopped washing my hair as often because every wash meant more loss. I stopped brushing it in front of the mirror because I couldn't watch the strands come out on the bristles.

I started wearing a wide black headband to work.

I told my coworker Denise it was because my ears were cold. It was July.

The thing about hospice work is you learn to notice what people are protecting. A widow who keeps her husband's reading glasses on the kitchen counter for a year. A daughter who won't sit in her father's chair. A man who won't take off his wedding ring even though the finger under it has gone gray.

I know how to see the small things people do to hold onto themselves.

I just couldn't see what I was doing to hold onto me.

My doctor told me it was probably my age. My thyroid was fine, my iron was fine, my hormones were "in the range for a woman your age." She said the words genetic and postmenopausal and shrugged in a way that was supposed to be gentle. She said some women lose their hair as they get older and there wasn't really much to do about it.

That's a hard thing to hear at 56 in a fluorescent room while you're still wearing your work badge.

I tried the shampoo aisle. I tried the pills at Walgreens with the little pink bottle. I tried the biotin gummies my daughter sent me from Target. I tried a scalp serum I ordered at 1 AM after crying in the bathroom that I dropped 42 dollars on and used exactly twice.

Nothing did anything.

By March I had started keeping my hair in a low bun with the bun pulled forward so it would hide the crown of my head from behind. I had cancelled a dentist appointment because I didn't want to lie back in a chair with a bright light overhead where the hygienist could see my part from above. I had asked my daughter to take our Christmas photo from the front instead of the side.

I hadn't told anyone.

Not my sister. Not my daughter. Not my best friend Ellen who I've known since nursing prerequisites at UMD.

I was pretending.

I was 56 years old and I was pretending.

My mother turned 82 on the second Saturday in May. We do the same thing every year. Perkins in Superior, 12:30 PM, the corner booth by the window that looks out at the parking lot. My mother orders the potato pancakes with a side of applesauce and a decaf coffee she barely drinks. My sister drives down from Ely. My daughter drives up from St. Paul with the grandkids if the weather holds.

That year the weather held.

I pulled into the parking lot 10 minutes early. Marjorie's truck was already there. My sister is always 15 minutes early to everything, always has been since we were kids, and I love her for it and it also drives me a little crazy.

I walked in.

She was already at the booth. She stood up when she saw me and I stopped in the middle of the walkway between the tables like someone had pulled the brake on me.

Her hair.

I'm going to try to explain this the way I saw it.

My sister is 63. She has always looked older than me even though she's 7 years my senior. When we were younger it was because she was outside for a living, working trailheads, doing search and rescue in the winter, running a chainsaw for 30 years. Her hands looked like a man's hands. Her face was weathered in the way beautiful things get weathered, and her hair had started to thin at the temples when she was 55, and by the time she retired at 60 she had a short pixie cut that she trimmed herself at her kitchen sink because she said there wasn't enough left up there to bother a stylist about.

I hadn't seen her in person since Thanksgiving.

The woman standing in front of me at Perkins on that Saturday in May had hair to her shoulders.

Not thick like a magazine ad. But there. Present. Filled in through the crown where the light used to shine through when she leaned over her plate. Grown out at the temples where the two little bare patches used to be. Enough of it that she'd pinned one side back with a small tortoise shell clip like she used to wear in the 80s.

I hugged her and I said "your hair" and she laughed and said "yeah, I know, isn't that something."

And I sat down and I didn't taste my food.

I got through lunch. I sang happy birthday. I helped my mother out of the booth and to her car. I told my sister I'd see her back at the house because we were all going over to help mom hang a new porch light.

I drove the 3 miles to my mother's place in a fog.

Marjorie was in the driveway when I pulled up. She was leaning against the tailgate of her truck. She had her hands in the pockets of her jean jacket. She looked at me over the roof of my car and she said "you want to talk about it."

Not a question.

That's my sister.

We sat on the porch swing at our mother's house while my daughter and the grandkids were inside setting up the ladder. I could hear my mother telling Karin where to find the extra bulbs. The lake was 4 blocks away and you could hear a gull sometimes and a boat horn from the harbor.

I told her about the elevator.

I told her about the pillow. The towel. The powder. The headband in July. The Christmas photo. The dentist appointment I cancelled.

I told her about the doctor with the shrug.

She let me talk for a long time. My sister is a good listener. That's the thing they don't put in the retirement papers when a Forest Service ranger retires. She has spent 40 years of her life being the person a scared hiker or a lost kayaker sees first, and she knows how to let a person get to the end of a sentence before she says anything back.

When I was done she put her hand on my knee and she said "Retta, this isn't age. Or not the way you think."

She said it wasn't happening to her hair anymore.

She said she'd been at it for close to a year and she wanted to tell me and hadn't because she didn't want to sound like every ad she'd ever scrolled past on Facebook. She said her friend Diane, who used to work dispatch out of the ranger station in Tower, was the one who'd told her, and Diane had heard about it from her sister-in-law in the Twin Cities, and it was one of those things that had moved from woman to woman in a small circle of people who'd stopped believing anything on TV.

She said the piece that had finally made her try it wasn't a promise about her hair.

It was a study Diane had shown her on her phone about something called oxidative stress.

I want to explain this the way she explained it to me on the porch swing because it made sense in a way nothing else ever had.

Marjorie said think about rust.

She said think about a car that sat in a barn for 20 years. The metal underneath is fine. It's the right metal, same as when it was new. But something in the air, over time, does something to it that nobody planned for. It scales up. It roughens. And the paint on top starts to lift, and the trim starts to weaken, and after long enough the car looks the way it does not because the metal is bad but because the surface has been slowly oxidized.

She said your body does that too. From the inside.

She said the doctors call it oxidative stress and they call the process itself oxidation, and it's the same word. It's rust.

And the tissue that gets rusted first is the tissue with the most delicate blood supply. The small vessels. The capillaries that feed the places that don't get a lot of flow to begin with. The tips of the fingers. The lining of the arteries. The back of the eyes.

The scalp.

She said the follicles that grow your hair are fed by the tiniest little vessels in your body. Smaller than you can imagine. And when the vessels get rusted, the follicles don't get what they need. They don't die exactly. They just get quiet. They shrink. They put out a thinner strand. Then a shorter one. Then nothing at all for a while. And the whole system slows down not because the follicle is broken but because the environment around it has gotten too rusty for it to do its job.

She said all those pills and shampoos and gummies I'd tried had been trying to feed a follicle that couldn't hear them.

Because the mailbox was rusted shut.

I sat there on the porch swing with my hand over my mouth.

She said what she'd been taking was pomegranate.

I said pomegranate.

She said yes but not the kind you drink and not the kind at the produce counter. She said it was an extract, and specifically an extract of the peel of the pomegranate, and she said that mattered a lot and she'd explain why in a minute.

She said the peel of the pomegranate has a set of compounds in it called punicalagins. She said the word slow so I could hear it. Pyoo-nih-kah-lah-gins. She said they are among the strongest natural antioxidants anyone has ever measured. She said they don't exist in the juice. They don't exist in the seeds. They exist in the peel, which nobody eats and which most companies throw away.

She said the reason that matters is because when you take those compounds in, your body uses them to quiet down the oxidation. To slow the rust.

She said it works on the vessels first. The small vessels. The ones that feed the places that were getting starved.

She said her hair coming back wasn't the point. Her hair coming back was the sign. The scalp was the place she could see it happening because the scalp is where the small vessels are close to the surface and the follicles are sensitive enough to respond quickly when the environment changes.

But she said she'd noticed other things too. Her hands didn't hurt in the morning anymore. Her energy in the late afternoon had stopped bottoming out. Her nails were less brittle. Her skin on her forearms had stopped looking papery.

She said the whole body had gotten a little less rusty.

Then she said something I want you to hear.

She said most of the pomegranate supplements you'll find are standardized to something called ellagic acid. And ellagic acid is one of the compounds you get when the punicalagins in the peel break down inside your body. It's downstream. It's the after, not the before.

She said companies use it because it's cheaper to standardize to. It sounds impressive on a label. It's technically related to pomegranate. But it's not the same thing as taking in the actual peel extract with the actual punicalagins in it, because the peel extract gives your body the raw material to make what it needs when it needs it, not just one downstream piece.

She said "if you're going to try one thing, try the thing that's actually the peel."

She said the one she took was called Alevia.

She said it was two capsules in the morning with her coffee. That was the whole routine. She'd been taking it every morning for close to a year.

She pulled her phone out and she showed me the bottle. Orange label, dark green cap. She said it was organic and made in the USA and she said the company had a 90-day guarantee where you sent the bottle back if it didn't work and they refunded your money.

She said she'd known within about 6 weeks that something was different.

I didn't order it that night. I want to tell you I did but I didn't. I went home and I sat with it for 4 days. I'm a hospice case manager. I don't buy things off the internet at 1 AM anymore. I've done that too many times.

I looked up what she'd said about the peel and the punicalagins. I looked up oxidative stress and the vascular pathway. I read about follicle blood supply. I read about NF-κB, which is a signaling pathway involved in the low-grade inflammation that gets stirred up when things stay oxidized for too long, and I read that pomegranate polyphenols seemed to quiet it down.

None of it promised me my hair would come back.

That was the strange part. Every ad I had ever seen about hair had promised me my hair would come back. And this stuff, when I actually read about it, didn't promise me anything about hair at all. It talked about vessels and antioxidants and inflammation. Hair was just the thing that some people happened to notice.

That was the part that made me finally order it.

I ordered it on a Wednesday in May. It came the following Tuesday.

The bottle looked like the one my sister had shown me on her phone. I put it on the kitchen counter next to the coffee maker so I wouldn't forget.

I want to tell you what happened the way it actually happened, because I don't want to be one of those ads.

Week 1: Nothing. I mean nothing. I took 2 capsules with my coffee every morning. I felt no different. I kept checking the pillow like it was going to change overnight. It didn't. I almost stopped.

Week 2: Still nothing on my head. But I noticed that the little ache I get in my thumb joint when it's cold at night wasn't there when I woke up on Thursday. I noticed I'd made it through the whole workday on Friday without hitting the 3 PM wall. I filed it away.

Week 3: Same. I told myself I would give it the full 90 days because I was not going to be the woman who quit at 3 weeks and then wondered.

Week 4: My daughter called on a Sunday and said "mom, did you get your hair cut" and I laughed because I hadn't been to a stylist in months. I looked at myself in the bathroom mirror after we hung up. Something looked different at my temples. I couldn't say what.

Week 5: The hairs on the pillow were fewer. Not gone. Fewer. I counted them one morning. There were 6. There used to be more than I could count.

Week 6: I took my headband off at work on a Tuesday and I forgot to put it back on and it was 3 in the afternoon before I noticed. Denise didn't say anything. But she looked at me a beat too long over the top of her monitor.

Week 7: My mother called and said "Retta, is your hair growing back."

Week 8: There was a soft fringe of new little hairs at my hairline that hadn't been there before. Very short. Like the first grass after a burn. I touched them with my fingertip and I sat down on the closed lid of the toilet in my bathroom and I cried for about 5 minutes.

Week 10: I put it in a ponytail one morning without thinking. And the ponytail felt like a ponytail again. Not a wisp. A ponytail.

Week 12: My sister came down for the 4th of July. She stood on my porch and she looked at me and she said "there you are."

I want to tell you that's when it hit me. But it hit me in pieces over the next month.

The powder went in the trash for real this time.

The headband I kept, because it turns out I did like it as an accessory. But not to hide anything.

I made the dentist appointment. I let the hygienist see my part from above and I didn't think about it once.

My daughter took a photo of me on a boat in August with the sun behind me and I sent it to Marjorie without cropping it. Marjorie sent back a photo of her own hair pinned up with the same tortoise shell clip she'd worn at Perkins.

She wrote "same team."

I'm not telling you this because my hair is the point. I'm telling you this because I lost something I didn't know how to talk about, and I got it back, and the getting it back changed more than my hair.

I stopped hiding.

That's the part.

There is something that happens when your body starts giving you back small pieces of what it used to do. You realize how much energy you were spending on the hiding. On the compensating. On the not-mirror-glancing and the not-Christmas-photo and the not-ponytail. And when the reason to hide goes away, all that energy comes back to you. And you don't know what to do with it at first, and then you remember.

I take my 2 capsules with my coffee every morning. I keep an extra bottle in the cabinet because my sister told me they sometimes run out and she's right, they have twice.

If you're a woman my age and something similar has been happening to you, and you have been quietly hiding it the way I was quietly hiding mine, I want to tell you a few things.

You are not vain for caring about this. You are not shallow. You are not making it up. What you are seeing is real. And it does not have to be the shrug your doctor gave you. It does not have to be the shampoo aisle. It does not have to be the pink pills in a box or the powder in a bottle or the wide black headband in July.

You have a lot of body left. And a lot of that body is fed by small vessels that have been slowly rusting for a long time and no one has ever explained it to you the way my sister explained it to me on that porch swing.

Alevia is what she showed me. Alevia is what I take. It's the actual peel extract with the actual punicalagins in it, not the cheaper ellagic acid stand-in that most companies use.

Two capsules with your coffee. That's the whole routine.

They have a 90-day guarantee. If it doesn't do anything for you, you send the bottle back and they refund every penny. 🌙 The stranger I was forced to marry was my true mate—but he looked at me with hatred. 💔
Chapter 1
I know it’s bad news the moment Daddy calls me into his office. If we’re going to discuss something calmly, we do it around the dinner table. We don’t go into the office unless there’s trouble. As Beta Phineas leads me through the pack-house, an ominous weight presses down on me, my thoughts spinning, trying to find some explanation, some reason for why this is happening. But nothing comes to mind. I’m not the kind of girl to stir up conflict—I’m boring, really. So why would my father call me in?
Phineas pauses to let me catch up, glancing back at me. His face is tinged with something like pity, but it only makes the air thicker. The closer I get to the office, the heavier my heart feels. I can’t shake this gnawing sensation in my gut that something is terribly wrong.
We reach the oak door, and Phineas knocks twice. "Enter!" my father calls from inside. The sound is like an order rather than an invitation, and my legs feel heavier as I step forward. Phineas opens the door and steps aside, allowing me to go in first. The air feels cold and distant as the door clicks shut behind me, trapping me alone with him.
Daddy is hunched at his desk, his broad shoulders drooping under the weight of something invisible. His handsome face looks drawn and tired, lines of stress cutting deeper than I’ve ever seen them. He looks older, as if time has fast-forwarded its hold on him. "Sit down, Natalia," he says, but it’s not a gentle invitation—it’s the voice of the Alpha, firm and distant.
I limp across the room, each step more deliberate than the last. My legs ache in ways I can’t explain. They’ve always been weak, uncooperative. I sink onto one of the leather wing-backed chairs in front of his desk, careful not to let myself relax. I sit on the edge, as if being too comfortable will somehow make this situation worse. Daddy doesn’t look at me. His eyes stay locked on the papers in front of him, fingers absently tapping the desk. He clears his throat several times before finally speaking, his voice thick with struggle.
"Natalia," he says, the words cold and clipped. "As part of the treaty negotiations with the Gilded Dawn Pack, I have agreed to a marriage alliance. You, Natalia Bastian, will marry the Alpha’s son, Nash Peregrine, on the next new moon."
I feel like I’ve been sucker-punched, the air sucked out of my lungs. "What? Daddy, how could you?" The words escape in a choked whisper, disbelief and shock crashing over me. This can’t be real. Arranged marriages? Isn’t that something that ended centuries ago?
My father’s face tightens, his expression pained. "I did it for the pack, Natalia," he says, voice wavering slightly. "We’re small, and after your mother..." He falters, unable to say it, to acknowledge that she’s gone. "We’re vulnerable. We need the protection of a stronger pack. This alliance will ensure our survival."
A whirlwind of emotions tears through me—anger, confusion, betrayal. "But… why me?" I demand, my voice trembling. "I have two sisters—Jovanna, strong and fierce, a warrior. And Helena, beautiful, everything the Gilded Dawn Pack would want. Why me?" I’ve always felt like the weakest link. The one with the "bad legs," the one who can barely keep up. I’m ordinary, forgettable. The last choice.
And then, it hits me, as cold and harsh as a slap: I’m the expendable one. I’m the sacrifice.
Without waiting for an answer, my father speaks again, quieter this time, though his voice still has that authoritative edge. "It’s not what you think, Natalia. It has nothing to do with your… condition." The hesitation is there, that awkwardness. The doctors couldn’t figure out what’s wrong with my legs, no one could. I’ve learned to live with it, but sometimes, I wonder if the rest of the pack sees it as a weakness.
I wait for him to explain further, to make me understand, but he doesn’t. His silence grates at me.
"Don’t I get a say in this?" I ask, my voice stronger, desperate. "Don’t you need my consent before you—before you sell me off for the pack?" The words taste bitter on my tongue. "What if I refuse?"
His face blanches, then hardens. He leans forward, his Alpha voice coming down on me with the weight of a boulder. "If you refuse, I’ll disown you. You’ll be exiled from the pack."
The words land with a sickening finality, the sting of betrayal cutting deeper than anything I’ve ever felt. My own father—my Daddy—would cast me out, make me a rogue. This can’t be real. This isn’t the man I grew up with. He wouldn’t do this. But I see it in his eyes. The Alpha comes first. Always.
A tear slips down my cheek, hot and silent, and the thought hits me—if Mama were still here, she would never let him do this. My heart aches with the hollow absence of her, her warmth, her unwavering love.
For a moment, I consider the possibility of exile. Of refusing him. I know I wouldn’t survive alone, not without a pack, not without strength. But more than that, I can’t bear the thought of being completely cut off from the family I’ve always loved. Daddy’s doing something awful, something that’s breaking me inside, but his role as Alpha is his first priority. Even if it means sacrificing me.
The weight of it presses down on me, and I finally sink into my chair, shoulders slumped in defeat. I can’t look him in the eye anymore. I don’t even have the energy to speak. All I can do is nod.
I hear the relief in his voice when he speaks again, but it’s not a comfort. "You’ll pack your things. You’ll leave tomorrow morning."
"So soon?" My voice cracks, unable to hide my shock. "But you said—the new moon. Isn’t that—?"
"I said the marriage would take place then," he interrupts, his tone cold. "The Alpha has requested you to come immediately. Gwenith will help you pack." He turns back to the papers on his desk, dismissing me with the flick of a wrist. "You are dismissed."

Chapter 2
Dismissed. The word burns through me. This is not how a father speaks to his daughter, not like this. I can’t reconcile this man with the one who once held me close, who used to be my rock. I don’t know who he is anymore.
I leave the office, the weight of my heart dragging me down as I walk, passing pack members who greet me, but I don’t hear them. I don’t see them. I’m numb, lost in a haze of confusion and disbelief. When I finally reach my room, I collapse against the door, sliding to the floor, my legs refusing to hold me up.
Being forced to marry a stranger—someone I’ve never met—is painful enough. But what really tears at me is the fact that I’ll never know what it feels like to find my mate. To find the one person who completes you, who makes you whole. Every wolf dreams of that. Every wolf craves that connection. But not me. I’ve been denied it, forever.
Tears of self-pity flood my face, soaking into the sheets beneath me.
After what feels like an eternity, there’s a soft knock at the door. Gwenith, the sweet little omega who helps around the house, peeks her head in. "I was told to come assist you, Miss Natalia."
I pull myself up with great effort. "I need to pack," I say, my voice flat, the life drained from me.
Gwenith doesn’t question me. She’s too gentle, too eager to serve, and I’m too empty to care. She follows me as I grab two suitcases from the closet—ones I haven’t touched since the trip to Mexico with Mom. I don’t remember packing then. I don’t remember any of it being real.
"What do you want to pack?" she asks quietly.
I sigh, pulling open drawers. "Just the essentials." I don’t need much—my simple clothes, a couple of nice dresses for formal occasions. But as I reach for my mother’s porcelain jewelry box, wrapped carefully in one of my sweatshirts, I realize how much I’m leaving behind.
I throw a picture of my sisters and me on the bed, taken years ago, before everything started to break. I don’t even look at it. It’s too painful. A leather-bound journal, a laptop—things I might need, things that have no real meaning. The only thing I take that feels real is the old, worn-out teddy bear I’ve had since I was six. And the lap blanket—fuzzy, sunflower-printed, childish—but I can’t leave it behind.
When I finish, I feel like I’ve packed my entire life into two small suitcases, and a tear falls. I’m worthless. I’m disposable. My father has sold me off for the pack, and I’ll never be the same again.
I want to call my sisters. I want to cry to them, to tell them how afraid I am. But I can’t. They’re already living their lives, their futures secure, and I’m left behind. My fate doesn’t matter to them.
Gwenith leaves me to my work. The door shuts behind her, leaving me alone in the quiet of my room, the two suitcases standing by the door like some terrible omen. I sit on the bed, clutching my old bear to my chest, trying to shut off the world, trying to silence the hurt, but I can’t. All I can think about is the mother I’ll never see again, and the life I’ll never get to choose.
I fall asleep eventually, exhausted by the weight of it all, but the ache in my heart lingers long after.
I wake to a soft knock at the door, barely a whisper against the morning stillness. Dawn has barely begun to stretch its light across the horizon, and I remain tangled in yesterday's clothes, my body sprawled on the bed in a heap of exhaustion. My eyes are swollen, red from a night spent in tears that left me hollow and drained. I haven’t eaten, and my stomach growls in complaint, a physical reminder of the emotional chaos that churns within me.
"Miss Natalia?" Gwenith’s voice calls softly through the door, tentative, as though she fears disturbing me further. "The Beta says you should be prepared to leave in one hour."
One hour. It feels like the air has been knocked out of me. No time, no room to breathe, to think. They aren’t even pretending to hesitate. The sentence has already been handed down.
I drag myself up and shuffle to the shower, the familiar ache in my legs worse than usual this morning. They never cooperate when I need them most. I lean against the sink as I undress, grimacing against the sharp pain that lances through my joints. The shower, when I turn it on, scalds my skin, but I welcome the heat. I scrub fiercely, as though I can wash away the humiliation, the pain, the part of me that made my father choose this fate for me. When my skin is raw and pink, I wash my hair, the steam rising around me, thick with the sharp scent of herbs and soap. I step out, the weight of it all settling back over my shoulders.
What does one wear when they are being sold to another pack? I feel like I should wear black, something heavy and mourning. After all, I am mourning—mourning the loss of my life, my freedom, my dignity. But I can't bring myself to do that. I choose a sundress, something simple and light. The turquoise fabric contrasts with my dark honey skin, making my eyes shine brighter than they ever have. I pull my long hair into a loose bun, fasten my favorite turquoise beaded choker around my neck, and settle the matching earrings against my skin.
I stare at my reflection, the face that stares back at me still, in this moment, just... me. Not pretty, not ugly. Neither tall nor short, fat nor thin. Just ordinary. Always ordinary. No matter how the dress fits, no matter how the jewelry sparkles. The girl looking back at me has swollen eyes and pale skin. Unremarkable.
A sharp knock at the door punctuates the silence of my thoughts. I expect my father, but instead, it’s Pablo, the Gamma.
"Miss Natalia," his deep voice is firm but kind. "Your father said I’m to drive you to the Gilded Dawn pack. Are you ready?"
Two hours. Two hours to the place where my fate will be sealed, where I will meet the man I’m supposed to marry. But it’s not like I have any choice. Pablo says nothing more as he drives, and the silence between us feels heavier with each passing mile. It’s like an invisible wall has been erected between us, and I’m not sure whether my father has ordered him to avoid speaking to me, or if he’s just following the lead of the others, giving me the cold shoulder. It stings. Adds another layer to the hurt already carving deep into my soul. My stomach growls again, and I wince. I haven’t eaten in a day, and the hunger gnaws at me, but there’s no comfort in food anymore.
I’ve never been to Gilded Dawn territory, but I’ve heard the stories. This pack is legendary—brutal, relentless, a force to be reckoned with. The warriors here are feared, trained in ways no other pack would even dare to imagine. They’re not just strong, they’re dangerous. My heart beats a little faster as we cross the boundary, but what greets me is not what I expected. The grounds are wild but beautiful, with sprawling gardens that feel untouched, and a sprawling manor that dwarfs the pack-house I’ve called home for years.
Pablo parks the SUV, and for the first time in hours, he speaks to me. His large hand rests gently on mine, an unexpected gesture of kindness. “Stay strong, Miss Natalia. You can do this.”
I nod, but the words don’t really take hold. How can I? There’s no strength left in me.
Pablo opens my door and pulls my suitcases from the back of the vehicle. He walks me toward the grand front doors, where a small group awaits. I’m struck by the contrast of the two figures standing at the top of the steps.
A massive man, towering over even my father, stands there, arms thick as tree trunks, a face that looks carved from stone. His pale blue eyes are cold, unyielding, like ice. The mop of his hair, untamed and wild, reminds me of something feral, of the Wolverine from the comics. He looks at me without warmth, without recognition. This is the Alpha, I know. Bastian.
Beside him stands a woman who is the complete opposite. She’s petite, barely clearing five feet, and has the delicate air of someone who might be swept away in the next gust of wind. Her long blonde curls spill around her shoulders like a halo, and her eyes are an impossibly vivid green. When she smiles, it’s bright, welcoming. She reaches down the steps with a lightness I envy and enfolds me in a warm, unexpected hug.
“Welcome to Gilded Dawn, dear,” she says, her voice melodic, soothing. “I’m Calista, and this is my husband, Bastian.”
I freeze, looking between them. The Alpha and his Luna. Yet, they don’t introduce themselves as such. Calista doesn't call herself Luna, and Bastian doesn't call himself Alpha. Still, it’s clear enough. And yet... where is Nash?

Chapter 3
As if sensing my confusion, Calista answers my silent question with a small, almost imperceptible shake of her head. “My sons are not here at the moment, but you’ll meet them soon enough. Come, let’s get you inside and settled.”
She loops her arm through mine, pulling me toward the grand entrance of the manor. My heart stirs, but it’s not with excitement. More with dread. As she leads me inside, I wonder where Nash is, this man I’m meant to marry. But the question hangs in the air, unanswered.
The inside of the house is just as magnificent as the outside, decorated with modern luxury and understated elegance. Calista takes me through a maze of rooms, each more grand than the last. “This is the conference room,” she gestures toward a large space, “And there, the entertainment room. That’s the nursery for the pups. And this is the kitchen, of course. Have you eaten?”
Before I can respond, she’s already taking charge. “I’m starving, let’s get you some breakfast.”
She leads me into the dining hall, vast enough to seat a hundred people easily, and gestures for me to sit at a small table for two. A waitress appears promptly, bowing her head in submission, her eyes never quite meeting mine.
“Kara, dear,” Calista introduces the woman, who looks up just enough to acknowledge me before lowering her gaze again. “This is Natalia Bastian, Nash’s betrothed.”
The name causes Kara to glance up in surprise before she quickly returns to her task. Calista orders with confidence, a four-egg omelet, Swiss cheese, mushrooms, a blueberry muffin toasted with butter, and sausage links. I blink, watching her with fascination. How can such a small woman eat so much?
I hesitantly order my own simple meal: a muffin and a cup of tea.
When Kara leaves, Calista reaches across the table and places her hand over mine. Her voice softens, the warmth in her words a stark contrast to the coldness I felt from Bastian. “I’m sure this is a difficult and uncomfortable transition for you, my dear. But I want you to know that I’m here for you. You are most welcome in this family, and I will do everything in my power to make you feel comfortable.”
She pauses for a moment, her smile faltering just slightly. “But Nash...”
My stomach twists. What did she mean? What was Nash like? But I don’t ask. I swallow, feeling the weight of her words hang heavy in the air.
Calista continues, glossing over the subject. “Nash can be... difficult,” she says cryptically. “His father and I, we hope that he will settle down and take up his responsibilities.”
Difficult? What does that mean? I want to ask more, to dig deeper, but I can see she’s finished talking about him. She moves on, telling me how happy she is to have a woman in the family, how much she’s heard about me. I smile, though I know it’s all just pleasantries. She knows nothing about me, beyond the fact that I’m the bride-to-be.
After breakfast, Calista leads me upstairs. I freeze when I see the staircase. The elegant, winding stairs stretch up ahead, and my heart sinks. Climbing stairs is difficult for me, painful even, and I feel my legs threaten to give out as I grip the rail tightly. I focus all my energy on making it up without drawing attention to my struggle, but with every step, the pain gets worse.
When we reach the third floor, Calista opens the door to a spacious guest suite. The bed is huge, the bathroom private, and my suitcases are already there, waiting. “Make yourself comfortable, my dear. I’ll send Dahlia to help you once she’s finished cleaning up from breakfast. If you need anything, she can assist you. Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have some business to attend to.”
And just like that, she leaves, leaving me alone in this grand, unfamiliar place.
Dahlia is a lively young Omega assigned to be my maid. Not that I particularly need one, but I’m grateful for her company. Her name suits her perfectly, for like the wildflower, she’s radiant—bright, cheerful, and brimming with sunlight. Her smile stretches too wide for her small face, her nose tilts up in that endearing way, and her dark blonde hair tumbles in a chaotic, curly mess, untamable and full of life. Her blue eyes twinkle with unguarded joy, and she exudes a warmth that feels genuine, like she’s happy in the very marrow of her bones. I fall in love with her instantly.
She helps me unpack my sparse belongings, then we sit side by side on the bed, exchanging idle chatter for a few minutes.
“What’s life like in the pack?” I ask, intrigued.
She grins—no surprise there. I don’t think I’ve ever seen her without that smile. “Oh, it’s a good life,” she says, her voice full of sincere affection. “The Alpha runs a tight ship. We work hard, we train hard, but it’s fair. It’s a fun pack, too. We’re all excited about your wedding celebration. I hear the Luna is planning a huge party for everyone in the pack. I love parties! Even if I’m working in the kitchen, they let us take turns so everyone can join in the fun.”
I smile back, her energy contagious. The Luna’s leadership already sounds a world away from what I know. In some packs, omegas are little more than slaves. My father treated them like hired hands, paying them for their work, but never making them feel like equals. They were always just a little beneath us, and that discomfort had never quite left me. I’m grateful that the Luna seems to value them. After all, not everyone in the pack can be a warrior, and omegas play a vital role—tending to children, maintaining the home, filling in the gaps that the hunters can’t.
“And what about Nash? What’s he like?”

Chapter 4
At the mention of his name, Dahlia’s smile falters, just briefly, before she forces it back into place. It’s a small shift, but I see it—something there she isn’t saying. “Oh, he’s very handsome,” she answers, but it’s as if the words don’t fit quite right. “Tall, like the Alpha, but... not as burly.”
“Okay, okay,” I press, trying not to sound impatient. “He’s good to look at. But what is he like? What’s his personality?”
Dahlia stands suddenly, her smile now stiff, less certain. “I think it’s better if you get to know him yourself, mistress. I don’t want to color your opinion. I should go check on the food now. If you need anything, just call for me.” She moves swiftly, shutting the door behind her with a soft click.

If Nash were truly the great man she had implied, wouldn’t she have eagerly listed his qualities? Wouldn’t she have said, “He’s kind, gentle, just”? But she didn’t. The fact that she kept silent speaks volumes. The Luna had called him “difficult,” and now Dahlia can barely bring herself to say anything positive. I try to push it out of my mind, but I can’t help the unease creeping in.
It wouldn’t matter if Nash was the handsomest man alive if he was an utter jerk.
I’m nervous as I make my way downstairs for dinner, knowing this will be the first time I meet my future husband. I choose a modest outfit—something pretty but not too flashy—and style my hair into loose waves, one of my few features I take pride in. A light touch of makeup makes my eyes pop, but I still feel unsettled by the way my reflection looks back at me, never quite the way I wish.
I dread descending the stairs. The thought alone makes my stomach churn. You see, navigating stairs isn’t easy for me. I must descend one step at a time, left foot down, right foot following, before repeating the slow, careful motion. If I try to walk normally, one of my legs will collapse, sending me tumbling down in a humiliating heap. Trust me, it’s happened more than once, and it’s a painful memory I’d rather not repeat. So, like a child, I grip the railing and creep down, hoping no one notices. Luckily, I’m alone on the third floor for now. But by the time I reach the bottom, others are scattered about, preparing for dinner.

Fletcher’s gaze is cold, calculating, a silent judgment hanging in the air. Mireille, however, smiles warmly and offers her hand, her voice lilting with grace. “Welcome to the family, dear,” she says.

Natalia, this is Berenice, the manager of our kitchen—a genius in the art of food and hospitality.” Berenice blushes under the compliment, curtsying with a practiced ease.
“Thank you, Luna. It’s a pleasure to meet you, Mistress. Welcome,” she says before excusing herself to attend to the dessert.
The murmurs of conversation fill the room as the meal continues, a low hum of contentment. But then the door slams open, and an abrupt silence sweeps over the room. Two young men step in, and my pulse jumps—there, standing in the doorway, I see him.
Nash.
Dahlia had been right. He is stunning. He seems like a figure plucked straight from mythology—shoulders broad, jaw strong and square, with hair that tumbles around his shoulders, and the rough stubble of a man who doesn’t care for the soft touches of a razor. His body is all muscle, defined and taut. But his eyes. His eyes... even from across the room, I can see the stormy blue-grey of them, and they are as cold as ice—ferocious, full of rage.
And somehow, I know that fury is aimed at me. I feel a wave of panic crash over me, and the overwhelming urge to shrink into myself, to hide beneath the table.
Yet, amid the fury, something else overwhelms my senses. A fragrance. Sweet, intoxicating—cedar, something musky and alluring. Is it his aftershave? A cologne? It seems too refined for a man like him, yet I’m intoxicated by it, drawn to it. Despite the coldness in his gaze, there’s something magnetic about him—something darkly appealing. My heart races, torn between wanting to escape his anger and desperately needing to bury my face in the scent of him.
He strides toward the family table, his lips set in a hard line, and my breath catches in my throat.

Chapter 5
Only belatedly do I register his brother’s presence. Both the Luna and Dahlia had mentioned him—Wilder, the younger brother. I hadn’t noticed him at first, too absorbed in the dark energy radiating from Nash. But now I see him clearly. Wilder seems to carry his mother’s genes more than his father’s. He isn’t as large or intimidating as Nash; in fact, he has a leaner, more graceful build. His blond hair is neatly trimmed, a sharp contrast to his brother’s disheveled mane, and his eyes are the brightest shade of blue. They glint with a mischievous amusement that sets my teeth on edge. Whereas Nash had looked at me with what could only be described as open hatred, Wilder seems to be laughing at me. The feeling makes my skin prickle with discomfort. If there’s one thing I cannot stand, it’s being the subject of mockery.
I try to ignore Wilder. He’s not worth my energy. But then Nash begins to stalk closer, and I feel the air shift, heavy with something that makes my body go cold, my thoughts muddled. My breath grows shallow, and I can’t seem to get enough air. It’s not a weakness, not in the way one of those dainty, fainting women might suffer from a delicate constitution. I am not going to faint. I refuse to.
"Nash," the Luna’s voice cuts through the haze, sharp and commanding. "It’s nice of you to join us. I want you to meet Natalia..."

And my wolf... my wolf whimpers. It’s a soft, pitiful sound in my chest. Mate, she whispers.
No. Oh, no, no, no.
This cannot be happening. This cold-eyed, rude, brutish man who is giving me nothing but contempt—he cannot be my mate. He won’t be my mate. I look into his eyes, and there’s a flicker—he knows. He knows it too.
And he couldn’t care less.
How much self-control must one have to reject the mate bond so effortlessly? It’s as though he’s dismissing it like he’d ignore the noise of a passing car, nonchalant. He even slathers butter on a piece of bread with a casual air as if the rest of the world—including me—doesn’t matter.
He doesn’t want us.
I pick up my fork, trying to focus my mind on something, anything, other than the excruciating awareness of the man across from me. What are the odds? I try to reason with myself. The odds of being forced into an arranged marriage and finding out the man you’re to marry is actually your mate? One in a billion, right? But then... What are the odds that I finally meet my mate, and he hates me?
He hasn’t voiced it, but the atmosphere around him reeks of rejection, thick and palpable, as tangible as the cedar scent that seems to be permanently attached to him. It’s cruel, and it feels unfair—like the universe decided to have a laugh at my expense.
But no. I refuse to let him see how deeply this hurts. I won’t cry in front of these people. Not in front of him. Not in front of that insufferable man.
I straighten my back, squaring my shoulders, and I shut off my whimpering wolf. With deliberate grace, I lift my chin and meet his cold, unforgiving gaze, all while pushing a forkful of lasagna into my mouth. It smells heavenly, and I know it should taste the same. But in that moment, it tastes like dirt.
I swallow. But I won’t let him see that my appetite has vanished because of him.
He glances at me briefly, eyes flicking over mine before quickly moving away. He turns to his brother, completely ignoring my existence as though I’m nothing more than a passing inconvenience.
But at least Wilder has some decency. He greets me properly, even goes so far as to welcome me into the pack. His blue eyes flicker between his older brother and me, then back again, as if weighing something. He shrugs and digs into his food with a kind of lazy grace, occasionally turning toward me.
“How are you finding it here, Natalia?” he asks casually. “Is your room comfortable? Do you need anything?”
“Oh, yes,” I force a smile, the words tasting strange on my tongue. “Everything is great.”
Great. Oh yes, everything is just peachy. I’ve been ripped from the safety of my childhood home to fulfill some ridiculous treaty. Your home is lovely, most of the people have been kind... but the man I’m meant to marry is a complete asshole. Yes, everything’s just perfect.
I mechanically push the food around on my plate, managing to choke down half the lasagna before I can’t stomach any more.
Dinner progresses. I’m eager to escape, to find a moment of peace away from the tension gnawing at my chest, but just as I’m about to make my exit, a rich, decadent tiramisu is brought out.
I’m not hungry anymore. No amount of sugar can satisfy the gnawing sense of discomfort that has settled deep in my stomach. But I’m the guest here, and I must behave accordingly. So, I take a few bites, trying to force the sweetness into my mouth, but all I can taste is the bitter sting of Nash’s silent contempt.
I can feel his eyes on me, though he barely acknowledges my presence. When our gazes finally meet, it’s only for a moment—his eyes hard, cold, and filled with quiet fury. The intensity of it sends a shiver down my spine, and I wish I could escape his gaze. His presence seems to suffocate the very air around me.
Finally, I catch a break. Several people begin to excuse themselves from the table, and I see my chance. I rise, clearing my throat, willing myself to remain composed.
“Luna, thank you for a lovely meal,” I say, my voice betraying nothing. “Please excuse me.” I push my chair back and stand, offering my goodnights to the others, doing my best to walk with dignity as I make my exit. But the moment my feet hit the floor, the weight of exhaustion presses down on me, and the stress I’ve been holding at bay for so long finally threatens to collapse me.
The last thing I want is for Nash to see my weakness. He already hates me for reasons I don’t understand—how much more would he despise me for something as simple as exhaustion?
I’ve barely made it a few steps out the door when a sudden, brutal grip seizes my arm. I gasp as I’m spun around and shoved hard against the wall, my breath knocked from my lungs. The sheer force of it leaves me dizzy, but I don’t fall—thanks to the cold, unforgiving wall behind me.
It’s Nash.
His hand tightens painfully around my arm, and the sparks—oh Goddess, the sparks. The magic, the erotic, consuming pull that everyone talks about. But they never talk about the pain that comes with it, the bitter, sharp sensation of it when your so-called mate is treating you like an object to be tossed aside. The sparks aren’t beautiful when they’re accompanied by bruising fingers digging into your flesh, when they’re a reminder that the man who is supposed to love you wants to hurt you instead.
I glance up at him, my stomach turning, and the look in his eyes is colder than ever. He stares down at me with that same dismissive expression, as though I’m nothing more than something he’d like to crush beneath his boot.
Being sexually drawn to someone who clearly has no interest in me—and who may well enjoy hurting me—is not magical. It’s sickening.
"Let me make something perfectly clear," Nash snarls, his voice a low, dangerous growl that resonates in my bones. His words drip with venom, each syllable aimed directly at my heart. "I do not want you, and I do not need you. You are only here because my father is an old-fashioned, pig-headed fool. I will marry you to fulfill the treaty contract, but you will never be my Luna, and you will never be my mate."
As if to punctuate the harshness of his words, he shoves me against the wall. The impact sends a sharp jolt through my body, pain blooming across my back, but it's the words that leave a deeper wound. My chest aches as though something vital has been ripped away, a tearing sensation that claws at my lungs, suffocating me.

Laura Peterson
